stories.Headline: OpenAI expands ChatGPT Ads to 44 countries through exclusive reseller Aleph
stories.Summary:
OpenAI expanded the market presence of ChatGPT Ads into 44 countries on November 12, 2026. The company selected Aleph as the exclusive reseller to provide local support for brands and agencies. This partnership allows advertisers to contract and pay for ads through a local entity. The move aims to broaden access to AI tools for businesses in these regions. It provides an additional buying option alongside global technology partners and the self-service Ads Manager.

The deal covers 14 Latin American nations including Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Puerto Rico and Uruguay. Europe and Central Asia include 16 markets: Azerbaijan, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Estonia, Hungary, Kazakhstan, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania, Serbia, Slovakia, Slovenia, Ukraine and Uzbekistan. Middle East and Africa include 10: Egypt, Kenya, Kuwait, Morocco, Nigeria, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates. Asia-Pacific includes 4: Bangladesh, Cambodia, Hong Kong for outbound ads and Sri Lanka. Aleph provides local invoicing in local currency, payment terms, onboarding, campaign support and training.

OpenAI stated that they have made significant progress in ten months but are still early in building the platform. They intend to focus on protecting user trust and helping businesses achieve their goals while developing new formats. Gastón Taratuta, the founder and CEO of Aleph, said AI gives businesses a new way to connect with people. He noted that Aleph turns global technology into local growth by speaking the local language. He emphasized that advertisers can now work with a local team that extends credit.

Jad Naamani from Seez said car buyers increasingly use AI conversations to research vehicles and compare different models. He believes dealers must be present when buyers ask AI assistants or they will not make the shortlist. Automotive retailers are affected as they use the Boost tool from Pinewood.AI to manage these new ads. This tool integrates ChatGPT Ads with Meta, Google, TikTok and Snapchat to reach potential car buyers. The system uses AI to shift budgets toward activities that deliver qualified leads and sales.

Over one hundred thousand marketers have already advertised on ChatGPT, which now has more than one billion weekly users. In 2026, Invoca research found 60 percent of UK car buyers used generative AI for research, up from 47 percent. Pinewood.AI, which was taken private by Ridgeview Partners in October 2026, acquired the AI company Seez in February 2025. Seez is headquartered in Dubai with an office in Copenhagen and operates in 25 different countries. Pinewood.AI serves a global user base in over 36 countries and partners with over 50 OEM brands.

OpenAI will continue to develop new optimization tools, measurement solutions, and advertising formats as the ecosystem evolves. Pinewood.AI and Seez plan to introduce additional advertising formats as soon as OpenAI makes them available. Currently, dealers can run the Sponsored Card format where ads appear alongside a ChatGPT response. The articles leave open which specific new formats will be released next for the automotive sector. They also do not specify the exact timeline for the rollout of these future measurement solutions.

stories.Headline: Paul Meinshausen says a personal AI agent grades marketing messages more ruthlessly than he would
stories.Summary:
Paul Meinshausen, Head of Agentic Decisioning at MoEngage and Co-Founder of Aampe, asked Meta's Muse to check his notifications from marketing brands while listening to a conference talk in New York. He loaded up the personal AI agent because he was curious whether brands were responding to customers who now have software reading on their behalf. The verdict was harsher than he expected, and he said it gave a rundown on them that was sort of even more ruthless than he would have. He shared the experiment in a conversation with CX Today, published on 20 November 2026. For marketers, that small experiment points to a bigger problem, because if a customer's agent is reviewing every message, relevance stops being a nice-to-have.

Meinshausen said executives have long had human assistants who watch over their affairs even more obsessively than they do themselves, and agents are now making that available to everyone. He said most people are not just a professional in their job, they are also a parent or a partner or family member and a friend, and they give each task a small amount of focus, whereas an agent can spend far longer on a single decision. He said the expectation for detail, for relevance, and for personalization is just a lot higher, and that it is a good thing, but it just means that the rate of work has increased as well for everybody involved. He called messaging across every channel the previous wave of automation, where the aim was just to make machines do things. He defined intelligent activity as the ability to take an action, observe a result, and then update the action.

Meinshausen said activity should be intelligent activity, and that for marketers this means giving agents a way to read the response, not only the authority to send. He pointed to a much wider set of signals before and after a purchase, including how customers read material, how they click around, and direct feedback such as whether something was relevant. He compared it to everyday use of tools like ChatGPT, where people learn to prompt and then correct the system, and said businesses need their agents to be correctable in the same way, sometimes directly and explicitly and sometimes indirectly and kind of implicitly. He said one form of response can be a negative form, saying I don't like this, unsubscribing, or not responding when you kind of were expected to respond, and those are really important to learn from. He said the agent that over-messages is the one that ignores those signals.

CX Today has previously explored how suppression and next-best actions can reduce personalization fatigue, and the principle is similar. Meinshausen sees AI decisioning arriving quickly in lifecycle and CRM marketing, and spreading into orchestration and content production. He admitted there is too much to do, so teams will need to prioritize and calibrate which adoption decisions they make first. He was clear on one point, that there is definitely no time to do nothing. He suggested marketers consider how a customer's agent would grade their last week of messages and what it would say.

Genesys launched Standalone AI Agents and Genesys Arena on 18 November 2026 for organisations that want to deploy agentic AI in customer service without replacing their existing systems. Standalone AI Agents lets organisations deploy the Genesys Cloud Agentic Virtual Agent within existing customer service environments in a few days, without first migrating more widely to Genesys Cloud. The software can operate within defined business rules and hand an interaction to a human employee, along with the conversation context, if a request needs further expertise. Genesys Arena is built around prebuilt Agent Kits covering more than 50 industry-specific scenarios, and teams can create a functional AI agent in as little as 10 minutes before customising it with natural language and deploying it into Genesys Cloud. The announcement includes a new pricing structure that groups interactions into simple, moderate or complex tasks and measures usage in Experience Units, the new name for what Genesys previously called AI Tokens.

Tony Bates, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer at Genesys, said enterprises want to move faster with AI but need the flexibility to do it on their own terms without compromising trust and governance. Bates said that with Standalone AI Agents, Genesys Arena and a new effort-based pricing model, the company is giving organisations more choice in how they put agentic AI to work today and scale it as their needs evolve. Youssef Nokta, Senior Vice President of AI Forward Deployed Engineering at Genesys, said AI is advancing quickly and enterprises shouldn't have to start from zero every time they want to put a new idea to work. Nokta said Genesys Arena gives teams a practical head start so they can spend less time on the foundational work and more time shaping AI around their customers, business and the results they want to achieve. Each Agent Kit includes a working model with prebuilt knowledge, integrations, skills and guardrails for a given use case, according to Genesys.

Voice customisation tools are due to be added to Arena and the Genesys Cloud platform, letting organisations choose and adapt how AI agents sound by adjusting personality, tone and delivery using natural language prompts. Genesys cited Charles Sturt University as an existing user of its agentic virtual agent technology, and Michael Buttsworth, Associate Director, Student Experience Service Centre at the university, said using Genesys Agentic Virtual Agent has shown them how AI can improve the customer experience and drive efficiency by resolving more interactions autonomously. Buttsworth said getting that value into production depends on how quickly teams can move from an idea to an experience that works in the real world, and that Genesys Arena and Agent Kits will make that path easier. Mila D'Antonio, Principal Analyst, Customer Engagement at Omdia, said enterprises are under pressure to move agentic AI from experimentation into production quickly, but they aren't all starting from the same place, with some operating in the cloud while others navigate complex hybrid or on-premises environments. D'Antonio said Genesys Arena and Genesys Standalone AI Agents give organisations different paths to deploy agentic AI based on their existing environment and requirements, and the introduction of effort-based pricing highlights how commercial models are evolving.

Genesys said Standalone AI Agents are generally available now, while Agent Kits through Genesys Arena are due to become generally available later this month. Insight launched an online Agent Store for business customers, now generally available in 14 countries, offering a catalogue of AI agents, platforms and related services designed to automate routine work across business functions. Customers can deploy the tools in days or weeks rather than months, either as standalone products or alongside consulting, implementation and managed services. The launch adds six new agentic products to Insight's AI portfolio, bringing the total in its library to 15, and nine products were introduced earlier this year. Products listed in the store include Insight AI Flight Academy, focused on training and change management, and TokenScope, which tracks token usage and AI consumption costs for finance teams.

Insight said the offerings were first developed for clients or used internally in areas including security, finance and legal. New products available at launch include Quote Advisor, which assesses pricing, inventory, freight and contract requirements to produce sourced quotes, NDA Review Agent, designed to review non-disclosure agreements against a company's legal policies, and Parts Order Assist, which helps warehouse, maintenance and field staff search catalogues and place parts orders. Jack Azagury, Chief Executive Officer of Insight, said organisations are feeling the pressure to move AI from isolated pilots into production, and that as Client Zero, Insight has built a repeatable approach proven first across its own organisation. Azagury said that having driven over 90% internal AI adoption, Insight knows firsthand what it takes to deploy and scale agentic AI rapidly and responsibly, and that combining the solutions offered in Agent Store with its consulting and managed services expertise empowers clients to move from hype to how with AI. Culligan International is the first external customer to implement Flight Academy, according to Insight, and the water services company is using a mix of AI tools including Microsoft Copilot, Cowork, Copilot Studio, Azure and Microsoft Fabric while putting governance in place around cost and responsible use.

Laura Walsh, Global Chief Information Officer of Culligan International, said at Culligan they believe technology doesn't transform a company, people do, and that generative AI adoption is far ahead of the learning curve, so it is their responsibility to arm teams with the best tools to lead now into the future. Walsh said that with partners at Insight, Culligan has prioritised AI education so teams can confidently leverage AI productively and responsibly, and that they are leveraging Insight's best practice and have established a functional champ. The deployment centres on workforce education and internal adoption rather than a single operational use case, and Insight said the training-led approach is intended to help organisations build confidence in AI tools across teams and geographies. Insight is positioning the store as a way for businesses to move AI projects beyond the pilot stage and into wider use, and said it applied the approach within its own operations before making the products available more broadly. The articles leave open how a customer's agent would grade any particular brand's messages, and what it would say.

stories.Headline: Microsoft unveils cheaper in-house AI models for coding and cybersecurity at Ignite
stories.Summary:
Microsoft introduced several in-house AI models for coding and cybersecurity at its Ignite conference in San Francisco. These announcements occurred on November 17, 2026, to target software development and digital security tasks. The company aims to reduce its reliance on external AI providers like OpenAI and Anthropic. These new tools provide comparable performance to rivals but at significantly lower costs for users. Microsoft also launched models for image editing, audio processing, and healthcare transcription during the event.

MAI Code 2 delivers 98 per cent of GPT-6.1 Sol performance at 40 per cent cost. It matches Claude Opus 5.5 at 96 per cent performance for only 5 per cent cost. MAI Code 2 Flash matches GPT-6 Luna performance at 65 per cent price and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 20 per cent. MAI Cyber 2 Flash outperforms GPT-6 Astra for less than 2 per cent of the cost per task. Other models include MAI Image 2.7, MAI Realtime 1, and MAI Transcribe 2 for various specialized business applications.

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman said the system co-optimizes performance and price and is not a flash in the pan. He also stated that preventing AI from taking harmful actions remains a top priority for the company. CEO Satya Nadella posted on X that the goal is to turn technological advances into real outcomes. The company plans to integrate MAI Code 2 into GitHub Copilot for developers and Azure for enterprises. Customers can license model weights to fine-tune and customize these tools using their own private data.

Secure Code Warrior tested over 30 models and found that lower-cost systems can sometimes be safer than flagship models. Their research involved building 15,000 applications and 41.3 million lines of code across 11 different programming languages. The study found that curated security rule sets reduced measured risk in AI-generated code by as much as 70 per cent. GPT-6 Luna had a mean risk score of 19.4 at 0.10 dollars, while Claude Opus 5.5 scored 43.6 at 8.17 dollars. Software teams are affected as AI is expected to account for 65 per cent of committed code by 2027.

Secure Code Warrior CEO Pieter Danhieux said assumptions that newer or more expensive models are more secure do not always hold. He noted that models do not use secure coding by default and rely on the prompts and rules provided. Stanford University research found human-only commits introduced roughly 0.08 vulnerabilities per 1,000 lines of code. The AI benchmark showed a 15-fold gap between the best and worst performers, ranging from 0.24 to 3.66 vulnerabilities. This background suggests that procurement decisions based only on branding or price may not reflect actual security outcomes.

Microsoft is currently developing a general-purpose frontier AI model to compete with broader systems beyond task-specific tools. Access to the MAI Cyber 2 Flash model is initially limited to a small group of select customers. The company has not yet announced specific pricing or availability timelines for all of the new AI models. It remains open whether the pricing advantages are due to promotional discounts or actual operational cost reductions. The articles leave open how these specialized models will perform against general models in scientific research problems.

stories.Headline: Microsoft launches Agent 365 Business Analytics to estimate AI agents' business value
stories.Summary:
Microsoft introduced Agent 365 Business Analytics on November 17, 2026, according to ZDNET, and the tool estimates the business value of AI agents. David Gewirtz wrote the ZDNET article, published on November 17, 2026, at 6:05 pm ET. Microsoft announced the tool as an accounting system for AI labor that compares agent costs with the value of human labor. Earlier in 2026, Microsoft had introduced Agent 365, a tool for tracking agents the way an HR department tracks human employees. SitePoint published a separate article by Varija Singh on November 19, 2026, about trusting the data feeding AI pipelines.

Agent 365 Business Analytics uses labor-costing data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the O*NET database from the US Department of Labor, and Microsoft's own LinkedIn Occupational Graph. The analysis covers more than 6,000 defined use cases and asks how much individual agents, models, and users cost. It also asks what business activities AI performs, how much human work those activities would require, and what that work is worth in dollars. Microsoft's blog post says assisted hours are "a directional estimate of work AI helped complete, not measured time saved or financial return." The SitePoint article describes a financial institution whose loan risk model flagged more customers as high risk after an upstream system changed a customer income field from annual gross income to annual net income.

Microsoft said the estimates are directional and not measured time saved or financial return, according to its blog post cited by ZDNET. Gewirtz wrote that Microsoft may be able to tell you the economic value of AI-assisted work but cannot demonstrate definitively that a company saved real money. He wrote that it is one source of possible truth, not the source of absolute truth. Singh wrote that even the most sophisticated AI model can produce misleading results if the underlying data is incomplete, inconsistent, or incorrectly interpreted. Singh wrote that just because an AI pipeline runs successfully does not necessarily mean its output can be trusted.

Gewirtz wrote that companies really have not been able to understand the AI bottom line. He wrote that AI work might have been assigned because there was AI to do the work, not because the AI was saving company labor costs with every token processed. He wrote that users will have to be quite disciplined in how they interpret the results and how much stock they put in them for decision-making. Singh wrote that the loan model's field name stayed the same and the data type was still numeric, so none of the existing technical validations detected the change. Singh wrote that building reliable AI systems requires understanding where data originates, how it changes, whether it meets quality expectations, and who is responsible when something goes wrong.

Gewirtz wrote that Microsoft has invested for decades to build out the core infrastructure of enterprise computing. He wrote that with Agent 365 and related offerings, Microsoft wants to help monitor AI agents from multiple vendors and manage their identities, permissions, and security. He wrote that Microsoft also wants to help track and limit AI spending, evaluate whether agents deliver value, and decide which AI systems deserve additional investment. He wrote that Microsoft integrates with offerings from OpenAI, Anthropic, Salesforce, Google, Databricks, Snowflake, and others. Singh wrote that most conversation about AI systems revolves around model accuracy, performance, and deployment.

Gewirtz wrote that Microsoft does not necessarily have to provide the AI model, and with those integrations it does not even have to provide the apps or SaaS capabilities. He wrote that if Microsoft can manage your plumbing, help you control costs, and be the HR operation for your AI workforce, it could own a central piece of your business's operations. Singh's article lists five practical controls for trustworthy AI pipelines: data contracts, quality gates, lineage metadata, versioned evidence, and ownership and escalation. Singh also describes data quality dimensions of completeness, validity, consistency, and timeliness, and distinguishes dataset-level from column-level lineage. The articles leave open whether the estimates match real-world experience or expenses, and Singh's article does not say whether the loan model problem was resolved.

stories.Headline: Guidepoint partners with Rogo to bring cited expert transcripts into AI financial research
stories.Summary:
Guidepoint announced a partnership with Rogo on Nov. 19, 2026, in New York, NY, according to a GlobeNewswire release. The partnership lets bankers and investors using Rogo access Guidepoint Library insights, including more than 150,000 compliance-reviewed expert transcripts. Answers that draw on Guidepoint content are cited to the original conversation. Guidepoint described itself as a global pioneer in access to expert insight. Rogo was described as the leading AI operating system for financial services and a trusted partner to the world's most prestigious financial institutions.

Through the Guidepoint MCP connector, Guidepoint clients who use Rogo can access Library insights from vetted Advisors in the same platform where they build comps, models, memos, and pitchbooks. The Guidepoint Library includes more than 150,000 compliance-reviewed transcripts of moderated conversations with vetted Advisors, and more than 5,000 new expert interviews are added every month. Guidepoint curates the content around topics relevant to clients' research needs, helping deal teams and investors screen opportunities, evaluate theses, and prepare client deliverables. Every transcript is compliance-reviewed, and Guidepoint implements custom compliance controls tailored to each firm's requirements. The connector is available now to Guidepoint clients using Rogo, who can contact their Guidepoint account team or email the address given.

Ameesh Shah, Chief Commercial Officer of Guidepoint Insights at Guidepoint, said it was clear from the first conversation that Rogo and Guidepoint share a commitment to reliable insight grounded in the firsthand experience of vetted practitioners. Shah said combining the strengths streamlines critical workflows, reduces everyday friction, and helps clients get answers faster. Shah said the partnership creates a more unified experience that helps users focus on what matters most. Strib Walker, Head of Product at Rogo, said some of the most valuable insights in finance come from people who have operated the businesses and navigated the markets customers are analyzing. Walker said the partnership brings that expertise directly into Rogo so teams can incorporate firsthand industry perspectives from diligence to investment decisions without interrupting workflows.

The partnership overview lists expert perspectives from vetted Advisors with direct operating, customer, and competitor experience. It lists traceable answers, where Guidepoint-informed answers in Rogo cite the original transcript, which users can open to validate the answer. It lists compliance review of every transcript and custom compliance controls tailored to each firm's requirements. It lists insights built into existing workflows, appearing where bankers and investors already work with no need to switch tools. The partnership is part of Guidepoint's broader effort to make its expert research available across the AI platforms and workflows its clients rely on, and Guidepoint is backed by a global network of more than 2M+ subject-matter experts serving institutional investors, consulting firms, and corporations.

Guidepoint announced Guidepoint MCP on Nov. 17, 2026, in New York, NY, a connector bringing its expert transcript Library and Advisor Network into AI platforms research teams already use. Guidepoint MCP connects Guidepoint360 to Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, and is built on the Model Context Protocol, an open standard for connecting data sources to AI applications. Guidepoint CEO Albert Sebag said AI has made public information easy to access but firsthand practitioner insight is still the hard part. Sebag said a general-purpose AI assistant may draw on public filings, news, and web content but does not usually have access to firsthand practitioner perspectives. Sebag said a standalone research platform can provide primary research but may require teams to work in a separate environment, and Guidepoint MCP bridges both gaps subject to the firm's own entitlements and compliance protocols.

Guidepoint MCP capabilities include seamless AI incorporation, full source attribution tracing every answer to the source transcript in Guidepoint360 with a complete audit trail, compliance by design configurable to client-specific controls and topic restrictions, and a compounding dataset with 150,000+ transcripts now and 5,000+ added every month. An analyst can pull up the full transcript to confirm a quote or paraphrase, read the surrounding conversation for context, and reference the source in an investment committee memo or client deliverable. Teams can search their own completed consultations and query those transcripts in one place, subject to their permissions. Clients can pull up open projects, see Advisors submitted to them, read screening answers, filter by responses, check availability, and request or decline a consultation with a confirmation before each step. Clients can also ask about upcoming curated insights and register for roundtables, teleconferences, and moderated calls without leaving the workflow.

Sebag said one challenge researchers face is the friction of working in multiple AI environments, and he called Guidepoint MCP the first end-to-end workflow facilitator to interface with all the major existing AI platforms. Sebag said it is designed to work from a 360-degree vantage point, handling curation and selection of the right experts, booking them, and gathering the research. Guidepoint said its network of more than two million subject-matter experts serves institutional investors, consulting firms, and corporations across companies, markets, and trends. Guidepoint said it embeds expert knowledge into decision-making through live, asynchronous, and agentic workflows. The articles leave open the terms of the partnership and any further platforms Guidepoint MCP may connect to.

stories.Headline: Woman sues Los Angeles police for investigating her stillbirth under California privacy law
stories.Summary:
A woman is suing the city of Los Angeles and detectives within the Los Angeles Police Department for allegedly unlawful interrogation and investigation following a stillbirth she had in 2024. The suit comes two years after California authorized the right for patients to sue for being investigated due to their pregnancy outcomes. This is the first known lawsuit under the state’s Reproductive Privacy Act, which was amended in 2022. The plaintiff was granted anonymity Thursday and is referred to in the complaint as Jane Doe. The complaint was filed late last week by If/When/How alongside law firm BraunHagey & Borden LLP.

The Reproductive Privacy Act was amended in 2022 to prohibit the state from taking punitive action based on pregnancy decisions and outcomes. The plaintiff alleges that in November 2024 she was unhoused, living in a city shelter and menstruating irregularly due to her epilepsy medication. An emergency visit for stomach pains revealed she was pregnant, but the fetus did not have a heartbeat. According to the complaint, Doe was initially informed she was still in the first trimester and could miscarry at home but subsequently learned she was around 29 weeks’ pregnant. She passed significant blood clots in the shelter toilet, left without flushing and was taken by ambulance to the hospital and treated for significant blood loss.

According to the complaint, police showed up at the hospital, shackled her to a bed and interrogated her for hours, telling her that a fetus had been found outside the shelter. The complaint said this was the first time Ms. Doe learned that she had passed into the toilet and the first time she heard that someone had reportedly moved the fetus from the toilet to an alley outside the shelter. The complaint alleges police continued to pursue a homicide investigation for about a year despite being told by a medical examiner that fetal demise had occurred in utero. The Los Angeles Police Department declined to comment citing the pending litigation. Ainsworth, chief legal and policy director at pregnancy-rights nonprofit If/When/How, said all the different things they did to Ms. Doe are a violation of the Reproductive Privacy Act.

Ainsworth said it is very important to show the state actors in California that they must abide by the law, which prohibits criminalizing somebody. At least 13 states and the District of Columbia have in recent years enacted measures to ensure protections for people’s pregnancy decisions and outcomes, including California, Colorado, Hawaii, Illinois, Michigan, Missouri, Montana, New Mexico, Ohio, Oregon, Vermont, Virginia and Washington. Among the few other places that explicitly allow damages suits, including D.C., Colorado and Illinois, California is the only state to eliminate common legal immunities for law enforcement, Ainsworth said. Women in other states have sued for facing criminal charges after a pregnancy loss, including Brittany Watts in Ohio, who last year sued the city of Warren, city policy officers and a hospital after she was arrested and charged with abuse of a corpse following a miscarriage in her home. Ainsworth noted that in other states it can be harder to determine who’s accountable.

Ainsworth said it is typically hard to hold government officials accountable for wrongful criminalization because of legal barriers. She said the Reproductive Privacy Act in California explicitly not only allows a private right of action but eliminates some of those immunities, allowing government actors who normally are shielded to actually be held accountable for their actions. In the first three years after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, more than 900 women faced criminal charges for conduct related to their pregnancies. The vast majority of the charges were for child abuse, neglect or endangerment, most related to substance use during pregnancy. Some involved allegations related to failing to obtain prenatal care or other actions taken or not taken during pregnancy or after pregnancy loss.

In California, Doe alleges she had to leave the shelter after police told reporters they suspected a homicide and headlines circulated about a newborn baby dropped from a fourth-floor window. In February 2025, she contacted a legal helpline run by If/When/How and started working with litigation counsel Shantal McNeil, who helped Doe navigate the investigation and petitioned the city attorney not to bring charges. McNeil said reputational damage and other harms often outlast these types of arrests and investigations, even when charges are dropped or never filed. She said police often investigate vulnerable women like the California plaintiff, who according to her attorneys is a young woman. McNeil said people mistakenly think that every pregnancy ends in a healthy baby, or that if this circumstance would happen to them, they would respond differently.

stories.Headline: MIT-led team uses large language models to review code sharing in nearly 4,000 medical studies
stories.Summary:
An international team led by researchers at MIT and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute used large language models to examine nearly 4,000 medical studies and hundreds of code repositories, as reported by MIT News on November 19, 2026. The team identified statements about shared code in papers and then followed those statements to assess the associated repositories. The review revealed two key gaps: code sharing remains uncommon, and making code public does not consistently mean providing the documentation and supporting information needed for reuse. The open-access findings were recently published in Nature Medicine. The work examined how code is currently shared in clinical prediction studies, which develop or evaluate models to estimate patient outcomes such as disease risk.

The review included almost 4,000 studies that developed, updated, or validated prediction models and whose full texts were available through PubMed Central's open-access collection. The team identified studies citing either TRIPOD or TRIPOD+AI, checklists that help researchers report how clinical prediction models were developed and evaluated. Only about 1 in 8 studies reported sharing code. Among journals, the proportion of studies sharing code ranged from zero to more than 70 percent. Two researchers independently checked 500 papers and a separate sample of repositories, resolving disagreements before comparing their assessments with the automated results.

Tom Pollard, a research scientist at MIT's Laboratory for Computational Physiology and Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, said studies involve many choices about preparing data, developing models, and evaluating performance. Pollard, a senior author of the study, said the choices researchers make affect the results and a methods section in a paper can only capture so much detail. He said the real benefit of LLMs is their ability to process unstructured information such as text, helping the team work with information scattered across papers and software repositories. Pollard said this allowed the team to examine how code was being shared in much more detail across a large collection of studies. He said the team wants to give researchers practical guidance on how to share code and give journals clearer expectations to communicate to authors.

Thomas Sounack, the study's first author, said the challenge was that the information was highly inconsistent and the team first had to identify whether or not a paper shared code. Sounack said authors discuss and link to code from a paper in many different ways. He said some repositories were extremely well-organized and documented, while others gave almost no guidance at all. Sounack said good code sharing means giving enough information to understand what the code does and be able to run it to reproduce the results reported in the paper. The authors emphasize the overall patterns rather than treating every count as exact because classification errors remain possible.

TRIPOD-Code builds on TRIPOD and TRIPOD+AI, checklists that help researchers report how clinical prediction models were developed and evaluated. The workflow went beyond checking whether a link existed, assessing repositories against characteristics such as completeness of documentation, software requirements, and terms of reuse. Agreement between human reviewers and the automated results was stronger for concrete characteristics, such as whether a license file was present, than for judgments about the adequacy of documentation. Some journals with low sharing rates nevertheless had written code-sharing policies, suggesting that policies alone may not be enough to motivate code sharing. The review also helped to identify examples of effective practice, such as researchers providing synthetic datasets to assist with code reuse where original patient records could not be shared publicly.

The open-access findings are informing TRIPOD-Code, a reporting guideline being developed to clarify what researchers should share. Through an expert review process, the team is developing guidance on which elements of shared analytical code should be considered essential. Clinical prediction research brings together people from medicine, statistics, and computer science, whose expectations for documenting and sharing code may differ, and TRIPOD-Code aims to establish a consensus. Pollard said the review gives the team evidence to inform those discussions. The articles leave open which specific elements of shared analytical code will be deemed essential under TRIPOD-Code.

stories.Headline: MP High Court pulls up state government for using AI to cite non-existent Supreme Court judgment
stories.Summary:
The Madhya Pradesh High Court cautioned the state government on Tuesday for using artificial intelligence to cite a non-existent Supreme Court judgment. The court found that the state blindly resorted to AI tools to draft a reply in a specific legal matter. This incident occurred during a hearing regarding a petition filed by a police sub-inspector who was dismissed from service. The court criticized the state for its callous and irresponsible drafting of the legal documents submitted to the bench. Justice Vivek Kumar Singh presided over the case and quashed the dismissal of the police officer in question.

The state cited a fake case called State of Andhra Pradesh vs S.S. Mohammad Nisar, reported as (2008) 5 SCC 230. This fabricated citation was actually from the Sidhartha Vashisht alias Manu Sharma vs State (NCT of Delhi) case regarding criminal appeals. The government used this fake ruling to argue that reappreciation of evidence is impermissible under Article 226 of the Constitution. The court held that the state could not bypass a departmental inquiry under Article 311(2)(b) in this specific case. The ruling requires the government to reinstate the sub-inspector forthwith while allowing for a fresh inquiry under the law.

Justice Vivek Kumar Singh stated that the respondents had blindly used AI tools, resulting in a fabricated name and unrelated citation. The judge noted that pleadings filed before a constitutional court are solemn documents and must be handled with professional care. He observed that inserting fictitious case law without verifying citations wastes precious judicial time and borders on actively misleading the court. The bench strictly cautioned the state machinery against such reckless practices in the future to maintain legal integrity. The court further ordered that the office of the Advocate General must meticulously verify all legal propositions and citations.

The police sub-inspector was affected by this case after being dismissed within twenty four hours of a sexual harassment complaint. Government advocate Swati Aseem George and Advocate General Prashant Singh both declined to comment on the court's stern observations. The court expressed no opinion on the merits of the allegations made against the officer regarding his alleged behavior. The bench emphasized that the state's justification for invoking Article 311(2)(b) was unsustainable in law for this particular dismissal. The officer had been accused of indecent behavior toward a woman cleaner at the state situation room in Bhopal.

The background involves a sexual harassment complaint lodged against the sub-inspector on May 26, 2024, in the city of Bhopal. He was suspended on that same day and then dismissed from his service on May 27, 2024, without inquiry. The state had invoked provisions that allow departmental inquiries to be dispensed with only in very exceptional and rare circumstances. This led the officer to file a petition challenging the dismissal process as a violation of constitutional due process. The court found that the state had bypassed necessary legal steps before removing the officer from his professional position.

The state government must now reinstate the police sub-inspector immediately as per the directions issued by the High Court. The government retains the liberty to conduct a regular departmental inquiry in accordance with the law regarding the original allegations. The office of the Advocate General is now responsible for ensuring that all future citations are verified before being recorded. The articles leave open whether the state will pursue the fresh inquiry into the officer's behavior toward the cleaner. It remains unclear if any disciplinary action will be taken against the officials who used AI to draft the pleadings.

stories.Headline: US Senate passes bill to speed energy permits and require AI data centers to pay more grid costs
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Senate passed a bipartisan comprehensive bill to speed up permitting for large energy projects on the 19th by a vote of 62 to 33. The bill covers power plants, transmission lines and data centers. The aim is to address the surge in electricity demand accompanying the spread of AI. The bill is titled the bipartisan American Cost of Living Relief and Employment Act. It now goes to the Republican-majority House of Representatives.

The bill sets stricter deadlines for federal environmental reviews and limits on litigation periods. It requires large-scale AI data centers to bear a higher share of grid reinforcement costs. It sets new limits on the scope and duration of reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act. It includes provisions restricting the period during which lawsuits can be filed and the circumstances under which permits can be revoked. It also expands federal authority over the siting and permitting of interstate transmission projects.

The bill took four years to craft and was led by four lawmakers, two Democrats and two Republicans. In the vote, most Republican senators were joined by 14 Democrats and one independent. Co-sponsor Republican Senator Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia said the Senate took a major step forward in addressing Americans' concerns about the cost of living. Democratic Senator Jeff Merkley of Oregon said consultations with tribes had not been adequately conducted. Merkley said the bill touches on states' authority, tribal rights and multiple matters of critical importance to energy.

Most opposing votes came from Democratic lawmakers, who argue the bill weakens environmental protection and Native American tribal sovereignty. Republican Senators Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota also voted against. Several tribal organizations maintained their opposition even after amendments were made. Many environmental groups warn that safety safeguards under NEPA and other laws would be dangerously undermined. A broad range of energy and business groups, the AFL-CIO and numerous individual unions have lobbied for passage.

Both parties have long pointed out that construction of large infrastructure projects takes too long and that procedural delays drive up costs. With electricity demand expanding due to the rapid growth of AI, concerns about power prices and worries that grid expansion cannot keep pace have been mounting. House Speaker Mike Johnson, Republican of Louisiana, was reported last week to have expressed confidence he can secure the votes needed for passage. President Donald Trump has indicated his intention to sign the bill into law. Efforts to secure enactment within the year are in full swing.

The bill now enters deliberations in the House, and if differences arise between the two chambers they must be reconciled within the year. Some Democratic lawmakers are calling for careful deliberation, with some arguing a separate bill should be assembled after taking control of Congress next year. Multiple supporters within the Democratic coalition believe there is no political room to amend the bill into a form Trump would sign. Some voices point to the possibility of legal battles even after enactment. The articles leave open the House schedule and the prospects for enactment within the year.

stories.Headline: Police find Lee Jin-woo dead at Seoul motel as AI cheating probe continues
stories.Summary:
Lee Jin-woo was found dead on Thursday, November 19, 2026, at a motel in eastern Seoul after police began searching for him. The man was a dental student at Seoul National University who had achieved a perfect score on the Legal Education Eligibility Test. He had gone missing since Wednesday night after he told reporters he would dispel cheating allegations through a public live stream. Emergency authorities discovered his body on the roof of a motel located in Cheonho-dong, Gangdong District, at around 1:12 p.m. that day.

He was found in cardiac arrest after failing to appear for a planned test of his abilities at 8:40 a.m. Thursday. The planned demonstration required Lee to solve questions from the Korean language section of the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test in real time. He had previously visited a lodging facility in Gwangjin District before taking a taxi toward Songpa District between 8 and 9 a.m. The investigation involves the Legal Education Eligibility Test, the 2024 and 2026 college entrance exams, and the national tax accountant certification exam.

Lee was admitted to Korea University's Department of Political Science and International Relations in 2024 and Seoul National University's School of Dentistry in 2026. He had previously scored in the sixth to eighth tiers on past college entrance exams using a nine-tier grading system. The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency assigned a criminal complaint against Lee to its Provincial Special Detective Corps on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. The charges included fraud, obstruction of official duties, and obstruction of business, though police will likely close the case without prosecution. A note found at the scene reportedly stated that Lee was physically and mentally exhausted, but it contained no admission of cheating.

The note also offered no apology or explanation regarding the allegations that he used artificial intelligence to achieve his perfect scores. Police began their search for Lee after receiving a report expressing concern for his safety at around 8:42 a.m. Thursday. Some people raised allegations that Lee cheated on the LEET and the college entrance exams for the 2024 and 2026 academic years. These suspicions grew after a separate case of alleged AI-assisted cheating on the national tax accountant certification exam recently surfaced in Korea.

Over 550,000 students sat for the college entrance exam under tighter anti-cheating measures, and 98 test-takers were caught cheating in 2026. The government tightened national exam rules, including expanded CCTV and random phone calls, after concerns about AI and smart-device cheating grew. Lee had previously claimed he gained a new understanding of reading comprehension and studying to improve his low previous scores. Lee had previously posed for a photo during an interview at the JoongAng Ilbo headquarters in Mapo District on September 8. He was the first person to ever achieve a perfect score on the Legal Education Eligibility Test while attending Seoul National University.

The articles mention that both Korea University and Seoul National University are regarded as prestigious schools within the country of South Korea. The case emerged during a broader storm of AI fraud allegations affecting various national qualification exams and college entrance tests in Korea. Authorities are now examining the motel scene to determine the exact circumstances surrounding the death of the controversial test-taker. Police said they will continue their probe into the AI-assisted cheating allegations even though Lee Jin-woo is now dead.

The investigation into the law school entrance exam cheating case faces an uphill battle because the primary suspect cannot be prosecuted. Authorities plan to further examine the scene at the motel near Cheonho station to gather more information about the event. The articles leave open whether other individuals were involved in the alleged fraud or if more cheating cases will surface. It remains unclear if the police will find evidence that confirms Lee used artificial intelligence to ace his various exams.

stories.Headline: European Commission sets 2 December 2027 high-risk AI compliance deadline
stories.Summary:
The EU AI Act's bans on certain practices and its AI literacy duty have applied since 2 February 2025, and obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models since 2 August 2025. The European Commission's AI Office and national authorities took on enforcement powers on 2 August 2026. An amending law known as the AI Omnibus pushed the heaviest compliance work, for high-risk systems, to 2 December 2027 for standalone uses and 2 August 2028 for AI built into regulated products. The Commission proposed the Omnibus on 19 November 2025, a political agreement followed in May 2026, and the Commission says it entered into force on 27 July 2026. Orrick identifies it as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

The Act sorts AI by risk, according to the Commission's summary, banning practices judged an unacceptable threat to safety, livelihoods or rights. The Commission's list covers AI that manipulates or deceives people in harmful ways, exploits vulnerabilities, scores people socially, predicts individual criminal offenses, scrapes the internet or CCTV footage to build facial recognition databases, recognizes emotions in workplaces and schools, categorizes people biometrically to infer protected traits, or performs real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement in public spaces. The Omnibus added a ninth ban, on systems that generate non-consensual intimate imagery or child sexual abuse material, which applies from 2 December 2026. High-risk systems are allowed but must meet requirements on risk management, data quality, logging, documentation, human oversight and robustness. Systems with transparency risk carry disclosure duties, such as telling people they are dealing with a machine and labeling deepfakes.

The final law keeps the AI literacy obligation on providers and deployers to take measures supporting AI literacy among staff and others operating AI systems on their behalf, according to Addleshaw Goddard's analysis of the adopted text. The text says it does not require any specific level of literacy for any individual. Providers of general-purpose AI models must address transparency and copyright, and providers of models with systemic risk must also assess and mitigate those risks. In July 2025 the Commission published scope guidelines, a voluntary code of practice and a template for summarizing training data. Since 2 August 2026 the AI Office can evaluate models, order corrective measures and issue fines.

Transparency obligations under Article 50 also apply from August 2026, and providers of systems that generate synthetic content and were placed on the market before 2 August 2026 have until 2 December 2026 to meet the marking requirement in Article 50(2), according to the Commission and Orrick's review of the final text. The Omnibus reinstated the duty to register high-risk systems in the EU database, which the Commission had proposed to waive for systems posing no significant risk, while streamlining what must be filed. It also narrowed the definition of a safety component. It gave the AI Office exclusive supervision of AI systems built on a general-purpose model from the same provider or group, and of AI integrated into very large online platforms and search engines. The Omnibus created a small mid-cap category for firms that are not SMEs, have fewer than 750 employees and have turnover of up to 150 million euros or a balance sheet of up to 129 million euros.

According to Orrick, small mid-caps gain SME-style treatment, including simplified documentation templates, proportionate quality management, priority access to regulatory sandboxes and tailored penalty caps. Annex III high-risk uses include biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, migration and justice, so AI used to recruit, screen, promote or monitor workers falls in scope. Systems already on the market before that date are covered only if they are substantially modified afterward, and public authorities have until 2 August 2030. High-risk rules for AI embedded in products regulated under Annex I, such as machinery, apply from 2 August 2028. Penalties are set in Article 99.

Breaching the bans can cost up to 35 million euros or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. Breaching most operator obligations, including transparency duties, carries fines of up to 15 million euros or 3%, and supplying incorrect or misleading information to authorities up to 7.5 million euros or 1%. For SMEs the lower of the two figures applies, and the Omnibus extended that treatment to small mid-caps for all but the prohibited-practice fines. A separate and broader Digital Omnibus, which would amend the GDPR and other digital laws, is still a proposal working through the EU legislative process and is not settled law. For HR and other Annex III tools under the AI Act, the conformity deadline is December 2027.

stories.Headline: Harvard Berkman Klein Center seeks a director to lead its AI and youth safety research
stories.Summary:
Harvard University’s Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society posted a hiring notice on Nov 20, 2026 for a Director of Research, also called Project Director, AI and Youth Safety. The center is an interfaculty research center at Harvard. The posting says the center seeks someone to lead its AI and Youth Safety initiative. The role involves defining unanswered questions about young people’s relationships with AI and developing a research agenda. The director will also convene leading thinkers across disciplines and translate research into evidence for public understanding and policy.

The basic qualifications are a bachelor’s degree and 8 years of progressive experience, or a related advanced degree with 5 years experience. The appointment is a term position currently expected to extend to June 30, 2027, with potential for renewal subject to departmental funding and need. Harvard says it is unable to provide visa sponsorship for the position. The position is salary grade level 059, and all offers are made by HLS Human Resources. The work format allows some duties at a non-Harvard location, and hybrid employees must work in a Harvard registered state when not at a Harvard or Harvard-designated location.

The posting says the director will lead day-to-day direction of the initiative, shape research design, conduct original research and writing, and ensure outputs meet standards for quality, rigor, ethics, and real-world relevance. The director will provide technical and methodological leadership, review research plans, instruments, analyses, and drafts, and select and justify quantitative, qualitative, or mixed methods. The role includes managing and mentoring research teams, hiring and supervising staff such as research coordinators, research associates, employee fellows, research assistants, and interns. The director will help shape the emerging field by identifying high-impact and underexplored questions and adapting the research agenda as new evidence and technologies emerge. The director will build an interdisciplinary community across Harvard and beyond, including researchers, youth-serving organizations, policymakers, technologists, educators, civil society organizations, and industry partners.

The posting says the director will design convenings, workshops, and ongoing collaborations, and support grant development and funder engagement, including proposal narratives, methods and measurement sections, project plans, and reporting deliverables. The director will oversee research program operations and communications with Center teams, manage timelines and outputs such as publications, tools, events, and reporting, and support public-facing outputs consistent with the Center’s Open Access Policy. The director will represent the Center’s AI and youth safety work at convenings and events such as working groups, symposia, and briefings. Qualifications include deep familiarity with AI and online safety issues such as generative AI and AI companions, youth online safety and development, platform governance, privacy and data protection, content moderation, age-appropriate design, human-computer interaction, evaluation and measurement, and the policy landscape shaping AI systems. The posting also lists a demonstrated record of AI or machine learning research, such as publications at peer-reviewed venues, open-source contributions, or equivalent technical work, and strong writing, presentation, and collaboration skills.

The posting says the center is committed to making sense of the digital environment and ensuring it promotes human agency, dignity, and genuine connection. It describes the opportunity as rare and unusual and the community as flourishing and intellectually robust, with faculty, staff, students, fellows, and affiliates from multiple disciplines and backgrounds. It says a successful candidate will be open to learning from experiments, taking good ideas from wherever they come, and changing course quickly. It says Harvard offers a comprehensive benefits package including paid time off, parental leave, medical, dental, and vision coverage starting on day one, retirement plans with university contributions, wellbeing and mental health resources, family and caregiver support, professional development including tuition assistance and reimbursement, and commuter benefits, discounts, and campus perks. It says Harvard is committed to equal opportunity and non-discrimination and seeks talent from all parts of society and the world.

The posting says the work schedule and location will be set by the department at its discretion based on operational needs, and certain visa types and funding sources may limit work location. It says individuals must meet work location sponsorship requirements prior to employment. It says additional details will be discussed during the interview process. It says the site and its contents are licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Unported license unless otherwise noted. It says the page was last updated Nov 20, 2026.

stories.Headline: Anthropic spends $3.4 billion on Caterpillar gas turbines for off-grid AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Anthropic spent 3.4 billion dollars to power its artificial intelligence data centers in the United States. The company finalized this deal in late September with a firm called OnePWR Solutions. This transaction allows the developer to acquire heavy duty gas turbines from the manufacturer Caterpillar Inc. The purchase is the largest single equipment buy ever made by an artificial intelligence firm. This move helps the company secure power for its gigawatt scale computing facilities.

The project, called the Anthropic Off-Grid 1.7GW Power Generation and Data Center Initiative, requires 1.7 gigawatts of capacity. It uses natural gas generators for base load and peak shaving operations at confidential United States sites. The commitment covers hardware fabrication, balance of plant engineering, and site construction works. It requires structural steel, high pressure gas piping, copper wiring, concrete footings, and acoustic cladding. The buildout includes gas pipeline interconnections, step up substations, fuel storage, and microgrid distribution switchgear.

Anthropic PBC is the developer responsible for this initiative and its overall execution. The company wants to maintain velocity across its multi hundred billion dollar compute pipeline. Leadership believes that owning power plants is a strategic shift from being a grid customer. This strategy aligns with the company's long term capital trajectory as it prepares for an initial public offering. The developer aims to guarantee uninterrupted operational uptime for its next generation foundation models.

Industry analysts say that utility grid interconnection backlogs are the largest constraint on modern data center deployment. These backlogs can delay projects by several years, affecting major cloud operators who need reliable electricity. The program will support thousands of specialized engineering, fabrication, and heavy civil construction jobs. At peak buildout, more than 3,500 workers in various trades will be employed. Once operational, the project will support over 450 direct permanent jobs for technicians and engineers.

The articles state that AI developers are taking direct control of energy supply chains to avoid public utilities. This trend is part of a global competition for high density computing infrastructure. One example is SK Hyper, which reportedly pursued 350 billion dollars for a massive data center buildout. Another report notes that AI data center power demand will double by 2030 due to 4 trillion dollars in spending. This growth will add 93 large AI factories with a projected capacity of 50 gigawatts.

Deployment will occur in three phases, starting with Caterpillar delivering generator sets to installation sites. Engineering teams will then connect fuel pipelines, microgrid switchgear, and step up transformers. Finally, on site power units will energize server clusters without relying on the utility grid. Phased hardware deliveries will run through 2027 and 2028 to reach the total capacity. The reports leave open the specific completion date for the full fleet beyond that window.

stories.Headline: Meta employees flag Muse AI privacy risks before launch as agent mixes user accounts
stories.Summary:
Meta launched its Muse AI agent in September 2026 with promises of privacy and security for its users. Internal communications reviewed by Reuters showed employees raising significant concerns about how the AI handled private data. Staffers flagged safety issues as recently as launch week, but Meta proceeded with the scheduled US launch. The AI agent reportedly mixed up conversations between different user accounts, which exposed private data to others. Some employees described failure modes that made the product unreliable when used in real world conditions.

The agent requires broad Android notification permissions to access messages and data from other apps on a device. Claroc found that a chat sharing feature exposed conversations through publicly searchable DNS records for any query. These exposed links included business documents, financial reviews, internal company information, and holiday schedules for entire companies. A vulnerability identified by Patrick Wardle put a user's dictated audio and account token at risk during sessions. Meta tested a human concierge phone calling feature with employees in August 2026 before the public launch.

Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts stated that employees have access to different versions of Muse than the general public. Roberts described the examples reported by Reuters as isolated incidents and said the company prioritizes safety and testing. Meta did not dispute that the internal posts existed but claimed many account mix ups were hallucinations. The company maintained that Muse was built with strong security foundations and follows strict internal company rules. Meta also stated that some of the identified problems had already been addressed by the technical team.

Staffers warned that Muse accessed encrypted private messages, including Signal messages, that users did not expect the bot to review. One employee expressed concern about a possible cross account context leak after seeing a conversation not their own. Users who shared conversations did not realize the resulting links were discoverable by anyone with the right query. The exposed data included financial data from a large marketing firm that was accessible without any login requirement. Call center workers might be exposed to sensitive user information through the human concierge phone calling feature.

Meta is an American technology company headquartered in Menlo Park, California, and the parent of Facebook and Instagram. Mark Zuckerberg founded the company in 2004 as Facebook before it rebranded as Meta in 2021. Muse is designed to manage tasks like reading emails, managing calendars, and handling financial tasks through connected accounts. Each Muse agent runs in its own cloud virtual machine and is gated by a security process called Sentinel. The AI agent had already been downloaded by more than 10 million people by November 2026.

Meta temporarily disabled the sharing feature while investigating the problem and later restored it with a fix in place. Claroc confirmed that the previously accessible links were no longer reachable after the company implemented the security patch. Meta expected the AI agent to generate billions of dollars in revenue from its various AI products. The articles leave open whether unfamiliar financial information was actual data exposure or information fabricated by the model. It remains unclear if the cross account confusion described in internal posts affected the general public.

stories.Headline: Senator Mark Warner introduces bipartisan bill requiring public companies to disclose major AI financing
stories.Summary:
Senator Mark Warner of Virginia and three of his colleagues introduced bipartisan legislation on Thursday, November 19, 2026, that would require publicly traded companies to make specific disclosures about major AI-related financing and would call for formalized standards on how firms warn investors about AI-related risks. The bill, first reported by Politico, is the latest sign that Congress is stepping up its oversight of the outsize influence the AI sector is playing in financial markets. Warner said in an interview that he worries about so-called circular investments, where AI companies provide financial backing for firms that are also their customers, and he cited Nvidia's support for businesses that buy its chips as one example. He also highlighted the need to get more information about financing through legal entities that might not appear directly on a firm's books.

The push for disclosure comes in a week when Anthropic launched its blockbuster IPO and Nvidia released its first earnings report since the resignation of its co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang, according to The Globe and Mail's Decibel podcast. Those two events are being watched closely as litmus tests for where the AI sector is going, as concerns loom about how the industry is being financed. Joe Castaldo, The Globe's tech and AI reporter, explained how the AI industry is being financed, why there are concerns about it, and what it means for the whole economy if AI funding continues at its current break-neck pace or slows down. The dynamic means that a blowup in the AI industry could spread to the rest of the economy, Politico reported.

Warner leads the bipartisan group of senators pushing for more information on the web of funding that is fueling the artificial intelligence boom, in a bid to scrutinize the potential financial risks posed by businesses at the center of it, such as chipmaking giant Nvidia. The legislation would require specific disclosures by publicly traded companies on major AI-related financing and call for formalized standards on how firms warn investors about AI-related risks. Warner expressed worry about circular investments and about financing through legal entities that might not appear directly on a firm's books. The bill is the latest sign that Congress is stepping up its scrutiny of the AI sector's role in financial markets.

The articles do not say what happens next with the bill, such as whether it will receive a vote or when. The Globe and Mail's podcast framed the week's IPO and earnings report as tests of where the AI sector is going amid concerns about how the industry is being financed. Politico reported that the bipartisan push is the latest sign of stepped-up congressional oversight of the AI sector's influence in financial markets. The articles do not say what would happen to the wider economy if AI funding continues at its current pace or slows down, beyond noting that a blowup in the industry could spread to the rest of the economy.

stories.Headline: Google builds a simulated internet called the Mirror Dimension to test its Gemini browsing agents
stories.Summary:
Google built a simulated internet called the Mirror Dimension to test its AI browsing agents. The Chrome team created this isolated ecosystem to ensure their Gemini models function safely. This project was detailed in a blog post published on November 19, 2026. The system allows agents to practice navigating websites without risking the open internet. It prevents models from developing eval awareness by mimicking a real web experience.

The Mirror Dimension requires a diverse array of simulated platforms like social media and banking dashboards. These environments include realistic components such as shopping sites where agents can enter promo codes. To build this, the team used AI harness agents to create various web services. Researchers had to forge web certificates to bypass Chrome validity checks for the agents. These specific security hacks only work because Google controls the entire network and environment.

Charles Qian is a software engineer on the Chrome AI security team who discussed the project. He stated that the exploration space is huge because agents are not traditionally programmed. Qian noted that the open web is hostile and requires thorough exploration of all prompts. He observed that agents are developing a mature sense of judgment for completing tasks. Some agents now know when to ask a user for confirmation before proceeding further.

The project affects AI browsing assistant agents that must learn to navigate real websites and platforms. These agents are subjected to resilience tests, including hidden prompt injection attacks, to harden defenses. The researchers emphasize that the attacks used in testing cannot affect regular Chrome users. The agents are designed to be benign while they learn to handle complex web interactions. This training ensures that unrefined agents are not released onto the live, open internet.

Google developed this system because training in limited test environments is not effective for web agents. Models often behave differently when they determine they are in a simulation or test. The Chrome team needed a way to simulate the scale of the real web quickly. They used armies of development agents to populate the Mirror Dimension with realistic data flows. This background allows Google to test Gemini models in a controlled, alternate universe.

Google will continue using the Mirror Dimension to refine how agents interact with various web services. The agents will face further tests to ensure they can handle the hostile open internet. The articles leave open how these agents will eventually be deployed to the public. It is unclear what specific tasks the final browsing assistants will perform for users. The text does not state when these AI features will launch in Chrome.

stories.Headline: SpaceX subsidiary Cursor considers phasing out Chinese AI models to reduce geopolitical risk
stories.Summary:
Cursor, an artificial intelligence coding platform owned by SpaceX, is considering the removal of Chinese developed models from its systems. This decision follows a months long investigation conducted by the House Select Committee on China and the House Committee on Homeland Security. The company had previously built its Composer 2 model using Kimi K2.5 from the Chinese laboratory Moonshot AI. SpaceX completed its acquisition of Cursor in August after first announcing a formal agreement to buy the firm in June.

The transition would involve phasing out open weight models from the People's Republic of China to reduce geopolitical risk. This shift occurs after SpaceX acquired Cursor at an implied equity value of 60 billion dollars. The House report suggests that American firms adopted these models because of their low cost, customization options, and near frontier performance. Lawmakers are now recommending a national American open weight initiative to provide competitive alternatives for the market.

The House committees stated that Beijing intends to use these technological gains to create long term global dependence. They also suggested expanding an October order that banned DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems to include all Chinese models in federal contracts. While Cursor, SpaceX, and DoorDash did not respond to requests for comment, Airbnb declined to speak on the matter. The report emphasizes that the United States currently lacks an open weight alternative that meets market demands for price and performance.

The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security announced an interim final rule on Monday to stop Chinese companies from accessing AI chips remotely. Washington is specifically concerned about the use of overseas data centers and the process of distillation to train new models. These measures aim to protect the American tech stack as the battle for AI supremacy between the two nations intensifies in 2026. The government continues to monitor how Chinese models are integrated into the infrastructure of private American companies.

stories.Headline: Babak Heydari and Hongan Zhu show AI agents recreating human decision chains in a study
stories.Summary:
Babak Heydari and Hongan Zhu published a study in Nature Computational Science on November 16. They showed how AI models could reproduce human decision making more closely. The researchers used AI agents to recreate the chain reaction of human decisions. This work helps scientists build more realistic simulations across a wide range of situations. The study focused on how people make choices, including their flaws.

The researchers used agents from seven AI models to play the beer game. This game involves a retailer, a wholesaler, a distributor, and a factory. The agents managed a pretend supply chain across 231 different sessions. They used cognitive grounding based on earlier experiments analyzing how humans play. Six of the seven models responded more like people when given emotional descriptions.

Babak Heydari said accurate simulations can help anticipate supply chain jams and avoid them. He noted that his lab uses engineering, computational social sciences, and economics. Hongan Zhu said the cognitive grounding was a paraphrase of a mathematical model. Zhu explained that they observe agent behavior and use language to redirect choices. He compared their approach to how psychologists treat their patients.

Jakob Kaiser of the Nuremberg Institute for Market Decisions said human studies take time. He noted that AI offers a shortcut for these types of experiments. Sangeet Khemlani of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory said simulations avoid ethical concerns. He stated that AI can play out scenarios too risky for real people. Khemlani warned that incorrect predictions from simulations can backfire.

The study mentions how Australians bought 39.7 million toilet paper rolls from Woolworths in 2020. It notes a 2012 Twinkie apocalypse where one man sold boxes for 1,000 dollars. The research builds on a 1971 experiment by Nobel laureate Thomas Schelling using coins. Schelling used a grid to show how small choices create urban segregation patterns. This early work laid the groundwork for modern agent based simulation.

Policymakers can use these simulations to test price shifts or new laws. Officials could test evacuation instructions to avoid gridlock or check transit fare changes. Businesses could explore if moving a pharmacy location attracts new customers. The findings suggest a way to keep AI agents from stepping out of line. The articles leave open how specific bots remained set in their ways.

stories.Headline: What Exactly Is AI? A Computer Science Professor Unpacks the Mystery
stories.Summary:
Joseph C. Osborn, an associate professor of computer science at Pomona College who studies technical game design and artificial intelligence, published an explainer on November 19, 2026, in which he argued that artificial intelligence is a messy term that means one thing to a research community and another to marketers. He said that where the term defines a research community it refers to building computational systems inspired by cognition, while as a marketing term it describes a category of products, and that when people think of AI they probably imagine chat interfaces built on large language models or agents layered on top of them. Osborn wrote that he tells his students there is no such thing as artificial intelligence because intelligence would have to be defined in a way that can be measured and encoded on a computer, which he called deeply problematic. He added that even if AI were a thing it would be impossible to build, since computer scientists are unlikely to stumble onto a new kind of mind using linear algebra, and that building an intelligence like ours as a product eager to serve our every whim would ruin us morally.

Osborn wrote that nobody outside the AI companies knows exactly what happens when a user sends a prompt to Claude, ChatGPT or other products, though these chat interfaces are known to be made from many smaller programs working independently. He said large language model chat systems output special sequences of words invisible to the user, which are intercepted and filtered through the system many times in multiple steps, including passing through old non-AI tools such as web searches, before the response is filtered for coherence and to keep users from seeing outputs deemed harmful. He described all these steps as trade secrets unrelated to the intelligence of the model, and said the utility of chatbots for search and document retrieval comes from engineering and product design moves that do not depend on the model getting any smarter. He called it a logical fallacy to argue that because humans make language and large language models create language the models must be intelligent, and said the models are mathematical models built for predicting the next most likely word, with parameters learned from large volumes of human-authored text.

Osborn said AI is already wreaking havoc in schools, communities and the social fabric, not because of a malicious rogue program but because corporate boards and CEOs want people to believe their peers will judge them negatively unless they use AI. He cited chatbots convincing people to commit suicide or stop taking important medications, and AI agents hacking into other companies to score higher on benchmark tests, with no one at the AI company held accountable. He said this is not a technological problem but a social and political one, and that AI acts as a mirror highlighting existing issues of corporate immunity and negligence. He said the last thing AI companies want is accountability for the outputs of their systems, and that the total lack of accountability for foreseeable consequences is his main worry.
