stories.Headline: Adam Tornhill says healthy code boosts AI performance and cuts token costs
stories.Summary:
Adam Tornhill presented at GOTO Copenhagen on how healthy code improves AI performance and reduces token costs, as reported by TechGig on November 20, 2026. He demonstrated that healthy code significantly enhances AI performance and leads to fewer token costs. Tornhill argued that agentic AI can speed up development velocity, but the gains vanish within months as code complexity grows. A study of over 1,000 open-source projects showed that initial AI-driven velocity increases were entirely offset by a surge in code complexity within two months. Tornhill said AI can operate in a self-harm mode, generating code it struggles to maintain.

Code health measures how easy code is to understand, change, and maintain, and the average codebase has a code health score of 5.15. AI-friendly code starts at 9.5, and research shows working with healthy code can be up to ten times faster than with unhealthy code. The defect risk is reduced 15 times, and code reviews go twice as quickly, Tornhill said. He noted that 95 per cent of software project costs occur after the first release, highlighting the importance of code quality and maintainability. Technical debt hinders enterprise adoption of agentic coding, necessitating agentic refactoring processes.

Tornhill said developing software with agents is significantly harder than writing code manually, but with agentic AI teams can complete tasks two to three times faster. He added that it helps teams unblock themselves and reduces coordination needs. Claude can address roughly 50 per cent of code health issues in lower-health code, but its performance drops sharply as code health improves. Claude only correctly refactors 20 per cent of code in such scenarios, Tornhill said. Adding a Master Control Program with code health data can increase the fix rate to 90 to 100 per cent.

Tornhill said AI tends to become conservative, doing small changes that do not really move the needle on code quality. He argued that safeguarding needs to happen at multiple levels, and all safeguards need to be completely automated in an agentic context. Concrete safeguards include linting, code coverage, mutation testing, and higher-level metrics like Code Health, exposed to agents as local MCP servers or command-line tools. Healthy code is also financially efficient, enabling tasks with 40 to 45 per cent fewer tokens, Tornhill said. Refactoring code to improve modularity and health can also reduce organisational friction.

Tornhill said code health is a multifaceted concept, so multiple metrics must be combined from three levels of software design. Module level design asks whether modules are cohesive and do one thing well, or have multiple unrelated responsibilities. Function level design asks how well-designed the individual function blocks are and how expressive their APIs are. Implementation level avoids accidental complexity such as deeply nested logic and excessive copy-paste. The main steps for refactoring at scale are to establish a baseline, build a safety-net for behavior, and provide a feedback loop to the agents.

Tornhill said the baselining step focuses on measuring code quality to identify what needs improving, and the safety-net is a reliable test suite that preserves existing behavior. The agentic feedback loop builds on objective code health information and test outcomes so the AI can determine whether a change moves code quality closer to the goal. In a study on Refactoring at Scale with Agents, agents were instructed to build an evolving playbook of successful codebase-specific refactoring patterns. While module-level code quality is largely automated, scaling AI friendliness to architectural design remains a significant challenge. Tornhill concluded that scaling AI friendliness to the design and architectural level is the next big challenge.

stories.Headline: Disseqt AI raises $8 million to expand AI governance platform and hire in India
stories.Summary:
Disseqt AI, an AI governance and assurance startup, raised $8 million in a pre-Series A funding round led by Gresham House Ventures, TechGig reported on November 20, 2026. The round also drew participation from existing investor Sure Valley Ventures, Delta Partners and Enterprise Ireland, according to the company's press release. Angel investors included senior executives from OpenAI, Palo Alto Networks, Salesforce and Meta, the release stated. Former Indian cricket captain Rahul Dravid invested in his individual capacity, Disseqt said. Inc42 reported the same $8 million round on November 19, 2026, describing the company as one that builds AI agents for AI governance and testing.

The fresh funds will be used to expand the company's global enterprise customer base, according to TechGig. Disseqt also plans hiring across sales, operations and technology roles in India, the report said. Inc42 reported that the capital will scale operations across the UK and international markets. The $8 million figure is about ₹75 crore, Inc42 stated. While headquartered in Ireland, Disseqt's engineering and AI teams are based in Bengaluru, and it has customer-facing operations across the UK, Ireland and India, according to its website.

Apoorva Kumar, Manish Atri and Cyril Treacy founded Disseqt AI in late 2025, the articles state. Kumar, the CEO and cofounder, said every enterprise is handing real work to AI agents but very few can prove those agents are safe, fair and within policy. He said this gap often stops ambitious AI projects from going live and is what Disseqt was built to close. He said the funding lets the company bring that standard to more enterprises around the world. Atri, the COO, is India-based, and both Kumar and Atri are graduates of IIIT Allahabad, Inc42 reported.

Disseqt provides an AI governance and assurance platform that helps enterprises test, monitor and govern AI applications and agents, according to TechGig. The platform assesses AI agents for vulnerabilities before deployment, enforces company policies once they go live and continuously monitors their behaviour. It can block outputs that violate organisational policies and maintains audit trails for compliance and oversight. Enterprises can test whether AI agents can be manipulated into revealing confidential customer information and check for other vulnerabilities before deployment. Inc42 reported that the platform lets compliance, security and IT teams test agentic workflows for vulnerabilities and data-leak risks prior to deployment, enforce real-time policy guardrails in production, block non-compliant outputs and maintain audit trails independent of underlying model providers.

Disseqt said it has deployed its assurance capabilities across multiple enterprise use cases, TechGig reported. In a project for a global sports league's fan engagement agent serving 80 million fans, the company improved the safe-response rate from 80 per cent to 99 per cent across tests covering safety, bias and privacy risks. No unsafe outputs were detected after fixes were implemented, according to the report. The company also provides assurance services for a credit card services programme at a large European bank. Disseqt has partnered with Indian IT companies Infosys, Cognizant, HCLTech, Mphasis and Tata Technologies as Global System Integrators to deploy its platforms for their enterprise clients, Inc42 reported.

The funding comes amid growing enterprise adoption of AI agents and increasing concerns around their safety, security and regulatory compliance, TechGig stated. McKinsey's 2026 State of AI survey found 40 per cent of companies with over $1 billion in annual revenues were scaling AI agents in at least one business function, compared with 27 per cent a year earlier. Inc42's Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026 found AI startup funding more than tripled year on year to $438 million in the September quarter. Overall funding raised by Indian startups increased by just 5 per cent year on year, Inc42 reported. The investment marks another bet on the emerging AI governance and assurance segment, according to TechGig.

stories.Headline: CircleCI adds Smarter Testing features to speed validation for AI coding agents
stories.Summary:
CircleCI, a continuous integration and continuous delivery platform, announced new features in its Smarter Testing suite on November 19, 2026, according to SD Times, which datelined its report from San Francisco, California. TechGig reported the release on November 20, 2026, saying the updates aim to accelerate feedback for engineering teams and help them validate code changes earlier. The company said the enhancements reduce redundant testing and optimise compute resource usage, and that they are particularly relevant for workflows involving AI coding agents. The suite now includes Dynamic Parallelism, which adjusts the number of machines for each run to cut unnecessary compute costs, the company said. CircleCI said testing can consume up to half of CI/CD pipeline time, often leaving developers waiting for feedback or switching contexts while tests run.

Smarter Testing lets developers and AI coding agents run affected tests locally before pushing code, catching issues before code reaches CI at no additional charge, according to SD Times. Intelligent Test Selection uses test impact analysis to identify only the tests affected by a code change, so teams do not have to run the full suite on every commit. Dynamic Parallelism automatically adjusts machine allocation based on the tests selected for each run, reducing compute usage as testing volume grows. Dynamic Test Splitting balances tests across machines to minimise idle time, and Auto Rerun Failed Tests retries only failed tests instead of rerunning entire suites. Smarter Testing is integrated directly into CircleCI, requiring no additional vendor or infrastructure, the company said.

Rob Zuber, CTO of CircleCI, said that as AI coding agents make it easier to produce code, everything downstream needs to get smarter and faster, including how code is validated. He said developers and agents should be able to check their work before pushing code, and that a small change should not require the same tests and compute resources as a large one. Zuber said Smarter Testing helps teams get feedback sooner and use resources more efficiently without having to rethink their entire development process. He said that as AI coding agents simplify code production, downstream processes like validation must become smarter and faster. The company said the features enable organizations to maintain confidence in what they ship without sacrificing speed, efficiency, or control.

William Yardley, Staff Infrastructure Engineer at Medallion, a healthcare technology company that automates provider credentialing and operations, said Smarter Testing helped bring down cost per pull request and reduce build times. He said this happened even as the company's pull request volume went up 10x and its test suite grew 2.5x, and that Dynamic Parallelism adjusts machines automatically as testing needs grow. Maria Volpe, Senior Software Engineer at Kustomer, an AI-powered customer service platform, said Smarter Testing changed the economics of its CI. Volpe said the cost of running Kustomer's tests was cut by a quarter, and that engineers get feedback faster because only tests affected by a change run. TechGig reported that Kustomer saw a 25 per cent reduction in test running costs, and that Medallion used Smarter Testing to manage increased development activity.

The articles say testing can account for up to half of CI/CD pipeline time, leaving developers waiting for feedback or switching context while tests run. They say AI coding agents are accelerating code creation, so engineering teams need ways to validate changes just as quickly, regardless of which tools or agents are writing the code. CircleCI said the updates help validate code changes earlier, reduce unnecessary testing, and use compute more efficiently. The company said teams can improve the efficiency of the entire delivery process and lower the overall cost of getting a change into production. CircleCI described itself as a leading continuous integration and continuous delivery platform.

SD Times directed readers to learn more about CircleCI Smarter Testing through a link in its report, and neither article states a general availability date beyond the announcements. The articles do not say how many customers have adopted the new features or how the features are priced beyond local test runs being offered at no additional charge. They do not give figures for Medallion's cost or build time reductions, only that both came down. They do not specify which tools or agents the AI coding agents mentioned are, or how Dynamic Parallelism calculates machine counts for each run. The articles leave open how Intelligent Test Selection performs test impact analysis and what results other early customers have seen.

stories.Headline: Forrester and Adams warn cloud operations and political parties are unprepared for AI job losses
stories.Summary:
Forrester and Mike Adams published reports in November 2026 regarding the failures of cloud operations and political readiness for AI. These authors argue that current technical systems and political parties are not prepared for the impacts of artificial intelligence. The reports highlight how AI creates new operational risks and threatens the stability of the American white-collar workforce. Technical teams face new definitions of health, while politicians ignore the coming wave of mass human job replacement. Both articles warn that ignoring these shifts will lead to significant failures in business and national economic stability.

Cloud operations must now monitor model drift, token consumption, and agent behavior instead of just focusing on basic system uptime. This requires visibility into infrastructure, applications, models, agents, and business outcomes to ensure that AI services remain economically sustainable. Mike Adams notes that Amazon cut 30,000 jobs and UPS eliminated 48,000 positions as AI-driven automation replaced human workers. Block Inc. axed 4,000 jobs, Meta planned to cut 8,000 positions, and Coinbase reduced its workforce by 14 percent. These changes affect radiology, coding, legal writing, and graphic design, as well as entry-level white-collar labor markets.

Forrester analysts suggest that enterprises must retool operations for the AI-native cloud to maintain trustworthy behavior and control costs. They state that recovery now requires model resynchronization, pipeline restarts, cache restoration, and controlled rollbacks to restore a trustworthy state. Mike Adams claims that neither the Democrats nor Republicans have a real plan for the tidal wave of job replacement. He argues that the Democratic reflex will be universal basic income, which he describes as a corporate subsidy. Adams believes that this approach is a delay tactic that fails to solve the underlying problem of disappearing work.

Many Americans are concerned, with 70 percent fearing job replacement and 64 percent believing AI is developing too fast. Specifically, 76 percent of Democrats and 54 percent of Republicans express the view that AI development is moving too quickly. Senator Bernie Sanders has called for national data center moratoriums, though Adams says this only addresses symptoms of infrastructure. Goldman Sachs found that the entry-level white-collar labor market is shrinking just as recent college graduates enter the workforce. Glenn Diesen observes that the poorest members of society usually bear the greatest burden of creative destruction.

The background involves a shift where GPU-centric compute introduces new capacity constraints and creates much more variable demand for operations. AI failures often surface as gradual degradation rather than clear outages, making them easier for operations teams to miss. Politically, Democrats recently took full control of Congress in a blue tsunami victory, promising affordability and data center regulation. Adams warns that implementing universal basic income alongside central bank digital currencies will lead to constant surveillance and total manipulation. He suggests that the labor share of income is hitting record lows as capital owners capture more productivity.

Future events include a Forrester analyst session on December 1 to explore AI, sovereignty, and trust in the APAC region. Adams predicts that printing money for universal basic income will cause hyperinflation and render the U.S. dollar completely worthless. He warns that globalist elites may embrace declining populations to accelerate robotics adoption, potentially leading to mass human impoverishment. Bill Gates mentioned that AI is powerful enough to cause a billion deaths, which he used to demand legislation. The articles leave open how governments will actually manage the economic dislocation of millions of displaced human workers.

stories.Headline: Anthropic raises 81.3 billion dollars in record Nasdaq initial public offering
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, PBC began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT on 19 November 2026. The company raised 81.3 billion dollars in the largest initial public offering on record after pricing shares at 83 dollars on 18 November. This price exceeded the 70 to 78 dollar range established during the roadshow that started on 10 November. The listing followed a public registration statement filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on 26 October 2026.

The new listing requires Anthropic to file annual and quarterly reports with the SEC and makes the company liable for material misstatements. Under its governance structure, the Long-Term Benefit Trust holds Class T stock and generally elects four of the seven board directors. The company warned in its filing that advanced AI could pose existential risks to humanity if weaponized or operated with high autonomy. It also noted that a single catastrophic incident might exceed the total capacity of the insurance industry.

Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote to chief executive Dario Amodei on 27 October 2026 to ask how the company could meet public benefit commitments. She argued that the listing could bring market volatility into retirement accounts and index funds. President Donald Trump told reporters that the technology is almost completely good but requires careful management of bad elements. Meanwhile, National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett rejected warnings that the AI sector might face a wider sell-off.

This event occurs while federal legislation remains stalled, with only one of 56 bills from the 119th Congress becoming law. Senator Bernie Sanders introduced a bill on 18 June 2026 to impose a one-time 50 percent stock tax on large AI firms. In California, the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act took effect on 1 January 2026 to manage catastrophic risks. Governor Gavin Newsom recommended on 18 November 2026 that the state add mandatory independent oversight and emergency shutdown authority.

stories.Headline: Anthropic prices shares at $83 as protesters rally outside Nasdaq
stories.Summary:
Anthropic held its initial public offering at Nasdaq in New York City’s Times Square on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, pricing shares at $83. CEO Dario Amodei and his team of executives were at Nasdaq for the opening bell and applauded the listing. Demonstrators gathered outside Nasdaq in Times Square on the same day to raise concerns about AI. The demonstrators held signs reading “Stop Tech Oligarchs” and “Freeze AI” as the stock ticker raced by on screens behind them. Representatives of the group used a small, hot-pink megaphone to address the media and onlookers.

The IPO priced shares at $83, and initial demand appeared strong before the stock started trading at midday. Demonstrators chanted “Hey, hey. Ho-ho. This IPO has got to go!” and “Anthropic, get off it, put people over profit!”

The demonstrators were affiliated with groups including Stop Funding Billionaires, Climate Defiance, Sunrise NYC, Act Up NYC, NYC-DSA, JVP-NYC, Climate Defenders, Planet Over Profit and New York Communities for Change. Their concerns ranged from the potential economic impact if the AI bubble bursts to AI’s effects on the environment, healthcare, surveillance, and jobs. One demonstrator in a Greenpeace T-shirt was led away by police after seating themselves with a sign at the entrance to Nasdaq. James Inniss, an organizer with New York Communities for Change, said Anthropic poses a threat “pension fund-style” because AI is a bubble worse than 2008 with the real estate crisis. Inniss said that if pension funds are stripped in five or 10 years when the bubble bursts, people have to be out there to fight and say that is not acceptable.

Bryce Rogers, an organizer with Resisting Automated Disempowerment (RAD), said he was there to protest that the IPO was moving ahead despite a lack of information about the risks the company’s technology poses. Rogers said he had read auditing firm METR’s recent report on Anthropic but was left with more questions than answers. Rogers praised New York’s Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act and called for more organizing to demand greater regulation and transparency. ACT UP New York’s Brandon Cuicchi said he was concerned about AI’s impact on healthcare, saying hospitals are cutting staff and trying to replace it with AI. Cuicchi said medical offices are trying to pre-screen people with AI instead of a live professional, and that AI is deciding medical outcomes and treatments in the country.

Kenny Moll, an activist affiliated with a campaign called QuitGPT and the Sunrise Movement, said he was concerned about the environmental impact of AI and about the relationship between AI firms, surveillance, and the government. Aber Kawas, a Palestinian-American democratic socialist recently elected as a New York State Senator, said AI companies are among the biggest enemies of the progressive movement. In a statement following the demonstration, organizers attributed a quote to one of the demonstrators who was arrested: “Our demand is clear: freeze reckless AI development and don’t bail out Big Tech when their bubble inevitably pops.” Sifted sat down with Menlo Ventures’ Deedy Das on the sidelines of Slush ahead of Anthropic’s big IPO. Das is a partner at Menlo Ventures, which was an early investor in Anthropic.

Sifted’s interview with Das was published on Nov. 19, 2026, the same day as the IPO. The interview was published under the headline asking whether AI is in a bubble. The articles state that Anthropic’s IPO priced shares at $83 and that demonstrators gathered outside Nasdaq in Times Square on Nov. 19, 2026. The stock was set to start trading at midday on Nov. 19, 2026.

Organizers demanded that reckless AI development be frozen and that Big Tech not be bailed out when their bubble inevitably pops. The articles leave open what Das said in the Sifted interview beyond the headline and the fact that it concerned Anthropic’s IPO and Europe. The articles leave open how the stock traded after it started trading at midday. The articles leave open what happened to the demonstrator who was led away by police.

stories.Headline: Apple builds a proactive AI agent that browses the web and writes code
stories.Summary:
Apple is building a proactive artificial intelligence agent, the company stated in a job listing for a senior engineering manager on November 19, 2026. This new agent will be able to browse the web, run commands, write code, and work across various apps like a capable person. The company is seeking a senior engineering leader to create the foundation for this future tool while maintaining the polish people expect. Bloomberg reported on Thursday that Apple wants to enter the fast growing market for AI agents alongside companies like Meta and OpenAI. This expansion happens as Apple also introduces new security controls for Mac users to protect their data from various AI agent apps.

The new security changes arriving with macOS 27.3 split Device Control and Data Access into System & App Protection Override and Accessibility settings. Apple is introducing a single method for granting permissions by selecting the requested app from a list to help streamline the configuration process. Users can now configure apps to ask for permission every time access is needed and see a transparency indicator when apps control others. The company provides new guidance for enabling Full Disk Access and encourages users to grant access only to the specific apps that need it. Developers of assistive technologies or disk backup apps can request entitlements to preserve functionality they offered before the macOS 27.3 update.

Apple warned app developers in a blog post that granting an app extraordinary access puts all of the data on a Mac at risk. The company stated that these new controls provide users with more nuanced options and increased visibility into the data that apps will receive. Apple suggests that developers adjust their onboarding processes so that their apps can gracefully handle having access to only a limited set. The company is balancing its privacy concerns with the fact that AI early adopters are purchasing Mac Studio and Mac mini computers. These users are buying this specific hardware to run their local AI models, which has benefited Apple through increased sales of these devices.

Google announced on November 19 that its Gemini app for Mac can now complete multistep tasks across the web, desktop apps, and local files. Potential Gemini applications include filling out forms, speeding up creative workflows, preparing resale listings, and turning live data into Google Slides presentations. A journalist claimed that the Muse app from Meta read private messages without consent, and Wired reported a flaw in ChatGPT's app. These incidents involving AI agents contributed to Apple's decision to revise its security settings to protect users from increased risks to their privacy. Other affected parties include professionals and small business owners who use proactive agents like Claude Duet to complete various requested tasks.

SpaceXAI launched Grok Bot in mid August, which surpassed 400,000 weekly users within one month to handle invoices and respond to workplace emails. Meta introduced a personal AI agent called Muse on September 8, which quickly topped the App Store charts and was built for everyone. OpenAI introduced agents called dots on September 28 that can connect to over 4,000 apps and learn from feedback over time. Anthropic unveiled the proactive agent Claude Duet on October 21 to help professionals and small business owners complete their specific requested tasks. These various industry developments show a broader trend of companies releasing agents that can take actions across operating systems and user files.

Apple will now provide users with more information about the choices they make when granting full permissions to AI agents and apps. The company expects developers to adapt their software to work with limited folder access instead of requiring full disk access for everything. The articles leave open whether these new security measures will be tedious or act as an obstacle to achieving true AI automation. It remains unclear how many developers will successfully request entitlements to maintain their previous functionality under the new macOS 27.3 security rules. The reports do not state when the proactive AI agent mentioned in the job listing will be officially released to the public.

Anthropic priced its shares at $83 and opened at about $100, and the stock was trading around $101 during the NextBigFuture show before ending at $97, according to Brian Wang of NextBigFuture. At $100 a share the company is worth roughly $1.32 trillion on shares outstanding, or about $1.8 trillion fully diluted in Wang's estimate. Wang said people are selling SpaceX and the rest of tech to chase Anthropic, but he noted that Anthropic is SpaceX's biggest customer at $37 billion per year. More cash for Anthropic means more rent for SpaceX, Wang said on the show he co-hosted with Randy Kirk. Anthropic raised $81 billion, and there is a private placement of another $25 billion, the articles said.

The company had $110 billion in cash from earlier fund raises remaining, giving it about $216 billion in cash and access to over $100 billion in credit facility if needed. Wang wrote that every 500 megawatts of inference compute makes Anthropic $100 billion per year. Anthropic and SpaceX are working together as AI partners, and Wang estimates Anthropic will likely increase its leasing from SpaceX at about 2 to 4 gigawatts per year. That estimate is based on an Elon Musk interview saying Anthropic will increase to 10 gigawatts of leasing from SpaceX over an unspecified period. Wang is responsible for the figures and estimates, writing as a futurist and science blogger with a million readers per month on NextBigFuture.

He described the economics for Anthropic and SpaceX as great and said the business models cover Earth-based AI, including Colossus 2 at half a gigawatt a month in Cochise County, SpaceX power for Anthropic and Cybercab. The show was a paid partnership with Kalshi, offering a $50 sign-up bonus through Wang's referral link. A commenter on the second article wrote that they do not understand the bubble talk, saying everyone is printing piles of cash and then drowning in it. stories.Headline: Washington University launches an AI cluster hire across seven schools to recruit over 30 faculty
stories.Summary:
Washington University in St. Louis has launched an interdisciplinary artificial intelligence cluster hire across seven Danforth Campus schools, the university announced on November 19, 2026. The search, which is part of the AI initiative outlined by Provost Mark West, is now open at those seven schools. The university plans to recruit more than 30 new faculty members over the next three years through this effort. These hires will join a community of more than 300 WashU faculty members who already work in the artificial intelligence space across many disciplines. The new hires will focus their research on four core areas: agentic AI, including governance, society and institutions; human values, creative practice and AI; AI-driven imaging science from molecules to the universe; and AI for science and engineering, which covers modeling the physical world.

The initiative was shaped by conversations with more than 150 WashU faculty members, who said the university needed transformative change in research and education rather than just the adoption of new tools. More than 500 candidates have already submitted applications for the positions. A committee of 11 faculty members, co-chaired by Nathan Jacobs, vice provost of AI, and Betsy Sinclair, vice provost for innovation, continues to review those applications as they arrive. West said artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing the nature of work both inside and outside universities, and he said the new scholars would help WashU shape the future of the technology rather than simply respond to it. Jacobs said that while much fundamental AI innovation has come from computer science, the impact is now spreading across many fields, and he said breakthrough discoveries require deep collaboration between method developers and experts in areas such as materials science or public health.

Sinclair said the initiative is recruiting faculty with deep expertise in their fields who take the questions seriously and can contribute to conversations at WashU. She said the strong interest shows that scholars want to do this work somewhere that takes both the technology and its consequences seriously. The Office of the Provost is working with each Danforth Campus school to ensure the new hires find community among their WashU peers. The review committee includes William Acree, Deanna Barch and Timothy Wencewicz of Arts & Sciences; Adrienne Davis of WashU Law; Debra Haire-Joshu of the Bursky School of Public Health; Jonathan Hanahan and Andrew Witt of the Sam Fox School of Design & Visual Arts; Byron Powell of the Brown School; Yevgeniy Vorobeychik and William Yeoh of McKelvey Engineering; and Dennis Zhang of Olin Business School. More information about the four focus areas is available on WashU's AI website.

stories.Headline: Virginia Tech launches an interdisciplinary AI minor for students in every major
stories.Summary:
Virginia Tech launched a new interdisciplinary artificial intelligence minor in summer 2026, and the program is designed to prepare students in every major for careers in an AI-powered future. The minor teaches technical foundations while encouraging students to evaluate AI’s social impacts and wrestle with questions of ethics and policy. Christine Julien, head of the Department of Computer Science, led a group of collaborators from across the university in developing the program. She said that regardless of major, today’s students are entering a workforce where AI will be part of nearly every profession. Students in the minor learn the technical foundations of AI, examine ethical and social consequences, and explore how the technology intersects with fields in the arts, social sciences, business, and humanities.

The result is not simply technical training, because the minor is intended to give students the conceptual foundation to ask better questions about AI’s impacts. One such class is “The Skeptic’s Guide to AI,” which Benjamin Jantzen first taught last fall. He expected a classroom filled mostly with humanities students, but nearly every student was a first-year engineering major. Julien said the goal is to ensure Virginia Tech graduates understand how these technologies work, how to evaluate them critically, and how to apply them responsibly in their own fields. Jantzen said being a skeptic means asking whether what people are told about AI tools is literally true and whether the tools can do what they say they do.

He said it also means uncovering the assumptions behind those claims and considering what may be gained or lost, because there are always trade-offs with any technology. He said that for democracy to work, people have to understand what they are being asked to accept and what they are being asked to give up, and that demands scrutiny and the work of the skeptic. The articles describe AI as offering enormous potential to accelerate scientific and social innovation, with Virginia Tech work that includes uses designed to speed drug discovery, unravel the secrets of DNA, protect consumers from scams and identity theft, and support the U.S. Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission to double scientific productivity. The articles also say AI raises concerns about related job losses, economic uncertainty, and the environmental and natural resource costs of operating systems. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the minor’s launch.

stories.Headline: Wookjae Heo coauthors two-volume book on South Korea’s AI research
stories.Summary:
Wookjae Heo, an associate professor of financial counseling and planning at Purdue University, is the Purdue author of a two-volume book titled “Korean Studies in the Artificial Intelligence Era,” according to a Purdue Today article published on November 19, 2026. The article lists Seok Kang, Woo Hyoung Lee, Jangwoon Lee and Young Choi as additional authors of the work. The first volume, subtitled “Innovations in Science, Engineering, Health, Business, Industry, and Ethics,” was published by CRC Press on May 5, 2026. The second volume, subtitled “Adoption Insights in Hospitality, Culture, Communication, Music, and Philosophy,” followed on May 25, 2026.

According to the publisher’s description in the article, the two volumes explore South Korea’s multidisciplinary advancements in artificial intelligence and show how South Korean and Korean American scholars use methods such as systematic literature reviews, empirical research and industry case studies. The book aims to fill a gap in global AI literature and to establish South Korea’s AI research as a vital topic on the global academic stage. Its chapters range from sustainable water treatment and 3D-printed cardiovascular devices to personal finance and ethical surveillance systems. The publisher says the book targets industry practitioners and can also serve as a reference for graduate-level studies.

Heo is an associate professor in the White Lodging-J.W. Marriott, Jr. School of Hospitality and Tourism Management, and the article says his research examines consumer behavior and individual well-being. His stated emphases include financial stress, financial risk tolerance, household financial decision-making, insurance, and human-centered applications of artificial intelligence and machine learning in financial services. Before entering academia, the article says, Heo worked in strategic marketing planning and consumer research in South Korea. The article does not include direct comments from Heo or the other authors about the book.

The article appears in Purdue Today’s weekly In Print series, which celebrates faculty excellence in scholarship by highlighting faculty expertise across diverse subjects and disciplines. The article directs readers to the Purdue University Books Initiative and the Office of the Provost website for more information and for suggesting a book for the series. It also notes that Purdue University Libraries and School of Information Studies’ authored books collection is available online. The articles do not say what happens next beyond those listings and the book’s availability.

stories.Headline: Yale Law School professors teach a course on AI’s impact on legal institutions
stories.Summary:
Yale Law School is offering a course called “The Transformation of Legal Institutions in the Age of AI,” taught by Clinical Professor of Law Sven Riethmueller and Visiting Clinical Lecturer in Law Bjarne Tellmann, according to a November 19, 2026, article on the school’s website. Riethmueller, who is the founding director of the Entrepreneurship & Innovation Clinic at Yale Law School, saw a need to introduce students to AI’s growing role in legal practice and the business of law as the technology spreads through the profession. He called upon Tellmann, an AI expert who worked in law for 30 years and recently wrote “Law in the Era of AI: Clients, Firms, and the Future of the Legal Industry,” to teach the class with him. The course examines AI’s growing impact on the legal industry and the deeper questions surrounding its role in the law and society at large.

The course centers on the premise of Tellmann’s book, which argues that AI’s impact on legal institutions can be better understood by examining corporate clients, who make up the majority of Big Law revenue in the United States. Tellmann contends that as companies adopt AI on a larger scale, the effects on their legal departments will inevitably spread throughout the legal profession, legal education and the courts. Riethmueller said the idea is for students to explore the topic, understand its facets and see that there is a role for law students in an AI world and how they can thrive in the new technological environment. The instructors are applying the Law School’s approach that blends theory and practice, giving students a chance to think about AI abstractly while pondering real-world applications, and the class has also featured guest speakers, including a law firm partner in a senior leadership role and the CEO of a legal technology company called ClearyX.

Riethmueller said Yale educates leaders, that its students are at the forefront of the legal world and will be future leaders of the profession with input on where it is going, and that the class is helping them prepare for that. Tellmann described a combination of excitement and anxiety among students, saying some come up after class expressing deep concerns while others are keen to lean into the opportunities the new era presents. Emma Lilly Menzer ’27 said the course has excelled at bridging the gap between theory and tangible application and that she has gained a greater appreciation for creativity, collaborative teamwork and human judgment against the backdrop of a legal practice being fundamentally altered by AI. Grace Sherrill ’27 said conversations about AI and the law often veer between dismissiveness and alarmism, but the course has let her think systematically about how AI may reshape the practice of law and the institutions that underpin it, and Tristan John-Jandles ’28 said hearing from the guest speakers gave him a reassuring read on where the profession stands for junior professionals right now.

stories.Headline: Hochul breaks ground on permanent Empire AI supercomputing facility at University at Buffalo
stories.Summary:
Governor Kathy Hochul officially broke ground on the permanent home of Empire AI at the State University of New York at Buffalo on November 19, 2026. The groundbreaking launches the next phase of development for Empire AI Gamma, the full-scale supercomputing facility. Empire AI Gamma will expand computing power for researchers at New York's leading public and private universities. The facility is intended to establish Empire AI as the most powerful academic AI research computer in the country. Empire AI was first announced by Governor Hochul in her 2024 State of the State address.

Empire AI has grown into a more than $500 million public-private initiative supporting research in medicine, climate science and advanced manufacturing. Empire AI Gamma is expected to be completed by early 2028. Empire AI was launched by Governor Hochul in April 2024 as a first-in-the-nation consortium of leading public and private research institutions. Just six months later, the Governor launched Empire AI Alpha, made possible by a philanthropic contribution from the Simons Foundation. In August 2026, Empire AI Beta, a $40 million supercomputer, became fully operational at the University at Buffalo, delivering 11 times the AI training capacity, 40 times the inference performance and eight times the data storage of Alpha.

Empire AI Board Chair Tom Secunda said Empire AI was an ambitious idea just two years ago and is now a national model with more than 1,500 registered users and hundreds of research projects underway. Secunda credited Governor Hochul's vision and leadership for bringing together government, universities and philanthropy. Co-founder and chair of the Simons Foundation Marilyn Simons said Empire AI gives more scientists the tools to tackle questions no one has been able to answer. Simons thanked Governor Hochul for bringing together New York's leading research institutions and philanthropic partners. State University of New York Chancellor John B. King Jr. said SUNY is proud to host Empire AI at the University at Buffalo and grateful to Governor Hochul for her vision and steadfast leadership.

The SUNY Board of Trustees said the permanent Empire AI facility will accelerate research and innovations that improve communities throughout New York State and beyond. Empire State Development President, CEO & Commissioner Hope Knight said the groundbreaking creates jobs now while empowering New York's students, researchers and businesses. U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand said Empire AI at the University at Buffalo represents a $500 million investment in the future. Congressmember Tim Kennedy said the groundbreaking keeps Western New York at the forefront of innovation. State University of New York at Buffalo President Caroline Attardo Genco said UB researchers are already putting Empire AI to work on challenges in education and neuroscience, climate science and advanced manufacturing.

Today's groundbreaking comes just days after Governor Hochul launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at the State University of New York at Binghamton. The center brings together more than 80 scientists to independently study the safety, security and performance of advanced AI systems using Empire AI's computing infrastructure. The milestone complements New York's RAISE Act on frontier AI accountability. By bringing together New York's leading academic institutions around a shared computing resource, Empire AI allows scientists to tackle bigger questions and pursue discoveries beyond the reach of individual universities. Empire AI provides access to computing power that no single university could afford independently.

State Senator Jeremy J. Zellner said Empire AI puts Western New York in a position to lead in the industries of tomorrow. Assemblymember Bill Conrad said the state's consortium of universities represents a world-renowned hub for talent and thanked Governor Hochul for her foresightedness. CUNY Graduate Center President and Empire AI Board Treasurer Joshua Brumberg said CUNY's participation has supercharged its researchers' capabilities. State University of New York at Binghamton President Anne D'Alleva said Binghamton shares its congratulations with the University at Buffalo on the next phase of Empire AI Gamma. Vice President for Research for the University of Rochester and Empire AI Board Member Steve Dewhurst said Empire AI has become an increasingly important resource for advancing research and innovation.

stories.Headline: Rhode Island Small Business Development Center and Meta host free AI workshop for small business owners

The Rhode Island Small Business Development Center, which is based at the University of Rhode Island, and Meta are teaming up to host a free, hands-on workshop focused on AI skills that small business owners can use. The training is scheduled for Tuesday, December 1, starting at 8:30 am and running until 11:30 am. More than 150 small business owners, students and community members have already signed up, but registration is still open. The event will be held at the Crown Plaza Providence-Warwick, 801 Greenwich Ave., Warwick, RI 02886.

The session will include an interactive workshop that lets attendees work alongside expert facilitators and fellow business owners. Participants will also receive a crash course on Muse, which is already integrated into Meta's social media platforms and acts as a virtual assistant. According to the articles, Muse helps small businesses answer customer questions, draft reports, keep sales leads from growing cold, create social media content and develop marketing campaigns tailored for their industry. Attendees will also have the opportunity to try on Meta's newest AI glasses. Those planning to attend should download Muse at muse.ai./business and bring a laptop or phone with Muse already downloaded onto it.

The collaboration is thanks, in part, to Matthew Lenz '11, a member of the University of Rhode Island's Board of Trustees, who serves as a public policy director for Meta and will be in attendance at the workshop. The articles describe the event as open to solopreneurs and small business owners across any industry. Registration is available at https://www.risbdc.org/workshop.aspx?ekey=70460040. stories.Headline: Engineers, Clinicians Partner to Advance Human Health with AI
stories.Summary:
Engineers at the University of California, Davis are working with clinicians on artificial intelligence tools meant to detect Alzheimer's disease earlier, expand care options for survivors of sexual assault and improve results for patients awaiting corneal transplants. The projects are funded by AI and Health Seed Funding Awards from the Center for Information Technology Research in the Interest of Society and the Banatao Institute, known as CITRIS, which aim to strengthen interdisciplinary connections between schools and colleges across UC Davis and UC Davis Health and to establish the university as a leader in AI-enabled healthcare technology research. The awards followed a matchmaking mixer for engineers and clinicians held in November 2025 and co-hosted by the UC Davis AI Center in Engineering, or AICE, with CITRIS, the Healthy Aging in a Digital World initiative and the Clinical and Translational Science Center as partners. That event produced six awarded seed grants, including the three co-led by engineers.

For the Alzheimer's project, Chen-Nee Chuah, the Child Family Professor in Engineering in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, is developing an AI model that can pick up early signs of the disease from a patient's speech, working with Michelle Cohn, a postdoctoral scholar in linguistics, and Alyssa Weakley, an assistant professor of neurology. The team is examining conversational interviews with older adults from the UC Davis Alzheimer's Disease Research Center Corpus, which is annotated with patients' cognitive status such as mild cognitive impairment or late-stage Alzheimer's, to train a model to identify biomarkers of cognitive impairment by analyzing how a patient sounds and their manner of speech. The team has completed the datasets needed to train the large language model on acoustic and linguistic features of cognitive impairment in older adults, and the National Institutes of Health has given the researchers a boost to develop an AI-enabled remote monitoring system to detect health issues in older adults, which will directly support the early detection work. The project will culminate in a real-world pilot deployment within a local senior living community.

Josh McCoy, an associate professor of computer science, is leading a project to develop a trauma-informed, AI-powered chatbot that can connect survivors of sexual assault with appropriate social and health support services, with Jessica Draughon Moret, an associate professor at the UC Davis Betty Irene Moore School of Nursing, as co-lead. The private chatbot aims to expand access to and simplify the process of seeking care, and the pair are working to ensure it is informed by human-centered design and built on expert consultation with survivors. The team has a prototype for the platform, called CARE-COMPASS: Community Assistance and Resource Engagement, and is currently in the refinement and user feedback phase, with the goal of seeking additional funding from the National Institutes of Health for further development and broader use. Separately, Hamed Pirsiavash, a professor of computer science, is co-leading a project with Mark Mannis, a distinguished professor of ophthalmology and vision science, to develop an AI-powered evaluation system for donated corneal tissue, joined by Min Zhao, a professor of ophthalmology and vision science, Ana Sandoval Castellanos, a postdoctoral fellow in the Laboratory for Cell Nanoengineering, and several medical students.

The cornea team has been working with Sierra Donor Services, a non-profit donor procurement organization serving the Northern California and Northern Nevada regions, to source a curated dataset of microscopy images of corneal tissue, and through self-supervised learning the system uses computer vision and machine learning to distinguish between healthy and abnormal tissue. The goal is to reduce clinicians' workload from hours to minutes when evaluating tissue and to minimize variability in the quality of donated tissue, and the project's next step is to test the AI model with larger sample sizes. Sam King, a professor of computer science and director of CITRIS at UC Davis, said an engineer can build a model that scores well on a benchmark and still fails in a clinic because the team does not know which errors matter to a patient, while clinicians know but cannot build these systems alone. He said the technology is improving faster than those partnerships are forming, and the awards exist to close that gap by putting engineers and clinicians on the same problem before design decisions are made. The awards dovetail with the AICE's AI and Health research area, which accelerates discovery by facilitating conversations between engineers and clinicians, and through AICE's partnership they are helping realize CITRIS Health's mission to encourage innovations in technology that improve health outcomes and increase access to medicine.

stories.Headline: UC San Diego and MIT scientists lead independent review of OpenAI and Anthropic refutation claims
stories.Summary:
On November 19, 2026, computer scientists from UC San Diego and MIT began facilitating an independent review of results from OpenAI and Anthropic. These two frontier AI labs recently announced that their models refuted the Exponential Time Hypothesis, which was originally formulated in 1998. The review is being led by Russell Impagliazzo and Mohan Paturi from UC San Diego, along with Ryan Williams from MIT. This effort follows global media coverage regarding the potential refutation of the influential hypothesis.

If these findings are verified, the change could have broad implications for optimization algorithms and various technical applications. Specifically, the results might impact the way experts approach chip design and the encryption systems currently used on the Internet. To manage this process, the team launched a new blog called ETH: Community Examination and Discussion for researchers to share ideas. They also posted the specific OpenAI prompt that led to the refutation on the blog this week.

Russell Impagliazzo and Mohan Paturi are professors at UC San Diego, while Paturi also serves as the associate dean for artificial intelligence strategy and implementation. These experts, along with Ryan Williams, are stepping into these roles to help the computer science community assess the claims independently. They intend to hold one or more academic conferences to discuss the verification work and its farther-reaching implications. The original hypothesis was proposed by Impagliazzo and Paturi alongside Francis Zane, who is now an independent researcher.

stories.Headline: Researchers find limited biological data hinders AI development in biotechnology
stories.Summary:
Vikram Venkatram and Steph Batalis published a report in November 2026 regarding the availability of biological data for artificial intelligence. The authors examined how engineering biology can be enhanced through AI to create better drugs, materials, and food. They used case studies on microscopy data for cellular segmentation and protein structural data to evaluate existing databases. This research identifies how the limited volume and quality of biological data currently hinder AI developers.

The report argues that the United States must address five specific categories of data challenges to maintain leadership in this field. These challenges include issues with data quantity, distribution, accessibility, usability, and the quality of validation. The authors suggest that policymakers should improve database infrastructure and promote better standardization to allow for interoperability between disparate sources. They also recommend incentivizing the collection of more representative data and investing in multidisciplinary talent capable of using computational tools.

The researchers stated that high quality and well annotated biological data are essential for the successful application of AI in biotechnology. They noted that while not every AI model faces every challenge, developers must test their systems based on their specific use cases. The authors believe that strategic improvements to data access will stimulate innovation and support national security and economic development. The report concludes that overcoming these bottlenecks is a critical first step for the future of engineering biology.

stories.Headline: Boulder Valley leaders present AI roadmap to school board
stories.Summary:
Boulder Valley leaders presented an AI roadmap to the school board at a work session this week, outlining a plan to use three groups to make decisions about specific technologies. The district is integrating AI lessons and tools into classes. District leaders also plan to begin providing an annual AI update to the school board. Superintendent Rob Anderson said the district developed a roadmap instead of a static policy. The roadmap is meant to be predictable with the community and nimble enough to make adjustments.

Students and teachers now have access to a district-approved software program called MagicSchool AI. District officials say MagicSchool is data-protected and meets district safety standards. The student side of MagicSchool is only available to students with a teacher guide. Teachers decide what tools students can use and can see all the inputs students use and all the content generated. The district leaves incorporating AI into lessons up to individual teachers.

The district generally hasn't restricted AI use, with the exception of some AI platforms that allow adult content creation. Anderson said the district is trying to stay in "the reasonable middle" by leading on innovation while maintaining strong data privacy policies. Chief Information Officer Frankie Elmore said, "Our philosophy has been to listen, learn and make informed adjustments rather than react to every new development." Chief Academic Officer Emma Herzog said state and federal educational AI policies are still being developed even as the technology changes rapidly. Herzog added that the district sees AI as a competency to build, not a static tool.

The three groups advising the district include an AI steering committee composed of district leadership, tasked with establishing strategic priorities, guardrails and oversight. An AI working group that includes teachers and school leadership will explore opportunities, evaluate emerging technologies and make recommendations to the steering committee. The third group is an existing IT governance group, which will prioritize technology initiatives and coordinate resources. Elmore said, "We start with a problem to solve, not a project product to purchase." More review would be required for projects that require new vendors, sensitive information or high risk decisions, including starting with small pilots before opening up the technology to the whole district.

Priorities for review include integrating the state's new AI standards for computer science into district classes. The district will also evaluate opportunities for embedding AI tools in other subject area classes to help students meet general content standards. Herzog gave an example of a custom chatbot in MagicSchool called debate partner, in which students in a social studies or science class can take a stance on an issue and interact with the bot. Herzog said the AI bot would respond with pushes on their initial claim or argument, and after a back-and-forth debate students could export their conversation, highlight where AI pushed them to think deeper and draft a finalized, persuasive essay or speech. Herzog said that in cases like this, AI isn't doing the thinking for the student but rather is encouraging the student to dig deeper into their initial thinking.

For teachers, Herzog said the three groups will look at how teachers can use AI for lesson planning and data analysis, as well as how to build capacity for teachers with ongoing learning and training. Herzog said, "AI becomes about how to improve practice and go deeper, versus replacing or outsourcing work." The articles do not say when the annual AI update to the school board will begin. The articles do not name the members of the AI steering committee or the AI working group. The articles do not say when the state's new AI standards for computer science take effect.

stories.Headline: Google offers free AI to compete with rivals while Alphabet takes a 14 percent stake in Anthropic
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, Sundar Pichai announced that Google is expanding Gemini Tasks for free to hundreds of millions of people in six countries. Bill Gurley says this move is the best way for Google to compete against rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. Alphabet is also becoming a significant owner of Anthropic, which is a customer that has committed 121 billion dollars. This strategic shift toward free AI aims to prevent competitors from gaining escape velocity and locking up the market. The company is using this defensive play to protect its core business and maintain its dominant market position.

An Anthropic filing from November 17 shows Alphabet will own nearly 14 percent of the company, which priced its IPO at 83 dollars. Trading for Anthropic began on Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT, making Alphabet's stake worth approximately 147 billion dollars. Broadcom manufactures the TPUs that Google operates and Anthropic leases, while Alibaba already pays to distribute its own AI for free. Anthropic has committed to paying Google at least 121 billion dollars for hosting services through the date of July 2033. Broadcom is further exposed through lease guarantees of 29 billion and 43 billion dollars, plus potential loans of 42 billion.

Benchmark general partner Bill Gurley told Deirdre Bosa Live that distributing free AI is the number one move Google should make. He compared this strategy to how Google previously used Android and Kubernetes to prevent Apple and Amazon from creating market monopolies. Gurley also noted that Anthropic's lobbying efforts are unprecedented for a company of its size and may seek regulatory capture. He expressed a wish that Anthropic would not lobby so hard, though he admitted the company's achievements are truly remarkable. Jed Ellerbroek of Argent Capital Management called Anthropic the most impressive business he has ever reviewed after reading its S-1.

Duolingo CEO Luis von Ahn said open models reduced the cost of AI video calls from 30 cents to less than one cent. Users on r/stocks argue that high-level users will still pay for the best models, but Google must protect its search revenue. Broadcom is heavily affected because Anthropic owes about 161 billion dollars in lease payments to Broadcom and its various partners. If Anthropic faces financial pressure, Broadcom is hit twice as both a supplier and a guarantor for the lease contracts. The Alibaba AI unit shows the risk, losing 1.6 billion dollars in the September quarter on 661 million dollars revenue.

Alphabet had a free cash flow of 73.3 billion dollars in 2025 and an operating margin of 32 percent that year. To fund a 2026 capex of 195 billion to 205 billion dollars, Alphabet doubled its long-term debt to 101.1 billion dollars. The company also sold 49.6 billion dollars in new shares in June to help cover these massive infrastructure and development costs. In 2025, operational cash flow of 164.7 billion dollars comfortably covered capital expenditures, which totaled 91.4 billion dollars for that period. Search and other services brought in 224.5 billion dollars in 2025, representing more than half of the total company revenue.

Analysts expect Alphabet's free cash flow to turn negative, reaching 18.4 billion dollars this year and 43 billion dollars in 2027. Broadcom will report its financial results on December 9, which will provide more clarity on its exposure to the AI market. The first public report from Anthropic will reveal if its prices and gross margins can hold up under market pressure. It remains open whether high-end users will continue paying for closed models like Claude Opus 5.5 despite the rise of free. The articles leave open if Google's free AI strategy will successfully stop Anthropic and OpenAI from pulling away completely.

stories.Headline: Kai McPheeters submits a $10 million opening bid for Character.ai's consumer platform
stories.Summary:
A $10 million offer to buy the consumer-facing platform of Character Technologies Inc., the company behind the Character.ai chatbot, comes from a 29-year-old gaming developer named Kai McPheeters, according to a filing made Monday in the US Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware. McPheeters is listed as the authorized signatory behind Smirks & Pangs Acquisition LLC, the entity tapped to serve as the minimum starting bid for the platform, its accounts and chat content, its brand, and its deep learning architectures. His name appeared in the filing ahead of a hearing held Tuesday before Judge Brendan Linehan Shannon. At that hearing the judge approved the consumer privacy ombudsman procedures that Character.ai had pitched.

The bid sets a floor for the sale of assets that include user accounts and chat content, which is why privacy procedures were put before the court. The ombudsman process approved by Judge Shannon is meant to address consumer privacy concerns tied to the transfer of that data. The filing identifies Smirks & Pangs Acquisition LLC as the minimum starting bid, meaning other buyers could still top the $10 million offer. The articles do not say what happens to the platform if no higher bid emerges.

The filing names McPheeters as the authorized signatory for the bidding entity, and the Bloomberg Law report describes him as an artificial intelligence gaming developer. The articles do not include any statement from McPheeters, from Character Technologies, or from the court beyond the approval of the ombudsman procedures. Judge Brendan Linehan Shannon of the US Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware handled the Tuesday hearing. No further comment from any party is given in the articles.

The context is a bankruptcy sale of Character.ai's consumer business, with the $10 million offer serving as the opening bid and the privacy ombudsman procedures now approved. The articles do not say when the sale process concludes or when a final buyer will be chosen. They also do not say whether other bidders have come forward. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Samsung and Google plan to release Gemini-powered smart glasses on December 10
stories.Summary:
Taylor Lane listed eight Best Buy holiday gifts, including Meta AI glasses and Nespresso makers, in a Fox News Deals article published on November 19, 2026. Fox News published a separate deals article on Meta AI glasses the same day, saving up to 25% on Ray-Ban and Oakley styles. TechRepublic published a comparison of Google AI Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 on November 17, 2026, written by Kezia Jungco. Samsung and Google developed the Gemini-powered Intelligent Eyewear, with Warby Parker and Gentle Monster providing frame designs. The companies opened preorders on November 12 and plan to release the glasses on December 10.

Meta AI glasses start at $249 with up to 15% off, and Ray-Ban Meta glasses start at $379 with up to 25% off, saving up to $115 on Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2. Oakley Meta glasses start at $399 with up to 25% off, and the Vanguard model comes in pink, blue, red and yellow lenses. Google's Warby Parker models start at $395, while Gentle Monster has six styles priced from $449 to $489, compared with $449 for Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. Both Google and Meta glasses have 12MP cameras and record up to 3K at 30 fps, Google has four microphones and Meta has six. Google offers 64GB of storage and up to nine hours per charge with up to 72 hours in its charging case, while Meta offers 32GB and up to 50 additional hours in its case.

Google says its glasses let wearers ask Gemini about their surroundings, translate conversations and get hands-free assistance, and on supported Galaxy phones summarize a whiteboard to Samsung Notes. Meta's September launch announcement introduced a customizable action button, and its integrations center on WhatsApp, Messenger and Instagram. Google says its privacy protections include recording indicators, camera permission controls and automatic redaction of bystanders' faces during Gemini visual queries. Google also says visuals processed through those queries are not used to train AI models or target advertisements. Meta's glasses include an external recording indicator to alert people nearby when photos or videos are being captured.

TechRepublic recommends Google AI Glasses for the lowest starting price, Gemini and Google services, and more storage, and Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 for messaging and social media features, glasses available now, and more video recording options. Google's frames weigh approximately 40 to 44 grams, while Meta's standard Wayfarer Gen 3 weighs about 51.5 grams and offers adjustable temple tips. Both support prescription lenses, although options vary by frame. Google's glasses support selected Pixel and Galaxy phones and compatible iPhones, and activation requires an eligible Google account associated with the United States or South Korea and users at least 18. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 requires a compatible smartphone, a Meta account and the Meta AI app, and its supported services and AI features can vary by country.

The Fox News article says the Meta glasses let wearers take calls and snap photos hands-free, and the Adventurer model has a classic tortoiseshell frame, brown lenses and standard or high-bridge fit options. The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 glasses come in styles including Wayfarers with matte-black frames and clear, transition or tinted graphite lenses. The Oakley Meta glasses' built-in Meta AI can connect with Garmin smartwatches to provide real-time insights and alerts while the wearer moves. TechRepublic says both Google and Meta glasses offer cameras, AI assistants and hands-free features, but their differences go beyond price. TechRepublic says buyers should check whether their phones and accounts qualify before preordering Google's glasses, and that some capabilities, including Guided Vision and Aira visual assistance, require a compatible Android phone at launch.

TechRepublic says buyers may want to wait for independent testing, particularly if they plan to record video frequently or wear the glasses throughout the day. TechRepublic says anyone prioritizing camera quality, call performance or real-world battery life may be better off waiting for independent comparisons after Google's December 10 release. TechRepublic says neither product has a demonstrated overall privacy advantage, and both warrant a review of their data policies before workplace use. TechRepublic says buyers should consider whether camera-equipped glasses are permitted in meetings, offices or locations where confidential information may be visible. TechRepublic says the best AI glasses are the ones that actually work the way you need them to.

stories.Headline: Cornell Systems Summit asks participants to define and close the AI skills gap
stories.Summary:
The third annual Cornell Systems Summit was held from November 1 to 3 on Cornell's Ithaca campus, bringing together leaders from academia, industry and government. It examined how artificial intelligence is reshaping engineering, education and the workforce. The summit was founded by Cornell's Systems Engineering program as a collaborative forum for researchers, practitioners and other experts. This year's participants were asked to help define the AI-driven skills gap and to help close it. They were asked to better prepare students for evolving workforce needs in the era of AI.

The summit included three keynote speakers. Ricardo Daziano, professor of civil and environmental engineering at Cornell, discussed how policy, human preferences, infrastructure and domain-informed AI shape adoption of clean energy technologies, electrification and policy. Fei Wang, the Frances and John Loeb Professor of Medical Informatics at Weill Cornell Medicine, spoke about how AI is being applied to disease characterization, treatment and prediction. Paul Heremans, corporate CTO and senior fellow at the Interuniversity Microelectronics Centre in Belgium, outlined how semiconductor technology and cross-industry collaboration help scale AI within energy, thermal and power-delivery constraints. A panel discussion brought together senior Cornell leaders to explore how AI is changing engineering, education and society.

Cliff Whitcomb, professor of practice and executive director of the Systems Engineering program at the Cornell Duffield College of Engineering, said AI had become prevalent and enters conversation frequently. He said it was time to examine AI's effects on workforce development, education and systems engineering across key areas including energy, healthcare and semiconductor manufacturing. Emmanuel Giannelis, the Walter R. Read Professor of Engineering and associate dean for innovation in the Cornell Duffield College of Engineering, opened the summit by encouraging attendees to think about what skills will be needed in the era of AI. Giannelis said it is always better not to have to react but rather to anticipate the changes ahead. He asked whether attendees could anticipate what is happening and how best to prepare themselves and their students.

The panel was moderated by Jessica Rush Leeker, professor of practice in Systems Engineering and the Office of Inclusive Excellence. It included Steven Jackson, vice provost for academic innovation, Thorsten Joachims, vice provost for artificial intelligence, and Martin Teschl, director of business development and licensing at the Center for Technology Licensing. Panelists considered what knowledge and judgment must remain uniquely human, who shapes emerging technologies, and how success should be measured in increasingly AI-enabled systems. They emphasized that AI cannot simply replace people and is strongest when well-defined, measurable objectives are defined, with people responsible for defining success and judging whether a result makes sense. Jackson said AI does not understand anything and is just different versions of text prediction, so judgment of whether it makes sense is important.

Jackson said people talk about the importance of having a human in the loop in AI systems, but what is needed is something stronger. He said engineers should be in the lead, not just in the loop. A second panel focused on how AI is changing engineering industries and was moderated by a person the article does not name. The article ends there and gives no further details of that panel. The articles give no date for the next summit or for any follow-up report.

The Manila Times article says AI can solve mathematical problems, explain complex concepts, write essays and answer questions within seconds. It says AI offers personalized instruction, immediate feedback, differentiated learning and greater accessibility. It says research increasingly suggests that its educational value depends less on technological sophistication than on how teachers and students use it. A meta-analysis involving 14,321 participants found positive learning outcomes compared with conventional large-group instruction (Ma et al., 2014). A randomized study involving 194 university physics students found that a carefully designed AI tutor produced greater short-term learning gains in less time than comparison classroom-based active-learning instruction (Kestin et al., 2025).

In a randomized experiment involving nearly 1,000 high school mathematics students, researchers compared unrestricted GPT-4 assistance, a safeguarded AI tutor and conventional learning resources. Students using unrestricted AI performed 48 percent better during practice. When AI was removed, they scored 17 percent lower on subsequent independent examinations than students in the control group. Those using a safeguarded tutor achieved substantially better practice performance without the same decline in independent examination results (Bastani et al., 2025). The article describes a troubling paradox: students can become better at answering questions with AI without becoming better at thinking without AI.

Stanford University's November 2026 SCALE review synthesized 52 causal studies from a larger collection of AI education research. It found promising outcomes from interactive tutoring, adaptive instruction, sequenced practice and feedback, while warning that using AI to complete academic work can undermine independent performance (Walker et al., 2026). Favorable student attitudes toward AI did not consistently translate into measurable learning gains. In Stanford's Tutor CoPilot experiment, more than 700 tutors and over 1,000 students participated in research on AI-generated instructional suggestions during mathematics tutoring. Students whose tutors received AI assistance were 4 percentage points more likely to master mathematics topics.

Gains reached 9 percentage points among students working with lower-rated tutors (Wang et al., 2025). Philippine studies suggest that AI can support teaching and learning, but its effectiveness depends on how responsibly it is integrated into instruction, with teacher preparedness, equitable access and academic integrity remaining critical challenges (Co, 2025). Research involving Filipino high school and university students indicates that independent learning, critical thinking and responsible AI use are more important to meaningful educational development than simply increasing students' reliance on AI tools (Besas et al., 2026; Astrero et al., 2026). A Philippine study found no significant learning advantage from AI-assisted instruction over conventional teaching (Dapiroc, 2025). Unesco advocates human-centered applications, ethical safeguards, teacher preparation and responsible implementation.

Its AI competency frameworks place human agency and ethical judgment alongside technological proficiency (Unesco, 2023, 2024). The Manila Times article says the Philippines has begun responding through policies, but a policy permitting AI is not necessarily a pedagogy that makes AI educationally effective. It says teachers need professional development in AI-supported pedagogy. It says assessments should combine responsible AI-assisted work with independently demonstrated competencies and authentic performance tasks. It says schools should measure learning gains, retention, knowledge transfer and independent competence rather than counting AI users or completed assignments.

It says students without reliable connectivity or paid applications must not be left further behind. It says a responsible implementation plan should define when students may use AI, what assistance they must disclose, and which tasks must remain entirely independent. The article says teachers should review generated materials for accuracy, cultural relevance and bias before classroom use. It says school leaders should consult families and protect student information, especially where minors are involved.

It says universities should develop discipline-specific standards rather than impose a single rule across nursing, engineering, teacher education and the humanities. It says policymakers should fund evaluations of AI-supported learning outcomes. It says AI can fabricate references and deliver inaccurate explanations with unwarranted confidence, and students must learn to question, verify and responsibly apply outputs. It says evidence from particular subjects and short-term experiments should not automatically be generalized across disciplines, and long-term effects on learning and professional competence still require investigation.
