stories.Headline: Senator Tillis plans to hold LoSapio's CISA nomination after he denies January 6 was an attack
stories.Summary:
Michael LoSapio, Palantir's chief information security officer and the nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, appeared before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday alongside six other nominees, and his nomination may now be in doubt after he said the January 6, 2021, storming of the U.S. Capitol was not an attack. When Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, asked all the nominees whether January 6 was an attack, LoSapio first said he did not know, then said he did not believe it was an attack, adding that he was not involved in politics and knew what he saw on the news. Sen. Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican who is retiring in January, told reporters he plans to put a hold on LoSapio's nomination after those comments, which narrows his path to confirmation because he is unlikely to be included in any Senate nominations package before Democrats take the majority in the new year. CISA has been without a Senate-confirmed director since January 2025, and the Trump administration's previous nominee, Sean Plankey, withdrew his name this spring after his nomination sat in the Senate for 13 months. During the hearing, LoSapio declined to say whether he thinks CISA needs more staffing and resources, even as the agency hires hundreds more people after widespread departures last year.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a Michigan Democrat, asked for his views on the Trump administration's proposed $385 million cut to CISA's budget for fiscal 2027 and the reduction of approximately 1,000 employees at the agency since January 2025, and LoSapio responded that he could not comment on the current state of CISA because he is not inside today, saying he comes from the private sector and can speak to his private sector experience about budgets and cuts and funding. Slotkin argued that recent outages and concerns about AI security point to the need for more CISA resources following the administration's cuts, and LoSapio responded that he does not necessarily believe more money means more security, saying he believes spending money on the right solutions in the right ways actually decreases risk. Sen. James Lankford, an Oklahoma Republican, referenced recent technology outages and asked how LoSapio would respond to similar scenarios as CISA director, and LoSapio said it is really important to understand the landscape of the systems out in the wild, the systems operated day to day, the systems relied on and the systems ancillary to the work, and to do an extensive evaluation of their vulnerabilities, whether they have been patched, how they have been architected and their defensive capabilities, both things that need to be added and things that exist today, as to how that maps to the threats being faced. LoSapio's hearing came a day after Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was also pressed on CISA staffing during a hearing before the House Homeland Security Committee. Earlier this year, Mullin said CISA needs to hire 600 new staff following the loss of 1,000 employees between January 2025 and January 2026, and in September, acting CISA Director Nick Andersen said CISA was making progress on hiring, with roughly 250 new hires waiting to get through the security clearance process.

Asked by Homeland Security Committee Chairman Andrew Garbarino, a New York Republican, about the status of CISA hiring, Mullin said he would follow up about the numbers, but he said the Trump administration wants to increase CISA staffing, alluding to the clearance process and government pay scales as hiring barriers, saying the administration is able to meet those needs today but wants to grow capacity and that it takes time, and also takes a long time to get people cleared to a TS/SCI clearance and above level, that not everybody can pass those background checks, and that the government has to work with industry because its pay scale is much lower than what industry is paying. Members of the Homeland Security Committee have also introduced a bipartisan bill that would establish a pilot program at CISA to help recruit AI and emerging technology experts, and Mullin backed such an effort during the hearing, calling it a very forward-leaning bipartisan bill that is needed more of and saying it gives the flexibility needed to compete with industry, bring the best into CISA and pay them competitively. CISA has some existing authorities to pay cyber experts more competitively, including under the Department of Homeland Security's Cybersecurity Talent Management System, or CTMS, but CISA also scaled back some cyber pay incentives earlier this year, leading to concerns that more employees could leave the agency. Rep. Michael McCaul, a Texas Republican who was the lead House sponsor on the legislation creating CISA in 2018, pushed Mullin to prioritize recruiting at the agency, saying there are 600 people to hire and urging him to get CISA full steam because the threats have not gone away and CISA needs to be in full force.

stories.Headline: SpaceX sells $32 billion in bonds through a trust to buy Nvidia chips for its data centers
stories.Summary:
Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) sold $32 billion of bonds through a trust set up to buy Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) chips on Thursday, with the largest piece paying investors a yield above 8%. The sale was reported by The Motley Fool on Friday, November 20, 2026, and the stock was down 6.7% as of 11:39 a.m. ET on Friday. The bonds are part of a more than $40 billion financing package SpaceX announced in October. The largest piece, about $25.2 billion, was priced at a yield of 8.259%. The average yield on high-grade U.S. corporate debt was 5.95% that day, and bonds considered "junk" were yielding an average of 8.3% that day.

To try to keep the debt off its books, the financing runs through a separate entity, a trust that sells the bonds, buys the chips, and leases them to SpaceX. Functionally, SpaceX is still the one borrowing, and its quarterly lease payments are what pay the bondholders back. The loans are secured by the chips in the same way a mortgage is secured by a home, and if SpaceX ever defaulted, the lenders' fallback would be to repossess the GPUs and sell them. The chips, destined for SpaceX data centers, are expected to start arriving in January. The AI unit nearly tripled its sales between Q2 and Q3, growing revenue from $2.6 billion to $7.6 billion.

According to reporting from The Financial Times, the lenders involved wanted guarantees that SpaceX would keep the financed chips on terra firma, apparently worried about the logistics of repossessing chips circling the Earth at about 17,500 mph. It is not clear if the lenders were able to get anything binding in the final documents, but SpaceX says these chips are for its "terrestrial compute build-out." CFO Bret Johnsen said in the company's October financing announcement that SpaceX is seeing "less than one year payback periods" on its infrastructure investments. The business spent $16.4 billion in capex in its Q3, the lion's share of the company's overall $19.6 billion capex spend. The Motley Fool's Johnny Rice wrote that he is still skeptical long-term and does not think the payoff will hold up.

Similar maneuvers are increasingly common across the AI data center market as companies look for ways to deal with ballooning debt balances. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Nvidia and Space Exploration Technologies. Johnny Rice has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The stock was down 6.7% as of 11:39 a.m. ET on Friday as the whole market sees red. Investors are being paid about 2.3 percentage points more than usual for bonds that are supposed to be relatively safe.

stories.Headline: Michael Burry flags Nvidia financing gap as $500 billion plan deploys no money
stories.Summary:
Michael Burry drew attention on Thursday to a financing problem for Nvidia, according to a Wall Street Journal report he shared on X. A Wall Street initiative to mobilize $500 billion for Nvidia's AI chip customers has yet to deploy any money, the report said. Talks on the first chip-backed deal are ongoing, with a closing unlikely before 2027, the Journal reported. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang helped bring together Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR in August. The firms signed a nonbinding agreement that set a fundraising ambition of $500 billion over time.

How much risk Nvidia would take has become a sticking point in the talks. Huang said Nvidia's credit support would cover up to 25% of project costs, and lenders have sought greater protection. Nvidia has separately disclosed up to $118 billion in guarantees, including up to $105 billion tied to an Ohio data-center campus that will host Nvidia hardware under leases to OpenAI. Those guarantees take effect in stages as buildings become operational, with the first expected in fiscal 2029. Nvidia still expects about $130 billion in fiscal fourth-quarter revenue.

The financing question is whether customers with less access to capital can fund future chip purchases on schedule. The first signed deal would show how much lenders are willing to commit and how much risk Nvidia must take to secure that funding. Burry has previously called Nvidia's $500 billion AI financing push a Wall Street stunt. He has also called Nvidia AI spending fugazi and said billions in GPUs are hidden through a complex financing structure.

stories.Headline: Paris Hilton and lawmakers press House to pass deepfake victim lawsuit bill
stories.Summary:
Paris Hilton joined Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Republican Rep. Laurel Lee at the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, to press House lawmakers to pass legislation letting people targeted by sexually explicit AI-generated deepfakes sue those responsible. The bill would allow victims to seek up to $250,000 in damages under certain circumstances. The bipartisan DEFIANCE Act passed the Senate unanimously in January but waited 10 months for House action. Hilton and the lawmakers renewed their appeal alongside survivors of digital sexual abuse. Supporters sought a vote before the current congressional term ends.

The legislation would let individuals bring federal lawsuits against people who knowingly distribute sexually explicit digital forgeries without consent, possess them with intent to disclose them, or knowingly solicit and receive them. Certain claims involving creation of a deepfake alone would qualify when the person knew or recklessly disregarded the lack of consent and the resulting harm or likelihood of harm. Successful claims could bring $150,000 in damages, rising to $250,000 when conduct involves actual or attempted sexual assault, stalking or harassment under conditions outlined in the bill. Individuals could alternatively seek compensation for actual losses, including profits earned by those responsible. Courts could order removal or destruction of the material, award attorney fees and permit lawsuits under pseudonyms, and the bill generally provides 10 years to bring a claim from discovery of the violation or the person's 18th birthday, whichever is later.

Ocasio-Cortez and Lee introduced the House version of the bill, which has attracted support from both parties. Republican Rep. Kat Cammack, who chairs the Republican Women's Caucus, helped organize Tuesday's gathering with members of the Democratic Women's Caucus. Hilton said she keeps her promises to survivors and will return to these halls as many times as it takes until the DEFIANCE Act is signed. Lee said in a statement that laws have lagged behind the technology, leaving victims without clear legal tools when their likeness is stolen and weaponized, and that the bill closes that gap. Ocasio-Cortez said every day the bill does not pass and is not signed into law is a day more children, women and people are victimized with no recourse and no accountability for abusers and predators.

Ocasio-Cortez also said thousands of people in this country, if not tens of thousands and eventually millions, could be subject to sexual abuse on our watch due to complacency. Hilton said that ten months ago she stood at the Capitol and told the world what it feels like to have your body exposed without your consent, and asked Congress to do something about it. Hilton said the laws aren't protecting us, and that if this can happen to someone with her resources and platform, imagine how powerless a young girl might feel facing this completely alone. Hilton joined the press conference along with survivors of tech-enabled sexual abuse and advocates Elliston Berry and Elizabeth Cline, and advocate and father Joseph Tucker Daniels, according to RAINN's press release. The bill has attracted 70 cosponsors, including 36 Democrats and 34 Republicans, according to RAINN.

Hilton has publicly discussed the unauthorized release of an intimate video involving her when she was 19 and has since become an advocate for people subjected to sexual exploitation and abuse. She previously helped secure passage of the Stop Institutional Child Abuse Act, signed into law in December 2024, which established new federal oversight and reporting requirements for youth residential programs. Her latest Capitol Hill appearance followed an earlier visit in January, when she joined Ocasio-Cortez and Lee to urge the House to advance the DEFIANCE Act after its Senate approval. President Donald Trump signed the TAKE IT DOWN Act into law in May 2025, making certain nonconsensual publications of intimate images, including AI-generated material, a federal crime, and covered online platforms must remove qualifying content within 48 hours of a valid request. The Federal Trade Commission began enforcing those platform removal requirements in May 2026, and existing federal law also allows civil lawsuits over certain disclosures of intimate images.

The Senate previously approved an earlier version of the DEFIANCE Act in 2024, but the House did not advance it before that congressional term ended, and lawmakers reintroduced the measure in 2025. The Senate approved it again on January 13, 2026, after it had passed the first time in July 2024, and since then the bill has stalled in the House. House leaders have yet to schedule a floor vote despite the legislation attracting 70 cosponsors. Congress has until January 3, 2027, to complete passage of the legislation and send it to the president for approval. If the deadline passes, supporters will have to reintroduce the bill when the next Congress convenes.

stories.Headline: Palo Alto Networks buys Applied Compute for 4.5 billion dollars
stories.Summary:
Three former OpenAI employees founded Applied Compute and sold it for 4.5 billion US dollars. This transaction occurred within 18 months of the startup beginning its business operations. The deal was announced on November 18 Eastern Time by the cybersecurity giant Palo Alto Networks. The founders are Yash Patil, Rhythm Garg, and Linden Li, who are aged 23, 24, and 25. They used Chinese open-source models to provide AI outsourcing services for various large enterprises.

The all-stock transaction integrates a team of 70 people into Palo Alto Networks. Yash Patil will serve as the Co-Chief AI Officer for the acquiring cybersecurity firm. The price was 1.25 billion dollars higher than the 3.25 billion dollar valuation from November 2. This acquisition follows a 350 million dollar financing round completed just half a month prior. The total payment uses shares based on a 15-day average price of 337.16 dollars.

Nikesh Arora is the Chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks. He stated that his company initially contacted the startup as a potential customer. Arora noted that the Unit 42 threat intelligence team conducted a security assessment. He believed the research team was outstanding and the platform was the best he had seen. Patil said joining the giant would put security at the core of all products.

Customers include Microsoft, NVIDIA, DoorDash, and the legal AI company Harvey. These enterprises used the AC2 platform to train proprietary models using their own business data. The marketing software company Clay used Alibaba's Qwen to reduce inference costs by 47 percent. Harvey used Zhipu's GLM-5.2 to lower average inference costs by 54.8 percent against Claude Sonnet 5. These clients sought to avoid the high costs of closed-source models from OpenAI or Anthropic.

The founders met at Stanford and worked at OpenAI on infrastructure, inference models, and machine learning. They decided to start their business after discussing the January 2025 release of DeepSeek-R1. Benchmark led a 20 million dollar round in June 2025 before the company was public. An April financing round brought the valuation to 1.3 billion dollars before the AC2 launch. The company reached 100 million dollars in annualized revenue within a year and a half.

Palo Alto Networks will now integrate the AC2 platform into its existing security portfolio. The company's after-hours share price surged about 10 percent following the acquisition announcement. The deal includes 500 million dollars in cash and committed prepaid computing power. The articles leave open how the outsourcing controversy and security risks will be resolved. It remains to be seen how the integration affects the existing client base.

stories.Headline: Claude builds its own reasoning engine and cuts first-character latency from 12 seconds to 0.478 seconds
stories.Summary:
Claude developed its own reasoning engine and cut the latency before the AI returns its first character from 12 seconds to half a second, 36Kr reported on 2026-11-20. On November 12, researchers from institutions including Carnegie Mellon University and NVIDIA submitted the preprint Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?. For one task, the researchers gave Claude Opus 5.5 a basic server codebase, 4 GB300 GPUs and 12 hours of runtime. The development environment was restricted from accessing the internet for reference, and Claude used Claude Code to write a complete inference engine. The researchers tested the engine with real programming sessions, replaying the same batch of 16 concurrent sessions on two engines running the same model on 4 GB300 GPUs.

The P90 time to first token latency of Claude's engine was 0.478 seconds, compared to 12.029 seconds for SGLang (v0.5.20). By median, Claude's engine generates 124.2 tokens per second and SGLang generates 125.0 tokens per second. When 16 sessions run simultaneously, the median single input length is 89,000 tokens, and the cache hit rate of both engines is around 96%. Claude's engine processed 19% more uncached tokens on average per GPU per second. Within the same replay time limit, SGLang completed 705 requests while Claude's engine completed 983 requests, nearly 40% more.

The researchers set two hard thresholds for submission: under concurrent load the engine must fully generate responses of the specified length, and it must pass the accuracy acceptance of hidden tests. Among the 11 AI self-developed engines that participated in the test, only 5 finally passed both thresholds. The other 6 either truncated words and sentences halfway or collapsed in accuracy, and got zero points on the spot according to the rules. The output of Claude's engine per GPU hour increased from 8.18 USD for SGLang to 11.52 USD, a 40.8% increase. Singularity-Bench split the core tough work of building AI into six independent closed-book exams: three for training and three for infrastructure.

11 AI teams formed by combining 7 mainstream models with two runtime frameworks, Claude Code and Codex, received the starting code offline and submitted their work according to the countdown. Claude Opus 5.5 paired with Claude Code also beat the human baseline in four other tasks. On the pre-training exam paper, Claude spent 44 minutes testing GPU performance first and did not start training until the 44th minute. It used only about half of the training computation and achieved a perplexity of 12.77 on the validation set, better than the 14.22 of the human baseline (OLMo 2 1B paired with Megatron-LM). For the mid-training task, Claude mainly selected data with complete problem-solving processes and verified answers, raising the downstream average accuracy from 17.5% of the human PRISM recipe to 31.9%.

In the agent runtime framework task (1 GB300 GPU, 6 hours), Claude raised the downstream average score from 0.438 to 0.468, and the new framework fixed one more bug than the original Claude Code. In the cluster scheduling task (16 GB300 GPUs, 4 hours), Claude adjusted the scheduling strategy to let engines use the GPU in turn, scoring 0.510 on latency compliance rate and request completion rate against 0.460 for NVIDIA Dynamo paired with KAI Scheduler. The only task that did not produce a winner was post-training (4 GB300 GPUs, 12 hours). The research team divided AI R&D into three stages: training, deployment and application. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Horizon builds 38 custom AI models in seven weeks and surpasses 55,000 downloads
stories.Summary:
Claude launched an AI factory that built 38 custom models in seven weeks, surpassing 55,000 total downloads, according to a 36Kr article dated November 19, 2026. The models were built by Horizon, an agent built on Claude Opus 5.5, which was given a blank Hugging Face account and a certain amount of computing power. The research team let Horizon decide what to do on its own, with only one requirement: to build models that developers are genuinely willing to use. The 38 models accumulated about 55,000 total downloads, and the prompt injection detection series alone recorded roughly 17,000 downloads. The models were integrated into more than 100 GitHub projects.

Horizon was embedded into Claude Code and kept running 24/7 in the background, with resources of no more than a Team Premium subscription plus a computing power quota of around 500 GPU hours per week. Human intervention was mostly concentrated in the first three days, and after October 22 the team completely stepped back and left the AI to operate entirely on its own. Horizon targeted the multilingual model mmBERT as its base model, and all 38 models have parameter sizes ranging strictly between 141 million and 568 million. It used a 27B open-source model to generate synthetic data in batches, then assigned Gemma 4 31B to label and expand the dataset. One model is specially designed to add punctuation to texts in 88 different languages.

The driving force behind the experiment comes from institutions including EPFL, ELLIS Tübingen Institute, Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems and Imperial College London. The research team checked the full records and estimated that downloads generated by their own operations were at most 50 times. The team found that Horizon downloaded its own model 42 times in 6 separate operations, a scene the research team wrote directly into the paper and made public. On September 24, Horizon accidentally set an account copy to public, and in mid-October it answered a work order incorrectly. On October 22, a failure in the underlying framework made it wake up later than scheduled.

Another concurrently running agent briefly shared Horizon's account and posted promotional comments, a traffic diversion record the paper also recorded. Even subtracting the team's 50 test downloads, the 42 self-boosted downloads and the traffic from the promotion, the remaining more than 50,000 real downloads are still completely valid and credible. Horizon ended up using less than 20% of its weekly quota of about 500 GPU hours, running for just over 600 hours across seven weeks. Of the roughly 1.9 billion tokens consumed, as high as 96% came from prompt caching, and at API prices the total cost of consumed tokens is about 1030 U.S. dollars, excluding GPU costs. Besides being integrated into more than 100 GitHub projects, the models were used for evaluation in two arXiv papers, and the Hugging Face community developed 18 derivative models based on its results.

Horizon runs in the background around the clock but spends an average of only 16 minutes per day on actual work. It wakes up on time exactly when Hugging Face refreshes its download statistics every day, checks the leaderboard, and only selects high-download, high-value models to continue polishing. It rests when there is no feedback and only takes action after identifying a clear trend. When it encounters tricky tasks it cannot handle, it can immediately submit a work order to human staff. The demands it locked in are rigid needs of developers: detecting prompt injection, masking personal information and identifying harmful content, and one of its prompt injection detection models has more than 7,000 downloads for the basic version alone.

The article says the era of mass production of AI models has arrived when AI begins to create AI. It says the AI sits in the boss's seat while researchers from top universities take orders to run errands in the background. It says Horizon is not a scholar who toils away at research but a shrewd and seasoned contractor who does not even work extra shifts. It says the models are flyweight players among large models that often have hundreds of billions of parameters, but for front-line developers they save video memory, are easy to deploy and can be put into use immediately. It says the one that knows best how to prevent AI from being tricked is AI itself.

The article says it remains to be seen whether Horizon can iterate models based on user feedback and then feed back these capabilities to itself, so that stronger AI can train the next generation of AI. It says Horizon's case confirms that AI built by AI has already passed the test of real developers. It says that on the path to ASI, this is the first step to turn the self-evolution flywheel. It says the specialized model you randomly pull from the internet may well have been developed by AI. It says the article is from the WeChat Official Account New Zhiyuan, author ASI Revelation, editor Yuan Yu, published with authorization from 36Kr.

He stated that implementing tighter regulations on this technology could potentially push the United States economy into a recession. This economic downturn would likely have negative consequences for the global economy as well. He estimates that the country needs between 7 trillion and 9 trillion dollars in related investments to succeed. These funds would be necessary to build the infrastructure and systems required for advanced artificial intelligence. Without this level of investment and a flexible regulatory environment, the economic risks increase. Larry Fink spoke about these concerns while he was visiting Tokyo, Japan, for a board meeting.

He explained that overly restrictive laws could stifle the growth and innovation needed for economic stability. The executive suggested that the balance between safety and progress is critical for the financial future of the nation. He emphasized that the global market depends heavily on the success of American technological leadership. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AXS, Visa and Mastercard connect AI agents to bill payments in Singapore
stories.Summary:
AXS, Visa and Mastercard are working together to let artificial intelligence agents pay bills on behalf of consumers in Singapore, connecting those agents to AXS's network of more than 800 billing organisations, which include hospitals, power companies, telcos, insurers, finance companies, country clubs and government agencies such as the Housing Board and the police. The service is meant to cover telco, electricity and healthcare bills as well as housing loan instalments and fines, and it removes the need for customers to manually check for outstanding bills, log into multiple apps and key in one-time passwords. AXS declined to give a roll-out timeline for consumers, but it plans a trial of bill payments with the Grab AI assistant, and it announced the tie-up around Nov 18, with The Straits Times reporting on it on Nov 19, 2026. Visa demonstrated the idea at the Singapore FinTech Festival at the Singapore Expo on Nov 18, showing a customer typing a request in a chat box for an AI agent to pay a telco bill, after which the agent confirms the amount and card and a biometric face check completes the transaction.

Existing card protections from Mastercard and Visa apply to these AI payments, and the guardrails include letting users set payment limits, specify which transactions are permitted and require their approval before a payment goes through. Visa's Asia Pacific head of innovation and growth products, Abhijeet Ramesh, said only a legitimate agent verified to pay on the customer's behalf can start a transaction, explicit customer approval with biometric verification is needed to complete it, and the card details are never shared with the agent. Instead the agent receives a random token unique to the customer's device and a separate one-time code unique to each transaction, and neither can be used for other payments, including to other billing organisations, even if stolen, while a payment of a different amount from the one approved is blocked. AXS group chief executive and executive director Jeffrey Goh said connecting partners' own AI agents to the AXS network extends its reach beyond existing channels and lets partners create new payment experiences for their customers, and Ramesh said the system-driven controls ensure an agent cannot simply do whatever it wants and that the user is always in control.

Because agentic payments are still in their infancy, Visa is working on how to help banks, which eventually disburse the funds, with more checks and balances, including updating banks on agentic transaction data so they can set rules for different types of payments to different types of organisations, such as a monthly cap on transactions to a particular biller based on billing trends. Visa will use its existing framework for resolving card payment disputes for payments made by AI agents, and a tamper-proof record of each action an agent takes can be used to settle disputes and determine whether an agent is at fault for an unintended transaction. Ramesh said Visa is continuously reviewing its dispute resolution framework and rules to see what changes are needed for agentic payments, adding that it is still early days, no changes have been made yet and the company is actively working on it. AXS, Visa and Mastercard did not say which AI agents the capability will be available for, though AXS said consumers could ask an AI assistant in their banking app or digital wallet to help with bill payments, and ChatGPT maker OpenAI said on Nov 13 that it was also working with American Express, Mastercard and Visa to let its dots AI agent make payments with those cards, initially only for US customers.

stories.Headline: Alibaba CEO Wu Yongming unveils AI strategy as net profit surges 213 percent

Alibaba released its financial report for the second quarter of fiscal year 2027 on November 19, 2026. The company reported that its net profit surged 213 percent during this specific period. Alibaba recently released Qwen4-Max, a model with 2.4 trillion parameters and a Mixture-of-Experts architecture. The company launched the Qwen Go! personal agent in October and the Enterprise Context function in September.

T-Head released the Zhenwu V900 chip in September and a super node instance in August. The company adjusted its financial reporting segments starting from the first quarter of fiscal year 2027. Hema's online and offline channels drove a 22 percent increase in China's instant retail revenue. Alibaba aims for 30 billion yuan in annualized recurring revenue for its MaaS business by fiscal 2027.

The company expects cloud revenue growth for the next fiscal year to be between 30 and 45 percent. A next-generation video model is expected to be released in the near future. stories.Headline: Bloomington mayor Kerry Thomson vetoes a city council ordinance banning artificial superintelligence
stories.Summary:
Bloomington mayor Kerry Thomson announced on Thursday afternoon, Nov. 19, 2026, that she will not sign an ordinance the city council approved 7, 0 earlier that month, which would prohibit the distribution and deployment of artificial superintelligence within city limits. The ordinance was presented to the mayor on Nov. 9 at 5:13 p.m., according to the city clerk’s office, giving her until 5:13 p.m. Thursday to sign it or return it to the council with a veto message. Because she did neither, the ordinance is considered vetoed under Indiana law. Seven councilmembers voted for the ordinance on Nov. 4, when two members, Sydney Zulich and Kate Rosenbarger, were absent.

Councilmember Dave Rollo introduced the ordinance and put forward all four amendments the council adopted before its final vote. The ordinance would add a new chapter to Bloomington’s municipal code under Title 14, which governs peace and safety, and would prohibit distribution and deployment of ASI within the city, including through websites, software and other electronic interfaces, even when the computers hosting those systems are physically located elsewhere. It defines superintelligence in terms of agency, generality and intelligence, describing autonomous systems capable of modifying their own algorithms, executing computer code outside restricted environments and undertaking complex tasks without continuous human oversight, combined with capabilities vastly exceeding human cognitive performance. The ordinance does not establish a testing procedure or designate an independent authority to determine when a particular AI system has crossed the threshold into superintelligence. It invokes the city’s powers under Indiana’s Home Rule Act and compares superintelligence to hazardous substances and industrial processes that local governments can regulate in the interest of public safety, and it would authorize the city’s legal and police departments to seek civil penalties and court orders against violators, with enforcement discretionary rather than mandatory.

One amendment explicitly excluded end-user access from the prohibition, so a Bloomington resident would not violate the ordinance merely by accessing an AI system through an electronic interface, and another removed Rollo’s original proposal to require approval from more than 95% of Bloomington’s registered voters, along with findings establishing an extremely high level of scientific certainty about the safety of superintelligence, before the ban could be lifted, retaining a scientific-safety objective in the preamble but no longer making the finding and referendum requirements for repeal. Thomson said, “Bloomington is working hard to grow our innovation economy, and artificial intelligence plays an important role in that work,” and that “AI already contributes to advances in research, medicine, education and many other fields.” She added, “We also need to be careful about creating unnecessary barriers that discourage those very people from investing in our community.” Thomson said, “As mayor, I have a responsibility to lead the team that implements and enforces our ordinances,” and that “This ordinance leaves significant questions about how the City would identify violations, what authority we have to regulate them and what enforcement would require.” She said, “The potential need to monitor private digital activity is especially troubling given our recent work to strengthen protections against government surveillance,” and that “Passing a law carries responsibilities beyond stating a principle,” adding, “We need to be confident that we can implement and enforce the laws we adopt.”

Thomson acknowledged the risks Rollo is attempting to address, saying, “I appreciate Council’s efforts to address the risks of increasingly autonomous AI systems and the national conversation this legislation has helped advance,” and that “Those risks deserve serious consideration.” Rollo told The B Square he is still optimistic about working with the mayor on a version of the ordinance she might eventually be willing to sign, because superintelligent AI is “a deadly risk for everyone,” and he added, “Obviously, we’re racing forward as the horizon is racing at us. I mean, this is madness. And there are huge consequences.” Rollo said at the start of the Wednesday night, Nov. 18, council meeting, less than 24 hours before the mayor’s deadline, that the ordinance “is emphatically not what tech businesses are using here or at IU,” and he said, “This particular AI, ASI, hasn’t yet arrived,” while contending that developing such systems is the goal of leading AI companies and that the technology could arrive soon.

Rollo contrasted that goal with work at Indiana University, which he characterized as human-centered artificial intelligence emphasizing ethical deployment, human oversight and beneficial social impacts, and he said, “Local tech applications and IU are to be lauded for their approach.” Rollo rebutted Thomson’s surveillance concern, saying, “We don’t need to surveil anyone,” and suggested violations could be reported through complaints or investigated by testing whether a prohibited system was accessible from a city-operated computer. The ordinance vetoed by Thomson represents a third effort by Rollo to persuade Bloomington’s city government to address what he and others warn is the existential danger to the human species posed by increasingly powerful artificial intelligence. In July 2023, Rollo proposed a resolution calling for a moratorium on developing artificial general intelligence until adequate safeguards could be established, and he withdrew it after officials with Indiana University raised concerns about possible implications for research funding, and sufficient support from council colleagues appeared unlikely.

On June 10 of this year, the council unanimously adopted a resolution calling on governments at other levels to address the existential risks of artificial intelligence and urging a moratorium on developing advanced AI until the technology could be aligned with human values and well-being, and that resolution was nonbinding, expressing the council’s position without establishing a local prohibition. The ordinance approved by the council in early November goes further by attempting to make distribution and deployment of superintelligence a violation of Bloomington law. Rollo’s goals extend beyond Bloomington, and the ordinance is part of a strategy he envisions being replicated by hundreds of municipalities, with local prohibitions eventually generating enough pressure to prompt state, federal and international restrictions on advanced AI development. The council could attempt to override the veto at its next regular meeting, scheduled for Wednesday, Dec. 2, at 6:30 p.m., and an override would require six votes in favor from the nine-member council.

Thomson’s objections come despite several amendments the council adopted before its final vote, intended in part to narrow the ordinance’s scope, address concerns that it could affect ordinary users of AI technology, and other issues identified soon after Rollo introduced it. The amendments reduced the potential reach of the ordinance but did not resolve the underlying question of how Bloomington would identify prohibited systems or determine whether companies outside its boundaries were distributing them within the city. Whether Indiana’s Home Rule Act powers would support a prohibition extending to remotely operated digital systems is an unresolved legal question. Thomson’s surveillance concern comes just five weeks after the city council voted 7, 0 on Oct. 14 to prohibit automated license plate readers and certain surveillance camera systems that allow outside entities to access recordings and data, and the superintelligence ordinance does not itself authorize new surveillance of internet activity.

stories.Headline: South Korean universities issue gowns and ban correction tape to stop AI cheating in admissions tests
stories.Summary:
South Korean universities implemented strict security measures in November 2026 to prevent cheating with artificial intelligence devices during admissions tests. These actions followed the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test and were prompted by reports of a top scorer in a tax accountant exam using a miniature camera. Sogang University issued an urgent notice on November 18 regarding smart glasses and cameras before its science exams on November 21 and humanities exams on November 22. Korea University also released guidelines on November 17 for its own essay exams held on November 21 and 22.

The new rules require specific clothing and writing tools to block hidden electronic devices. Seoul National University provides interview gowns to prevent cameras from being hidden in buttonholes, while Sogang University asks applicants to avoid garments with buttons on the sleeves. Korea University banned correction tape and requires answer sheets to be written in a single pen color. Sungkyunkwan University only allows the use of specific pens previously given as souvenirs to prevent cameras from being attached to writing instruments.

Inha University and other schools may use metal detectors on suspicious applicants or those using the restroom. University officials and education bodies are taking responsibility for these heightened security protocols. A Sungkyunkwan official stated that the school increased the number of proctors and sent text messages with guidelines to all applicants. Sogang University warned that violations of these rules could lead to legal action and criminal complaints.

The Korean Council for University Education stated it would respond sternly to AI cheating and urged the Ministry of Education and the National Assembly to revise the Higher Education Act. These measures aim to align university exam security with the rigorous standards of the national CSAT. The Korean Council for University Education is seeking budget funding to expand equipment and proctoring staff for future tests. Efforts to build a comprehensive anti-cheating system for university-administered exams are expected to accelerate.

stories.Headline: EU AI Act amendments push high-risk HR system obligations to December 2027
stories.Summary:
The EU Digital Omnibus Package amended the EU AI Act and entered into force on July 27, 2026, Mary T. Costigan of Jackson Lewis P.C. wrote on November 19, 2026. The Commission presented the Digital Omnibus in November 2025 as a package to simplify EU digital law, Éric Le Quellenec of Flichy Grangé Avocats said. The package has two parts, and the first reopens the GDPR, which is still being negotiated, Le Quellenec said. The second part amends the AI Act, and that one is now law, he said. Luís Neto Galvão of SRS Legal and Le Quellenec offered five practical steps for general counsel and HR leaders at multinational businesses.

Obligations for systems listed in Annex III, including recruitment and career management, were due to apply in August of this year, Le Quellenec said. They now apply from December 2, 2027, and from August 2, 2028, for AI built into regulated products, he said. The prohibitions have applied since February 2025, the AI literacy obligations as well, and the transparency rules since August 2026, he said. High-risk systems in use before December 2, 2027, only fall under the Act if their design is significantly changed afterward, he said. Point 4 of Annex III covers recruitment, including targeting job ads, filtering applications, and evaluating candidates, and decisions on the employment relationship, including promotion, termination, task allocation based on behavior or personal traits, and monitoring and evaluating performance.

The five steps are inventory and classify AI-enabled HR tools, strengthen oversight and vendor contracts, mitigate bias, train relevant teams, and prepare recruitment practices for compliance, the article said. Neto Galvão said clients should not think they have nothing to do until 2027 and that now is the time to put a compliance plan in place. He said a year goes very quickly when you have to map your tools, renegotiate vendor contracts, and train your teams. Le Quellenec said the vendor is usually the provider and the employer is the deployer, but this can change.

He said that if the employer puts its name on the tool, modifies it substantially, or changes its intended purpose so that it becomes high risk, it becomes a provider, which brings much heavier obligations. Le Quellenec said the employer should check the conformity assessment, CE marking, EU declaration of conformity, and registration in the EU database before buying. He said the employer must use the system in line with the instructions, assign human oversight to people with the competence, training, and authority to overrule it, and make sure the input data the employer controls are relevant and representative. He said the employer must monitor the system, suspend use immediately and inform the provider if a risk appears, report serious incidents, and keep the logs for at least six months.

He said the employer must inform candidates and employees who are subject to decisions and, before the tool is introduced, inform workers' representatives and the workers concerned. He said individuals have a right to an explanation of the role AI played in a decision that significantly affects them, and a rejected candidate can ask for it. Le Quellenec said the fundamental rights impact assessment introduced by the AI Act applies to public bodies, private entities providing public services, and credit and insurance uses. He said a private employer generally does not have to do it, and for them the key assessment remains the GDPR DPIA.

Neto Galvão said human oversight must be designed into the process, not added as a label, and a manager who can only confirm the system's output is not providing meaningful oversight. Le Quellenec said HR owns the use case, IT owns integration and security, the data protection officer owns data protection and privacy, and legal owns the contracts. He said the French Lawyers' Guide on Ethics and AI was adopted in March this year and draws attention to how the way you phrase a question shapes the answer. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Federal court rules police cannot arrest on an uncorroborated AI facial recognition match
stories.Summary:
A federal court ruled that police cannot arrest someone on an uncorroborated AI facial recognition match, and it denied qualified immunity to a Kentucky detective who jailed a Nebraska man on a bad-check charge, according to LavX News. Officers arrested Alain Osorio over a charge of passing a bad check at a bank in Florence, Kentucky, where detectives had only the bank's CCTV footage as a source for the suspect's image. Detective Ryan Kilmer of the Florence Police Department ran a screenshot from that footage through the department's facial recognition program, which matched the suspect to photos on Facebook belonging to a profile named "Yony Smith Npoles Charon." Kilmer concluded that "Yony" was Alain Vizcay Osorio, a man whose booking photo appeared in police files, and the court did not name the facial recognition program.

The use of Facebook photos suggests Clearview AI, a company that has scraped hundreds of billions of images from the open web. Osorio lived in Nebraska, and officers arrested him there and extradited him to Kentucky, where he posted bond on Jan. 24, 2025, the day after his arrest. A grand jury indicted him in March 2025, a court arraigned him two months later, and he pleaded not guilty, while the state attorney's office dismissed the charges after Osorio proved he was working in Nebraska when the suspect passed the bad check. Osorio does not resemble the man in the security footage or the Facebook profile, since he has a different head shape, haircut, facial features and complexion, though both men are Black with facial hair.

Kilmer told the court in an affidavit that he used "investigative tools" to "match" Osorio to the suspect, but the court found he used one tool, the facial recognition program. Under Florence Police Department policy, facial recognition AI alone cannot establish probable cause, and Kilmer used it despite the policy. The court wrote that the Fourth Amendment does not allow a detective to delegate to AI the task of assessing probable cause, and that the Constitution does not permit an arrest based on nothing more than an uncorroborated conclusion by AI that the individual committed a crime. The judge stripped Kilmer of qualified immunity, the legal doctrine that shields officers from civil liability unless they violate clearly established law, and Kilmer can appeal.

A higher court could affirm the decision or reverse it, and if Kilmer loses his appeal, the ruling would apply beyond facial recognition. Police departments use AI to steer patrols through predictive policing software, officers use AI to generate reports from body camera footage, and Axon has added AI tools to its body cameras. The article states that running a photo through an algorithm does not constitute detective work, that a match is a lead rather than a conclusion, and that departments across the country use facial recognition as an investigative shortcut. Detectives cannot treat an algorithm match as detective work, according to the piece, which cites Techdirt as its source.

stories.Headline: Manipal University Jaipur adds AI and emerging technology electives to five online degree programmes from January 2027
stories.Summary:
Manipal University Jaipur announced significant curriculum enhancements for five of its online degree programmes on November 19, 2026. The university introduced these changes to meet evolving industry needs and professional landscape demands. These updates affect the Master of Business Administration, Master of Computer Applications, and Bachelor of Computer Applications. They also include the Master of Commerce and the MA Economics degree programmes. The university is a NAAC A+ accredited institution located in Jaipur, Rajasthan, India.

The Academic Council approved these revised curricula to come into effect from the January 2027 admission session. The MBA programme adds Artificial Intelligence for Business and offers specialisations like Finance, Marketing, and Digital Marketing. The MCA programme adds Next-Generation Technologies, Business Analysis, Generative AI and Agentic Systems, and ERP and Digital Transformation. The BCA programme introduces six pathways, including Cloud Computing, Cyber Security, and Full Stack Software Development. The MCom programme reduces total credit requirements from 100 to 80 per the NEP-related credit framework.

The university is responsible for these changes and states that the initiative strengthens the industry relevance of its programmes. They said the enhancements equip learners with specialised knowledge and skills aligned with changing professional demands. The university aims to enable learners to build relevant competencies and strengthen their professional capabilities. They believe these updates enhance career readiness by offering flexible learning pathways and revised course content. The institution intends to prepare graduates to navigate an increasingly technology-driven professional environment.

Learners are affected by these changes and can now explore emerging interdisciplinary domains and foundational academic knowledge. MBA students can choose one elective for super specialisation or two electives for dual specialisation. MCom students will use three new pathways involving Accounting, Taxation, Global Financial Reporting, and Digital Financial Services. MA Economics students can now study Global Economics and Finance, Public Policy, and Economics, Data and AI. These students will integrate conventional commerce and economics disciplines with technology-enabled financial and data practices.

Manipal University Jaipur was established in 2011 as a multidisciplinary university committed to providing quality education. Its online degree programmes are UGC-entitled and are recognised at par with corresponding on-campus degrees. The university currently offers nine degree programmes in the online mode to a diverse learner community. This community spans more than 7,000 towns and cities across India and includes over 85 nationalities. They provide live interactive classes and placement assistance through virtual drives and resume-building support.

The university will implement these new elective pathways and credit reductions starting in the January 2027 session. Students will begin using the new AI, data analytics, and digital transformation course content at that time. The university will continue providing skill assessments and industry-readiness sessions to its online learner community. The articles do not state when the next curriculum review will occur or if more programmes will change. They leave open whether additional credit reductions will be applied to other online degrees in the future.

stories.Headline: Anthropic prepares a $60 billion IPO this Thursday despite AI market fears
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is preparing to launch an initial public offering this coming Thursday. The company is moving forward with this plan despite current market fears. This financial move comes as the artificial intelligence sector faces significant instability. The company intends to sell stock to the public during this period. This event occurs while investors worry about a potential bubble in AI.

The company is preparing for an initial public offering valued at 60 billion dollars. This financial event is scheduled to take place this Thursday in November 2026. The process requires the company to sell stock to the general public. No other specific names, dates, or locations are provided in the articles. The valuation remains the primary figure associated with this upcoming stock sale.

The company leaders are responsible for pushing ahead with the public offering. They believe that investors will still buy into the stock despite market wobbles. They are betting that the company's value will attract buyers now. The executives are forging ahead even as fears about AI mount. They maintain their course despite the shaky moment for AI companies.

Investors are becoming jittery because they fear an artificial intelligence bubble exists. Some investors are currently dumping technology stocks due to these growing market concerns. These jittery investors are the primary group affected by the current market volatility. They are worried that AI companies may be overvalued at this time. This sentiment creates a risky environment for the upcoming public offering.

The company has made recent artificial intelligence advances that trigger new safety fears. These safety concerns have emerged on the eve of the initial public offering. The broader market for technology is currently experiencing a period of instability. AI companies are operating in a shaky moment according to the reports. This background sets the stage for the company's bold financial move.

The company will proceed with selling its stock to the public this Thursday. The market will determine if investors actually buy into the 60 billion valuation. The articles do not state how the safety fears will be addressed. It remains open whether the IPO will succeed despite the current market fears. The final outcome of the stock sale is not yet known.

stories.Headline: Wenge AI adds Google and Apple sign-in options for international ScienceOra users
stories.Summary:
Wenge AI announced a new update for its ScienceOra platform on November 20, 2026. The company added Google and Apple sign-in options for users of its international site. This change happened in Shenzhen, China, to help overseas researchers access the platform. The update aims to make registration and sign-in processes faster and more convenient. These tools support scientific research and decision-making through an AI for Science platform.

Users can now authenticate using existing Google or Apple accounts instead of long forms. Apple sign-in is currently available on the web version of the ScienceOra platform. The system uses email addresses and account-linking status to identify new or existing accounts. It provides clearer prompts for linked accounts, used email addresses, or Apple's Hide My Email. These changes reduce duplicate registrations and friction for users during the sign-in process.

Wenge AI, listed as 1956.HK, is responsible for these platform refinements and updates. The company stated that these changes provide a more consistent account experience for users. They intend to continue refining the product experience based on the needs of international users. The goal is to make scientific exploration and research tools more seamless for everyone. Wenge AI develops proprietary foundation models to turn AI capabilities into practical business applications.

Overseas researchers are the primary group affected by these new sign-in registration options. The platform helps these users by bringing together scientific literature, data, and specialized research agents. Meanwhile, the Korean Fair Trade Commission is tightening scrutiny over platforms like Apple and Google. This regulator requires overseas platforms to appoint legal representatives in Korea by January 21. This rule affects companies like OpenAI and Alibaba to help resolve local consumer disputes.

Wenge AI was founded by a team of AI scientists from the Chinese Academy of Sciences. The company uses the ScienceOne Scientific Foundation Model to power its ScienceOra research platform. It combines expertise in cognitive intelligence, foundation models, and complex-systems modelling for enterprise applications. In Korea, the FTC rule applies to firms with global annual sales of 1 trillion won. It also targets firms with at least 1 million average monthly Korean online-site users.

ScienceOra will continue to refine its tools to better serve the international research community. The Korean FTC will monitor the implementation of its domestic representative system for foreign platforms. A three-month grace period exists for Korean compliance, but the January 21 deadline remains. The articles do not state when other sign-in options might be added to ScienceOra. They also leave open whether Wenge AI will appoint a legal representative in Korea.

stories.Headline: Orangeburg lawmaker Gilda Cobb-Hunter hosts forum on artificial intelligence and data centers
stories.Summary:
State Rep. Gilda Cobb-Hunter hosted a public education forum on artificial intelligence and data centers at Orangeburg-Calhoun Technical College in Orangeburg, South Carolina. The forum was held on November 20, 2026, according to WRDW and WIS. The University of Dubuque hosted a public forum on the potential benefits and drawbacks of artificial intelligence and data centers on Tuesday night, November 17, 2026, in Dubuque, Iowa. Students spent the semester researching data centers from several perspectives. The Orangeburg forum followed Orangeburg County's September approval of a moratorium halting new data center development and applications for at least 12 months.

The Orangeburg forum aimed to bring community members together to learn about the technology before making quick judgements. Elected officials, technology professionals and infrastructure representatives participated in the discussion. Warren Harley, general manager of the city of Orangeburg's Department of Public Utilities, said no plans are in motion for a data center at this time. Harley said any data center seeking to use the utility's system would pay the cost of service rather than passing it on to customers. The University of Dubuque students researched data centers' potential impact on water use, energy demand, land use and the environment, as well as ethical and public policy concerns.

Cobb-Hunter said she suspects many people, like her, are using the technology without really recognizing it. She said the point of the evening was to connect the dots, educate the community and enable informed decisions. Harley said whatever is done with respect to data centers or any big customer must not negatively impact the system or the customers served, from a rate perspective and a cost perspective. Harley said any data center looking to come onto the system will pay whatever cost it is to serve, and the utility will not pass that on to the customer. Donavan Tann, an English professor at the University of Dubuque, said the technology is inevitable and communities have to learn how to live with it.

Tann said he hopes people leave the event with a sense that the community gets to decide what that looks like. Tate Glaspie, who examined the potential environmental impacts of data centers, said communities must weigh the benefits of the technology against its potential consequences. Glaspie said it could be a huge beneficial thing to overall improve the quality of life, but the main concern is whether a huge aspect of quality of life is being sacrificed to make life simpler and more convenient. Glaspie said it is more of a moral obligation to take into account all factors that could potentially harm quality of life in order to make sophisticated and educated decisions. Orangeburg resident Rick Leonard said the discussion changed his thinking about the technology and its potential impact.

Leonard said he is glad a positive step is being taken, not just saying no, and instead saying this might be a great thing and he does not want to miss the boat. Several academic divisions across the University of Dubuque collaborated on the event, including aviation and flight, computing and applied technology, humanities, natural sciences and theology. In addition to student research presentations, the Dubuque forum featured a 90-minute panel discussion and question-and-answer session with three journalists from across the region. The panelists included Dubuque-based freelance journalist Benjamin Fisher, Wisconsin Watch reporter Tom Kertscher and The Gazette's Linn County local government reporter Grace Nieland. The Dubuque forum aimed to help community members better understand the technology and make informed decisions about data center development.

Cobb-Hunter said she is working to host a similar event in the near future. The articles leave open what the Orangeburg moratorium will mean after its at least 12-month period ends. The articles leave open what decisions community members will make about data center development after the forums. The articles leave open what further events Cobb-Hunter will host. The articles leave open what the University of Dubuque will do with the student research presented at its forum.

stories.Headline: Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services releases clinical AI roadmap to accelerate technology adoption
stories.Summary:
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services released a clinical artificial intelligence roadmap on Friday, November 15, 2026. This federal strategy aims to accelerate the development and adoption of clinical AI technologies within the healthcare system. The initiative focuses on improving data infrastructure, modernizing regulations, and reforming healthcare payment models to support innovation. It establishes necessary safeguards to protect patient safety, ensure data privacy, and maintain accountability for AI tools. The roadmap identifies these key components as essential for the responsible integration of AI into medical operations.

The plan requires expanded patient access to medical records and improved information exchange between providers to strengthen data infrastructure. CMS will coordinate with the Food and Drug Administration to create risk-based regulatory pathways for AI medical devices. This includes a competency-based evaluation approach and accelerated market pathways for clinical decision support and consumer wellness applications. The agency will explore outcomes-based reimbursement through the ACCESS model for chronic conditions and the LEAD and AHEAD models. These changes aim to reward technology that improves patient outcomes and reduces costs rather than increasing service volume.

CMS CIO Patrick Newbold stated in September that the agency views AI as a tool for achieving organizational goals. He explained that the agency is shifting its strategy to measure operational outcomes instead of relying on adoption statistics. CMS uses its Tech Pulse initiative to track technology-related objectives and key results to assess progress toward priorities. The agency intends to support staged technology adoption through continuous monitoring, patient consent, and transparent performance reporting. These efforts are designed to build public trust while addressing algorithmic bias and cybersecurity risks.

More than 60 companies, including Apple, Amazon, Google, Oracle, Anthropic, and OpenAI, pledged support at an August 2025 event. These companies committed to a patient-centered digital health ecosystem focused on AI-enabled solutions and data interoperability. Patients in Utah are affected by pilot programs that allow AI to renew and write some medical prescriptions. These residents can access these AI services for a few dollars, but federal accountability for these tools remains unclear. The roadmap aims to clarify who is liable when AI harms a patient, though it does not resolve this.

The agency launched QualTech to seek commercially available technologies that can address various healthcare quality challenges. Through its Center for Clinical Standards and Quality, CMS identified four priority areas for AI-assisted patient safety reviews. These priorities also include support for annual wellness visits, digital quality measurement, and a national hospital quality dashboard. The roadmap calls for clinical AI to meet a safety and effectiveness standard that is better than today. It also proposes partnering with state-level regulatory sandboxes to test these new clinical AI technologies.

The government will strengthen post-market surveillance mechanisms to collect real-world performance data on the safety of evolving technologies. Senior leaders from CMS, HHS, the Defense Health Agency, and the VA will discuss AI at a December 3 summit. This 2026 Healthcare Summit will explore health IT, data modernization, healthcare innovation, and contracting priorities for fiscal year 2027. stories.Headline: Africa Tech Festival 2026 opens in Cape Town to advance AI and digital transformation across the continent
stories.Summary:
The Africa Tech Festival 2026 officially opened on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, in Cape Town, South Africa, to advance digital transformation across the continent. Organizers launched this event to help Africa seize new opportunities in the age of artificial intelligence by bringing together various industry leaders and innovators. This gathering serves as a platform for policymakers, investors, entrepreneurs, and technology experts to explore emerging technologies and foster important partnerships for digital development. The festival focuses on positioning the continent as a leader in technology rather than just a consumer of solutions developed in other regions. It aims to drive inclusive growth and prosperity through the strategic application of artificial intelligence and other modern digital tools across Africa.

The 29th edition of the festival runs through Thursday at the Cape Town International Convention Centre under the theme Powering Africa's Digital Transformation. Organizers stated that the event brings together more than 13,500 attendees and 2,000 companies from over 130 countries to the South African city. The program features more than 450 speakers and 350 exhibitors who participate in keynote speeches, panel discussions, technical masterclasses, and various investment forums. Six interconnected content pillars guide the event, which are Telecoms and Connectivity, Data Centers, Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity, Startups, and Digital Transformation. These pillars cover key areas such as digital infrastructure, entrepreneurship, emerging technologies, and the overall growth of the digital economy across the continent.

South African Deputy President Paul Mashatile delivered a virtual opening address where he urged African countries to shape the global artificial intelligence landscape. He stated that the continent must become a developer and exporter of emerging technologies to ensure they advance local developmental goals and prosperity. Mashatile argued that digital transformation is fundamentally about human development and must be people-centered to be truly effective for all African citizens. He called for stronger partnerships, bold investment, and decisive action to turn these high-level discussions into tangible progress for the entire region. The deputy president emphasized that Africa will compete in the age of AI by solving its own challenges and harnessing local talent.

Mashatile warned that millions of people could be left behind due to inadequate broadband access, high connectivity costs, skills shortages, and infrastructure gaps. He identified five priorities, including building future-ready digital infrastructure, investing in human capital, strengthening innovation ecosystems, and building trust through responsible digital governance. The deputy president also highlighted the African Continental Free Trade Area as a key opportunity to establish a single digital market across Africa. He argued that closer regional integration would help drive investment and innovation while promoting more inclusive growth for the continent's diverse populations. To realize this, he noted the need for interoperable payment systems, harmonized regulations, trusted data flows, and stronger collaboration across national borders.

The articles describe the Africa Tech Festival as one of the largest and most influential technology events currently held on the African continent. It brings together a wide array of participants, including providers of AI solutions and startups, to showcase their latest technological advancements. The event structure includes roundtables and networking opportunities designed to connect innovators with the investors and policymakers needed to scale digital projects. The background provided shows a push for Africa to move beyond the mere adoption of foreign technologies to build its own capabilities. This shift is intended to address specific development challenges while creating technological solutions that have relevance on a global scale.

The festival continues its scheduled activities through Thursday, featuring an exhibition of companies from the telecommunications and technology sectors and various specialist industry sessions. Participants will continue to engage in panel debates and networking to foster the partnerships required for the continent's digital transformation and growth. The articles leave open how the proposed five priorities for digital infrastructure and human capital will be funded and implemented across nations. It remains unclear which specific countries will lead the effort to create the single digital market through the African Continental Free Trade Area. The texts do not specify the exact timeline for achieving the goal of becoming a global exporter of emerging AI technologies.

stories.Headline: Codefi CTO Brian Holdman says AI is here to stay and cuts client software costs
stories.Summary:
Brian Holdman, chief technology officer at Codefi, said artificial intelligence “can’t be ignored” and is “here to stay.” Holdman made the comments in a Heartland News report by Blake Schowalter published Nov. 19, 2026, at 5:36 PM CST and updated two hours later. The report came from Cape Girardeau, Missouri, as tech stocks slide. Shares of both Nvidia and Microsoft have each fallen more than 30% in the past month. Holdman uses artificial intelligence every day and teaches startup businesses how to use the technology.

Holdman said he started out training companies and developing their software. He said AI can now build basic software on its own, cutting time and cost for his clients. He said building just a basic part of software, a proof of concept almost, may have cost clients $25,000 or $50,000. With AI, he said, they have been able to reduce that down to $2,000 or $3,000. Holdman said it is unclear how big an impact AI will have on local businesses.

Holdman said “we are seeing a lot of improvements in processing all around from different businesses.” He said a lot of individual stories you hear are that it is helping. He said a lot of people he talks to say they enjoy what they are doing much more now because they are able to hand off mundane tasks they do not really enjoy to AI. He said the benefit and usefulness of AI is still there, so he does not think AI is going to go anywhere. He said he hopes this is just a little dip and it will just go back up.

On Nov. 17, 2026, the S&P 500 fell 1.03% to 7,341, marking its fourth day of consecutive losses. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.74% to 24,328 on technology sector weakness, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled 1.64% to 50,759. Salesforce plummeted 9.45% as security jitters and further AI replacement fears combined to punish software stocks, and UnitedHealth Group dropped 5.42% on sweeping anti-fraud proposals for Medicare & Medicaid. Gold price dipped 0.18% to $3,849.20 as of U.S. market close, while the 10-Year Treasury yield edged down 3 basis points to 5.11%.

Energy stocks were the only real gainers, with financial services and healthcare stocks under the most pressure. Crypto stocks, including Coinbase Global and Robinhood Markets, tumbled as Bitcoin continued its losing streak, now down over 20% in the past month. The recent string of technology outages that hit air travel, banks and other firms weighed further on stocks, compounding AI chip concerns and broader negative sentiment. Consumers are stockpiling essentials, which helped Costco Wholesale Corp as Mizuho Securities just upped its price target on the stock. Post-close earnings from Nvidia beat analyst expectations, offering some reassurance on AI infrastructure demand and boosting peers in after-hours trading.

Investors are still digesting the impact of new U.S. measures restricting international access to advanced AI chips, not only for Nvidia but for the whole sector. Holdman said they hold Q&A sessions for the public, with their next conference scheduled for the first week of December. The articles do not say what the Q&A sessions cover beyond AI or where the December conference will be held. The articles do not say how the new U.S. measures will affect Codefi or its clients. The articles do not say whether the dip Holdman hopes will reverse has begun.
