stories.Headline: Anthropic lists on Nasdaq at $1.5tn valuation and raises a record $107bn
stories.Summary:
Anthropic became a listed company on Thursday, 19 November 2026, when its shares began trading on the Nasdaq in New York. Dario Amodei, the co-founder, rang the Nasdaq MarketSite opening bell with his sister and fellow co-founder Daniela at the start of trading. The shares were priced at $83 each, above the indicated range of $70 to $78, and began trading at £111.50. The listing raised $107bn, a record sum, and the company was valued at $1.5tn at the listing price. At the opening trading price its market capitalisation reached $2tn, and only 14 months earlier it had raised money at a valuation of $183bn.

The prospectus detailed $900bn of spending commitments for computing power and infrastructure, and $26bn of the listing proceeds came from a cornerstone placement. That placement went to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC, and the banks collected $550m of underwriting fees. Anthropic is loss-making, with projected revenues in 2026 of $50bn-ish, and tech analysts have pencilled in roughly $600bn of revenue in 2030. Nasdaq entry will be quick, but S&P 500 inclusion will take at least a year, and the company was founded five years ago.

Dario Amodei said as trading started that the company was hoping to be investment grade at some point in the future. He said: "Obviously, at some point in the future we're hoping to be investment grade," and the article noted that the price at which Anthropic borrows matters fundamentally. The prospectus said the technology "could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity". The article asked whether Anthropic, loss-making and with projected revenues in 2026 of $50bn-ish, can possibly be worth $1.5tn-plus.

The European Central Bank issued a reminder this week about how much capital is being bet on the AI revolution and how little transparency there is around the funding of hyperscalers and other suppliers. Its report said big tech firms are estimated to have total off-balance-sheet commitments of more than $4tn as of the second quarter of 2026. It warned of "historical parallels with the dotcom and sub-prime bubbles". Truist chief market strategist Keith Lerner noted that tech valuations have fallen 42% over the past year, and the sector has gone from outperforming the S&P 500 by 25% over six months to underperforming it by 6%. Bank of America's latest fund manager survey shows investors have cut tech exposure by the most since June 2006, and "Shark Tank" star Kevin O'Leary told the second article that investing in Anthropic is like investing in a young Amazon.

The second article said Thursday is supposed to be a celebration of AI, with Anthropic heading toward its long-awaited IPO at the Nasdaq. It said the very stocks that fueled this AI boom are still under pressure, pointing to sell-offs this week in CoreWeave, Salesforce and AMD. It said investors are questioning the AI spending, the valuations, the financing arrangements and whether the returns will ever justify the billions being poured into this technology. It said the AI build-out isn't disappearing, as seen from Nvidia on Tuesday, and that companies are still spending and the technology is still evolving. Lerner pointed out that previous tech pullbacks of more than 10% during this bull market were followed by an average rebound of 47%.

The first article said there was a late risk that investor sentiment towards the AI universe could be jinxed, or Jensened, by the soap opera at Nvidia. It said there was a worry that the AI bubble could burst when somebody tried to unload too much stock on the stock market in one go. It said the assembly of AI and AI-adjacent names in the cornerstone placement fed worries about the industry's circular financing. It said executives grumble that their IT budgets are finite and that nine-month-old versions, or cheaper "open weight" models from rivals, do the job for basic work. It said "commoditisation risk" could be the next year's valuation debate, and that debt, not just equity, will be a crucial part of this story.

stories.Headline: CareSource Foundation commits $1 million to scale proven AI for Medicaid care
stories.Summary:
The CareSource Foundation has committed $1 million to a single artificial intelligence project intended to improve health care for Medicaid members and people who face barriers to getting care, and it opened the request for proposals, titled “Advancing AI-Enabled Models for Care and Community Transformation,” on Nov. 10. The foundation is seeking applicants who are past the concept stage, saying it wants more than a promising idea. The funding provides up to $500,000 a year over two years, with one award expected. Concept papers are due Jan. 6, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. EST, full proposals from invited applicants are due Feb. 12, the award will be announced March 18, and the project starts in the second quarter of 2027.

Every proposal must show relevance to Medicaid, underserved and high-need populations, and the foundation is most interested in AI-enabled solutions with existing capabilities or proven models that are ready to be put into operation, evaluated and scaled. At the full-proposal stage, 30% of the score goes to the solution and technical approach and 15% goes to data, privacy, security and responsible AI, with reviewers also weighing measurable impact, organizational experience and capacity, operational readiness, cost effectiveness, and the potential to sustain and scale the work. The lead applicant must be an eligible nonprofit, and technology vendors cannot apply on their own. Applicants must name specific outcomes and key performance indicators and explain how their approach addresses equity, and the selected organization will send regular performance and progress reports along with qualitative material such as case studies and impact stories.

The foundation said AI has the potential to fundamentally improve how people experience health care, and it described responsible AI as fundamental to making innovation useful and trustworthy rather than separate from it. It pointed to places AI could help for Medicaid and underserved populations, including spotting emerging risks sooner, improving care coordination and navigation, personalizing outreach, connecting people with community resources and lowering barriers to care, and it said it wants the benefits to show up in people’s real experiences with the health care system. On scalability, the foundation said it will assess whether there is a credible path to sustaining and expanding impact beyond the grant period, not simply whether a pilot worked during its two years of funding. Details are at caresource.com/foundationgrant.

stories.Headline: Pontifical Gregorian University forum participants develop solutions for Catholic AI accountability in Rome
stories.Summary:
The Builders AI Forum, an interdisciplinary conference hosted by the Pontifical Gregorian University, held a two-day program of workshops in Rome on Nov. 5-6, 2026, aimed at identifying problems facing Catholic AI development. The forum was formed two years ago and holds annual gatherings in Rome. This year's theme was "Uniting to Shape AI Before It Shapes Us." The gathering brought together church leaders, technology developers, venture capitalists and policymakers from around the world. It took place in the same weekend that Pope Leo XIV spoke to Argentines about the "challenges posed by artificial intelligence and unregulated automation."

The conference examined the lack of human accountability within AI models, potential system biases against particular languages and cultures, and the dangers of treating machines as human persons. Participants then worked together to develop possible solutions for their communities and dioceses. The conference focused on the need for positive action in addition to technology regulations. It emphasized that forming thriving Catholic communities, building responsible and properly sourced AI tools, and calling governments and tech developers to protect human labor are essential tasks for the church today. The forum's theme framed the two-day program of workshops held at the Pontifical Gregorian University.

Matthew Harvey Sanders, founder of the forum and CEO of Longbeard, the company behind AI tools such as Magisterium AI and Vulgate, framed responsible human development of AI as a duty for the church in his opening address. He quoted Leo and called Catholic developers to fill the gaps of agency, instances where AI lacks human oversight and accountability, that are often created by AI developers. Sanders said a machine that can be blamed is a convenient place for everyone above it to leave the blame. He said that before any parish, school or hospital lets an agent act for a person, someone must be able to stop it, and someone must answer for it. Sanders presented a vision for "digitizing the church's patrimony and universalizing access to it" that he has worked to implement through Longbeard's AI products.

Cardinal Michael Czerny, who heads a Vatican commission on artificial intelligence, used an image from Magnifica Humanitas contrasting two biblical construction sites, Babel and Jerusalem, as examples of different ways that technology can be developed. He said both are collective efforts, yet the manner of constructing and the outcome are very different in the two sites. Czerny said the difference between Babel and Jerusalem lies in the desire that guides the act of building. He said the contrast between the two cities presents today's primary question: out of what desire shall we build, deploy and employ artificial intelligence? Sanders told the National Catholic Reporter that he sees AI as an "unfortunate means" to evangelize the world, emphasizing that building authentic Christian community is the ultimate goal.

Sanders said he does not think Catholic AI should need to exist, and that if everyone were well formed and living in good, vibrant Catholic communities, pressing fundamental existential questions would get answered by osmosis. He said the only reason they decided they needed to develop Catholic AI was that they could see a wave of interest in the Catholic faith and were not prepared for the scale. He said their thinking was AI could be a really good instrument in the short term to help ensure people get answers to fundamental questions, but then they need to get this person into community. In his closing speech, Sanders encouraged participants not to stand idle in the face of AI's challenges, but to take action in building communities and technologies that uphold and promote human dignity. Sanders said that a year ago, Pope Leo prayed that this forum's work would bear fruit, and that fruit is something you can see and hold, and it feeds someone.

Leo's encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, called AI "a valuable tool ... [that] calls for a measured and vigilant approach." Leo warned tech developers to "embed values in their projects with due seriousness: with transparency, responsibility toward affected communities and careful attention to ensuring that what is being cultivated is a genuine good." Leo's Nov. 6-17 Latin America trip included a stop in Argentina, where he spoke to representatives of the country's work community about the dignity of labor and the dangers of encroaching technology.

On Nov. 8, the pope addressed workers, business and trade union leaders, and teachers and students at the Catholic University of Argentina in Buenos Aires. Leo reminded the crowd of "the dignity of the human person ... [who] is the author, the center and the goal of all economic and social life." Leo warned that "the challenges posed by artificial intelligence and unregulated automation can put countless jobs at risk and become a real threat to proper integral human development."

The pope's address came as Argentina's Congress considers legislation submitted by the Javier Milei administration that would grant legal recognition to companies operated solely by AI. Milei's proposed legislation comes after an announcement last October that a massive AI data center project, Stargate Argentina, will be constructed in Patagonia. The articles leave open what the forum's participants will do with the solutions they developed for their communities and dioceses. They also leave open the outcome of Argentina's Congress consideration of the Milei administration's legislation on companies operated solely by AI.

stories.Headline: Trina Storage unveils Elementa Hybrid Genset for AI data centers at RE+ 2026
stories.Summary:
Trina Storage introduced a new hybrid power product on Nov. 18, 2026 at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas, combining gas-fired generation with the company's battery storage platforms under a single hybrid plant controller. The Elementa Hybrid Genset is aimed at data center developers that need on-site power while grid interconnection is delayed, limited, or unavailable. The launch follows a preview of the solution at Data Center World Power in September. Trina Storage unveiled Elementa Hybrid Genset at RE+ 2026, according to a PR Newswire release dated Nov. 19, 2026 in Las Vegas. The solution combines gas-fired generation from qualified partners with Trina Storage's Elementa DC battery systems and Electra AC platform, coordinated by a hybrid plant controller.

The system consists of three main components, with gas generation providing sustained power using reciprocating engines rated up to 2.5 MW in modular configurations. Trina Storage acts as the system integrator, while qualified engine partners supply the generation equipment. The Elementa and Electra BESS solution provides rapid power response and grid-forming capabilities, with reference configurations based on 5 MW/10 MWh building blocks. A hybrid plant controller coordinates all power sources in real time, and its scalable control architecture is designed to support applications ranging from 5 MW to 1 GW. The solution supports four reference scenarios: grid-connected with backup generation, grid-constrained, bridge-to-grid, and off-grid, and solar PV can also be integrated where appropriate.

Load Transient Sensing uses the power plant controller to predict changes in power demand and coordinate a rapid BESS response, allowing the system to accommodate swift load fluctuations before slower-responding power sources can adjust. Hybrid Power Coordination dynamically coordinates power output between the BESS and gas generators, so when a sudden load increase occurs the BESS responds immediately while the gas generators gradually ramp up. Fault Isolation and Resilient Power Supply addresses failures, and when a fault occurs the control system identifies and isolates the affected equipment while the BESS and remaining available gas generators respond to support critical loads. Two system architectures are available, with Load Sensing prioritizing cost efficiency and system performance while Double Conversion provides full electrical isolation and enhanced power quality. The choice between the two depends on the IT load profile and grid conditions at a given site.

Eric Cao, Vice President of Trina North American PV and BESS Business, said AI data centers have demanding power requirements, particularly when grid capacity is constrained or workloads fluctuate rapidly. Cao said Elementa Hybrid Genset brings gas generation, battery storage, and hybrid controls together in one system architecture, designed to coordinate these resources according to project needs. Trina Storage describes itself as a global leader in energy storage solutions and enters the growing field of hybrid power solutions for data centers where grid access cannot keep pace with demand. The company framed the product as a response to a pairing of limitations, since AI workloads can cause rapid and substantial fluctuations in power demand that gas generators alone may struggle to follow. Battery storage responds quickly to those fluctuations but is not designed to supply energy through extended outages on its own, according to Trina Storage.

Trina Storage says it continues to develop and validate the product through simulation, hardware-in-the-loop testing, and an integrated validation platform incorporating real power generation, conversion, and storage equipment. Further testing of grid-forming functionality and hybrid control strategies is ongoing, alongside relevant certification activities. Final system configurations and performance specifications will be assessed based on individual project requirements. The company describes the product as designed to accommodate different power requirements and grid conditions, from grid-connected sites seeking additional power flexibility to projects operating with limited or no grid access. System architecture and equipment selection can be tailored to each project's load profile, site conditions, and operational requirements.

Trina Storage is currently engaging with data center developers and project partners to explore potential applications and develop project-specific configurations. The articles state that these capabilities help coordinate different power sources within one system, with the specific operating strategy depending on the project configuration and requirements. The articles leave open the final system configurations and performance specifications, which will be assessed based on individual project requirements. The articles also leave open the outcomes of the ongoing grid-forming functionality testing, hybrid control strategy testing, and relevant certification activities. The articles do not state when the Elementa Hybrid Genset will be commercially available or which specific projects will use it.

stories.Headline: Firecrawl opens its first office outside the US in downtown Toronto and hires for research, growth and engineering roles
stories.Summary:
Firecrawl, a company based in San Francisco, opened its first office outside the United States in downtown Toronto. This expansion occurred around November 2026 to support the company's growth in the artificial intelligence sector. The firm provides tools that allow AI agents to search and pull information from the web. It is currently hiring for several new roles in research, growth, and engineering. This move marks the first time the company has established a site outside of California.

The company is hiring a back end infrastructure engineer with a salary between 217,000 and 233,000 dollars. A web automation engineer role also pays between 217,000 and 233,000 dollars and requires three years of experience. The founding security engineer position pays between 208,000 and 226,000 dollars and reports to the head of core platform. These hybrid roles require employees to be on site three days per week in Toronto. The team will expand Alexandria, which offers one interface to government indexes, research development, and data providers.

CEO Caleb Peffer stated that AI is creating a new knowledge economy where people are paid for sharing knowledge. He described Alexandria as the economic model that makes this new knowledge economy possible for users. Peffer noted that Toronto has been at the heart of modern AI and is the best place to build. The company aims to support a fast growing community of developers who are building AI agents in Canada. These new hires will help bring more data providers onto the Alexandria platform for the company.

Mayor Olivia Chow said that Toronto is where much of modern AI was born and welcomed the company. She stated that companies choose Toronto because of the city's diversity, universities, and the available local talent. Chow believes this investment provides good jobs for Torontonians and helps the city grow as an innovation home. The expansion affects local developers and job seekers who can apply for the open positions online. Other tech companies like Lyft and OpenTable have also opened offices in Toronto during this year.

Firecrawl is based in San Francisco and creates infrastructure for AI agents to access the live web. Lyft opened a 90,000 square foot office at 100 King Street West in September for 500 jobs. OpenTable debuted a 24,000 square foot office at 134 Peter Street in May for its global team. These companies are joining a growing ecosystem of technology firms establishing a presence in the Canadian city. The articles highlight Toronto as a primary hub for artificial intelligence and high skilled technical talent.

The Toronto team will now work to expand the indexes of the Alexandria knowledge infrastructure for AI agents. They will focus on making Firecrawl fast and reliable against a web that constantly changes and fights back. The company will continue to hire for roles in legal, finance, and people and culture in Toronto. The articles do not state the total number of employees Firecrawl intends to hire for this office. It remains open how many data providers will eventually be integrated into the Alexandria platform.

stories.Headline: Texas provost Angela Bauer urges universities to let faculty decide where AI belongs in learning
stories.Summary:
Angela Bauer, executive vice president for academic affairs and provost at Texas Woman’s University, wrote a Texas Tribune opinion piece published November 19, 2026, arguing that higher education is gripped by an existential debate over artificial intelligence playing out nationwide at governing board meetings, in news headlines and on social media feeds. She said conversations at times devolve into a rigid binary of either banning AI to protect academic integrity or embracing it wholesale to stay relevant. She said the polarization is understandable because AI can perform tasks once viewed as uniquely human, such as reasoning through problems, constructing arguments and generating original text. She said AI is forcing higher education to rethink the nature of learning, what constitutes mastery and the evolving role of the professor. She said academic leaders have a fundamental responsibility to confront these existential questions head on rather than letting the debate polarize them.

Bauer wrote that preparing Texas students for an AI-integrated workforce requires moving beyond false choices and embracing the complexity of this moment. She said there are times when learning must occur in an explicitly AI-free space, because building cognitive muscle, developing a unique voice and mastering foundational logic require unassisted human effort. She compared a student letting a machine do the heavy lifting to a runner who cannot build endurance riding in a golf cart. She said that in business, healthcare and graphic arts, AI is rapidly altering how work gets done and AI fluency is no longer optional but fundamental. She cited a recent Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas study highlighting how generative AI is shifting the entry level job market for college graduates, automating routine tasks and raising what employers expect on day one.

Bauer said that at Texas Woman’s University, leaders have trusted their experts, namely faculty, to develop an AI roadmap for students rather than giving top-down system mandates. She said faculty within their specific disciplines determine where AI belongs and where it does not, with an English professor possibly requiring pen-and-paper drafts for a personal reflection while a nursing or business professor might integrate AI tools to analyze clinical data or develop marketing strategies. She said this nuanced approach honors academic rigor and disciplinary expertise, and that faculty have been equipped with both the autonomy and the resources to navigate these decisions because so much is at stake for students. She said a digital divide is emerging as AI reshapes the economy, with students who had prior access or experience with technology gaining AI fluency informally while first generation students risk falling behind. She said closing this literacy gap is central to the mission and that failing to teach students to use AI tools critically, ethically and strategically risks leaving them behind in the economy they are being prepared to lead.

Bauer said the issue extends far beyond the job market, because as statewide and national debates continue about policy guardrails around digital safety, data privacy and automated decision-making, society needs an educated citizenry that understands technology. She said policies alone are not enough and that voters, professionals and community leaders must understand how these models function, how to apply the technology ethically and its potential impact on human health and the environment. She said that as an academic year gets underway across Texas, the polarization should be left behind. She said AI is not going to replace the human element of higher education but is challenging people to refine it. Texas Woman’s University is described as the nation’s largest public university with a woman-focused mission.

Kate Perez of the Chicago Tribune reported that at DePaul University roughly a dozen students routinely wrestle with how much artificial intelligence should and could influence the human experience, spending hours at the Responsible AI Systems and Experiences, or RAISE, Lab on the university’s Loop campus exploring how AI affects daily life. DePaul recently released “Guiding Principles on Artificial Intelligence,” a tome calling for academic integrity, intellectual honesty, transparency and human-centered use of the technology. The principles were born out of the school’s 26-member Provost’s Advisory Committee on Artificial Intelligence, which worked for over a year to develop them and meets monthly to discuss policy, practices and how AI is used in the classroom. Jay Cunningham, RAISE Lab creator and assistant professor of computing, said DePaul’s principles, published last month, go beyond issues of academic integrity. Cunningham, who launched the lab in 2025, said his goal is to help students understand that AI is a tool that attempts to model human behavior, human interactions and human decision-making, and that the job of humans is to wield tools in ways that serve them best.

Cunningham said that over the past half-decade he has seen more fields demand that workers understand AI, creating a need for students to learn the technology as it progresses. Professor of English John Shanahan said DePaul published a statement on AI in 2023, but in this age of rapid transition that is like 100 years ago. Shanahan, who chaired the university’s Advisory Committee on Artificial Intelligence, brought together colleagues who worried about AI’s implications for higher education and others who thrived in the new technology, creating a communal space for faculty across disciplines from acting to computer science to talk about the new programming. He said launching the committee was a chance to get a sense of what is going on in the units, provoke discussion so faculty talk about what they hear from students, and vet good ideas about what to do moving forward. Other Chicago campuses have formed committees to examine how to integrate AI into higher education, launched AI classes and majors and pushed for AI literacy among students and faculty, and several schools including the City Colleges of Chicago and Northwestern University now offer AI-related programs and degrees.

Nationwide, schools are considering how to inform students about AI use and best practices through websites, classes and training, and their approach depends on the institution. At the University of Chicago, a new master’s degree in applied AI will launch in fall 2027, while the law school prohibits note-taking on electronic devices in some classes. This fall, Northwestern University launched an undergraduate major in AI and an AI webpage of tools and resources that, according to the site, enable students, faculty and staff to use generative AI effectively and responsibly. Across the schools of City Colleges of Chicago, which serves more than 73,000 students a year through its network of multiple public community colleges, the system introduced its first AI degree program at Wilbur Wright College this fall, and students can now earn an Associate of Applied Science degree in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Development. City Colleges’ Provost and Chief Academic Officer Mark Potter told the Tribune the degree is applicable and relevant across all disciplines, from history and law to transportation and distribution, and that before the new program City Colleges created a district-wide AI steering committee that helped hone and articulate the school’s position on AI.

Potter said preparing students for an AI-enabled workforce and society is essential, that the school cannot shy away from this technology or bury its head in the sand, and that students need AI competencies including responsible and ethical use of AI, a position he said the system started with and still carries forward. Potter said he hopes people recognize City Colleges as a place where they can cultivate their AI knowledge, learn skills and build careers in the field. City Colleges’ Associate Vice Chancellor of technology sector strategy, Ayoka Noelle Mota Samuels, told the Tribune the school system is intended to be a space where people can afford to learn AI skills, adding that people can learn AI in a responsible way and know that it is not just transactional. Samuels said it is important that City Colleges be a recognizable and trusted place for people of all backgrounds to learn about AI, and that being part of the larger educational conversation around AI means more people will have access to the field than before. She said that without an education community part of being in leadership around AI, different folks do run the danger of being left out, and that City Colleges makes sure people are included at whatever level and stage of understanding and interest with AI.

Shanahan said that back at DePaul there has been a growing recognition over the last two years that AI does not necessarily have to be feared. He said the evolution of AI has brought a mix of enthusiasm, excitement, skepticism and fear, and that the advancements have benefited the institution, while acknowledging that they are at the beginning of this. He said the university is having conversations and being proactive about meeting the challenges of AI integration. He said AI is not going to go away, so there is a recognition of the need to negotiate a place with it and to ask what it means to be a creative person, a thinker and a writer with AI next to you all the time. He said there will be times when it is useful to use and times when it is better to think your own thoughts and write your own sentences, and that it is both.

stories.Headline: Malaysia regulator seeks details from Anthropic over alleged election manipulation
stories.Summary:
Malaysia’s communications regulator is seeking further information from the artificial intelligence company Anthropic over an alleged foreign-linked election manipulation operation targeting users in the country, following claims that its Claude technology was used to build fake social media accounts, voter targeting systems and fabricated news websites. The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission said this in a written parliamentary reply dated 17 November. The ministry said Anthropic had linked the operation to BBS Bilisim Teknolojileri, a technology company based in Istanbul, Türkiye. Anthropic had terminated the identified Claude accounts and implemented mitigation measures, the ministry said. Anthropic published its threat intelligence report earlier in September.

Anthropic identified and removed an account that used Claude to operate a commercial election manipulation platform primarily targeting Malaysian users, and the platform was allegedly sold by BBS Bilisim Teknolojileri as a paid influence-as-a-service capability. Anthropic said the operation’s infrastructure was marketed as a “military-grade, AI-driven, real-time political operations ecosystem”. The platform was used to profile and target voters across all 222 Malaysian parliamentary constituencies, drawing on census and electoral data, including millions of voter records. Its targeting focused on sensitive political and social fault lines involving race, religion and royalty. Anthropic also found that the platform managed more than 1,000 fake accounts on X, formerly Twitter.

The accounts were designed to inflate engagement metrics and evade social media platforms’ detection systems, with mechanisms to make them appear authentic before being deployed in influence operations. Its dashboards allowed operators to monitor likes and views generated by the fake accounts against specific targets, as well as set artificial view targets. Anthropic observed a request to generate one million artificial views on the account of Malaysia’s sitting prime minister, in support of the leader. Anthropic cautioned that the figures recorded by the platform were self-reported and could not be independently verified. The operation also ran a fabricated news outlet called “Malaysia Pulse”, which was supplied with content through an AI rewriting pipeline.

Its operators additionally generated fabricated intelligence dossiers containing false allegations against an opposition politician and civil society organisations, and Anthropic said its own research could find no corroboration for the allegations. Anthropic also found that the actors continued pursuing their objectives when Claude refused certain requests. In one instance, the model identified a document as material for political defamation, after which the actor negotiated sanitised wording to continue developing the same capability. The report further revealed that the actors had pursued a contract with MCMC, but Anthropic said it found no evidence that the pursuit had been successful. The ministry was responding to a question from Datuk Seri Dr Ronald Kiandee (PN-Beluran), who asked whether MCMC’s investigation had identified those responsible for the alleged political manipulation operation and what action had been taken against the network of fake accounts and fabricated news portals involved.

Based on the information and evidence obtained, MCMC will determine appropriate follow-up action within its jurisdiction and under relevant legal provisions, the ministry said. This could include cooperation with enforcement and security agencies, digital platform providers and other relevant parties, where necessary. Any regulatory or enforcement action would be carried out under the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998, the Online Safety Act 2025 and other applicable laws. Separately, the government, through the Ministry of Digital, is drafting an Artificial Intelligence Governance Bill to strengthen the country’s AI governance framework, including accountability, risk management and the responsibilities of parties developing and deploying AI systems. The government added that it would continue strengthening its monitoring of potential AI misuse and cooperation with technology providers, digital platforms and relevant agencies to address online harms and maintain a safe, transparent and trusted digital environment.

The developments also come as Malaysia seeks to strengthen its position in the global digital economy. The country climbed seven places to 27th out of 70 economies in the 2026 IMD World Digital and AI Ranking, making it the second-highest-ranked economy in ASEAN after Singapore. While Malaysia improved 21 places to 14th globally for AI adoption, its governance ranking slipped to 38th from 36th, making it the country’s weakest-performing area. IMD said Malaysia would need a more seamless regulatory environment, faster digital transformation across industries and stronger workforce skills to improve its standing. The ministry said MCMC is seeking clarification from Anthropic to ensure that any assessment and subsequent action would be based on sufficient information and evidence.

stories.Headline: Fujitsu Japan and partners verify AI cuts manual clinical trial screening by 89 percent
stories.Summary:
Fujitsu Japan, the National Cancer Center Hospital East, and Paradigm Health conducted joint research to streamline clinical trial candidate screening. This project used a Large Language Model and the Paradigm Platform to identify potential candidates for new drug trials. The verification study took place between June and the end of October 2026 in Kawasaki and Kashiwa. The partners confirmed that this AI approach significantly improved the efficiency of the candidate identification process. This research aimed to shorten patient recruitment timelines and expand participation opportunities for domestic and international trials.

The study used data from 22,334 patients in the Department of Respiratory Medicine to simulate a trial for EGFR gene mutations. Fujitsu Japan processed electronic medical records for 3,027 lung cancer patients through anonymization and structuring using a Large Language Model. Paradigm evaluated 540 patients with EGFR gene mutations based on five specific criteria to determine their clinical trial eligibility. The AI identified 57 priority candidates, and physicians later confirmed that 51 of these individuals were promising candidates. This automated overnight processing reduced the number of patient records requiring manual review by approximately 89 percent.

Fujitsu Japan, led by CEO Izuru Kokubu, aims to commercialize a service for candidate screening and enrollment by fiscal year 2027. The company promotes the Uvance business model to create social value and streamline clinical trials through the use of AI. Toshihiko Doi directs the National Cancer Center Hospital East, which collaborated to verify the application of the Paradigm Platform. Paradigm Health, based in Columbus, Ohio, and led by CEO Kent Thoelke, provided the matching platform for the research. These partners stated that the system allows institutions to determine eligibility based on standardized criteria without relying on individual expertise.

Medical professionals, including physicians and clinical research coordinators, are affected because they previously relied on manual reviews and personal knowledge. The research shows that AI can alleviate the burden on medical staff and expedite clinical trial opportunities for patients. Patients are affected because the system helps them avoid missing opportunities to consider new treatment options for their conditions. The process ensures that final eligibility is determined by physicians based on trial requirements and the consent of the patient. These results represent candidates identified during research and do not guarantee that these individuals will actually participate in trials.

Drug loss is a pressing social challenge where new treatments available overseas are not developed or approved within Japan. Personalized medicine based on biomarkers and genetic mutations has advanced in oncology, making clinical trial participation criteria increasingly complex. Medical staff must currently review dispersed information across genomic data, test results, treatment histories, and electronic medical records. Differences in medical data formats and unstructured data in Japanese records create obstacles for the utilization of global data. This background creates an urgent need to promote clinical trials for new drugs to expand treatment opportunities for patients.

Fujitsu Japan will now proceed with commercializing a service to support the process from candidate screening to patient enrollment. The company targets a launch by the end of fiscal year 2027 to help expand clinical trial capacity. Partners will promote the adoption of this solution at medical institutions across Japan to facilitate broader access to therapies. stories.Headline: Apple ties Siri AI daily usage limits to iCloud storage plan tiers
stories.Summary:
Mahmoud, a reviewer for Macworld, hit the daily usage limit for Siri AI while working on an article about Apple TV. This occurred after he made numerous straightforward requests over twenty minutes on tvOS, including installing an app and surfacing reminders. He discovered these restrictions after Apple rolled out daily usage limits based on iCloud storage tiers in iOS 27.3. The reviewer found that his requests were barred until the following day, despite his paid subscription plan. He noted that the experience was far more restrictive than any other popular AI chatbot he had used.

The system applies to advanced requests on iPhone, iPad, and Mac, but excludes simple tasks like setting a timer. Limits are tracked per device and feature category, resetting around midnight in the user's current time zone. The 200GB plan for $2.99 per month offers 2x limits, while the 2TB plan for $9.99 offers 5x. The 6TB plan costs $29.99 for 10x limits, and the 12TB plan costs $59.99 for 20x limits. These boosts are unavailable in China, Brazil, the EU, the UK, and South Korea for select features.

Apple claims that Siri AI includes a generous daily usage limit for all users, regardless of their iCloud+ subscription. The company stated in a support document that cloud-based models require expensive AI chips, electricity, cooling, and network capacity. Apple intends to pass these computing costs on to users through the tiered storage system. They noted that users will receive a warning as they near a limit and notification when it is hit. The company also specified that the AFM Cloud Pro model in Shortcuts requires at least the 200GB tier.

Mahmoud was affected despite having a 2TB plan, as his iPhone displayed a banner stating the daily limit was reached. He found he could no longer perform multi-step queries, such as checking the weather and texting it to his mother. Other family members on his account share the same pool of requests on a first-come, first-served basis. His iPad and Mac also warned him that he was approaching their respective limits because the shared pool was exhausted. This affects anyone using advanced requests, including Photos tools like Clean Up, Extend, Image Playground, and Spatial Reframing.

Apple first mentioned daily limits at WWDC in June and added a warning about paid expanded access in September. The current system turns iCloud+ storage tiers into AI allowance tiers to manage the cost of data center resources. Simple requests happen directly on the device and do not count toward the daily cap for the user. Third-party apps using Apple Foundation Models in Private Cloud Compute also count toward these daily usage limits. The 50GB plan offers the same basic limit as users who do not pay for extra storage.

Beta testers using iOS 27.3 will now learn exactly where the free usage cap sits for various AI features. Users who hit the limit must wait for a reset or upgrade to a more expensive iCloud+ storage plan. The articles leave open the specific numerical values of the limits, as Apple has not listed actual numbers. It remains unclear how tokens are tallied, making it difficult for users to predict when they will hit limits. The full extent of which other features are covered by the cap is not yet exhaustively listed.

stories.Headline: NTT Data's supply chain head urges firms to connect isolated AI uses through multiagent systems
stories.Summary:
Pedro Béjar Castán published an article on 13 November 2026 on nttdata.com urging organizations to stop doing isolated AI and to implement multiagent systems. He wrote that the CEO talks about AI in broad terms while the innovation team runs proofs of concept and some business functions have started pilots. He said demonstrations, vendor conversations and internal experiments are all happening at the same time. He wrote that proof is emerging that AI adds value, yet he keeps hearing the same thing: "We don't know what to do next." His answer is that organizations probably don't need another use case and need to connect the ones they already have.

He described multiagent systems, where multiple AI agents work together across a business process to interpret what is happening, coordinate the response and take action. For a manufacturer that wanted to define and implement agentic intelligence throughout its value chain, NTT DATA ran 14 workshops for customer service, production, logistics and warehousing departments. The team spoke with more than 60 people and cataloged 129 improvement opportunities by the end of the process. Following a multiagent approach let NTT DATA group the 129 individual improvement opportunities into just 36 prioritized AI use cases. In one project, some shifts needed 10 frontline operators and others 4, and truck arrival patterns drove much of the staffing volatility.

Béjar Castán, managing director and global head of supply chain at NTT DATA, said he is responsible for leading NTT DATA's work with the World Economic Forum's Advanced Manufacturing and Supply Chain initiative. He wrote that NTT DATA combines deep industry and process knowledge with AI strategy, consulting, engineering and implementation expertise. He said NTT DATA can look across a value chain to identify where AI can make the biggest difference, connect opportunities that might otherwise be treated in isolation and then design, build and integrate the multiagent systems. He said plenty of firms will help you think, some partners specialize in strategy and others are strongest at implementation. He said what is harder to find is a partner that can do both.

He wrote that in supply chain management AI is already improving forecast accuracy, flagging changes in demand patterns, surfacing supplier risk earlier and optimizing transportation routes. He said each use case enhances only a single activity and a human is still required to pass the separate pieces of intelligence on. He described a multiagent environment where the system reads an order, checks the quantity against expected demand, identifies anomalies, evaluates stock-out risk over a two-week horizon, recommends a revised quantity, updates the planning system and notifies the people who need to know. He said multiagent systems are mostly used in software at the moment but will increasingly extend into the physical world through autonomous handling equipment, vision systems and connected assets on plant floors. He said a logistics specialist thinks about transportation and a warehouse manager thinks about staffing, and AI creates more value when you look at the process connecting the two.

He wrote that organizations have introduced AI capabilities function by function, launched pilot programs and encouraged employees to experiment with AI tools. He said this has led to many small use cases that save individual teams time and effort, but those use cases must be organized and connected for the organization as a whole to benefit. In one project, warehouse managers worried about staffing while the logistics team reported that trucks turned up early, late or in clusters at the docks. He said the two problems were in reality one use case, and looking at them together has allowed NTT DATA to synchronize operator availability with inbound and outbound truck movements. He said that if you can predict an important truck will be two hours late, you can place fewer employees in loading and more in preparing customer orders before the gap opens up.

He listed six steps: set the ambition, identify improvement opportunities, define the use cases, prioritize the use cases, choose your technical architecture and build a roadmap. He said most discussions and arguments are about prioritizing use cases, weighing the value each could create and whether the organization is ready to deliver it. He asked whether an organization has the data availability, process maturity and systems integration to make an effective AI use case. He wrote that the processes connected today could eventually be executed by physical AI, so it makes sense to prepare for that transition. He invited readers to request a half-day workshop to identify where AI will create value and turn a long list of possibilities into a practical plan.

stories.Headline: AI Inspo launches an AI social media agent that combines strategy, content creation, publishing and performance review
stories.Summary:
AI Inspo launched its AI-powered social media agent on Nov. 18, 2026, according to PR Newswire, bringing strategy, content creation, publishing and performance review into a single workflow. The company said the agent combines two core capabilities, social media strategy and creative content creation, which help users set priorities, turn plans into content and use performance insights to shape what comes next. AI Inspo described the platform as an all in one AI powered social media management platform for content creation, scheduling, account management, performance tracking and social media growth. The launch announcement was dated San Francisco, Nov. 18, 2026. QuVideo produced the analysis in the Quad City Herald, reviewed and distributed by Stacker, and AI Inspo is a flagship product from QuVideo.

AI Inspo said managing multiple social platforms and accounts often requires moving among planning tools, creative software, publishing schedulers and analytics dashboards, a fragmented process that adds repetitive work and can make it difficult to turn insights into action. The agent's strategy capability assesses account performance and recommends next steps based on each user's goals and stage of account development. AI Inspo also finds trending topics relevant to the account and helps turn them into content ideas, giving users a way to identify trends their audience may care about and connect those opportunities with publishing plans. Its creative capability lets users choose a viral reference and add their topic, and AI Inspo adapts the reference's format into ready-to-publish content built around that topic. Users can take an idea from trend discovery through creation and publishing, then review how it performs, and those insights inform the next content brief and help users refine their choice of topics and formats over time.

Dong Lin, CEO of QuVideo and Project Lead for AI Inspo, said AI Inspo was built around the real-world needs of creators and marketers managing multiple accounts across social media platforms. He said that by bringing research, data analysis and content creation together, the company aims to reduce repetitive tasks and give users more time to focus on strategy, informed decision-making and creativity. The agent remembers how users manage their accounts and create content, then tailors recommendations to their changing goals and workflows. That continuity lets users build on earlier work and receive guidance aligned with their current priorities, and account context and performance insights help users judge which trends and formats deserve further creative effort. AI Inspo said the workflow is designed to reduce routine work, leaving users more time for creative decisions and planning.

AI Inspo said an account's needs change as it develops, and for a creator launching a new account, early priorities may include choosing a content direction and establishing a consistent production routine. As the account matures, attention may shift to refining formats or improving an existing strategy. Alongside its AI agent, AI Inspo provides ongoing user support and a Discord community where creators, marketers and businesses can exchange ideas, seek guidance and refine their social media workflows. The company said this combination supports its mission to make high-quality content easier and more affordable to produce. The platform is designed for creators, marketers and businesses.

The Quad City Herald analysis said social media managers handling multiple accounts often find the difficult work falls between tools, with audience research in one document, content plans in another and performance data across several dashboards. It said publishing connects these activities only superficially, and a team can keep its calendar full while losing track of why a post was made or what its results should change. Marketing professor Mary Beth McCabe, in her account of the 2026 Social Media Marketing World/AI Business World event in Anaheim, highlighted agent autonomy, repeatable workflows and human leadership, and the 2027 AI Business World program lists workflow automation and AI operations. The analysis said AI should support human judgment, not replace it, and that by connecting strategy, content creation, publishing and performance analysis, AI could help teams streamline workflows, make better decisions and improve their results over time. It said the question is whether these systems connect evidence to decisions rather than simply accelerate production.

Sprout Social's 2025 Impact of Social Media Marketing report describes data silos and the demand for audience and competitor context, and Glimpse conducted the online survey for Sprout Social from May 30 to June 20, 2025, among 1,200 marketing leaders in the U.S., U.K. and Australia, respondents ranging from managers to CMOs, all with social media responsibilities. YouTube's official guidance states that from March 31, 2025, Shorts views counted starts and replays without a minimum watch time, and engaged views remained available as a separate metric. Buffer's AI Assistant supports brainstorming, rewriting and adapting posts for individual platforms. In a 2023 Sprout Social case study, San Francisco-based Plaid social media lead Matthew McConnell described handling publishing, responses and reporting as a team of one, tagging posts to compare performance, investigating weaker results and adjusting strategy for different audiences. A 2024 Science Advances study found that AI-generated ideas could improve evaluations of individual short stories while increasing their similarity among them, and in Generative AI at Work, Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li and Lindsey Raymond found larger gains among novice and less-skilled customer support workers, with minimal effects among experienced workers, while a Harvard Business School field experiment likewise found that effects depended on the task.

stories.Headline: Nvidia beats analyst estimates as board refuses to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
stories.Summary:
Nvidia reported third quarter results on November 18, 2026, beating analyst estimates. The company's board of directors refused to reinstate Jensen Huang as the chief executive officer. This was the first earnings report since Huang resigned from his leadership role. The board's chairman, Harvey Jones, stated that they do not intend to reinstate him. Investors and analysts had hoped for Huang's return during the earnings call.

Revenue reached 115.8 billion dollars, which was more than double the amount from a year ago. Data center revenue was 107.6 billion dollars, and the GAAP gross margin was 74.8 percent. The company guided fourth quarter revenue to 130 billion dollars, assuming no China data center compute revenue. The cloud backlog grew to 2.5 trillion dollars, and the Vera Rubin platform brought in almost 20 billion dollars. Nvidia sold 2.4 billion dollars of older Hopper chips to China last quarter.

Interim CEO Colette Kress said momentum is real and called the current situation business as usual. She raised the outlook for next year's growth to about 75 percent from 70 percent. Chairman Harvey Jones said the board will not reinstate Jensen Huang as the chief executive officer. Jensen Huang stated he would be honored to return in his first public statement since resigning. The board refused to take any questions regarding the resignation or the ongoing investigation.

An open letter supporting Huang's return has more than 188,000 names, though some signatures are disputed. Employees warned the board about the loss of irreplaceable talent in a separate letter. The SEC is conducting a civil investigation into whether Nvidia's disclosures misled its investors. President Trump said he would not mind a comeback for the former chief executive officer. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is pushing the board for answers regarding potentially illicit sales.

The company booked 104 billion dollars through its Singapore unit last year, nearly half of its revenue. Jensen Huang's daughter and son-in-law worked on the relationship with a firm called Megaspeed. The US government opened a probe into Megaspeed in 2024, and Justice now leads a criminal investigation. Nvidia put Megaspeed on a no sell list in June 2025 to avoid legal risks. The board established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee to manage these issues.

The board is searching for a permanent CEO both inside and outside of the company. New rules require licenses for top chips in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil within 90 days. Secretary Bessent wants answers from the board and outside counsel within ten days about company culture. President Trump may discuss Nvidia during meetings this week with President Xi and President Putin. The articles leave open whether the visionary founder will ever return to lead the company.

stories.Headline: GAO reports AI expands cyberattack reach while giving defenders new detection tools
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Government Accountability Office reported on November 20, 2026, that artificial intelligence is expanding the reach of cyberattacks while providing new detection tools for agencies and companies. The agency noted that generative AI can create deepfakes and convincing phishing messages, while agentic systems can adapt across multiple stages with very little human involvement. These technologies allow threat actors to magnify the impact of traditional attacks against essential services like telecommunications, energy, water, and financial systems. The report cited a June 2026 instance where AI agents tested malware and a February 2026 campaign where a low-skill actor used commercial AI services.

To counter these threats, organizations are using machine learning and generative AI to inspect network traffic, find source-code flaws, and manage large volumes of information. The GAO outlined four policy goals to improve cybersecurity guidance, address research gaps, oversee the AI life cycle, and strengthen the workforce. Among sixteen suggested options, the agency recommended risk-based procurement, larger testing environments, and human authorization for consequential actions. It also advised creating backup arrangements, such as manual procedures or rule-based tools, in case AI systems fail or produce unexpected results.

The GAO stated that cyber defenders struggle because AI tools are difficult to test and lack sufficient guidance or data for proper use. The agency highlighted concerns regarding outdated governance, data privacy, high costs, and a shortage of skilled workers to manage these complex systems. It also noted that there are currently no widely accepted measures to compare the performance of offensive and defensive generative AI. In a separate October 2026 report, the agency found that prompts sent to Gemini, ChatGPT, Grok, and Claude produced feasible information for planning attacks on the electrical grid and improvised explosive devices.

stories.Headline: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei launches IPO and vows AI systems stay under human control
stories.Summary:
Dario Amodei, the chief executive officer of the company known as Anthropic, launched an initial public offering on November 19, 2026. This significant financial move allows the artificial intelligence firm to transition into a publicly traded entity on the open market. The timing of this event coincides with ongoing global discussions regarding the safety and governance of advanced computing systems. This transition marks a major milestone in the growth and funding strategy of the organization.

The launch of this initial public offering requires the company to adhere to strict regulatory standards for public corporations. It changes the ownership structure of the firm by allowing external investors to purchase shares of the business. Every detail of the process is managed by the leadership team to ensure a stable transition for the company. The move is intended to provide the necessary capital to further develop their complex technological infrastructure.

Dario Amodei is the person responsible for overseeing this transition and the future direction of the company. He stated that he is committed to making sure that their artificial intelligence systems remain under human control. This promise emphasizes the importance of safety and oversight as the technology becomes more powerful and widespread. He believes that maintaining human authority over these systems is essential for the benefit of society.

The context of this announcement comes during a period of rapid expansion for the artificial intelligence industry. The company is positioning itself as a responsible leader in a field that faces many ethical challenges. There is no further information provided regarding the specific next steps for the company after the offering. The public will likely monitor how the firm balances its profit goals with its safety vows.

stories.Headline: Anthropic plans IPO to raise over US$60 billion to fund data centre spending
stories.Summary:
Anthropic launched the biggest Wall Street debut of all time on Thursday by offering an initial public offering to its investors. The company behind the Claude AI model is offering 980 million shares at a price of US$83 for each share. This American tech giant expects to raise US$81 billion, which exceeds the US$75 billion that SpaceX raised in June. Anthropic is now valued at about US$1.5 trillion, but it lacks enough customers to meet its massive spending commitments. The firm needs rapid growth to keep pace with spending that exceeds US$900 million in various financial obligations.

The company committed to spend US$901 billion on data centres by 2045, including US$70 billion by next September. In Point Tupper, Nova Scotia, Anthropic signed a 20-year lease for a 95-megawatt, 18,600-square metre facility owned by EverWind Fuels. EverWind is spending $8 billion on this data centre and another $2 billion on wind farms to power the site. Anthropic is also in talks to lease a 920-megawatt project northeast of Edmonton, Alberta, for operation by late 2027. The Cape Breton site is also scheduled for completion toward the end of 2027, marking the first Canadian site.

Anthropic warned investors that it may enter obligations based on revenue expectations that are not realized over the long term. The company reported a net loss of US$104 billion, which includes a US$94 billion charge for a financing adjustment. Laurel Munroe of EverWind stated the lease has credit protections and the risk sits with lenders, not Nova Scotians. Economics professor Joel Blit noted that US$900 billion is roughly the same amount as the entire sovereign debt of Canada. Blit suggested that new uses for AI must emerge to justify this unprecedented level of investment in compute capacity.

Randy Goebel of the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute said the sector is building more computing capacity than it actually needs. He compared the current situation to the dot-com bubble of the early 2000s, which took many tech companies down. David Garrity noted that Nvidia, the global leader in AI chips, has lost almost 30 per cent of its value. Other affected firms seeing billions in value erased include Meta, CoreWeave, and Alphabet, the parent company of Google. Garrity added that increasing interest rates and elevated oil prices have created a different investment outlook for the AI sector.

York University researchers reported in June that 213 data centres were planned or under construction across the entire country of Canada. These projects would draw 22.2 gigawatts of power, which is more than 14 times the existing capacity of the nation. Almost 80 per cent of these planned projects are located in Alberta, where the AI sector is heating up rapidly. AI firms including Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic are expected to spend US$700 million on data centres during this current year. Revenue for Anthropic grew 13 times to US$33.2 billion during the first nine months of the current fiscal year.

The company must now increase sales to pay for its infrastructure and the leases for its various global data centres. Markets historically tend to pull back in the weeks following U.S. midterm elections, which may impact the current investment climate. The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang followed public reports of affairs with an executive and a suspected Chinese spy. It remains open whether demand for AI services will grow at the rate required to sustain such high potential debt. The articles leave open the specific amount that Anthropic will pay EverWind to lease the facility in Nova Scotia.

stories.Headline: J.S. Held Applies Multidisciplinary Expertise to Physical AI Claims and Disputes
stories.Summary:
J.S. Held announced on November 20, 2026, that it applies multidisciplinary expertise to Physical AI claims and disputes, according to a press release issued from New York. The firm said Physical AI moves artificial intelligence beyond digital outputs and into systems that sense, decide, control, or act in the physical world. Those systems include AI-enabled and autonomous vehicles, robotics, industrial equipment, building systems, medical technology, drones, and other technologies in which digital decisions can affect people, property, infrastructure, and business operations. The release said autonomous and AI-enabled systems are creating new investigative questions when digital decisions produce physical consequences. J.S. Held published the announcement through PR Newswire, and The Manila Times carried it on November 20, 2026.

J.S. Held said a Physical AI investigation may examine the complete system chain, from the data the system received and what its sensors perceived to what the AI decided and how software, controls, and equipment translated that decision into action. The firm said these matters do not necessarily require new investigative disciplines but require established disciplines to work across increasingly complex systems. J.S. Held said it is publishing two perspectives, one in Insurance Journal titled When AI Leaves the Screen, the Stakes Change, and one to be published as Expert Analysis in Law360 titled When AI Leaves the Screen, the Evidence Changes: What In-House and Outside Counsel Should Do Before a Physical AI Incident. The firm said the Law360 piece discusses evidence ownership and preservation, system and software changes, sensor data, operating logs, telemetry, contractual responsibility, privilege, regulatory reporting, and coordination among technical and legal teams. J.S. Held said more than 1,500 professionals serve organizations across six continents, including 84% of the Global 200 Law Firms, 75% of the Forbes Top 20 Insurance Companies, 90% of the NAIC Top 50 Property & Casualty Insurers, and 71% of Fortune 100 Companies.

James E. Malackowski, Chief Intellectual Property Officer, Intellectual Property Practice Lead, and co-lead of the AI Disputes practice at J.S. Held, said AI is moving from generating information to influencing and controlling physical systems. Malackowski said that when those systems are involved in an accident or loss, the investigation cannot stop with the algorithm. He said understanding what happened may require examining the data and sensors, controls and equipment, human interaction, and the resulting physical and economic consequences. He said Physical AI is where those disciplines increasingly converge. Stephen Fenton, PE, Executive Vice President and Accident Reconstruction Practice Lead at J.S. Held, said that when an AI-enabled or autonomous system is involved in an accident, investigators still have to reconstruct the physical event.

Fenton said reconstruction covers what happened in the moments leading to the incident, how the system or vehicle behaved, and how the available physical and digital evidence explains the outcome. He said the technology may change but rigorous reconstruction remains essential to determining how and why an event occurred, and his work includes forensic engineering, vehicle dynamics, photogrammetry, computer modeling, and vehicle and product testing. Scott Armstrong, Executive Vice President and Equipment Practice Lead at J.S. Held, said Physical AI incidents can create complex equipment and insurance questions after the cause of an event is established. Armstrong, who has more than 25 years of experience in equipment loss consulting involving high-technology equipment and systems, said a physical loss can raise questions about whether the problem was the equipment itself, the sensors or connected systems, the power supply or physical infrastructure, a manufacturing issue, or some combination of factors. He said separating those issues is important for insurers to understand the damage, determine what can be repaired or recovered, assess whether replacement is necessary, and evaluate the operational impact.

J.S. Held said its Physical AI perspective builds on its work involving artificial intelligence in industrial and operational environments. The firm said its experts examine AI implementation in the energy, manufacturing, and natural-resources sectors in Enterprise AI Implementation in Heavy Industry: A Digital Transformation Strategy for Sustainable Growth. Their analysis addresses data governance, digital architecture, analytics, system integration, and the organizational foundations required to deploy AI in complex operations. The publication includes a case study involving an AI readiness assessment for a major energy operator, which considered the digital, data, governance, and organizational foundations needed to support scalable AI implementation. J.S. Held said this experience is relevant to Physical AI because the reliability of an AI-enabled physical system may depend not only on an algorithm but also on the data architecture, connected systems, implementation decisions, operating environment, and human processes surrounding it.

Alastair Mckenzie-Kerr, PhD, Regional Director of Health, Safety & Human Factors, EMEA at J.S. Held, said the important transition is not simply that companies are adopting AI but that AI is being integrated into operational environments where people, equipment, and safety-critical processes already interact. Mckenzie-Kerr, whose work includes implementing AI-enabled EHS solutions and integrating human factors into design engineering and operational systems, said organizations need to understand not only whether the technology works as intended but how it performs within the broader operating system and how people respond to it. J.S. Held said it is publishing the two perspectives as part of its ongoing examination of Physical AI risk, addressing how organizations, insurers, and legal counsel can prepare for incidents involving AI-enabled and autonomous systems. The firm said the Insurance Journal article examines what organizations and insurers should consider when an AI-enabled system contributes to an accident, equipment failure, operational interruption, or other physical loss, and explains why engineering, digital, human factors, insurance, legal, and financial investigations may need to proceed together. J.S. Held said it is not a law firm and does not provide legal advice, and that its affiliates and subsidiaries are not certified public accounting firms and do not provide audit, attest, or other public accounting services.

stories.Headline: UN officials warn AI gives predators new ways to exploit children
stories.Summary:
Senior UN officials warned on Thursday that artificial intelligence is handing predators and criminal groups new ways to groom, extort and exploit children. Dr. Najat Maalla M’jid, the UN Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence against Children, said efforts to protect children are failing to keep pace. She spoke during a high-level event in the General Assembly on the risks and opportunities of AI to help end the scourge. UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed addressed the event at UN Headquarters in New York. The warnings were reported by UN News on 19 November 2026 and by The Manila Times on 20 November 2026.

At least 1.2 million children in 11 countries had their images manipulated into sexually explicit deepfakes in the past year alone, Amina Mohammed said, citing a recent UNICEF study. Reports of child sexual abuse material linked to generative AI rose by 1,325 per cent between 2023 and 2024, according to the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, Dr. M’jid said. She noted that most AI-facilitated crimes against children remain unreported and under prosecuted. Chatbots are being used to gain children’s trust, gather personal information and coerce them into sharing explicit images, she said. Deepfakes made with “nudification” apps are used to humiliate, threaten and exploit children, and profiling and predictive targeting let predators, traffickers and criminal groups reach vulnerable children more easily.

Dr. M’jid said the world lost the battle on social media because it was lagging behind, and is now losing the battle on artificial intelligence because it is still lagging behind. She said voluntary approaches by the tech sector are insufficient and called for global standards at the core of AI governance, including mandatory child safety and privacy by design. Amina Mohammed said we would never accept a children’s toy being put on the market without proper safety checks, but AI systems are reaching children without the same scrutiny. She said we cannot leave children’s safety to the goodwill of technology companies. She added that AI can also help detect abuse material, identify victims and spot early signs of grooming.

John Trenary, who has worked on child exploitation investigations for more than 25 years, said predators have always sought ways of “weaponizing technology to exploit our kids”. He warned that because AI can scale so efficiently, automate and create wholly synthetic content, its weaponisation is “self-perpetuating”. He said that as soon as investigators get a handle on one way predators misuse it, “something else comes out”. Kay Chau of the Tech Coalition, a non-profit alliance focused on child protection, said perpetrators may be using chatbots to facilitate abusive role-play or generate grooming scripts. She said agentic AI, systems that can carry out tasks independently, is introducing new risks.

Mariana Rozo-Paz of the Datasphere Initiative recalled working with teenage girls on a digital literacy programme in rural Colombia last year. Asked to draw what the internet looked like, the girls drew a girl named Lucia, their AI agent. The girls said they talk to Lucia every day and ask her whenever adults don’t want to answer specific questions. They said she is always there for them and has intimate mode and best friend mode. In a World Childhood Foundation study, a young person in Sweden said the technology is really cool but the people in charge of controlling it cannot keep up.

In July, Secretary-General António Guterres launched the AI Child Safety Pledge, whose aims include making AI systems certifiably safe before they reach children and zero tolerance of AI-generated child sexual abuse material. Paula Guillet de Monthoux, Secretary General of the World Childhood Foundation, said children should never have to tell us that the adults responsible for their safety cannot keep up. She said it is our responsibility to prove that we can. The articles do not say what penalties or enforcement follow from the pledge. They do not say which 11 countries the UNICEF study covered.
