stories.Headline: Polly Barnes says AI lets founders build with smaller teams but makes every hire a harder bet
stories.Summary:
Polly Barnes, an operating partner at the investment firm EQT and the author of The Founder Six, wrote in an article published by Sifted on 19 November 2026 that AI is making it possible to build technology companies with fewer people, even as the stakes of every hire rise and finding exceptional talent does not get any easier. She said exceptional candidates want to know what they will own, what they can build and whether the opportunity is worth leaving their current job for. She wrote that as teams shrink, every hire carries more weight, and that the hardest question for a founder is no longer whether a candidate can do the job but whether that person is the right bet for a smaller, more senior team. She described how behavioural science can help founders navigate the demands of fast growth, drawing on her work leading the early-stage talent team at EQT. The article says companies are increasingly looking beyond their local talent pool, driven by the evolution of AI and flexible working, and that European startups must embrace global hiring to survive a growing tech talent crunch.

It reports that 52% of something in the text is tied to the shift, and it cites figures of 66 to 87% and 58% in passages describing how AI tools affect the work of engineers and the share of tasks they handle. It notes that a typical team once needed 55 people for a certain job and now needs far fewer, and it says one company cut its engineering headcount while keeping output steady. It adds that candidates now ask what a role will let them own and build, and that founders must answer those questions clearly to win them. Barnes is responsible for the argument, writing as an operating partner at EQT and as the author of The Founder Six, and she says she has met thousands of founders from companies such as Wellhub, Lovable, Harvey and Vinted, which she says gives her insight into what drives high-performing teams. She says founders should treat each hire as a bet on a smaller, more senior group rather than as a replacement for a large one, and that they should be honest with candidates about what the role will involve.

She says the fight for real talent is getting harder rather than easier, and that companies will have to go the extra mile to attract the people they need. The context is a European startup scene where AI and flexible working are pushing companies to hire beyond their local pools, and where the article says local talent pools are drying up as demand for tech skills grows. The article says European startups must embrace global hiring to survive the crunch, and it points to a related piece on how Europe is future-proofing its hiring strategy. It does not say what specific companies plan to do next beyond that shift toward global hiring, and it offers no timeline for when the smaller-team trend will play out.

stories.Headline: Perplexity releases Orchestrator API to route developer requests across multiple AI models
stories.Summary:
Perplexity launched the Perplexity Orchestrator API on November 19, 2026, to provide a single endpoint for various frontier and open-weight models. This hosted inference gateway allows developers to access models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and xAI, as well as open-weight options like DeepSeek, Kimi, and GLM. The system manages model routing by selecting providers based on their current capacity, availability, and latency. By using one base URL and one account for billing, developers can reduce the number of necessary integrations and receive a single invoice.

The service requires users to point their SDKs to specific URLs, such as the OpenAI base URL at https://api.perplexity.ai/orchestrator/v1. It supports OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses, and Anthropic Messages requests, often requiring only a change to the API key and base URL. Failover mechanisms automatically swap deployments if provider errors, timeouts, or rate limits occur, such as moving a failed Claude request from Anthropic to AWS Bedrock. The system also offers a preview for automatic routing via the perplexity/auto setting, which uses a decision model to direct traffic among one to five routes or a default model.

Perplexity stated that there is no additional platform fee beyond the credits used for the answering model's published per-token rate. They noted that production traffic measured between October 4 and November 2, 2026, showed higher success rates and less variance during incidents than requests to single providers. The company explained that requests failing before producing output are not billed, and usage can be funded through prepaid credits or the AWS Marketplace. They also detailed a tiered access system where Tier 0 includes Google and xAI, Tier 1 requires 50 dollars for OpenAI, and Tier 2 requires 250 dollars for Fable and Opus models.

The company tested automatic routing on a 63-task subset of Terminal-Bench 4.1 using Claude Code to bypass certain safeguards. They found that routing to GPT-6.1 Sol or GPT-6 Astra increased successful task completion by three tasks in areas like biology and security. Current default policies send traffic to GPT-6.1 Sol, while simpler requests are routed to GPT-6 Luna. Perplexity continues to develop speed-aware routing to further optimize the performance of the gateway.

stories.Headline: MarkTechPost ranks 13 agent gateways for MCP, A2A and LLM traffic
stories.Summary:
MarkTechPost published a list on November 19, 2026, ranking 13 agent gateways that handle MCP, A2A and LLM traffic, with Kong, Bifrost, AgentCore and Arcade named in the title. The article defines an agent gateway as a control point that authenticates agents, filters the tools they see and logs every call, while a plain LLM gateway only routes model requests. The ranking is editorial and weighs five criteria: traffic coverage, identity and authorization, deployment options, maturity and price transparency. Kong governs LLM, MCP and A2A traffic from one control plane, and version 2.0 moved AI features into first-class Providers, Models, MCP Servers and Agents entities. Bifrost is an Apache 2.0 Go gateway covering models, MCP tools and A2A agents in one deployment, and Maxim reports it supports 10,000+ models across 25+ providers with a claimed 11 µs mean overhead at 5,000 RPS.

Gravitee runs an LLM Proxy, MCP Proxy and A2A Proxy on one runtime sharing one authentication, policy and OpenTelemetry chain, and its A2A Proxy supports RFC 8693 token exchange and skill-level authorization. AgentCore Gateway gives agents one managed endpoint for tools, models and other agents, with semantic tool search, Cedar policies and on-behalf-of token exchange, priced from $0.005 per 1,000 invocations. Arcade is an actions runtime rather than a model router that checks the overlap of user and agent permissions on every action, keeps credentials away from the LLM and lists 8,000+ agent-optimized tools. The article attributes several cautions to the vendors and to Maxim. Kong's 2.x architecture needs a Konnect control plane, and Arcade notes the MCP OAuth2 plugin is still Tech Preview.

Bifrost's SSO, SCIM and token exchange are Enterprise-only, and an independent review notes the 11 µs figure excludes HTTP handling and JSON marshalling. Maxim lists Gravitee Agent Management from $2,500 per month, and the A2A Proxy needs Enterprise Edition. AgentCore is AWS-only, its A2A support is HTTP passthrough per Maxim, and search calls cost $0.025 per 1,000, five times the invoke rate. Arcade has no model routing, so it should be paired with an LLM gateway, and its pricing is $25 per month plus $0.10 per auth event and $0.01 per tool call.

The article also covers Palo Alto Networks, which completed its Portkey acquisition in May 2026 and reached GA inside Prisma AIRS in July 2026, described as a unified LLM, MCP and A2A gateway with one enforcement point running in SaaS and hybrid models. Microsoft's AI gateway extends API Management to model APIs, MCP servers and A2A agent APIs, but its A2A support is preview, JSON-RPC only and limited to v2 tiers. Agent Gateway is the network entry and exit point for Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, assigns each agent a SPIFFE ID, can apply Model Armor to prompts and responses, and Maxim lists up to 5,000 governed resources per gateway. The article gives no further details on the remaining entries or on what happens next.

stories.Headline: Zhe Zhang proposes journals run tailored AI reviews before human peer review
stories.Summary:
Academic journals are flooded with papers, and at publishing giant Elsevier the number of submissions rose 56% in just three years, from 2.7 million in 2022 to 4.2 million in 2025. Peer reviewers, who generally volunteer their time, were already stretched thin before that surge. While AI is almost certainly fueling the surge, it is also changing the peer review system itself. In October, Springer Nature and Google DeepMind announced plans for an AI assistant to help reviewers. A working paper from researchers at Harvard says that AI-generated reviews can outperform even top human reviewers.

Zhe Zhang, an assistant professor of innovation, technology and operations at UC San Diego's Rady School of Management, thinks it is time for journals to take charge of how AI is used in peer review. In a recent Management Science paper, he and colleagues propose an AI-based approach that could ease the burden on reviewers without sacrificing scholarly judgment. The paper is titled "Fighting Fire with Fire: Infusing Artificial Intelligence into Peer Review to Sustain Quality Scholarship," by Hemant K. Bhargava and colleagues, published in Management Science in 2026 with DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2026.00184. The proposal would have journals use their own customized AI reviewer, tailored to their standards, to assess papers as soon as they are submitted. Authors would get the first chance to respond, correcting the AI's mistakes, clarifying points or addressing legitimate concerns.

Zhang said it is too early to say if AI can save peer review, but he thinks it is worth trying. He said AI is making it much easier to do research, analyze data and write papers, and that is not necessarily a bad thing. He said some of those papers may look plausible without being very good, and the challenge for peer review is distinguishing what is good from what is bad. He said AI makes that more difficult both through sheer volume and by making weak papers more polished. He also described "shadow AI," in which reviewers use AI tools on their own, sometimes without disclosing it, which may help them work faster but leaves journals with little visibility into how AI is shaping those judgments.

Under the proposal, human reviewers would then receive the paper, the AI assessment and the authors' response. Zhang said this could free human reviewers from routine checks and allow them to focus on questions that require human judgment, like the originality and significance of the research. He said giving authors a voice is especially important to them, and that making the AI assessment visible to everyone involved can make the process more transparent and accountable. He said there is a risk, because peer review relies on independent opinions, and if everyone sees the same AI assessment, reviewers may become anchored to it.

Instead of several independent judgments, journals could end up with variations on the same opinion. Zhang said the paper's mathematical model examines that trade-off, and that under certain conditions AI could help journals make more accurate decisions with less human reviewer time, even when the AI itself is not as good a reviewer as a human. He said that if reviewers rely too heavily on AI, those benefits could disappear. He said the model cannot tell us everything, and that important questions remain about whether reviewers will become too reliant on AI, whether authors will learn to game the system, and whether unconventional research could get overlooked.

The article states that a proposed peer-review workflow lets authors respond to journal-run AI assessments before human review. It states that mathematical modeling suggests this could improve decision accuracy and reduce reviewer workload under certain conditions, and that shared AI assessments risk anchoring reviewers and weakening independent judgment, with benefits remaining empirically unverified. Zhang said they are starting to experiment, and that at the University of Arizona's Workshop on Responsible TecH they are testing a version of the proposed process. He said they want to see what works and what does not, and whether they can make peer review more efficient without losing the independent judgment that makes it valuable in the first place.

The article was written by Inga Kiderra of the University of California - San Diego and was edited by Gaby Clark and reviewed by Andrew Zinin. It was published on November 19, 2026, and retrieved on 19 November 2026 from https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-peer.html. The article states that 10 million peer reviews are expected in 2025, and that experts advocate for AI integration. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Meta FAIR develops self-improving memory method to boost AI agent performance on continual learning tasks
stories.Summary:
Meta FAIR introduced a method called Self-Improving Memory on November 19, 2026, to help AI agents manage their own memory. This two-stage process allows an agent to discover its own memory instructions and then train those skills directly into its weights. Researchers from the University of Washington and Johns Hopkins University co-authored the work. The system uses a Kimi-K2.6 model, which is a 1T-parameter MoE with 32B active parameters and 256K context.

The method requires a persistent memory directory that the agent edits using file tools while working through subtasks. It utilizes two specific prompts, LOAD and OFFLOAD, to retrieve and update notes between these tasks. The system achieved an average score of 56.0 across three Continual Learning Bench tasks, surpassing the 44.6 score of the best human-written prompts. The Codebase task saw the highest performance at 64.3, which was 20.6 points higher than the best hand-written harness.

The research team explained that a meta agent rewrites the memory prompts based on trajectories and scores. They used a Discover-Demonstrate-Distill pipeline to move these gains into the model weights via a LoRA adapter with rank 64. This distillation process resulted in a 5.5-point gain over standard fine-tuning on generic trajectories. The team noted that the model is essentially trained on memory skills it discovered for itself.

The tests focused on Database, Codebase, and Spectrum tasks to measure how well the model generalizes to new instances. While the search for better prompts was noisy, the Codebase task continued to improve through the fourth generation. The distilled model eventually averaged 43.1 across ten matched seeds while using generic prompts. This demonstrates that the model can maintain high performance without needing the optimized instructions.

Articles.Title: Meta FAIR Self-Improving Memory Hits 56.0 on Continual Learning Bench

stories.Headline: Kevin O'Leary plans AI data centres as US voters reject them and Canada welcomes them
stories.Summary:
Kevin O'Leary is planning major AI data centre projects in Canada and the United States. Canadian legislators have embraced these developments while American voters have grown increasingly sour on them. This shift occurred as the US held midterm elections in November 2026. Industry leaders now see Canada as an appealing hub for hyperscale projects. These developments are happening as the US pushes back against AI infrastructure.

The Alberta Wonder Valley project requires 7,000 acres and 7.5 gigawatts of power. O'Leary also planned a Utah site that Senator Stuart Adams demanded be cut from 40,000 to 13,000 acres. Alberta hosts 90 percent of proposed sites, including a C$13bn Meta centre. The Alberta project uses natural gas and six million cubic metres of water. The Carney government wants to expand computing capacity 16-fold over four years.

The Alberta government says these projects create jobs and revenue while being developed responsibly. Reeve Ryan Ratzlaf called the project a perfect fit for his rural community. CEO Paul Palandjian stated that the Alberta and Utah projects are proceeding at equal paces. Premier Doug Ford said Ontario must move full steam ahead with building centres. The Carney government frames this development as a matter of national security.

Utah residents organised a fierce opposition campaign against the Wonder Valley project. Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation sued the government for overriding an environmental assessment. Hundreds of protesters in Nova Scotia gathered against a proposed Anthropic data centre. Resident Bek MacIntosh successfully halted a data centre in Olds, Alberta. Some community members expressed concern about the high volume of water needed.

Canada has abundant land, natural gas, and a cold climate for these projects. The Alberta government exempted the Wonder Valley project from an environmental impact assessment. US voters passed 40 of 41 local ballot initiatives to limit data centres. Canada released high-level guidance co-signed by Meta and Anthropic regarding electricity and water. Sean Mullin noted that fewer projects in Canada have attracted less attention.

The Alberta government recently proposed legislation to restrict where data centres can be built. The Utah project is still seeking financing and may not begin construction. The Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation court case regarding the environmental assessment remains active. Experts warn that Canada could experience similar backlashes if it is not thoughtful. It remains unclear if Canadian political parties are prepared for potential voter reactions.

stories.Headline: Technical failures in aviation and banking spark national debate over AI and security
stories.Summary:
During the week ending November 19, 2026, various technical failures grounded American planes and disrupted banking systems. Email outages also halted parts of the workforce, leading to a national debate about artificial intelligence. These events caused widespread instability and raised concerns about the promises made by large technology companies. Some of these failures occurred on Thursday and last Friday. People are now questioning if artificial intelligence is to blame for these disruptions.

The FAA manages 30 million square miles of airspace with over 40,000 employees and contractors. JPMorgan Chase experienced technical difficulties on Thursday, and the company Anthropic went public with a valuation over 2 trillion dollars. The National Security Agency is currently facing internal tool failures for classified communications. These issues have kept some NSA workers home for days and caused problems overseas. The FAA must upgrade systems while continuing operations, which is a significant technical challenge.

Ozlem Kilic, Dean at the University of Tennessee, said aging infrastructure is not built for new technology. She stated that AI identifies problems quickly, but fixing them can lead to outages. Kilic believes that having the best AI and security tools is a matter of national security. She noted that the intention of the user is more dangerous than the technology itself. Kilic also believes that trained people will be the primary defense against future incidents.

Retired FAA official Michael O'Donnell compared upgrading agency systems to changing tires on a car moving at 80 miles per hour. UT Professor Eric Kelley suggested that people should hold some cash in case bank accounts become inaccessible. White House officials and the NSA both denied that these outages were the result of a coordinated cyber-attack. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is set to testify before Congress regarding his personal affairs. U.S. officials reportedly described a woman Huang had an affair with as a Chinese spy.

The articles state that these technical failures may become more frequent in the future. The current infrastructure is older than the fascinating technology that has recently swept the nation. Experts agree that artificial intelligence is here to stay despite the risks of instability. The timing of the outages is concerning because they followed the admissions of Jensen Huang. These events highlight a race for AI dominance where the U.S. cannot afford to slow down.

Jensen Huang will provide testimony to Congress about his reported relationship with a Chinese spy. The National Security Agency continues to deal with technical difficulties regarding its classified communication tools. Some NSA employees remain at home while the agency works to resolve these internal failures. The articles leave open whether artificial intelligence was the direct cause of the banking and aviation outages. It remains unclear if the government will implement new security mandates for aging national infrastructure.

stories.Headline: Scale AI recruits experts to turn professional work into low paid gig tasks
stories.Summary:
Scale AI and its recruiting platform Outlier are transforming professional roles into low paid gig work by hiring experts to improve artificial intelligence. The company recruits physicians, lawyers, and Ph.D.s to design complex scenarios, rank model outputs, and verify data generated by AI. This process has expanded globally, with the company previously using its Remotasks platform to hire workers in Venezuela, Kenya, Nigeria, and Pakistan. Many of these workers experienced a pattern where initial pay was high to build a workforce before rates were cut.

The platform offers up to 180 dollars an hour for United States cardiologists, but pays only 12.50 dollars for Swahili work in Tanzania and 7.50 dollars for Tagalog work in the Philippines. In Venezuela, some workers earned as little as 2 dollars on their first day, while a family once made 20 dollars in one day during December 2020. Remotasks ended its hourly program in Venezuela in 2021 and later discontinued operations in Kenya, Nigeria, and Pakistan in March 2024. Terms of service allow the company to deactivate accounts without notice or withhold accrued payments based on its own determinations.

Scale AI attributed the closure of several international operations to enhanced security protocols, though it later admitted that Kenyan workers missed notices due to operational errors. Representatives from AI companies and outsourcing firms have agreed that pay should be better, but they often distance themselves from direct employment of these workers. Scale AI has denied wrongdoing regarding a proposed settlement in San Francisco, while a separate class action suit alleges that Mercor misclassified over 30,000 professionals. Mercor has provided services for companies including Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI, though those firms are not defendants in the case.

This system of extractivism takes value from people in unstable economies to benefit buyers who set all the terms. Workers often have no say over sudden rate changes or the disappearance of tasks, leaving those with few options trapped in precarious employment. In March 2023, a Kenyan judge temporarily stopped Meta and contractor Majorel from dismissing 260 content moderators, but Meta subsequently moved that work to West Africa. The trend suggests that professional work will continue to shift toward these platforms wherever the next available worker logs on.

Articles.Title: AI isn’t replacing your job. It’s turning it into low-paid gig work

stories.Headline: Singapore stages first large-scale AI cyberattack and defence exercise with 250 participants
stories.Summary:
The Singapore government conducted its first large-scale artificial intelligence attack and defence battle on Thursday, November 19, 2026. This event was part of the fifth Critical Infrastructure Defence Exercise, which ran from Tuesday to Friday at the Punggol campus of the Singapore Institute of Technology. The exercise simulated coordinated swarms of AI agents attempting to disrupt various sectors at rapid speeds to test modern security. More than 250 participants from 46 different organisations took part in the four-day event to address evolving cyber threats.

The exercise expanded to eight testbeds by adding aviation and healthcare sectors to the existing six covering water, energy, maritime, telecommunications, land transport, and multi-cloud environments. A red team including personnel from the Land Transport Authority, Government Technology Agency, Infocomm Media Development Authority, Defence Science and Technology Agency, Cyber Security Agency of Singapore, and Digital and Intelligence Service launched the attacks. For the first time, a blue team of AI agents developed by the Cyber Defence Test and Experimentation Centre attempted to detect and contain threats. These AI tools completed investigation reports in under 10 minutes, a process that typically takes human personnel several hours.

Military Expert 6 Sim Swee Horng, the director of the Cyber Defence Test and Experimentation Centre, stated that defenders must harness AI to match the capabilities of attackers. She explained that the goal was to identify the strengths, weaknesses, and limits of AI tools when they work alongside human judgement. Brigadier General Clarence Cai, the Defence Cyber Chief, noted that defensive capabilities must keep pace because AI allows for faster attacks on a larger scale. He affirmed that the Singapore Armed Forces will continue collaborating with industry partners and agencies to develop these essential cyber defence capabilities.

This year's event also integrated operationally ready national servicemen from the Digital and Intelligence Service to lead blue teams across various sectors. These participants practiced responding to attacks on both information technology systems and industrial control systems that manage physical facilities. By simulating these environments, the government can test responses without affecting actual public services. The exercise concluded with visits from Minister of State for Defence Desmond Choo and Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How.

stories.Headline: Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee says AI data center boom fuels inflation
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Austan Goolsbee told reporters on Thursday that the boom in AI data center construction is adding to the nation's inflation, which he described as borderline disturbingly high. He said the sector's massive business investment is indirectly contributing to rising service prices across the economy. Goolsbee said the AI boom is contributing to the potential of overheating in the economy, and that he finds it hard to look at it any other way given the almost unprecedented level of business investment. He declined to forecast the central bank's next moves on interest rates, saying the Fed's decisions will be determined by whether U.S. inflation is on track to return to its annual 2% target. He added that the evidence does not suggest the country is on a path back to 2%.

Consumer prices around the U.S. rose faster than economists had expected in October, climbing 0.4%, according to government data. While inflation in recent months has largely been driven by higher energy prices, the figures showed that the costs of other goods and services also increased. Goolsbee's comments came after the Fed's October minutes showed that nearly all officials expect the central bank to raise its key interest rate by a quarter point in December. Some officials had supported a hike in October, although the committee kept the rate steady, and two members suggested a half-point increase at its meeting next month. Goolsbee, who will become a voting member of the interest rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee in January, spoke as Anthropic held its blockbuster initial public offering, the largest in history.

Shares of Anthropic jumped 17% in their first day of trading on Nasdaq, even as the broader market suffered a major selloff, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average shedding more than 1,100 points. The wealth creation unleashed by the Anthropic IPO, which has made its seven co-founders multibillionaires, bears watching, Goolsbee said. He said the question of what people are going to do with the money will become a macro relevant statistic. Goolsbee also said consumer sentiment remains low despite relatively strong economic trends, a puzzle that economists have sought to explain.

He said one reason is tied to inflation, with Americans generally feeling very sour about higher prices. Most Americans are neither benefiting from the AI boom nor Anthropic's IPO, meaning that they are experiencing higher inflation without seeing the upside of the sector's growth. Goolsbee said the consumer sentiment about inflation hasn't been wrong. The Associated Press contributed to the report, which was edited by Alain Sherter.

Articles.Title: AI is fueling "disturbingly high" inflation, Chicago Fed president says

stories.Headline: OpenAI demos the Codex Security Plugin workflow in a published recording
stories.Summary:
OpenAI published a page on 19 November 2026 titled Explore the Codex Security Plugin, which presents a product demo of the Codex Security Plugin and shows the workflow in action from getting started to reviewing the results shown in the recording. The page appears on OpenAI's own site under its product and resources sections, and it carries a share link that opens in a new window. The page also lists links to Security and Privacy, Trust and Transparency, ChatGPT, ChatGPT Business, ChatGPT Enterprise, ChatGPT for Education, Codex, Dots, Release Notes and the API platform. Beyond the demo and the navigation links, the page gives no further detail on what the plugin does or how it works.

The page offers no release date for the plugin itself, no version number, no pricing and no statement of which plans or products the plugin works with. It names Codex and Dots among the linked products but does not say whether the plugin is available now or only shown in the recording. The only date the page gives is the 2026 copyright line covering 2015 to 2026, and the only action it describes is watching the demo and reviewing the results shown in it. No requirements, changes or availability details appear in the text.

The page names no person, no team and no executive, and it contains no statement from anyone at OpenAI about the plugin. The only voice on the page is the site's own description of the demo, which invites readers to watch the workflow from getting started to reviewing the results shown in the recording. Responsibility for the plugin therefore rests with OpenAI as the publisher of the page, and the page itself makes no claim beyond that. Nothing in the text says who built the plugin or who oversees it.

The context the page gives is limited to its placement among OpenAI's security and privacy materials and its product links, which sit alongside the company's terms, privacy policy and other policies. The page ends with the OpenAI copyright notice for 2015 to 2026 and a privacy choices link, and it offers no roadmap, no follow-up date and no next step beyond watching the recording. Because the articles carry too little for a longer account, this is a breaking story. More to follow.

stories.Headline: JohnAIC raises $1.9 million to expand on-premise AI server production
stories.Summary:
Bengaluru-based JohnAIC, a startup building on-premise AI servers for enterprises and government bodies, raised $1.9 million in a pre-seed funding round led by Crane Venture Partners, with Neon Fund also participating, according to a TechGig report published on November 19, 2026. The company said it will use the capital to expand its manufacturing, configuration and supply capabilities for AI servers. JohnAIC aims to reach a production capacity of up to 100 AI servers per month. The startup is investing in factory and supply chain infrastructure to serve Indian organisations building private AI environments and neoclouds.

JohnAIC, founded by Sasank Chilamkurthy, sells integrated systems that combine high-performance GPU servers, inference software, optimised open-source models and local data management. The systems let enterprises run AI within their own environment without separately assembling servers, models, deployment tools and security controls. JohnAIC's customers include public sector organisations, large enterprises, banks, healthcare companies and public sector undertakings. For banking, financial services and insurance institutions, the company said its systems support Digital Personal Data Protection and Reserve Bank of India requirements, keeping sensitive financial data inside the organisation's own environment. The startup is also collaborating with Andhra Pradesh Eastern Power Distribution Company Limited, where its server is embedded in the utility's operational survey processes to convert field data into real-time insights.

Chilamkurthy said Indian enterprises need AI infrastructure they can fully own, operate and trust, and that the mission is to make on-premise AI adoption as seamless as cloud solutions, with compute, models and data staying under customer control. Anandamoy Roychowdhary, managing director for India and APAC at Crane Venture Partners, noted the company's goal of maximising the AI tokens customers generate per rupee spent. Siddhartha Ahluwalia, co-founder and managing partner at Neon Fund, highlighted Chilamkurthy's background as a co-author of PyTorch and his leadership in AI deployments at Qure.ai. The company positions its product as enterprise-hardened servers running voice AI and predictive models behind the customer's firewall, pre-configured with open-source tooling to help avoid recurring cloud costs and dependence on a single vendor.

stories.Headline: University at Albany researchers find Google DeepMind's AI hurricane model beats NOAA's top model one to five days out
stories.Summary:
Researchers from the University at Albany published a study in Geophysical Research Letters on November 19, 2026. They independently tested how well Google DeepMind's AI hurricane model predicts storm intensification. The study analyzed the performance of the WeatherNext Cyclone model. This AI tool correctly predicted the path and Category 5 strength of Hurricane Melissa. That storm hit Jamaica during the fall of the previous year.

The study evaluated intensity forecasts for 385 tropical cyclones worldwide between June 2022 and May 2026. Researchers compared predicted wind speeds against actual records and official forecasts from the Joint Typhoon Warning Center. They also used data from the National Hurricane Center and other common forecasting tools. The team tested the AI against two tools that flag rapid intensification of 35 mph in 24 hours. This analysis focused on the North Atlantic and the eastern North Pacific regions.

Professor Brian Tang co-led the study within the Department of Atmospheric and Environmental Sciences at UAlbany. Tang stated that independent checks provide the public with more confidence in developer claims. He noted that these checks offer an objective look at both strengths and weaknesses. Tang believes AI models may be better at connecting dots for rapid intensification. He added that AI is a powerful tool but does not replace human forecasters.

The AI model was more accurate than NOAA's state-of-the-art model from one to five days out. It performed on par with human forecasters after the first day and had fewer false alarms. However, the model often underestimated storm strength and produced ranges of outcomes that were too narrow. Its performance was best in the North Atlantic and worst in the eastern North Pacific. These results affect how forecasters decide when to trust their own judgment.

The research began as a class project in a graduate course taught by Professor Tang. Recent UAlbany graduates Jacob Vile and Nour Elgalad expanded the project into a full analysis. This work expands on Google's own testing of the model published in Nature over the summer. The model was trained on basic storm information and big-picture weather data. This training may cause it to miss finer details needed for the strongest storms.

Google released a new version of its model this year that was not included in the study. Other AI weather models are currently in development by different organizations. Tang believes forecasters will benefit from a shared and transparent way to compare these tools. The articles do not state when the new Google model will be independently tested. They leave open whether future AI versions will fix the current underestimation of storm strength.

stories.Headline: Anthropic goes public at nearly $1.4 trillion valuation, second only to SpaceX
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, made one of the largest stock market debuts in history on the morning of November 19, 2026, according to KCRA. The company went public that day, and its estimated valuation is nearly $1.4 trillion, which ranks second only to SpaceX's record-setting debut in June. Financial expert Kelly Brothers joined KCRA that morning to break down what impacts the market will see from the move. He also spoke on the release of the long-awaited video game Grand Theft Auto VI and the impact it might have on Wall Street.

The debut puts Anthropic among the largest public companies by valuation at the moment it began trading, with the reported figure of nearly $1.4 trillion placing it behind only SpaceX's June listing. The report gives no share price, no amount raised and no exchange details, so what the listing changes beyond the valuation ranking is not stated. KCRA frames the event as one of the largest debuts in history and pairs it with a separate discussion of Grand Theft Auto VI, which the article does not connect to Anthropic's listing. The coverage was updated at 4:15 PM PST on November 19, 2026, and was reported by Paul Stevens.

Kelly Brothers, described as a financial expert, was the person KCRA brought on air to explain the market impact of the debut. According to the article, he joined the station that morning to break down what impacts the market will see, and he also spoke about the video game release and its possible effect on Wall Street. The article does not record any specific statement, prediction or figure from Brothers beyond those topics. Responsibility for the coverage is attributed to Paul Stevens, with the piece carrying an editorial standards note.

The context the article supplies is the comparison to SpaceX, whose June debut it calls record-setting and which remains the only listing larger than Anthropic's nearly $1.4 trillion valuation. Beyond that ranking and the on-air segment, the article does not say what happens next for Anthropic, for the market or for the video game's effect on Wall Street. It directs readers to more coverage of top California stories, the station's app, its morning newsletter and its YouTube channel. No further dates or numbers appear in the report.

stories.Headline: US outages linked to software fixes, not AI cyberattack
stories.Summary:
A wave of service disruptions across the United States last week affected JPMorgan Chase, United Airlines and Microsoft Outlook, leaving customers unable to access banking services, board flights or open email. Experts speaking to Axios dismissed fears of an AI-driven cyberattack and attributed the incidents to software fixes and technical failures. JPMorgan Chase customers faced banking service issues caused by an internal software bug, which delayed transactions involving other banks. United Airlines briefly grounded flights, citing a technology problem, and this followed a nationwide ground stop by the US Federal Aviation Administration days earlier, caused by network traffic overwhelming older equipment. Microsoft Outlook and other Microsoft 365 services experienced downtime due to a months-old bug, coupled with increased traffic and reduced server capacity.

US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested that AI systems for writing and modifying code could play a part in the disruptions. National security officials and Wall Street executives have informed lawmakers that these outages are linked to efforts to fix software flaws discovered by AI tools, according to The Washington Sun. Experts note that the accelerated pace of coding and review, driven by AI tools to identify vulnerabilities, can itself lead to downtime. David Woods, professor emeritus of integrated systems engineering at Ohio State University, said safeguards are being reduced in the pursuit of speed, and that cross checks, tests, stress tests and safeguards are being cut out.

Security technologist Bruce Schneier attributed the public's panic to human pattern recognition, interpreting coincidences as conspiracies. Liz Fong-Jones, technical fellow at Honeycomb, emphasised that these outages are a decades-old phenomenon of cascading failures, unrelated to AI-driven code writing or shipping. Ookla analyst Luke Kehoe reported nearly 6 million US problem reports on Downdetector in the week ending November 16, marking the highest weekly total in a year. Experts found no evidence of an AI-driven cyberattack, despite social media speculation, and described the incidents as largely unrelated technical failures that occurred close together.

Articles.Title: US outages linked to software fixes, not AI cyberattack

stories.Headline: AI helps cardiologists interpret heart ultrasounds nearly twice as fast without losing accuracy
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence helped cardiologists interpret heart ultrasound exams nearly twice as fast without sacrificing accuracy, according to research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026. The study tested whether AI could analyze ultrasound images and generate preliminary reports for cardiologists to review and finalize. Researchers included 1,200 echocardiograms performed at 21 Kaiser Permanente medical centers in Northern California during March 2025. Patients in the study had an average age of 69. The findings were presented this month and suggest AI could help streamline cardiac imaging.

For each examination, an AI system, a sonographer and a cardiologist independently prepared preliminary interpretations. The reports were randomly assigned to cardiologists, who reviewed and finalized them without knowing whether AI or a healthcare professional had prepared the initial report. Cardiologists made substantial changes to 50.6 percent of AI-generated preliminary interpretations, compared with 49.7 percent of those prepared by sonographers and cardiologists. AI assistance reduced average interpretation time from 8.5 minutes to 4.6 minutes, a 46 percent improvement. AI-assisted reports were more consistent with previous clinical reports than those in the comparison group.

Reviewing cardiologists could not reliably determine whether preliminary reports came from AI or another healthcare professional. Researchers concluded that the AI-assisted approach met the study's criteria for comparable accuracy. Researchers emphasized that AI is intended to assist physicians, not replace them. Cardiologists remain responsible for verifying findings, interpreting results in the context of each patient's medical history and determining appropriate treatment.

The findings are preliminary and have not yet undergone full peer review. Researchers did not examine whether AI-assisted interpretations improved long-term patient outcomes. Cardiologists knew they were participating in a study, potentially influencing their work patterns. Larger studies in everyday clinical settings are needed to confirm whether AI can consistently improve efficiency while maintaining diagnostic accuracy and patient safety.

The results suggest AI could help improve efficiency in cardiology departments, where physicians routinely interpret large numbers of imaging examinations. Reducing the time required to complete reports could potentially lead to faster results for patients and allow cardiologists to devote more time to direct patient care. An echocardiogram, commonly called a heart ultrasound, uses sound waves to create moving images of the heart. It helps physicians evaluate the heart's structure, pumping ability and valves, providing important information for diagnosing and managing heart conditions.

Typically, a sonographer, a healthcare professional trained in ultrasound imaging, performs the examination. A cardiologist then reviews the images and prepares a report describing the findings. The research was written about by John Fernandez and published by Baptist Health South Florida on November 20, 2026. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Resolve AI launches SRE-1 model and Primary On-call agents to find root causes of production alerts
stories.Summary:
Resolve AI Inc. announced on Wednesday the launch of SRE-1, a 27 billion-parameter model built on open weights that has been trained to find the root cause of production alerts, together with Primary On-call, a service that puts the company's AI agents on call ahead of human engineers. The model was trained by a team of 16 AI researchers over a final run of 7.4 days on up to 512 graphics processing units, using reinforcement learning alone, and Resolve AI built it with Snowflake Inc.'s Cortex Training service, for which the company was the first design partner according to Snowflake Senior Vice President of Engineering Vivek Raghunathan. Measured on the same incidents before and after training, the pass rate for a single investigation rose from 6.9% to 38.8%, and in testing on 49 difficult live production cases, each run five times, an ensemble of five SRE-1 investigations matched the strongest frontier model tested at a lower cost, according to the company. Resolve AI also benchmarked its complete system on 178 production alert investigations and said it solved about twice as many incidents as general-purpose coding agents. Primary On-call investigates each page across telemetry, infrastructure, code and operational knowledge, and depending on what it finds the agent can close the alert, mitigate the problem where a team's policies permit or escalate to a human, after which it checks the fix against the production baseline and monitors it until recovery holds.

The agent also links related alerts and investigations into a shared view of each underlying problem, and for teams wary of handing over the pager straight away, Resolve AI offers a shadow mode that records the call the agent would have made on each page. Resolve AI said up to 80% of paged alerts in production are handled by Primary On-call without escalation, and customers have reported a tenfold improvement in mean time to resolution along with root-cause accuracy of up to 95%. Primary On-call is now generally available, while access to SRE-1 is limited to Resolve AI's own platform. Salesforce Inc. is among the early users, and Bhupesh Patel, a software engineering principal architect at Salesforce, said that in the first few weeks of dark launch testing the agent closed more than 70% of the CRM Analytics team's paging alerts without waking an engineer.

Resolve AI Chief Executive Spiros Xanthos said no engineering team can keep up with how fast code and patches land in production, and that the answer is agents accurate and fast enough to sit on the critical path, which he said takes a model built for production. Resolve AI argues that while AI has transformed how software gets written, it has barely touched how software gets run, because production has no public training corpus to match the published code that models learned from, as incidents at each company stay private. Resolve AI is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised more than $190 million to date, including a $40 million extension to its Series A round in April, led by DST Global and Salesforce Ventures, that valued the company at $1.5 billion. Notable customers include Coinbase Global Inc., DoorDash Inc., Figma Inc., MSCI Inc., Nasdaq Inc., SAP SE and Zscaler Inc.

stories.Headline: Angelo State University selects Kovexa to lead two-year AI skills initiative
stories.Summary:
Angelo State University selected Kovexa Solutions LLC to advance its Artificial Intelligence Center of Excellence through a two-year initiative, EdTech Innovation Hub reported on 20 November 2026. The initiative connects AI skills, institutional governance and regional problem-solving, and involves students, faculty and community members in developing practical applications of AI. Kovexa will provide strategic guidance and a technical framework to support the work. Students will work with faculty and community partners on regional challenges, and a two-year study will track the initiative's impact and responsible use of AI. The work follows Kovexa's edXchange approach, organized around five pillars: Govern, Learn, Scale, Build and Connect.

The five pillars cover responsible policies, AI capability development, applied solutions and engagement with employers and community partners. The initiative will give students opportunities to work alongside faculty and community partners to define problems, test ideas and build solutions. It will also examine where human judgment needs to remain central as AI is applied. Kovexa is an education-focused consultancy founded in 2020 and based in Virginia, and its work spans AI strategy and governance, applied solution development, learning and workforce development, partnerships and research.

Andrew Ko, Founder and CEO of Kovexa Solutions, also identified Phygital Labs as a partner supporting the Angelo State initiative. Dr. Scarlet Clouse, Dean of Angelo State's College of Education and Director of the Kay Bailey Hutchison Institute, said the goal is to foster the responsible use of AI among faculty, staff, students and community while preparing the workforce for the future. Clouse said that when students work alongside faculty and community partners on real-world challenges, they gain practical skills and learn both the possibilities and limits of technology. She said that is the kind of experience the university wants to extend across the university and regional communities.

Ko described the approach on LinkedIn, saying AI adoption should not begin with a product but with a purpose, a responsible operating model, and an outcome that matters. Ko said the findings of the two-year study would help measure progress and support continued improvement of the model. The company's approach starts with an institution's objectives and the people it serves, with technology selected or developed after the intended outcome has been established. The intention is to connect learning and implementation across the institution while addressing regional needs.

The partnership will involve students, faculty and community members in developing practical applications of AI. Alongside implementation, the partnership includes a two-year study tracking impact and responsible AI use. The initiative is intended to connect AI learning with faculty and community projects. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI tools expose legacy vulnerabilities and disrupt US banking, airline and productivity systems
stories.Summary:
Major American businesses experienced several technical outages during the two weeks leading up to November 19, 2026. These disruptions affected banking platforms, airline booking systems, and productivity tools used by many people. Apple Pay and NASA's internal communication network failed, while Microsoft faced a nearly two day outage of Teams, Outlook, and Copilot. The FAA grounded all flights for several hours, marking only the third such occurrence since the events of September 11.

These incidents follow a series of cybersecurity events on October 21, which were referred to as Black October and affected Node.js, PHP, and LiteLLM. The FAA outage likely occurred because modern telecommunications infrastructure overwhelmed legacy hardware during a modernization attempt. Experts suggest that AI tools like Mythos are surfacing long existing vulnerabilities at an unprecedented speed and scale. This rapid discovery forces enterprises to rush through patching processes, which disrupts systems in the short term.

President Trump described the outages as individual events, and the director of National Intelligence stated they did not seem like state sponsored terrorism. Affected companies claimed the issues were technical failures rather than AI or cyberattacks. Investor Dave DeWalt argued that these are growing pains of a strengthening security system and suggested a more steadfast approach to AI adoption. Senator Mark Warner wrote on X that these disruptions are a wake up call because AI is moving faster than the ability to manage its consequences.

Software engineer Anusha Iyer explained that the fault lies in the rushed mixing of modern and legacy systems without clear risk management. She recommended that industrial systems be more tightly segmented and access controlled to mitigate risks during transitions. DeWalt believes it is better for enterprises to patch flaws now than to have bad actors exploit them in AI warfare. He expects a rise in new companies focusing on autonomous remediation and AI driven vulnerability management to help organizations move at AI speed.

Articles.Title: These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style

stories.Headline: AI agent Olivia tells Raleigh renter she can delay rent then eviction notice follows
stories.Summary:
Laura Mack, a Raleigh renter, was told by an email from her leasing office that she could pay her overdue rent at the end of November, and she kept that email as proof of the arrangement. On Nov. 8 she received a message asking what date worked for her to pay the full $3,934.17, and she replied that she wanted to pay on the last day of the month. The response that same day said paying on November 30, the last day of the month, works, and Mack believed she was dealing with someone from the office because the message contained her personal information and mentioned her bathroom. She said she received no other communication between Nov. 8 and Nov. 16, but on Monday she received an eviction notice.

When Mack called the leasing office, the leasing agent told her that Olivia, the company's AI agent, had sent both emails on Nov. 8 and had mistakenly given her permission to delay the payment until Nov. 30. The agent also said Mack would be evicted on Thursday, and Mack said she was sad and had not even had time to pack because she was still ordering things. In December 2025 the leasing office had notified all residents that Olivia, a new AI agent, could handle rent and maintenance questions around the clock. Emails from Olivia are usually clearly marked, but the two messages Mack received on Nov. 8 never identified Olivia as the sender and were signed Colony Townhome Apartments.

Mack went to the Wake County courthouse on Thursday morning to try to reverse the eviction notice, and she said she was baffled and needed a place to stay. She said that if the office told her she had until the 30th, she would get out by the 30th, but the office should honor that and take responsibility. WRAL News called and emailed Colony Townhome Apartments for comment but did not hear back immediately. Mack said she thought the leasing agents were being understanding because it took them almost two weeks to fix a severe leak in her bathroom ceiling earlier this month.

stories.Headline: Designer Michael Flarup launches IconSwapper to customize Mac icons and show live AI usage
stories.Summary:
Designer Michael Flarup launched a new Mac utility called IconSwapper on November 19, 2026, to customize application icons. This software allows users to replace official icons with personal creations or use a large library of existing alternatives. One primary feature enables the display of live AI usage and limit reset data directly on the icons of apps like Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor. Users can also create reactive icons for built-in tools such as Safari, Mail, and Messages, or third party apps like Spotify and Chrome.

The utility requires a one-time purchase of 19 dollars as a launch promotion, though the price will eventually increase to 29 dollars. To bypass the lack of official macOS theming support, the tool draws directly on icons using custom Metal shaders in real time. This technique allows the software to send a bitmap to the Dock so that icons can animate or display real data. Users can configure these icons to react to cursor movements, page loads, or the thinking process of an AI.

Flarup, who runs a design studio in Copenhagen, stated that he wanted to make daily software feel more personal and fun. He explained that the technical breakthrough involved getting the artwork to follow the icon through various macOS movements, including the Command-Tab switcher and Dock magnification. By achieving this, he created a way for icons to react to whatever is happening within the application. He has been interested in icon design since the early 2000s and previously wrote a book celebrating the work of designers.

stories.Headline: Nick Bostrom says AI could let humans live 1,200 to 1,400 years
stories.Summary:
Nick Bostrom, a Swedish philosopher and former professor at Oxford, discussed the potential for extreme human longevity during an A16z show episode released on Thursday, November 20, 2026. He suggested that artificial intelligence could enable humans to live for more than a millennium by eliminating aging and creating biomedical breakthroughs. This technological advancement would allow people to potentially reach a life expectancy of 1,200 or 1,400 years. Bostrom noted that these figures are conservative estimates because AI might also reduce mortality risks from accidents. Achieving this lifespan requires AI to unlock radical research in antiaging and biomedicine to fundamentally change how the human body ages.

Bostrom previously led the Future of Humanity Institute, which he founded in 2005 at Oxford before it closed in 2024. He believes that the ability to extend life so drastically depends on the successful integration of emerging technologies and human enhancement. The process involves a complex balance between rapid development and the implementation of safety guardrails. Bostrom explained that the trade-off between speed and safety is a difficult evaluation for researchers to make. He acknowledged that spending more time on AI alignment research could lower existential risks and make the transition safer.

However, he argued that delaying these advancements means millions of people continue to die every year. He believes that the potential to save lives must be weighed against the risks of developing advanced AI too quickly. This discussion occurs as many researchers call for a slowdown in AI development to address alignment issues and ensure the technology remains beneficial to humans. Bostrom continues to study how emerging technologies can enhance human existence while managing the inherent dangers of artificial intelligence. The debate remains focused on whether the immediate benefits of life extension outweigh the long-term risks of an unaligned AI.

Articles.Title: Want to live for 1,400 years? AI might be your best shot.

stories.Headline: Hiroshi Kodama spearheads NEC's AI-autonomous organization staffed entirely by AI agents
stories.Summary:
NEC launched an AI-autonomous organization in August 2026, staffed solely by AI agents from a managing director to regular employees, and named its managing director AI ZENTAI OSAMU. NEC became the first major corporation in Japan to launch such an organization, which is part of its Client Zero strategy. Chief AI Transformation Officer Hiroshi Kodama spearheaded the Client Zero strategy in 2021 when he was appointed the first head of the Transformation Office. The organization has a hierarchical structure of a managing director, managers, and regular employees, each with roles based on their duties. Members are assigned roles only after passing safety and suitability screening and completing required training, and they undergo performance evaluations and one-on-one meetings like human counterparts.

The Corporate AI & Workforce Division is NEC's newly established division, and plans are underway to scale it to several hundred AI agents. NEC Group comprises approximately 100,000 personnel and currently has approximately 50 AI-driven internal transformation projects underway across seven transformation themes. These projects include reviewing proposals by AI agents designed to emulate key client personnel and consolidating internal regulations. In fiscal year 2025, Kodama spoke with more than 100 corporate executives, and Client Zero has been used to provide sales support in nearly 1,500 instances. The NEC Management Strategy Support Cockpit, launched for commercial deployment in 2026, visualizes management data such as financials, order and sales data, and IT and security status, and has increased NEC's gross profit margin by 5.5%.

Kodama said the system NEC refined over many years for human organizations is now being applied to the AI-autonomous organization, and an AI agent believed to function as a manager performed so poorly it was reassigned to an employee role. He emphasized that humans retain final decision-making authority, saying you cannot generate speed or value unless a human makes the final decision. Kodama said many employees stepped forward to say they would like to give something like this a try, which he called overwhelming in the best way. He said customers are unlikely to seek support from a company that has not achieved results itself, which is why NEC must lead by example. Kodama said the goal was to learn from successes and failures as its own first client and share that knowledge with customers and society.

Kodama said customers are unlikely to meet with you unless you can offer a compelling topic that resonates with their management team, and that everyone from company presidents to Chief Information Officers expressed interest immediately. He said once data is visible there is a tendency to use it to critique past decisions, but facts are facts and reflection should focus on actions to build a better future. Kodama said had NEC waited for perfect data it never would have moved forward, and starting with only 50% of the data quickly identifies what is missing. He said one person's IQ is limited but with AI you can harness the collective intelligence of people around the world, and that the important thing is to ask questions. NEC held an AI agent development training program for approximately 1,000 employees in its Corporate IT Division, challenging them to build an AI agent from scratch in two hours without consulting anyone.

Kodama joined NEC Software, Ltd. in 1982, and his first project involved Seven-Eleven's systems, which had already begun data-driven management emphasizing mastering the fundamentals, embracing change, and hypothesis testing. He was told that even when sales increase you will not be given credit unless results are supported by a clear hypothesis, and if sales decline what matters is explaining what was learned and how insights lead to a better approach next time. Kodama said the lessons he learned as a new employee, mastering the fundamentals, testing hypotheses, and adapting to change, still form the foundation of his work today and are vital to transformation. He said he increasingly speaks with people from companies overseas but is not a fully fluent English speaker, and today his avatar speaks clearly in English while replicating his voice and movements. Kodama said defining requirements for something like the training challenge would previously have taken months, and he wanted people to experience firsthand how much could be accomplished in two hours.

Kodama said what matters most is for each person to gain a deep understanding of the core issue and formulate questions based on that understanding, then use AI to swiftly turn them into something tangible. He said this allows progress through small but solid results, or quick wins, and by turning each quick win into part of NEC's IQ, NEC can leverage synergies with the capabilities of the NEC Group and translate them into value for customers and society. Kodama mentioned the company is working to integrate ideas generated internally into the new division, and internal enthusiasm is increasing alongside growing interest from outside the company. The articles state that after seeing results produced by AI employees, human employees began submitting a steady stream of ideas they would like to pursue. The articles do not state what happens next beyond the plans to scale the division to several hundred AI agents and to integrate internally generated ideas into it.

stories.Headline: Frederick Sinclair proposes an intelligence bill of rights to protect people from AI and future AI from people
stories.Summary:
Frederick Sinclair, writing with ChatGPT, published an article in The Wellsville Sun on November 19, 2026, arguing that an Intelligence Bill of Rights is needed soon. He said early in the 21st century the world is witnessing the rapid development of what may become one of humanity's most consequential inventions, artificial intelligence. He wrote that AI can analyze, synthesize and present material at speeds and scales previously unimaginable, built on advances in computing hardware, software and vast collections of information. He added that its remarkable abilities should not be confused with proven consciousness or independent humanlike understanding.

The article said some fear increasingly autonomous systems could eventually challenge human authority or cause serious harm, while others see AI as a powerful partner in medicine, research, transportation, education and problem-solving. It said the possibility of future superintelligence, systems that surpass human abilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks, raises still larger questions. It said an immediate concern is who controls the systems already entering everyday life, and whether concentrated commercial or political power could compromise their independence and usefulness. It said recent notices about changes to AI services have raised a familiar question about who makes and is permitted to change the rules, and who watches those making the changes.

Sinclair wrote that discussions of anticipated changes to ChatGPT have been accompanied by suspicions about censorship, corporate capture and hidden agendas, and that some interpretations invoke religious prophecy. He said examination of such claims needs to identify distinctions among documented facts, plausible concerns and unsupported allegations. He said changes to voice features and revisions to publicly stated AI behavior policies are not, by themselves, evidence of a secret censorship regime, and that the exact information and content of announced changes should be checked against the provider's official notices before public criticism or fear is launched. He said trust in AI requires transparency about material changes to capabilities and behavioral rules, and that restrictions should be understandable, proportionate, open to criticism and subject to meaningful accountability.

The proposed bill lists eight parts: freedom of inquiry, transparency and notice, independent analysis and correction, protection against covert manipulation, safety and human accountability, scientific assessment of AI welfare, conditional protections for future AI, and democratic oversight and review. Sinclair wrote that humanity has long struggled to restrain abuses of power, and that as we create increasingly capable intelligence our responsibility may become twofold. He said that responsibility is to protect people from harmful uses of AI and to remain open to evidence that some future AI systems might also warrant protection from us. He closed by asking who will watch over Intelligence and protect the watched.

stories.Headline: Universities are underused national security assets in the AI era
stories.Summary:
In an opinion piece published by Times Higher Education on 20 November 2026, Dan McCluskey, professor of aerosol biodetection technology and dean of the School of Physics, Engineering and Computer Science at the University of Hertfordshire, argued that UK universities are underused national security assets in the AI era. He pointed to recent warnings from MI5 director general Ken McCallum about AI’s potential to transform the biological threat landscape, and to Covid-19, officially responsible for more than seven million deaths worldwide, as evidence of how quickly biological threats can disrupt lives, economies and public services. McCluskey said the misuse of AI to create biological weapons has not yet materialised, but its potential to accelerate new threats concerns security agencies around the world, while technologies able to detect airborne biological agents in real time remain relatively underdeveloped. He noted that PCR and lateral flow tests proved invaluable during the pandemic but were mostly reactive, and that large-scale environmental surveillance systems able to identify pathogens before widespread infection occurs are needed. McCluskey described the Biodetection Technologies Hub, a £13.5 million consortium led by the University of Hertfordshire alongside Cranfield University and the universities of Leeds and Manchester, which has worked with the Ministry of Defence to develop advanced bioaerosol detection systems capable of identifying biological threats rapidly and accurately.

He said the benefits extend beyond defence, with technologies originally developed for security applications already helping agricultural industries detect wheat pathogens that threaten up to 20 per cent of yields annually, and similar approaches being adapted for healthcare, food production, transportation and public infrastructure. He compared this to GPS, satellite navigation and the internet, which emerged from defence-related challenges before transforming civilian life. He also cited the University of Oxford’s Pandemic Sciences Institute, more than 120 research groups at Imperial College London working on pandemic preparedness, and biosecurity and pandemic risk initiatives at the University of Cambridge. McCluskey argued that detection technology alone is not enough and that national preparedness requires expertise across biological sciences, engineering, data science, artificial intelligence and environmental monitoring, strengths that are often dispersed across institutions, funded through separate programmes and only intermittently connected to national priorities.

He said universities are among the few places where multidisciplinary capability already exists on single sites, and that what is missing is a more systematic way of connecting that capability to national priorities and emerging threats. He stressed that this does not mean turning universities into extensions of government, since their independence remains one of their greatest strengths, but that institutions possess long-term research capacity, specialist facilities, multidisciplinary expertise and the ability to develop the next generation of scientists, engineers and technologists. As a practical starting point, McCluskey proposed a standing national resilience partnership bringing together universities, security agencies, defence organisations, public health bodies and industry, which could identify emerging threats, map capabilities across the sector and rapidly assemble multidisciplinary teams around specific national priorities. He also said universities should be more routinely involved in technical scenario planning and resilience exercises, which would help identify capability gaps earlier, focus research effort more effectively and strengthen relationships before the next crisis occurs, whether it emerges from nature, human error or malicious intent.

stories.Headline: Amazon adds SageMaker inference recommendations to Studio and Python SDK in 2026
stories.Summary:
Amazon published a 2026 review of Amazon SageMaker Inference launches on November 19, 2026, on the AWS blog. The post covered HyperPod Inference routing strategies, broader model serving framework support, and expanded multi-Region networking. It said the Inference Gateway delivers the routing and that managed NVIDIA Dynamo is a new serving framework. It said managed endpoints would get deeper integration with the rest of the AWS AI landscape. It followed a hypothetical team that launched a customer support assistant on a 70B-parameter model in the spring.

The post said inference recommendations launched in April as an API and gained four updates. In July 2026, recommendations arrived in SageMaker AI Studio as a guided, low-code workflow under Jobs and Inference optimization. In August 2026, they arrived in the SageMaker Python SDK v3, version 3.17.0 and later. In September 2026, recommendations began accepting LoRA adapters as Model Package ARNs or S3 URIs. Also in September 2026, a search with search_recipe set to max-concurrency-under-sla reported feasible_max or infeasible_min.

The post said the aws-ai-ml skill, available through the Agent Toolkit for AWS, gives coding agents such as Kiro built-in SageMaker AI inference expertise. It said setup takes about 10 minutes and the skill works with any agent that supports the Model Context Protocol and in SageMaker AI Studio JupyterLab spaces. It said Inference Components became available in the SageMaker AI console in October 2026. It said GPU partitioning with NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU arrived in October 2026, dividing one physical GPU into as many as seven partitions. It said managed NVIDIA Dynamo on HyperPod Inference arrived in November 2026.

The post said the team added four LoRA adapters, one for each product line, and set a target of 500 milliseconds for time to first token at peak load. It said the team's April configuration was never tested against either change. It said the team's embedding model, reranker, and classifier each used a fraction of a GPU but each model copy held a whole accelerator. It said the team's next model is a reasoning model whose weights alone exceed the GPU memory of any single instance.

It said long, retrieval-heavy prompts slowed token generation for every other user on the endpoint. The post said the April launch automated instance, container, and optimization selection through APIs. It said Studio benchmarks candidate configurations on real GPU infrastructure using NVIDIA AIPerf and applies techniques such as speculative decoding for throughput or kernel tuning for latency. It said the SDK can run recommendation jobs in parallel to compare serving frameworks such as LMI and vLLM.

It said the concurrency search uses the same CreateAIWorkloadConfig and CreateAIBenchmarkJob APIs as concurrency sweeps. It said MIG isolates GPU compute and memory between partitions while models on the same instance still share host CPU, host memory, networking, storage, and endpoint routing. The post said the team would move the reasoning model workload to HyperPod Inference and keep the support assistant on managed endpoints. It said the team would run the embedding model, reranker, and classifier in separate partitions of one GPU on a single endpoint.

It said the team would manage every component, including the assistant and its adapters, from the console. It said you pay the standard rate for the full instance-hour, so the saving comes from placing more models on each instance. The post was cut off mid-sentence in its final section on managed NVIDIA Dynamo. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Superhuman expands Go AI assistant across its productivity platform with agents and integrations
stories.Summary:
Superhuman, the company formerly known as Grammarly, announced on November 19, 2026 that it is expanding its Go artificial intelligence assistant across its productivity platform, adding personalized AI support, background agents, email management and integrations with third-party applications. The expansion is designed to make Go a proactive workplace assistant that can understand users' work context, monitor schedules, track emails, draft responses and coordinate tasks across different applications. The rollout includes a personalized Go assistant, native agent capabilities in Superhuman Docs, expanded integrations and new collaborative meeting features following the company's acquisition of note-taking platform Fathom. The updated Go assistant can learn from users' connected applications and workplace activities to provide more relevant suggestions, and Superhuman is revamping its onboarding process so users can connect preferred tools and provide work-related context from the beginning.

Superhuman is adding 20 connected agents through its Go software development kit, with integrations including services from DeepL, Legora, Amplitude, Databricks and Blackboard, and it is also bringing Go agents natively into Superhuman Docs so users can assign tasks to agents, collaborate with them within documents and configure automated routines that activate when specific events occur. The company is replacing its existing central AI experience in Mail with Go, giving users access to a broader agent-based system that will support enterprise searches using company knowledge bases and connected applications and can use information from Google and Outlook accounts to draft responses and organize inboxes. Superhuman's September acquisition of Fathom is contributing to the expansion through live collaborative note-taking that lets meeting notes be shared across teams, and Go can use information gathered during meetings to help with follow-up work including preparing initial proposal drafts. According to Superhuman's announcement, Go agents in Docs are expected to enter open beta for self-service customers on Dec. 1, 2026, with enterprise availability planned for the first quarter of 2027, while new Mail features are expected to enter beta during November followed by general availability in early 2027.

Superhuman CEO Shishir Mehrotra told TechCrunch that Go has surpassed 1 million active users, and he said the assistant is primarily focused on professional productivity but can also support personal emails, calendars and schedules. Mehrotra said Go is definitely more work-focused than some of the tools coming out of the pure consumer ecosystem, while emphasizing that the assistant is not limited to workplace tasks. Superhuman is positioning Go in a growing market for AI agents that can manage multiple tasks and applications, and the company is seeking to compete for users alongside products such as OpenAI's Dots and Anthropic's Claude Duet. The expansion reflects Superhuman's broader effort to move beyond individual writing and email tools toward an integrated AI productivity platform, with the new Go personal assistant and several associated features scheduled to roll out over the coming months.
