stories.Headline: Anthropic raises 81.34 billion dollars in record Nasdaq IPO
stories.Summary:
Anthropic launched its initial public offering on the Nasdaq exchange on Thursday, November 20, 2026. The company priced its shares at 83 dollars, which valued the artificial intelligence giant at 1.5 trillion dollars. The stock opened at 111.50 dollars, which was 34 percent above the initial price. It later closed up 17 percent at 97.17 dollars per share. This debut gave the company a market capitalization of 1.3 trillion dollars.

The record breaking IPO raised 81.34 billion dollars, or 107.34 billion dollars including a 26 billion dollar private placement. Menlo invested over 1 billion dollars for a 1.5 percent stake worth over 20 billion dollars. Lightspeed invested over 3 billion dollars and holds more than 2 percent of the company. The company reached a market cap of 2 trillion dollars, edging past the June listing of SpaceX. This valuation made Anthropic the sixth largest company in the world.

CEO Dario Amodei said he and his co-founders started the company to benefit humankind. He mentioned that AI will have a positive human impact on gene editing and CRISPR. He stated that the mission requires everyone to work together for future generations. Amodei noted that he and Daniela Amodei lost their father to a disease. He believes the most powerful technology of our time should be built for people.

Protesters rallied against the company in New York and San Francisco after the stock market debut. Some AI safety advocates challenged the safety branding used by the company. Over 400 employees are estimated to be worth more than 100 million dollars each. Some insiders say these new millionaires are too science obsessed to buy mansions. Others worry that these wealthy employees might leave the company.

The company is a public benefit corporation and was founded by seven co-founders. Emily Zhao invested 50 million dollars in March 2023 when the company was pre-revenue. Iconiq changed its mind and invested after previously passing on the Series E round. Yasmin Razavi of Spark Capital was the only venture capitalist listed in the S-1. The company launched the first version of Claude before its early funding rounds.

The IPO could deliver 156 billion dollars to charity according to some reports. The stock is now live with external pricing and 10x leverage. Some analysts believe the age of unicorns is over now that multiple startups exceed one trillion dollars. The articles leave open whether the company is worth 1.1 trillion or 1.5 trillion dollars. It remains unclear how the company will handle its safety fears.

stories.Headline: Check Point Research publishes a principle it calls gatekeeper asymmetry doom
stories.Summary:
Check Point Research published on November 19, 2026 an exposition of a principle it calls gatekeeper asymmetry doom, stating that if the system vetting adversarial input has strictly less power than the system processing that input, without leveraging some hard problem, this will inevitably lead to doom. The article lists examples of the principle in action, including the limits of static binary classification, the proliferation of sandbox evasions and Check Point's own PuzzleMask research for bypassing external AI guardrails. It also gives a short exposition of how the Time Hierarchy Theorem exemplifies the same principle. It concludes with a recommendation that doomed attack surfaces should be noticed and the gap narrowed as much as possible, by upgrading gatekeeper power or using its existing power more comprehensively. It notes that frontier LLMs, with scaffolding, extended reasoning and code execution in the chain of thought, have significant power in this sense and can meaningfully contribute to narrowing doom gaps, though they themselves are still subject to the principle.

The principle is offered in the same spirit as Moxie Marlinspike's Cryptographic Doom Principle, and the article says leveraging a hard problem excludes cases such as signature verification for binary files, which is many times simpler than executing the file but can still in a certain theoretical world determine whether the binary is malicious. The article phrases the principle more glibly as every quick sanity check involving either cryptography or a silent prayer, and shortens gatekeeper asymmetry doom to doom. Its warm-up example is hash comparison, which it says someone in the industry must have thought solved malware at some point during the 1990s, by collecting all hashes of malicious binaries in a large database for an antivirus to check each executed binary against. The gap there was truly huge, the article says, because the target is the full Turing-complete execution of a binary and the gatekeeper is a simple observation of whether the binary is in some set of known files. Threat actors' counter was infamous and trivial, randomizing the value of some non-load-bearing byte for each compiled binary.

The article says pattern matching and regular expressions underlie YARA rules and act as a backbone of binary classification still to this day, and that as of 2026 AI-augmented YARA rule generation has already improved the throughput of signature authorship considerably, though coverage and consistency are not close to a defender-optimistic utopia. It says regular expressions are not powerful enough to parse HTML and are also not powerful enough to capture the class of assembly subroutines that perform some action, or that perform some action using some specific algorithm, or that perform some action as implemented by some specific sequence of instructions subject to moderate mutation. It says the projected end state would be some malware generation process that takes care to inject this moderate mutation into every subroutine, a new kind of polymorphism. It says static reverse engineering, also known as reading the disassembly, is considered the apex form of static analysis, and that even frontier LLMs have historically struggled with dynamic-equivalent static analysis and in the worst case still do. It says the target victim machine can run the malicious binary but the gatekeeper, human or LLM, cannot natively, and through this capability gap came packers, opaque predicates, control flow flattening, the movfuscator and the Rust Programming Language.

The article says basic computability theory tells us the gap can't disappear outright, and that in the static reverse engineering utopia of a human-expert-level LLM analyzing every new binary in the wild, the new equilibrium lives in the gap, with binaries universally obfuscated to such a degree that a debugger is strongly required. It cites the SolarWinds compromised update, which it says unabashedly attempted to brainwash anyone reading its source code into compliance with the idea that they are looking at benign software. It says mitigations exist for this technique in both LLMs and humans, but it is representative of the general shape of the gatekeeper asymmetry that emerges there. It says malware has traditionally had the property of not wanting to be read, and we do not quite yet live in a world where selection pressures have pushed it to either adopt bleeding edge obfuscation or perish. It describes a possible post-equilibrium world where we miss the old days when we could unpack binaries to make code readable, where our favorite disassembler becomes the vessel of a futile hope, and where an LLM told to reverse engineer a binary ends up forced to reinvent the sandbox from first principles.

In an interlude on what gatekeeper asymmetry doom is not, the article cherry-picks disastrous phenomena in information security that it says have absolutely nothing to do with the principle. It says fuzzing being viable as a vulnerability discovery strategy involves typically no gatekeeper standing between adversarial input and the target application. It says the possibility of supply chain attacks is out of scope, because gatekeepers by definition exist to vet untrusted input, and facing trusted adversarial input is very bad but out of scope. It describes the lagging race for automatic detection of fast flux domains, with detection models advancing from an ineffectual shrug to calculating domain entropy to catch xrewrgfuvhnadfsajkaldsfj.biz, then n-gram frequency engines, then weird edit distance to the dictionary hacks to catch Kwyjibo. It says attackers evolved to use concatenations of randomly generated dictionary words, and the text of the article ends there, mid-sentence, with defenders could have re.

The article leaves open what defenders could have done next in the fast flux domain race, since its text stops at that point. It leaves open how the gap should be narrowed in each of the examples it lists, beyond the general recommendation to upgrade gatekeeper power or use existing power more comprehensively. It leaves open what the post-equilibrium world of obfuscated binaries will look like in practice, beyond the shape it says we can see and find little to like about. It leaves open how frontier LLMs will fare as contributors to narrowing doom gaps while remaining subject to the principle themselves. It gives no date for when the projected end states it describes might arrive, and no figures beyond the 1990s and 2026.

stories.Headline: Waswo X Waswo uses AI to expand photographs in Delhi exhibition
stories.Summary:
Waswo X Waswo’s solo exhibition Long Short Stories opened at Latitude 28 in Delhi and runs until November 20, 2026, bringing together photography, miniature painting, old engravings, a video installation and sculpture. The show is built around an imagined American traveller called Dandy, played by Waswo in Mughal robes, who arrives in a fantastical Indian city with a telescope, befriends a prince, survives battles of magic and finally flees with the prince on an old scooty with arrows flying behind them. The story is funny, absurd and in parts autobiographical, and the photographic works follow Dandy as he is welcomed into a royal court, grows too powerful, is exiled and escapes with the prince. The exhibition also includes a series called Other Stories, which begins with pages from an 1804 Belgian book, The Costume of Hindostan by Baltazard Solvyns, featuring 60 hand-coloured engravings of 18th century India.

The show takes forward the Udaipur-based artist’s long interest in India, the outsider’s gaze and the small personal stories that official history leaves out, which he says build up the larger narrative and give the exhibition its title. Waswo shoots black-and-white photographs that are then hand-coloured and worked on with miniature painting techniques, with flowers, birds and other details painted onto them by his collaborators, a process he says took a year and involves considerable handcraft. The biggest departure this time is the use of AI, which he used to expand his usual square-format photographs into panoramas, and he is wary of the assumption that AI does all the work, saying the craft is still there. He now works with a new team in Udaipur including Dalpat and Banti Jingar, Shankar Kumawat and Chirag Kumawat, with Bhavesh Jingar contributing to the video installation, and he makes sure their names appear alongside his in the gallery and catalogue.

Waswo says he certainly realises he is an outsider here, an American very far from his distant land, though he is now accepted in the Indian art world and treated almost like family in Udaipur, where he has lived for about 20 years. He is also conscious that being a white American has opened many doors for him, and he believes Indians can recognise themselves in this outsider because India is so diverse that people can feel foreign even when they move from one part of the country to another. On his team he says they are stronger together than apart, like a rope that is the sum of its individual strands. Of the Other Stories works, in which he and his collaborators add contemporary details and symbols to the Solvyns engravings to make them satirical and sometimes funny, he says viewers are invited to construct their own stories about those, with no single narrative and each work leaving room for the viewer to imagine one.

Articles.Title: Waswo X Waswo’s Long Short Stories blends AI, miniatures, photography in Delhi show

stories.Headline: TiE Bangalore and the Aerospace Industry Association of India call for integrated AI adoption in aerospace and defence
stories.Summary:
A report released at the Bengaluru Tech Summit on November 19, 2026, said India’s aerospace, defence and space industry needs to move beyond isolated artificial intelligence experiments toward integrated, production-ready applications. The report, titled “Intelligent by Design: AI Adoption in India’s Aerospace, Defence and Space Industry,” was brought out by TiE Bangalore and the Aerospace Industry Association of India. It identified AI as a significant opportunity to improve engineering productivity, manufacturing efficiency, maintenance and operational performance across the sector. The study also cautioned that adoption across the industry remains uneven, with significant differences in technological maturity, investment capacity and organisational readiness.

Drawing on practitioner perspectives gathered through interviews, working sessions and written contributions, the report identifies four major constraints: fragmented data access, inadequate integration with existing engineering systems, shortages of specialised talent and concerns around accountability in safety-critical applications. It pointed out that aerospace and defence manufacturing involves complex engineering processes, stringent certification requirements and long product lifecycles, so AI-generated outputs cannot be accepted without adequate validation, traceability and human oversight. Applications with potential include predictive maintenance, engineering design optimisation, quality inspection, supply-chain analytics, digital twins and automated documentation, and AI could also help analyse large volumes of engineering data, identify anomalies and improve decision-making. The report highlighted that access to reliable, structured and integrated data was fundamental to successful adoption, since fragmented records, inconsistent data formats and legacy systems often prevent organisations from deploying AI solutions at scale.

The report also underlines the importance of protecting sensitive technical information, intellectual property and operational data, and it flags the non-availability of skilled manpower as another major concern. It says the industry needs engineers who combine domain expertise with knowledge of AI, machine learning, data science and digital engineering tools, and it calls for stronger collaboration between industry, academic institutions and technology providers to develop these capabilities. It also stresses that smaller suppliers and MSMEs could face greater challenges because of limited resources, technology access and investment capacity, and it suggests shared infrastructure, collaborative platforms and targeted support could help them participate in the emerging AI ecosystem. The report was published on November 19, 2026, and the articles do not say what steps, if any, have been taken since its release.

stories.Headline: Sudhanshu Trivedi says AI can predict Rahul Gandhi's repeated remarks and suggests sending an AI version abroad
stories.Summary:
BJP spokesperson and Rajya Sabha MP Sudhanshu Trivedi held a press conference at the party headquarters in New Delhi on Thursday, November 19, 2026, and criticised Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over remarks he made during a two-day visit to the United States. During that trip, Gandhi interacted with students and faculty at Columbia University in New York on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, and at the University of Chicago on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. At the University of Chicago, Gandhi said Indian democracy is sacred and that the Congress is ready to face electoral defeats until people realise the system has been completely demolished. He also said that boycotting elections over alleged flaws in the system would bring an end to Indian democracy, which the Congress does not intend to do.

Trivedi said it was unfortunate that Gandhi was making remarks against India in Chicago, the city where Swami Vivekananda had once brought glory to the country, and that a leader of the opposition was lowering the prestige of Mother India at the same place. He was responding to Gandhi's remarks questioning the 2024 Lok Sabha elections and concerns over electoral irregularities, and to Gandhi's claim that a Brazilian model voted 23 times in India, asking whether anyone coming from abroad should not have an immigration record. Trivedi accused Gandhi of making what he called Hawai allegations about India's electoral process and of lowering the country's image on foreign soil. Taking a swipe at Gandhi's frequent foreign visits, Trivedi said the Congress should stop spending money on sending him abroad.

Trivedi said it is the age of AI and that the Congress should simply send an AI-generated version of Gandhi because he has to repeat the same sentences and words again and again. He suggested an AI model could be programmed with four options, namely making derogatory remarks against India, saying something against the prime minister, creating an uproar over democracy, and embarrassing his own party by raising something anti-India. He claimed artificial intelligence could do a better job than Gandhi's repeated remarks and that AI models were now capable of predicting what the Congress leader would say and the responses to his statements. The BJP also said the Congress should consider sending an AI-generated version of its leader abroad because he keeps repeating the same words.

Articles.Title: BJP mocks Rahul Gandhi's U.S. remarks, says AI can predict his speeches

stories.Headline: Riddhipratim Basu wins 2026 Infosys Prize in mathematical sciences
stories.Summary:
Riddhipratim Basu, an associate professor at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, has been awarded the 2026 Infosys Prize in the mathematical sciences category. The ICTS is part of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, and before joining it Dr. Basu was an assistant professor at Stanford University. In his work he uses mathematics to understand how random events produce predictable patterns in physical systems. He corresponded with The Hindu by email after the Prize, and the newspaper presented the exchange after editing it for length.

The interview asked Dr. Basu whether there are important phenomena in nature or society for which we still lack the mathematical tools to understand them, and what it would take to develop those tools. He replied that nature has endless mysteries and that we have barely scratched the surface, adding that there are many phenomena we still lack a precise understanding of. He said the systems mathematicians study are more often than not highly simplified versions of the real-world phenomena they are trying to model. He added that mathematicians nevertheless believe these simplified systems capture the essential features of those phenomena.

The 2026 Infosys Prize in mathematical sciences is the award named in the headline, and Dr. Basu is the laureate it refers to. The article gives no further detail on the prize money, the citation or the award ceremony, and it does not say when or where the prize will be presented. It also does not say what Dr. Basu plans to do next with the award or how the recognition might change his research. The published material is limited to the announcement of the award and his edited email remarks on the limits of mathematical modelling.

The article does not report any statement from Dr. Basu on keeping humans at the centre of mathematics as we adapt to artificial intelligence, beyond what the headline indicates. It also carries no comment from the Infosys Prize organisers, from ICTS or from Stanford University on the award. No date is given for when the prize was announced beyond the publication date of November 19, 2026, and no other numbers appear in the text. The article says nothing further about what happens next, so the only follow-up it supports is the interview itself.

stories.Headline: Sociologist William Robinson says AI capital drives global crisis and links with fascism
stories.Summary:
The Cockroach movement in India and cost of living protests across France and Germany in recent weeks express a broader crisis of global capitalism, according to William I. Robinson, professor of sociology at University of California, Santa Barbara. Robinson said the crisis includes a social reproduction dimension that has catalysed movements from below through an explosion of critical consciousness and social solidarity. He said agents of the transnational elite have tried to divide working classes through propaganda, threats and mass psychology. He said the protests resist capitalism's bid to enhance the power of the transnational elite at the common man's expense. He said the system's trajectory, felt through intensified intra-capitalist competition and class wars, is undermining its capacity to reproduce itself and leading to a point of no return.

Robinson's latest book, Pax Silica: The New Ruling Class, explores the emergence of new lords of the world in the age of AI and how they reshape the world to consolidate power. He said AI turbocharges capital's centuries-old drive to deskill and cheapen labour and threatens to eliminate labour altogether. He said AI is extremely expensive, with data centre construction requiring hundreds of billions of dollars in investment, so constant capital grows enormously relative to variable capital. He said the tech sector extracts surplus value from labour and rents from other sectors of capital that do the exploitation. He said the newest and most important source of profits worldwide now, and the accumulation strategy of the new hegemonic block of capital, is repression, warfare, genocide, conflict and chaos.

Robinson said historical figures such as Modi and Trump generate political, social and cultural conditions that deflect from the epochal crisis of global capitalism and disorganise, atomise, divide and confuse the labouring masses. He said the hegemonic block of AI capital brings together tech capital, military-industry repression capital and transnational finance capital, all linked to the new ruling class in the US and worldwide. He said that block decided over the last four to five years to link up with fascism in the state, with Trumpism, with Modiism, with Javier Milei in Argentina and with Netanyahu in Israel. He said the fascist project allows capital to accumulate, including through repression of the working class, and capital in turn supports fascism's political project. He said capital no longer needs our social reproduction.

Robinson said masses of people do not need to read Capital or call themselves Marxists to understand what is going on, and people are in rebellion worldwide without having read Marx. He said the ruling class wages psychological warfare at every level, and AI lets them wage new age warfare through social media, the attention economy and intervention in electoral processes. He said capital has fragmented and atomised people and turned them against one another, so mass struggles need new ways to recompose the global working class. He said a crisis of social reproduction and social disintegration is taking place in India, the US and Africa, and billions of people cannot survive or reproduce themselves and their communities. He said the students' rebellion in France is a working-class struggle against AI and a restructuring of global capitalism driven by digitalisation.

Robinson said the more global capital does not need workers, the more workers become surplus humanity and surplus labour. He said the more AI, machinery and constant capital take over, the less transnational capital needs young people trained to read and think in the abstract. He said there is no need to educate people who become surplus labour, only to control them, lock them up in mass incarceration or even commit genocide against them. He said education is being savagely defunded in France. He said the transition from precariatisation of labour, the shift towards unprotected employment, to the elimination of labour could in theory end capital-labour relations and therefore capitalism as known.

Robinson said AI, like fossil fuel extraction, represents an ability to concentrate disparate sources of value under centralised control and extract rent. He said Harry Braverman, building on Karl Marx in Labour & Monopoly Capital, laid out how capital seeks to deskill labour, cheapen it and take control of the labour process. He said Yanis Varoufakis's Technofeudalism: What Killed Capitalism is really brilliant, but the problem is that it is not feudalism, which is very distinct. He said rents are not new to capitalism and were always there, and super-profits come from profit made in different sectors migrating to the super-profits sector. He said globalisation unleashed an unprecedented historical centralisation and concentration of capital on a world scale in transnational capital and the transnational capitalist class.

Robinson said these people appear as lords of the world because they are the lords of the world, but they are capitalist lords, not feudal lords. He said the construction of data centres means fixed capital is enormously expanding relative to living labour, and the decline in the rate of profit in the long run is new territory. He said AI capital is constructing AI to expand profits, continue to accumulate and control global labour, and it will backfire on capital in the long run. He said we are moving towards World War III and towards a dystopic future nightmare society that previously existed only in Hollywood films. He said the more the struggle pushes forward, the more counter-consciousness to fascist consciousness expands.

stories.Headline: UBS forecasts S&P 500 reaching 8,200 by end of 2027 while cutting US equities to neutral on AI uncertainty
stories.Summary:
UBS Global Wealth Management said on 19 November 2026 that it expects the S&P 500 to reach 8,200 by the end of 2027, an upside of around 12% from current levels, according to a Livemint report. The brokerage based that target on resilient economic growth and continued expansion in corporate earnings across the US equity market. At the same time, UBS shifted its rating on US equities to neutral, citing elevated valuations, high market concentration and growing uncertainty around the artificial intelligence investment cycle. The report said the year-end 2027 target is broadly in line with Wells Fargo's outlook but remains below the more bullish projections from Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley. UBS estimated that S&P 500 earnings will rise 29% in 2026 and then expand a further 15% in 2027, even as it anticipates a moderation in earnings growth.

It expects global AI-related investment to keep expanding, rising to $1.4 trillion in 2027 and reaching $1.5 trillion in 2028. Within the AI ecosystem, the brokerage favours well-capitalised hyperscalers and select semiconductor and chip-equipment companies with strong competitive positions and clear opportunities to generate revenue from AI adoption. UBS cautioned that the path to further market gains could be volatile, flagging rising risks around AI-related disruption, financing and execution alongside elevated investor expectations. UBS explained its move to a neutral stance by saying that cannibalization, financing and execution risks around AI have increased while expectations and index concentration remain high. The brokerage added that while it expects gains, the path could be volatile.

The report noted that the AI trade has come under pressure amid opposition to large data-centre projects and concerns over the returns generated by heavy investment in the technology. Regulatory uncertainty following the US midterm elections and developments surrounding Nvidia have also contributed to investor caution, according to the report. The sustainability of the AI investment cycle is emerging as a key consideration for equity investors as markets assess whether substantial spending on AI infrastructure can translate into lasting earnings growth beyond 2027. UBS said the ability of companies to convert heavy AI spending into sustainable revenue and profits will be crucial in determining whether the current market momentum can be maintained. The brokerage's outlook suggests that while AI investment and corporate earnings could continue supporting US equities, investors may need to be more selective as expectations remain elevated.

stories.Headline: JPMorgan co-president Doug Petno calls AI market swings expected as winners and losers emerge
stories.Summary:
JPMorgan Chase co-President Doug Petno discussed the current state of artificial intelligence and the Japanese market during a recent exclusive interview with Nikkei. He addressed the significant market swings currently affecting companies related to artificial intelligence on November 20, 2026. Petno explained that these fluctuations are a normal result of a sector that has expanded very rapidly. This growth has been driven by massive amounts of capital moving through the industry and substantial funds being raised.

The situation requires an understanding that volatility is expected when so much money enters a new technological space. While the bank is very keen to adopt these new technologies, Petno emphasized that the human element in banking is not going away. He believes that the emergence of clear winners and losers within the AI field will naturally cause these price swings. The bank continues to monitor how these shifts impact the broader financial landscape and the Japanese market.

Doug Petno is the person responsible for sharing these views on behalf of the leadership at JPMorgan Chase. He stated that the current instability is simply the expected volatility of a space that has grown dramatically. By highlighting the movement of capital, he suggested that the market is adjusting to the scale of AI investment. He maintained that the integration of technology will not replace the essential role of human professionals.

stories.Headline: Researchers find regulators increasingly rely on legitimate interest to justify AI training data use
stories.Summary:
Wenlong Li and Yueming Zhang wrote an article on November 19, 2026, about AI training and GDPR compliance. They analyzed how data protection regulators are recognizing legitimate interest as a legal basis for training AI models. This trend has developed over the past two years into a form of regulatory orthodoxy. AI companies use this legal basis to process personal data without obtaining direct consent. The authors argue this approach to enforcement is fragmented and increasingly minimalist.

The GDPR serves as the global backbone for AI governance while the EU AI Act faces institutional uncertainty. Controllers must justify training on large personal data volumes using either consent or legitimate interest. The study mapped 19 guidelines and instruments alongside public enforcement actions against AI providers. Regulators like the French CNIL and the EU EDPB name check legitimate interests regarding web scraping. These authorities often view consent as operationally fragile or impracticable at a large scale.

Li and Zhang state that the convergence on legitimate interest is largely symbolic and lacks coherence. They argue that enforcement is dialogic rather than decisive and fails to resolve lawfulness conclusively. The authors claim that legitimate interest risks becoming a façade that obscures meaningful accountability. They suggest that the legitimate interest assessment should be a foundational pillar of GDPR compliance. The researchers believe a forward looking governance framework and minimum safeguard bundle are necessary.

Data protection authorities often focus on minimal safeguards like transparency and opt outs for AI providers. This focus leaves gaps in operational clarity for controllers and ignores thornier issues like hallucinations. Children's data has also been mostly dropped in the early stages of data protection enforcement. Meta paused AI training on European public content in June 2024 after engaging with the Irish DPC. Meta later revised its transparency and objection mechanisms after discussions with the UK ICO.

The authors identified a significant disconnect between official regulatory guidance and actual enforcement actions. They noted that regulatory responses remain uneven and fragmented across different global jurisdictions. The study mentions a withdrawn OpenAI fine as a pessimistic example of how GDPR operates. The researchers analyzed the prospects of global convergence based on levels of practical difficulty. They found clear convergence on dark patterns and the right to object.

The authors propose a strategy to align interpretations of reasonable expectations and the relevance of consent. They suggest pooling expertise to address divergences regarding the necessity of web scraping and accuracy. Future work will compare generative AI and personalized advertising using jurisprudence from the CJEU. The articles leave open whether minimalist safeguards are adequate given technical complexities and global diversity. They seek to formulate realistic goals for cooperation at global and sub global levels.

stories.Headline: Andrew Lloyd Webber says AI cannot create original musicals like Cats
stories.Summary:
Andrew Lloyd Webber told reporters in Seoul on Nov 19, on his first visit to Korea, that artificial intelligence would not have come up with Cats or The Phantom Of The Opera, because true musical success depends on original ideas and a strong story rather than on anything drawn from musicals of the past. He said that if he had asked such a system what to write after Evita 45 years ago, it would have based its answer on earlier shows, and he added that the originality a person brings is what matters. He also said AI would not have suggested the subject of his next show, the 1911 theft of the Mona Lisa from the Louvre, an idea that came from a story he read in The Times of London about how the painting drew little attention until it was stolen and disappeared for more than two years, with the publicity making it world-famous. He said the story made him think about what fame is and what the value of any piece of art is, and he plans to present the new musical in 2027. He was blunt about Broadway, saying that all the associated costs with a Broadway musical have become prohibitively high and that no new work of any consequence is really being done there any more.

He said he believes a good story can carry a musical score that may not be great, but a bad story cannot carry great music, because the story is in the end what people really come for. He said music has to add something to the story and be the reason for it being a musical, otherwise there is no point, and he welcomes new directors' takes on his previous shows as long as the music stays exactly as he wrote it, citing Jamie Lloyd's minimalist Sunset Boulevard and Cats: The Jellicle Ball. He called The Phantom Of The Opera the exception, saying the original production by Hal, meaning director Harold Prince, is so phenomenal that he does not think it will ever be bettered. The Phantom Of The Opera is returning to Seoul for its 40th anniversary in a Korean-language production that opens Dec 22 at Blue Square's Woori Bank Hall and runs through Feb 28, with Choi Jae-rim, Jeon Dong-seok and Park Kang-hyun rotating as the Phantom, sopranos Lee Hae-won and Choi Seon-ho making their musical debuts as Christine, and Song Won-geun and Kim Sung-sik playing Raoul.

The musical's Korean-language premiere in 2001 drew a record-breaking 240,000 people and generated 19.2 billion won, or S$18.6 million, in revenue, exceeding the country's entire musical theatre industry's annual revenue of 14 billion won that year, according to producer S&Co, and there have been six productions of Phantom in Korea drawing more than 1.5 million cumulative admissions. Seol Do-yoon, who produced the 2001 iteration, recalled trying to fund the show while Korea was still emerging from the 1997 financial crisis, saying he ran around everywhere trying to raise money but nobody would invest, though everyone who heard the music said the show would do really well and was so moving. Lloyd Webber attended a rehearsal on Nov 17 and called the cast absolutely excellent, saying the Korean language sat beautifully on the music and that it was stunning, and that he almost wished he could hear it in Korean all the time. He said he would return in 2027 to hear the musicals being written in Korea, adding that he is older now and loves hearing what young people are doing in musical theatre, which is the thing he loves most.

stories.Headline: Researcher warns AI could displace 19,000 jobs in the Worcester metropolitan area
stories.Summary:
Bhaskar Chakravorti discussed how artificial intelligence could disrupt thousands of local jobs and billions in wages on November 18, 2026. He spoke at the DCU Center during the 41st annual meeting of the Worcester Regional Research Bureau. The researcher warned that AI could displace more than 19,000 jobs in the Worcester metropolitan area. These projections suggest that an estimated 1.55 billion dollars in annual wages are at risk. The disruption is expected to occur over the next several years.

The American AI Jobs Risk Index examines over 700 occupations and the industries concentrated in different regions. Nationwide, 9 million jobs representing 757 billion dollars in annual wages could be displaced in two to five years. Massachusetts is the most vulnerable state due to its high concentration of data analysis, writing, and technology work. Boston faces a projected displacement rate of 7.8 percent, while the national average is 6.15 percent. Worcester ranks 106th among U.S. metropolitan areas with a projected displacement rate of 5.6 percent.

Chakravorti, the dean of global business at the Fletcher School at Tufts University, described the current moment as the eye of the hurricane. He stated that the region is less exposed in industries on the firing line but over-exposed in other sectors. He noted that AI requires a human to steer and prompt it because the technology makes mistakes. He explained that the current market is a no-hiring economy for entry-level positions rather than a firing economy. He argued that Massachusetts should take the lead in figuring out a re-education program for workers.

Hiawatha Bray, a technology writer for the Boston Globe, questioned the values embedded in AI systems. She suggested that American AIs are trained with American values, whereas Chinese AIs might reflect an authoritarian perspective. Professional services firms, including law practices, consulting companies, and information technology businesses, are reconsidering their entry-level hiring needs. Fresh graduates from graduate schools are particularly affected by the significant drop in the job market. Highly skilled workers who can effectively use AI may see increased demand and higher pay.

The research indicates that Worcester is protected by its mix of trade transportation, healthcare, social assistance, government, and manufacturing. AI can augment human work by refining presentations, writing speeches, and analyzing information, but it can also reduce staff. The debate involves those favoring caution, those focused on economic activity, and those racing against China. American-developed systems have shortcomings, including biases that can affect consequential decisions about hiring. Past retraining initiatives during previous waves of automation did not always produce successful transitions for workers.

Actual job losses will depend on how businesses adopt AI and whether new employment opportunities emerge. The researcher expressed concern that students may not develop independent thinking and writing skills if they rely on ChatGPT. He worried that there is currently no plan to re-train people because new jobs have not been defined. Policymakers must balance security concerns, energy demands of data centers, and the need to remain competitive globally. The articles leave open exactly how educators and employers will prepare for these unknown consequences.

Articles.Title: AI could put 19,000 Worcester-area jobs at risk, researcher warns - The Worcester Guardian

stories.Headline: MAS chief Chia Der Jiun warns consumers against giving AI agents financial login credentials
stories.Summary:
Monetary Authority of Singapore managing director Chia Der Jiun warned on Nov 19 at the Singapore Fintech Festival that consumers should not give artificial intelligence agents their financial account login credentials, because safeguards are still too weak to ensure such tools act safely and within their users' instructions. He noted that some payment service providers and financial institutions are building agent interfaces into their offerings, but many financial institutions have yet to set terms or channels for agents to access financial services. Chia said a financial institution cannot tell whether an agent acts on the customer's full authorisation and control, or whether it transacts within its mandate and instructions, and he asked who bears responsibility if agents transact incorrectly or beyond their instruction. Chia said a trusted protocol and a secure channel are needed for AI agents to access financial services, drawing on lessons from the first phase of MAS' Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime initiative. These lessons include giving agents enough autonomy to do useful tasks within clearly defined boundaries, establishing their identities and authority to act for users, and specifying in their instructions what actions they can take along with any limits and conditions.

He said the greater the discretion and impact of action given an agent, the stronger the assurance and controls needed. MAS will develop a common "know your agent" protocol for trusted information exchange between customer agents and financial institutions, covering the agent's identity, whom it represents, its authority, its mandate, and its origins and reliability, so institutions can set permitted terms and a dedicated secure channel. MAS will also set up a sandbox with the Future of Finance Institute to bring together AI agents and programmable money in two use cases, corporate treasury management and payment services. In treasury management, banks could let an agent monitor a company's liquidity positions and due payments, decide when and where funds move, and use tokenised deposits to execute permitted actions, with companies setting mandates and participating banks setting controls and terms. In payments, banks and payment service providers could let customer agents execute payment instructions using digital money such as tokenised deposits or stablecoins, verifying the agents' identities and authority and applying risk controls first.

Chia said consumers and businesses need to retain meaningful control over the objectives, mandate and actions of their agents, adding that autonomy has to be bounded and actions and outcomes have to come with accountability. MAS also announced on Nov 19 that it had successfully issued $100 million of tokenised MAS Bills on Nov 6, four-week bills issued on the Singapore Dollar Test Network and settled using wholesale central bank digital currency. Five primary dealers, DBS, HSBC, OCBC, Standard Chartered and UOB, took part in the auction, with applications amounting to more than double the issuance size, and the bills will mature on Dec 4. MAS said it intends to scale up tokenised MAS Bills issuances, bring on board more participating financial institutions and expand their use for collateral management, and interested institutions and financial market infrastructure providers can join the next phase of live trials in 2027.

Articles.Title: Don’t give AI agents your financial account login details, warns MAS chief Chia Der Jiun

stories.Headline: Klarna claims its chatbot absorbs 700 agents as AI drives data centre energy use
stories.Summary:
The article, published by The Straits Times on Nov 19, 2026, and written by Roy Ka-Wei Lee, examines the energy dilemma that artificial intelligence poses for Singapore as companies increasingly adopt AI assistants for corporate efficiency. It recalls that the Swedish fintech firm Klarna claimed in 2024 that its chatbot had absorbed the workload of 700 customer service agents, a claim that drew fair questions from sceptics. According to the International Energy Agency, global data centre electricity consumption could more than double by 2030, with AI as a major driver of this growth. The piece frames the challenge as balancing productivity against energy efficiency, a task it says will not be easy.

The article states that AI assistants have fast become the watchword of corporate efficiency, and it describes the trajectory towards autonomous, agentic AI assistants replacing human agents as seemingly inevitable. It gives the Klarna figure of 700 customer service agents as the example of what such systems are claimed to absorb, while noting that sceptics raised fair questions about that claim. The International Energy Agency projection that global data centre electricity consumption could more than double by 2030 is presented as the energy side of the dilemma. The article places the issue under the themes of climate change, environmental issues and renewable energy.

The author, Roy Ka-Wei Lee, frames the central difficulty as balancing productivity and energy efficiency, which the article says will not be easy. The piece does not name any other person or organisation as responsible beyond Klarna, the International Energy Agency and the author himself. It presents the doubling of data centre electricity consumption by 2030, with AI a major driver, as the consequence that Singapore must weigh against the efficiency gains AI assistants promise. The article was published on Nov 19, 2026, and updated on Nov 20, 2026, at 05:53 AM.

The context the article supplies is the rapid corporate embrace of AI assistants, illustrated by Klarna's 2024 claim about its chatbot and the scepticism that followed. It sets that embrace against the International Energy Agency's warning that global data centre electricity consumption could more than double by 2030, with AI a major driver of the growth. The article does not say what Singapore will do next or what policy follows, beyond describing the balancing of productivity and energy efficiency as not easy. It closes its framing with the themes of climate change, environmental issues and renewable energy.

stories.Headline: 45% of young people in Japan use AI as a social companion, Gallup survey finds
stories.Summary:
A new poll has found that 45% of young people in Japan reported using artificial intelligence as a social companion, the second-highest rate among the countries surveyed behind Australia. Researchers with Gallup and Boston Children’s Digital Wellness Lab surveyed 15,925 young people between the ages of 15 and 22 across 16 countries, examining patterns around friendship, well-being and their digital relationships. The survey was reported by The Japan Times on November 19, 2026, in a story by staff writer Elizabeth Beattie. Japanese respondents gave AI companionship the second-lowest quality scores even as their usage ranked near the top.

Japanese young people also reported some of the highest usage rates of AI overall, reaching third place behind Brazil and Italy, with 35% of those surveyed saying they used it once a day or more. In-person relationships are central to the social lives of young people and receive the highest ratings for strength, according to the researchers. Young people associated higher levels of happiness, safety and sense of connection with their in-person friendships while reporting higher levels of anxiety around their online relationships. The report said higher loneliness is more common among young people who frequently communicate online with strangers or online-only friends than among those who frequently communicate with in-person friends or family members.

Friendships are increasingly spanning offline and online worlds, with young people reporting that they maintained relationships through online communication or had built relationships through online communities. Young men more often meet online friends through gaming and young women through social media platforms, according to the researchers. The report said digitally mediated friendships generally add to, rather than replace, in-person relationships, and that the two most common friendship configurations both include an in-person friend alongside at least one digitally mediated friendship. The most common online activity young people around the world reported was scrolling, with 72% of respondents saying they frequently scroll short-form content, and the report said scrolling through online content is the response young people report most often when they feel lonely.

Articles.Title: Young people in Japan more inclined to seek AI companionship but skeptical of quality

stories.Headline: GIGABYTE launches AI TOP AERO and AI TOP ATOM desktops for local AI development and content creation
stories.Summary:
GIGABYTE announced the launch of the AI TOP AERO and AI TOP ATOM desktops on November 16, 2026, in Taipei. These new machines are designed to bring local AI development, content creation, and gaming to personal workspaces. The company aims to expand its range of local AI solutions for developers, creators, and AI users. The AI TOP AERO is a personal AI studio powered by the NVIDIA RTX Spark platform. The AI TOP ATOM is now available in a new 64 GB unified memory version.

The AI TOP AERO features a 20 core NVIDIA Grace CPU and an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU in a one liter chassis. It offers up to 128 GB of LPDDR5x unified memory and a PCIe Gen5 SSD with up to 4 TB of storage. The AI TOP ATOM uses the NVIDIA DGX Spark platform with 64 GB or 128 GB of unified memory. The 64 GB ATOM model includes M.2 NVMe PCIe 4.0 SSD options of 1 TB or 2 TB. Connectivity includes USB Type-C, 10 GbE Ethernet, and Wi-Fi 7 for the AERO model.

GIGABYTE stated that the AI TOP AERO combines a compact format with the performance needed for prolonged computing use. They noted that their cooling design maintains performance during demanding AI tasks and professional content creation workloads. The company explained that the AI TOP ATOM allows users to maintain better control over project data. They said the AI TOP Utility supports local development workflows through model downloading, inference, and retrieval augmented generation. GIGABYTE claims these tools help users develop and validate AI applications within a dedicated local environment.

The AI TOP ATOM is intended for AI developers, machine learning engineers, researchers, educators, and AI enthusiasts. These users can select memory capacities that best fit their specific model sizes and various computing workloads. The AI TOP AERO targets creators who use tools like ComfyUI for generative AI and NVIDIA Broadcast for audio. Gamers are affected by the inclusion of NVIDIA DLSS 5, which brings neural rendering to compatible game titles. Developers can use the NVIDIA CUDA platform to prototype and run the latest open models locally.

The company developed these systems because generative AI is moving beyond conversational assistants toward AI agents and workflow automation. Users want personal AI computing to improve data privacy, response speed, and overall usage costs. The AI TOP AERO integrates the NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X Superchip to combine high performance with low power consumption. The AI TOP ATOM uses NVIDIA ConnectX-7 and NVIDIA Sync to group up to four units for more power. These products build upon GIGABYTE's existing experience in hardware integration and system design.

The AI TOP AERO is scheduled for release on November 10, 2026, while the AI TOP ATOM 64 GB is available. Users can use NVIDIA PAIR to distribute inference tasks across available devices in homes and creative studios. Developers may use NVIDIA Nemotron models, LM Studio, and Ollama to create tailored local AI environments. The articles leave the specific pricing and regional availability of the products open for local announcements. They do not state the exact cost or the specific distribution channels for these new desktop computers.

stories.Headline: LS Electric secures a $93.83 million order to supply switchgear for a US AI data center
stories.Summary:
LS Electric announced on Monday, November 16, 2026, that it had secured a contract worth USD 93.83 million to supply power distribution systems for a hyperscale artificial intelligence data center in the United States. The customer is an unnamed global technology company, and the agreement covers 38-kilovolt high-voltage switchgear as well as low-voltage switchgear, which will be delivered in phases. Switchgear controls and protects electrical circuits so that power can be distributed safely across large facilities. The contract is a repeat order that broadens LS Electric's role in the client's data center project, carrying its participation beyond the initial construction stage into a later expansion phase. The award comes as the rapid spread of AI applications drives up demand for computing capacity, making time to power a critical factor in project execution.

To meet compressed delivery timelines, LS Electric runs manufacturing plants in Cheongju, South Korea, along with facilities in Utah and Texas, which the company says give it the capacity to keep up with such schedules. Beyond its conventional alternating current distribution business, LS Electric is developing direct current systems that limit the number of power conversions needed to run servers and can thereby cut energy losses. Its Cheonan plant hosts a DC-powered factory featuring solid-state transformers for voltage conversion, solid-state circuit breakers for protection and energy storage systems, which the company describes as a proving ground for next-generation power grids and data center applications. An LS Electric official said the latest contract reflects the quality of the company's power equipment and its ability to execute projects in North America, and that it will continue expanding its business by providing solutions tailored to the needs of major technology customers. The additional contract reflects an ongoing commercial relationship between LS Electric and its technology-sector customer, and its involvement in both the original development and the subsequent expansion gives the manufacturer an extended role in the project's electrical infrastructure requirements.

Repeat orders of this nature can also give equipment suppliers opportunities to maintain long-term relationships with major data center operators. The expansion of AI-focused data centers is changing the requirements for electrical infrastructure, since larger computing environments need dependable power distribution systems capable of handling substantial electrical loads while supporting continuous operations. As technology companies increase their investment in hyperscale facilities, demand for high-voltage and low-voltage electrical equipment is also gaining importance in data center development. The latest contract adds to LS Electric's business activity in the North American digital infrastructure sector, and with US technology companies continuing to expand their AI computing capabilities, the company is positioning its electrical equipment portfolio to address the associated infrastructure requirements. Further opportunities in this market could support its efforts to expand its overseas business and establish stronger relationships with major technology customers.

stories.Headline: STN commissions its first fully integrated AI infrastructure campus in Odessa, Texas
stories.Summary:
STN One Incorporated, a company based in Pleasanton, California, announced on November 12, 2026 that its operations now cover the full AI infrastructure stack, from securing land and power through building data centers to operating technology, and it said its first fully integrated campus had been commissioned in Odessa, Texas. Construction at the Ector County site, a former industrial property that had sat largely unused for years, began in May 2026, and STN placed its first Elemental Data Center there on June 11, 2026 before fully commissioning it by July 31, ready to accept compute. The facility pairs on-site power generation and battery storage with a utility connection, is designed to meet its own energy needs while following Texas' requirement that large power users cover their associated costs, and relies on sealed, closed-loop cooling built for an arid climate that produces no process water discharge. The company said the expanded capabilities respond to what it calls one of the industry's biggest challenges, access to reliable power and suitable facilities as AI demand grows, and that reducing reliance on outside providers lets it bring new computing capacity online faster.

The Odessa project currently supports 375 jobs and is expected to create 200 permanent, highly skilled Dark AI Factory positions as operations expand, with STN also planning skilled employment and workforce training for Permian Basin workers. Elemental Data Centers are factory-built structures engineered and manufactured by STN with essential operating systems already installed, and production runs while site crews work in parallel, which the company says shortens construction time. The first unit is designed for 2 megawatts and 1,024 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs, and with a single change to the same footprint it can support 1,008 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GB300 GPUs. Beyond Odessa, the company has additional projects underway in Marshfield, Missouri, and Orangeburg, South Carolina.

Sabur Mian, founder and CEO of STN, said AI companies need more than compute and need facilities ready to support them, and that getting those facilities built has become one of the industry's biggest challenges. He said the company is taking responsibility for the entire process so customers do not have to depend on multiple companies to get the capacity they need, and that it can now build, power and operate the infrastructure customers need for AI all under one roof. Mian said STN ONE is already part of how the company runs its own operations every day and is the same intelligence it brings to every customer environment, adding that anyone can host a workload but STN operates it with customers from the facility to the application. Ector County Judge Dustin Fawcett said the company engaged with community concerns early, including confirming the build will rely on its own water supply, and that STN is prepared to be a good partner by bringing an emerging industry and opportunities to a community that has for decades relied solely on oil and gas.

STN ONE, which the company describes as its agentic operating system for AI infrastructure, manages the entire operation from engineering and infrastructure to the computing systems customers use, and the company views it as a first step toward autonomous data centers. The platform is already in use across support, finance, security and engineering operations, where its AI agents work alongside employees to monitor systems, identify potential problems and automate routine tasks, and as capabilities expand it will help manage infrastructure and services more efficiently while sensitive actions remain subject to human oversight and approval. STN describes itself as a vertically integrated AI infrastructure company that owns powered land, generates its own power, manufactures its own data center buildings, delivers them as Elemental Data Centers and operates AI compute through GPU One, and it began as a managed service provider for regulated industries. STN is working with regional education and workforce organizations, including Odessa College and the University of Texas Permian Basin, to develop training programs aimed at advanced computing equipment maintenance, data center facility operations and the specialized electrical and technical roles required to run AI data centers.

stories.Headline: Hyperscale Data sells its last Bitcoin to fund Michigan AI data center and cut debt
stories.Summary:
Hyperscale Data, Inc., which trades on the NYSE American under the ticker GPUS, confirmed on November 10, 2026 that it had finished selling off its Bitcoin holdings, disposing of approximately 211.56 Bitcoin at roughly USD 76,000 per coin for gross proceeds of about USD 16.0 million. The liquidation was completed as of November 8, 2026, and it closed out a process that began in late July 2026, during which the company sold approximately 1,113 Bitcoin in total for approximately USD 74.4 million. The cash generated by the sales is earmarked for two purposes, which are reducing the company's debt and advancing construction of its artificial intelligence data center in Michigan. The company said the proceeds would go toward paying down debt and funding the Michigan buildout.

Chief Executive Officer Will Horne tied the sales directly to the company's near-term operational target, saying that energizing the first 10 megawatts of critical IT capacity at the Michigan data center in December is the company's highest priority and the quickest path to profitability. Horne also cited risk management as a reason for the sales, saying that selling the Bitcoin reserves reduces the company's exposure to Bitcoin price swings while providing cash to pay down debt and fund the Michigan work, which he called the best use of this capital for all stockholders. Although the balance sheet reserves are gone, Hyperscale Data has not abandoned digital assets altogether, because the company continues to mine Bitcoin at its Montana site. Looking ahead, the company expects any Bitcoin held on its balance sheet to come primarily from its own mining operations rather than from purchases or other accumulated reserves.

Hyperscale Data anticipates filing its Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026 on or before Monday, November 23, and because of the recently announced proposed Exchange Offer for its Class A common stock, the company also plans to shift its virtual Investor Day from November 12 to November 23. Management intends to brief investors then on debt reduction progress and the status of the December energization goal at the Michigan facility, and when the Exchange Offer is commenced, offer documents will be filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. Hyperscale Data's data center operations run through wholly owned subsidiary Sentinum, Inc., which offers colocation and hosting services for emerging AI ecosystems and other industries, while a second wholly owned subsidiary, Ault Capital Group, Inc., operates as a hybrid private equity firm and operating company. The company currently expects to divest ACG in 2027, after which Hyperscale Data would be an owner and operator of data centers supporting high-performance computing services, along with holding digital assets and a third wholly owned subsidiary, Omnipresent Robotics, LLC.

stories.Headline: DeepMind researchers argue AI is on pace to move from AGI to superintelligence
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind researchers argued on 20 November 2026 that AI development is on pace to move beyond human-level AGI to ASI, which consistently outperforms groups of human experts. The researchers published the argument in a DeepMind Institute article titled "What comes after AGI? From AGI to Superintelligence." Tim Genewein of the DeepMind Institute was named in connection with the article. The article said AGI is coming within reach and that looking past it can no longer be put off.

It said AI could continue to advance at its current pace, and possibly accelerate, towards ASI. The article defined ASI as an advanced system that consistently outperforms large groups of human experts on tasks that could take them years, using fewer resources and less time. It gave as examples making the same scientific progress as an entire research field in a fraction of the time, or chip design developments on par with what large companies can do in a year. It said ASI would need to meet this bar across virtually all tasks of human interest, not just narrow domains such as Chess, Go, protein structure prediction or proving theorems. It said fundamental limits lie far beyond both today's AI systems and humans.

It said the space between human-level AI and theoretical limits, encompassing expert AGI and more advanced superintelligent systems, is largely uncharted. The article said compute per dollar has increased by roughly 1.5x per year for six decades under Moore's law and related trends. It said training compute required to reach a fixed AI performance level has fallen at roughly 3, 6x per year over the last decade, while inference efficiency improved by roughly 3x per year. It said spending on AI hardware has grown by roughly 2.5x per year over the past decade, and training compute of the largest frontier runs grows by more than 4x per year. It said multiplying these factors gives overall growth of global effective compute stock of at least 10x per year, a factor of 10 billion over ten years.

It said a recent Epoch study finds the consumer price for a fixed benchmark score has fallen by more than 13x per year since 2023. The article said practical ceilings on compute build-out and speculative ceilings on algorithmic efficiency might allow the effective population of today's AI agents to scale up by more than a thousand-fold by 2030 and more than a billion-fold within ten years. It said a cognitive workload costing $1 billion in compute tokens today would cost just $1000 in ten years. It said that if other dimensions were frozen and today's AIs were only scaled in speed and number, the result might not even count as full AGI. It said a quantitative leap in speed and scale might itself bridge the qualitative gap from AGI to weak ASI.

It said digital intelligence benefits from more and faster compute through processing speed, working memory, substrate independence, lossless replication and high-bandwidth sharing of experiences. The article said scaling laws are extrapolations that hold only within familiar boundaries and cannot confidently predict the scale required for AGI or ASI. It listed bottlenecks including data exhaustion, diminishing returns on model scale, and physical and economic resource limits in power plants, electrical grids, chip fabrication plants and low-latency hardware interconnects. It said today's models fall short of humans on continual learning, certain forms of world modeling, decision-making and sample efficiency.

It said researchers are divided on whether these problems can be solved with simple extensions of today's paradigm or require deep technological paradigm shifts. It said coordinating thousands or millions of AGI instances into group agents or virtual agent economies could produce collective capabilities. The article set out four pathways from AGI to ASI: scaling models and data, technological paradigm shifts, improving agent coordination and recursive self-improvement. It said preparing for a potential shift requires mapping the possible roads from AGI to ASI and building rigorous, reliable ways to track progress.

It said solving chess perfectly requires far more computing power than exists on Earth, yet a thumbnail-sized chip can play well enough to defeat any human. It said it remains unclear whether hardware and software efficiency gains can compensate for real-world limits on training compute. It referred readers to an in-depth discussion in its From AGI to ASI report. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Anthropic begins trading on Nasdaq with a board overseen by a long-term benefit trust
stories.Summary:
Anthropic priced its initial public offering last night and began trading on the Nasdaq today. The company published a corporate prospectus called an S-1 that extends over five hundred pages. This document provides potential investors with an outline of the business model and financial situation. It also includes lists of hypothetical events that might adversely affect investments and foreign securities law. The filing explains that large-scale corporate decisions are overseen by a long-term benefit trust.

The long-term benefit trust is a five-person purpose trust that appoints a majority of the board. This body is entitled to a special class of corporate stock and manages the company purpose. That purpose is the responsible development of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. Trustees include Ben Bernanke, Neil Shah, and Richard Fontaine, who joined the trust in 2025. Fontaine is the CEO of the Center for a New American Security and a Trilateral Commission director.

The long-term benefit trust is intended to operate as an independent body of specialized experts. These trustees are selected for their competence in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise. They are responsible for promoting the best interests of all living humans materially affected by company conduct. The company uses a public benefit corporation structure to balance humanitarian interests against shareholder pecuniary interests. This innovation hands the responsibility of enforcing these competing interests over to the trust members.

Critics of the US-aligned international security community describe the Trilateral Commission as having a dark reputation. Some leftists cite a 1975 report that suggested a greater degree of moderation in democracy. Daniel Boguslaw reports that Anthropic plans to deploy AI to surveil, predict, and stifle protest activism. These plans include collaboration with law enforcement to monitor activists. This approach aligns with historical calls for digital surveillance from AI safety lobbyists with company ties.

The Trilateral Commission is a private membership organization including senior government officials, business executives, and academics. The Center for a New American Security is a Washington-based think tank with ties to both major parties. This center has received funding from military contractor firms and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Coefficient Giving has provided over 100 million dollars to the Center for Security and Emerging Technology. It also gave grants of over 5 million and 8 million dollars to CNAS in 2022 and 2025.

Anthropic executives may soon donate large portions of their wealth to Coefficient Giving and similar organizations. This funding could flow to distant beneficiaries like the Center for Security and Emerging Technology and CNAS. The company continues to collaborate on the CHIPS Act and export controls against China. The articles do not state how the company will manage future conflicts of interest. They leave open whether the trust will maintain its independence from the national security establishment.

stories.Headline: BrightAI raises $97M led by Smith Point to grow internationally
stories.Summary:
BrightAI Inc., a Palo Alto, California-based startup that helps industrial companies detect malfunctioning equipment, raised $97 million in a Series A round led by Smith Point Capital, according to the company's Wednesday announcement of the deal. A number of other venture capital firms also contributed to the round, and they were joined by GE Vernova Inc., an energy equipment company that emerged from the 2024 split-up of General Electric Co. The company said the new capital brings its total funding to $184 million. BrightAI's products monitor hundreds of thousands of industrial assets across 50,000 sites, and investor GE Vernova, which is also a customer, plans to expand its use of the technology in connection with this week's round. BrightAI develops hardware and software tools that help customers spot problems earlier, because many industrial machinery malfunctions affect internal components that are not visible to an outside observer and often go unnoticed until they cause a major disruption. The first part of its portfolio is a collection of sensors called State Stickers, small rectangular devices with a ruggedized case and a long battery life that technicians attach to equipment to monitor for issues that cannot be detected visually.

The sensors detect when a machine diverges from its usual operating pattern and wirelessly transmit measurements to a device called the Stateful AI Hub, which runs artificial intelligence models that analyze the data for signs of hardware failures. The company says its models become more accurate as the number of sensors deployed at a site grows. BrightAI also offers software that lets companies augment sensor data with drone footage, so a utility could use a BrightAI-powered drone to detect erosion at the top of an electric pole, and its models automatically draw a square around damaged components to spare technicians the hassle of manually analyzing footage. The software can read meters attached to assets such as data center coolant tanks to check their internal pressure, and built-in support for infrared cameras enables it to spot overheating equipment. The third core component is an AI wearable called the Stateful Wearable, which provides technicians with troubleshooting advice in the field, checks whether they follow safety guidelines during inspections and automatically turns maintenance data into reports.

Founder and Chief Executive Alex Hawkinson said the company's infrastructure is under more strain than it has ever been and that Physical AI has finally become reliable enough to work in the field, calling the combination of those two facts a once-in-a-generation opportunity. BrightAI will use the capital to grow its international presence, while GE Vernova plans to expand its use of the company's technology in connection with this week's funding round. The round was led by Smith Point Capital, with other venture capital firms contributing alongside GE Vernova, and the company announced the deal on Wednesday. BrightAI says its products monitor hundreds of thousands of industrial assets across 50,000 sites, and the new funding brings its total raised to $184 million. The company is based in Palo Alto, California, and its sensors and software are aimed at catching equipment problems before they cause major disruptions.
