stories.Headline: Accenture cuts token spend 40 to 85 percent on Amazon Bedrock across four client engagements
stories.Summary:
Accenture applied six levers for optimizing token spend in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment, as described in an AWS blog post published on November 19, 2026. The post says Accenture applied these levers in production on Amazon Bedrock. Where savings were measured, token spend fell by about 40 to 85 percent, the post says. Accenture withheld the client names to protect client confidentiality. The post says results are specific to each client's workload and may vary.

The post describes cost allocation tags applied through Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles, one profile per application or workload, tagged by team, cost center, and environment. It names AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0) delivered through AWS Data Exports, Amazon CloudWatch, and Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging as the telemetry. It describes Accenture's Cost per Business Transaction framework, which aggregates model invocations, retries, tool calls, and agent handoffs into one fully loaded cost figure. It says Amazon Bedrock prompt caching is designed to reduce cached input token costs by up to 90 percent for supported models. It says Amazon Bedrock batch inference runs at 50 percent lower cost than on-demand pricing for select models and writes results to Amazon Simple Storage Service.

The post says Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing can reduce costs by up to 30 percent without compromising accuracy, and it points readers to Amazon Bedrock Pricing for any routing charges. It says semantic caching can be implemented on AWS with a vector store such as Amazon ElastiCache in front of the model. It cites an AWS benchmark on 63,796 real chatbot queries where a 0.90 similarity threshold produced a 74.5 percent cache hit rate, 92.3 percent accuracy, and 72.5 percent cost savings. It says distilled models in Amazon Bedrock are up to 500 percent faster and up to 75 percent less expensive than original models, with less than 2 percent accuracy loss for use cases such as RAG. It says Amazon Bedrock Guardrails should stay on every route and semantic cache expiry should be set so users do not receive outdated answers.

The post says the first engagement was a large enterprise deployment where every request went to a frontier model with no caching, model tiering, or batching, and three changes together cut monthly token cost by 85 percent. It says about 15 percent of tasks still needed the top model for hard, open-ended reasoning and the rest ran on lighter models. It says the second engagement was a telecom operator with $12 million in annual token spend, where input tokens fell by 70 percent and annual token spend fell from $12 million to $3.8 million, a 68 percent reduction. It says Accenture validated output quality against the operator's pre-change performance benchmarks. It says the third and fourth engagements each applied a single cache layer, an insurer using model-layer prefix caching and a mining operator using an application-layer semantic cache, and token spend fell by about 40 percent combined without model routing changes or training investment.

The post says the Linux Foundation has launched the Tokenomics Foundation to develop open standards for AI cost economics. It says token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall, and that without cost allocation tags a cloud invoice shows AI spend as a single line item rather than by team, workload, agent, or model. It says cheaper tokens expand adoption and agentic workloads multiply invocations, so consumption can rise faster than unit prices drop. It says the economic question is whether business value grows faster than the cost of the intelligence required to produce it. It says the six levers are organized into three phases and that AWS and Accenture recommend working through the phases in order, and it says two of the engagements applied several changes at once so those results reflect the combined effect.

The post recommends connecting consumption to owners and outcomes, applying one lever at a time, measuring cost, quality, and business value, and building on what works. It lists four operating tenets: establish a quantitative baseline for cost and quality before applying any lever, validate output quality with held-out evaluation sets drawn from actual production traffic rather than synthetic benchmarks, apply one lever at a time per workload to attribute results and roll back cleanly, and document quality test results and rollback procedures in regulated industries such as financial services, insurance, and healthcare. It says Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is an environment to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model, and it mentions AgentCore Evaluations, a capability that provides batch e. The post does not give the outcome of the fourth engagement separately or name the clients.

Articles.Title: Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture’s sequenced approach

stories.Headline: AI bug hunting prompts rushed patches that overwhelm systems and cause outages
stories.Summary:
A series of recent technology outages affecting JPMorgan Chase transactions, Microsoft Outlook and a classified National Security Agency network may stem from a rapid effort to patch security vulnerabilities, according to officials who briefed members of Congress. Wall Street executives and the NSA told lawmakers that the disruptions were caused by attempts to fix flaws identified by artificial intelligence models, The Washington Sun reported. The outages do not appear to be cyberattacks, and officials said the sheer volume of fixes temporarily overwhelmed the systems they were designed to protect. A congressional official noted that AI models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, which increases the urgency for immediate patching.

Microsoft fixed a record 1,400 security flaws in a single monthly update recently, a significant jump from about 170 a year earlier, The Wall Street Journal reported. That increase is linked to AI bug-hunting models such as Anthropic's Mythos and similar models from OpenAI. The NSA's classified internal network, NSANet, went offline because of a software patch for major PHP vulnerabilities discovered last month, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton confirmed. PHP powers approximately 70 per cent of the world's websites, and Clayton stated that the incident was not a cyberattack or a coordinated nation-state action.

Not all the outages fit that explanation, since Microsoft's Outlook disruption, which affected over 450 million Microsoft 365 users, was traced to a latent bug on its networking gateway servers. The Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop resulted from a data flood hitting its network, possibly linked to a new router, and the FAA blamed legacy equipment. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin indicated that pushing new technology onto older systems seems to overwhelm them, suggesting more such incidents are likely. Companies and government agencies are using powerful AI models to find weak spots before hackers exploit them, and that pressure has led to faster rollout of fixes, according to The Washington Sun.

Articles.Title: AI-driven bug fixes overwhelm systems, causing major outages

stories.headline_source: AI-driven bug fixes overwhelm systems, causing major outages

stories.Headline: Onlook lets designers build and edit real app code visually with AI
stories.Summary:
Onlook, an open-source AI-first design tool, was published on GitHub by the onlook-dev organisation, and TechGig reported on it on November 20, 2026. The tool lets designers and visual engineers build, style and edit code visually with AI on a canvas. It works directly with real app code running live from any Git repository on a user's machine. The GitHub repository, onlook-dev/onlook, had 1,644 commits, 27.3k stars, 121 watchers and 2.2k forks when the articles were written. TechGig published its report on November 20, 2026 at 04:51 AM IST, and the GitHub page was dated November 19, 2026.

Onlook is released under the Apache 2.0 License, and the license covers source code but not every asset in the repository. Artifacts can be exported as self-contained HTML, PNG, JPEG or PDF files, with PNG and JPEG captured through Electron capturePage and PDF through Electron printToPDF and pdf-lib. The macOS desktop application is available for download for Apple Silicon and Intel x64, while Windows and Linux versions are planned, with waitlists for both. The source build needs no Onlook account, cloud keys or .env file, and a build from source asks before collecting usage analytics, which can be turned off in Settings or with STUDIO_TELEMETRY=0. The desktop app is built with Electron, React 19, Astryx, React Flow, Zustand and CodeMirror, and uses Git, node-pty, Bun and Turborepo.

The GitHub page says Onlook is the developer tool for designers and describes it as a free, local-first editor where designers craft exceptional experiences in code. It states that Onlook does not ship its own model, and that users connect the Claude Code or ChatGPT/Codex account they already have so that agent does the work inside their project. It says Onlook opens any Git repository on a machine and runs the user's own dev server, so what is designed is the actual product, not a mockup someone has to rebuild later. It says the app runs on the user's computer, code stays there, and more tools can be plugged in through MCP connectors. The page also says the team is hiring engineers and designers in SF.

TechGig describes Onlook as an open-source alternative to Figma, V0, Replit Agent, Base 44 and Webflow, and the GitHub page lists the same alternatives. The GitHub page says users can design apps, websites, posters and graphics with local fonts and assets, work on multiple design tasks at once across repos and pages, and use mobile, tablet and desktop frames side by side. It says a safe worktree copy means the user's folder is never touched, and that projects run as parallel tabs. It says users can ask about any element on the canvas, have the agent arrange the canvas for variations, states and flows, reference images on the canvas, and sketch and share artifacts for quick HTML sketches outside the repo. It says users can import a GitHub repo, start entirely new codebases from scratch, and make one-press pull requests from checks to merge.

The GitHub page says Onlook works with all web frameworks or languages the user's dev server already supports, because it runs the project with its own tooling. It describes a workflow where a user starts a new empty project with the New Draft button in the upper left corner of the projects page and writes a request in the input box in the lower right corner. It says the user answers clarifying questions from the agent and waits for it to build, then clicks frames for context in follow-up prompts or double-clicks an element to use inline chat. It says the user selects a frame, asks the agent to convert it into an Artifact, exports it as HTML/CSS or PNG with the export button in the upper right corner of the frame, and pastes it into Slack, email or any messaging tool. It says changes show up on the canvas as the dev server reloads, and Git keeps track of everything that changed.

The GitHub page says the previous browser-based version of Onlook, v1, lives on the v1 branch of the repository, and the first desktop version is at onlook-dev/desktop. It says Onlook's icons come from Central Icons by Iconists and are licensed to Onlook for its own product, a license that does not extend to forks, and that brand marks, DMG art and sounds are not covered either. It points to ASSETS.md for what is covered and what to replace when forking, and to NOTICE for third-party notices. It says the official download has product usage analytics on by default, and points to the privacy policy for details. It lists contact channels including Discord, email, Twitter, LinkedIn, YouTube and Substack, and the website onlook.com.

The GitHub page invites users to fork the repo and create a pull request, browse open issues, and read CONTRIBUTING.md for instructions and a code of conduct. It says security issues should be reported by following SECURITY.md instead of opening a public issue. It says Windows and Linux users can join waitlists to be emailed when there are updates, and that the team is still gauging demand for Linux. It says SOURCE_BUILD.md covers building and running Onlook on a Mac. The articles do not say when Windows or Linux versions will be released, and they do not give a release date for the macOS app.

stories.Headline: Researchers warn AI may entrench clinical evidence monopoly without data access reform
stories.Summary:
Researchers Shenwei Wan and Xiaoguang Lei published an opinion in PLOS Digital Health on November 19, 2026. They evaluated if artificial intelligence will dismantle the global concentration of medical evidence or establish a new monopoly. The authors examined how AI could reshape clinical evidence production systems. They focused on the resources required to generate authoritative clinical evidence. This evidence currently remains skewed toward high-income nations and well-funded institutions.

The authors cite 784,585 trial sites from 2006 to 2012, where 83 percent were in 25 OECD nations. Meanwhile, 91 low-income or lower-middle-income countries hosted only 5 percent of these sites. They note a median trial cost of 19 million US dollars for US drug approvals between 2015 and 2016. Wan and Lei propose an AI-enabled evidence commons to allow more institutions to produce and challenge evidence. This requires secure data access, documented methods, and local research capacity.

Wan and Lei state that an evidence monopoly is the structural concentration of funding, data, and expertise. They argue that this imbalance shapes global practice guidelines, regulatory approvals, procurement choices, and reimbursement policies. The authors suggest that academic journals require structured statements documenting software versions and validation protocols for AI synthesis. They advocate for design fitness, where methodological choices match the specific research question. They claim technical refinements alone cannot resolve the geographic concentration of clinical research.

The authors note that clinical AI models and triage algorithms are subject to software revisions and algorithmic drift. They mention that automated depression detection tools showed narrow linguistic and geographic coverage. Large language models shifted emotional category distributions when applied to online cancer-support posts. The authors warn that AI can produce fabricated claims, inconsistent data extractions, and search omissions. They state that AI cannot recover patient populations that were never recorded.

Evidence-based medicine was established to integrate research evidence with clinical expertise rather than professional authority alone. Randomized controlled trials are indispensable but demand substantial capital, personnel, ethics oversight, and infrastructure. A scoping review identified 388 AI tools across 137 studies for evidence synthesis. These tools may reduce workloads like searching literature, screening citations, translating text, and extracting data. However, this experimentation has not yet demonstrated reductions in overall synthesis costs.

Funders and international bodies must invest in local trial infrastructure, regulatory frameworks, and community partnerships. This should align with the World Health Organization 2025 action plan for sustainable clinical trial ecosystems. The authors suggest using quasi-experiments, implementation science, and target-trial emulations as complementary approaches. The articles leave open whether AI will actually reduce systemic global research inequality. They do not state if the proposed evidence commons has been implemented.

Articles.Title: Researchers Examine How Artificial Intelligence Could Reshape Clinical Evidence Production Systems

stories.Headline: GC Evans president Mark McNamer uses AI to help small manufacturers compete globally
stories.Summary:
GC Evans, an automated packaging manufacturer tucked into a wooded area just off Interstate 530 in Little Rock, has been building custom systems for the food and beverage industry since the 1950s, and it is now using artificial intelligence to reshape both what it builds and how it operates, according to a November 19, 2026 article by Jeremy Harper in Arkansas Money & Politics. Company president Mark McNamer said that with AI, GC Evans can offer the same resources and capabilities that previously only very large companies could offer, and that work a staff of 10 once did can now be done more efficiently by just one or two engineers. AI-assisted tools let the company's engineers create three-dimensional floor plans and visualize custom packaging solutions with considerably less time and effort, while tasks that once required hours of coding can increasingly be accomplished through simple prompts. Manuals, instructions and technical documentation can also be generated in a fraction of the time, which the article says leaves a smaller company capable of offering services, speed and pricing that can compete with much larger international manufacturers.

Artificial intelligence is also becoming part of the machinery itself, with GC Evans manufacturing inspection and rejection systems that identify flaws in packaging as products move through a production line. Those systems can increasingly incorporate AI cameras, meaning machine-vision cameras paired with artificial-intelligence software capable of analyzing products and packaging almost instantaneously, and rather than relying exclusively on traditional programming, the systems can be trained to recognize acceptable products and identify defects or inconsistencies. On a beverage line, that might include damaged cans, improper labels, faulty closures or other packaging problems, and McNamer said the AI cameras enable the systems to process 2,000 12-ounce standard aluminum cans per minute. He said the cameras are programmed through prompting rather than tedious coding, which means a person does not need to be a computer scientist to make an adjustment.

McNamer is the person responsible for the effort described in the article, and he said many food and beverage companies would very much like to work with USA-based manufacturers, but overseas conglomerates have acquired many of the companies providing automated packaging solutions. He said AI is one tool GC Evans uses to even the playing field and bring manufacturing to Arkansas, and he believes the effect on jobs could look very different for small and midsize companies than for large ones. While very large companies will likely reduce workforce, he said, smaller companies like GC Evans will increase hiring due to added productivity, and what is happening is a shift of workforce to where it is most needed. He added that like any technology, companies will adapt to it and be better for it.

The article places GC Evans in the context of a national conversation that has focused on the possibility that automation will eliminate jobs, and it says the combination of speed and accessibility shows why AI could prove especially consequential for smaller manufacturers. It is not simply automating individual tasks but giving smaller teams access to capabilities that once required significantly more personnel, specialized expertise and capital. For Arkansas manufacturers, the article says, that may ultimately be one of AI's greatest opportunities, because the technology can give smaller companies productivity, engineering capabilities and sophisticated tools once available primarily to multinational corporations. That allows Arkansas businesses not simply to compete globally but to bring more of that work home, according to the article.

stories.Summary:

stories.Headline: Google AI search answers push marketer Marshall Evans to cut search ad spending
stories.Summary:
Marshall Evans, a North Carolina marketer who has bought Google search ads for small businesses like home repair companies and fitness studios for more than a decade, has moved ad dollars away from those ads over the past six months because AI-written responses now often appear above the usual links and ads. For one trophy company he now allocates $500 a month to search ads, down from $2,000 a month about a year ago when Google introduced a feature called AI Mode, and he is shifting money toward streaming services such as Tubi, other search engines like Bing and social media sites like Reddit and Nextdoor. Last month Google reported for the first time that search advertising had fallen to less than 50% of its $128 billion in quarterly revenue, with search ad revenue rising 12% and falling short of the 15% Wall Street expected. Google CEO Sundar Pichai said during the earnings call that the company is focused on building the best search user experience, followed by monetization, and Google has said it wanted to make AI search features appealing to users and would think about advertising later.

Users now often see AI Overviews, an AI-written answer to their query, at the top of the search results page, and the bottom of the summary invites them to interact with a chatbot through AI Mode, but advertising in those AI answers and chatbots has not yet taken off. Advertisers can pay more for the chance to feature their ads in AI Mode, but there is no guarantee the promotion will show up, and Google does not offer advertisers a way to buy guaranteed placement in AI Overviews. Google spokesperson Thomas Schoenfelder said AI is driving an expansionary moment for Search, with AI features leading to increased usage and overall query growth including commercial queries, and that the company's ads experiments have shown promising results. Google also said users were flocking to its AI search tools and that the number of search queries was growing faster than it had in the past five years.

Thomas Monteiro, a senior analyst at Investing.com, said Google is trying to take a business that was the best in the world for 10 years and transform it into a different business without the same advantages, and that making the transition is a lot harder than management thought it would be. Valerie Schlosser, a marketing executive at the global creative agency VML in New York, said what is being seen is arguably the biggest change in searcher behavior, with people spending more time in conversation with chatbots and less time surfing the web. She added that advertisers are not abandoning Google search but are trying to figure out how to survive in the new system, and that clients want to test new things like ChatGPT and Perplexity without totally pulling back from Google. Max Anderson, CEO of OnlyFinder, a service that helps users find creators on the adult entertainment site OnlyFans, said his ads either will not show on the page at all or will show down the page below an AI Overview, and that his costs have probably tripled or quadrupled in the last three years.

Anderson said he is gradually and mathematically pulling back as costs rise and now devotes about half as much spending to Google ads as he did in the early days of the business, declining to discuss specific spending because the numbers were proprietary. He is not planning to abandon Google but is flummoxed by how to get his business mentioned in AI Overviews, saying he would love a way as a business to predictably play there but has not seen one yet. The article describes AI as a double-edged sword for even the biggest companies, with Google standing to benefit enormously from the technology including in its booming cloud computing business while AI takes a toll as the company adjusts. The articles do not say what happens next beyond Google's stated focus on the user experience first and its confidence about its trajectory.

stories.Headline: AI agents make Spec-Driven Development effective again by shortening feedback loops
stories.Summary:
AI agents are making Spec-Driven Development effective again by shortening the feedback loops that long challenged the Waterfall Model, according to a recent analysis reported by TechGig on November 20, 2026. The approach moves the main effort from writing code to the discovery and design phases of software development, which enables faster iteration. Better large language models over the past year fixed earlier problems where correcting generated code cost more time than it saved. The method closely mirrors the sequential phases of the Waterfall Model, including specification, requirement analysis, technical planning and system design. Both methodologies stress structured, detailed documentation and move to the next phase only after the current one is completed and approved.

The historical problem with the Waterfall Model was feedback loops lasting weeks or months, along with unclear upfront requirements. AI agents cut individual phase durations to minutes or hours, letting developers quickly rework specifications, turn intents into structured documents and check that requirements stay consistent. The faster cycles allow iterative work on smaller increments, so unsatisfactory outcomes can be easily reverted or discarded. Documentation such as specifications and decision logs is now cheap and central to the method, a benefit that often suffered in agile environments because of time constraints. The articles do not name who is responsible for the analysis or attribute any statements to a person.

The analysis says the improved quality of large language models over the past year addressed the earlier issue where fixing generated code outweighed the time savings. It also says AI helps quickly rework specifications and validate requirement consistency. No further context or next steps are given beyond these points. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Amazon says Connect Talent uses structured questions and evidence-based scoring to run AI-led job interviews at scale
stories.Summary:
Amazon published a blog post on November 19, 2026 describing Amazon Connect Talent, an AI-led structured interview service. The post says Connect Talent uses structured questions, adaptive follow-ups and evidence-based scoring to gather consistent, job-related information. Amazon built the service around three core design principles and evaluated it through internal research and independent expert review. The post says the service brings established hiring science to AI-led interviews at scale. The article appears on the AWS blog under the Artificial Intelligence topic.

Connect Talent builds each interview around the competencies required for the role, using job requirements and established occupational frameworks to create behaviorally anchored scorecards. The AI interviewer checks after every answer whether the candidate has provided enough evidence and asks targeted follow-up questions when details are missing. A separate evaluation process identifies demonstrated behaviors, cites supporting transcript passages and calculates each competency score from 1 to 5 using a fixed formula. When the transcript lacks sufficient evidence, Connect Talent flags the competency instead of producing a score, and missing evidence does not automatically count against the candidate. The service evaluates transcribed responses without video, voice tone or physical appearance, excludes candidate identity information from scoring and evaluates each competency separately.

An independent I-O psychology firm reviewed Connect Talent's baseline output before human editing and found it retained critical job information in 100% of the job descriptions reviewed. The firm found 91% of generated competencies were clearly traceable to the job description, 98% of interview questions targeted the intended competencies and 94% of rubric signals clearly measured the intended competency. Hiring teams can review, select and edit the competencies, scorecards and questions before using them. The post says this human oversight gives organizations control over the interview process while helping them apply structured hiring practices at scale.

A second independent review covered 36 interviews assessing specific strengths and concerns, creating 252 rubric signals, and Connect Talent aligned with expert scoring decisions in 89.3% of cases. Scoring alignment reached 97.6% when candidates provided clear evidence and 92.9% when only considering candidate concern signals. The evaluation produced a Cohen's kappa of 0.79, which the post calls substantial agreement and just under the 0.81 standard for almost perfect agreement. In a preliminary evaluation, scores based only on the first response were up to 1.14 points lower on a five-point scale than scores based on the full conversation. Connect Talent's structured scoring used all five points of the rating scale, while holistic LLM-as-judge scoring concentrated its ratings within the middle three points.

The post cites decades of research in industrial-organizational psychology, including Schmidt and Hunter, 1998, and Sackett et al., 2022, showing structured interviews help organizations evaluate candidates and predict job performance. It says delivering structured interviews at scale requires significant time and expertise to develop competencies, create questions, train interviewers and evaluate responses consistently. It cites Zhu et al., 2026, finding that some AI scoring approaches concentrate ratings within a narrow range, making differences harder to recognize. It also lists Booth et al., 2021, on bias and fairness in multimodal machine learning, as a reference. The post says a traditional one-way video interview gives a candidate a fixed question and only one opportunity to answer it.

Amazon will present BIZ332, "Every Candidate, Every Time: AI-Led Structured Interviews with Amazon Connect Talent," a Chalk Talk led by Sunitha Srivatsa and Gerald Friedland at AWS re:Invent 2026. Session 1 runs Monday, November 30, 2026, 10:00, 11:00 AM at Caesars Forum, Level 1, Academy 409, with a repeat Thursday, December 3, 2026, 3:00, 4:00 PM at MGM Grand, Premier 309. The post says the session will explore structured interviewing, adaptive follow-up questions and evidence-based scoring. The post does not give pricing, availability dates or customer names for Connect Talent. The post does not say how many candidates or organizations have used the service.

stories.Headline: Open-source BehaviorLock blocks unproven API behavior to counter AI-driven attacks
stories.Summary:
BehaviorLock, a new open-source library for ASP.NET Core, was released to block unproven API behavior as a defense against fast-moving, AI-driven exploitation of vulnerabilities, according to a TechGig report published on November 20, 2026. The library records SQL statements and outbound HTTP calls for each API endpoint into a behavior.lock.json file while running in a Learn mode. In an Enforce mode, it blocks any access not present in that recorded profile, returning a 403 error and raising an alert. The approach is meant to counter attacks that outpace traditional patching cycles, including SQL injection, mass assignment, forgotten debug switches, Server-Side Request Forgery and compromised dependencies, whenever those attacks produce new endpoint behaviors.

The articles give several numbers on how quickly exploitation now follows disclosure, and they show why the library's authors see patching alone as insufficient. Attackers needed 63 days on average to exploit a vulnerability after its patch release in 2018-2019, according to Google's Mandiant team, but that duration dropped to 5 days in 2023 and was negative for 2024 and 2025 estimates. In August 2025, DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge saw automatic systems find 54 of 63 planted vulnerabilities and patch 43 of them, while also discovering 18 real vulnerabilities at a cost of about $152 per task. Anthropic announced in April 2026 that its Mythos Preview model found thousands of zero-day vulnerabilities in major operating systems and web browsers, with the count exceeding 10,000 high or critical findings by May 2026.

BehaviorLock runs inside the application process and currently supports EF Core and IHttpClientFactory for .NET 11, with future plans to extend coverage to Dapper, raw ADO.NET, direct HttpClient, file access and background jobs. The library does not replace existing security practices such as parameters, authorization checks or patching, and instead serves as an additional defensive layer against rapid, unknown attacks. Its code is available on GitHub under the Apache-2.0 license. The report does not name the individuals behind the library or attribute any statements to them, so responsibility for the project rests with its open-source contributors as a whole.

Articles.Title: BehaviorLock shields APIs from AI-driven zero-day attacks

stories.Headline: Texas regulator restarts data center permits before ERCOT audit finishes
stories.Summary:
Texas environmental regulators restarted data center permit reviews in November 2026. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality resumed processing after the Governor's office gave notice on November 13. This action ended a pause that began with Governor Greg Abbott's September 21 directive. The agency issued an air permit for a data center and gas plant on November 16. This restart occurred before the grid operator ERCOT finished its full audit.

The pause required the agency to halt permits until ERCOT completed an audit of data centers. ERCOT plans to file two reports by December 10, including the Community Impact Review Report. The Batch Zero Eligibility Verification Report will decide which loads of 75 MW and above remain eligible. The Public Utility Commission of Texas is expected to discuss these reports on December 17. A new Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, takes office on January 19, 2027.

The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality is responsible for evaluating applications under state and federal laws. A spokesperson for the agency stated that they will follow all applicable laws during reviews. Governor Greg Abbott previously directed the agency to stop permits until the ERCOT audit was finished. The Governor's office later told the agency that ERCOT finished gathering information on community impacts. Gibson Dunn confirmed that the permit pause described in its alerts has ended.

Public Citizen and other watchdogs claim that the agency is issuing permits unilaterally and prematurely. Kathryn Guerra of Public Citizen said that agency leadership began issuing these permits on its own. These critics argue the restart is early because the final audit reports are not yet filed. Developers waiting on the grid are affected by the ERCOT study and the April 9, 2027, deadline. AI builders who depend on Texas capacity must track these changing regulatory and political conditions.

Governor Abbott directed the PUC and ERCOT to audit data centers in August 2026. The agency took its electronic filing system, STEERS, offline after some approvals were flagged in October. ERCOT reviewed responses from 257 developers and about 5,140 questions by November 5. Bipartisan proposals filed between November 9 and March 12, 2027, seek to repeal data center sales tax exemptions. These proposals also aim to require water-use disclosure and bar local tax incentives.

The 90th Texas Legislature convenes on January 12, 2027, and the regular session ends May 31, 2027. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa may rescind or replace the directives issued by Governor Greg Abbott. TCEQ chair Paup's term expires August 31, 2027, and two PUC terms expire September 1, 2027. It remains open whether the restart covers every permit type or only some specific ones. The articles leave open which specific projects will benefit from the resumed permit reviews.

stories.Headline: OpenAI launches GPT-6.2 Astra, which builds working websites from written prompts
stories.Summary:
OpenAI introduced GPT-6.2 Astra, a new frontier model that can build functional, interactive websites from written descriptions, the company announced on Tuesday. TechGig published its report on the model on Nov 20, 2026 at 05:00 AM IST. OpenAI's own announcement of GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol is dated 2026-11-17. The model shows improved coding, visual design, and handling of complex projects that require multiple steps. A test used a single detailed prompt to build a family command center website.

The test site included a calendar, meal planner, grocery list, and chore tracker, and it was fully functional, interactive, mobile-friendly, and remembered changes. GPT-6.2 Astra is available through ChatGPT Work for eligible Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users. Users can customise prompts to build simple web applications such as vacation planners or budget dashboards. OpenAI also introduced GPT-6.2 Sol, an efficient, versatile model for everyday work, and both models deliver better results with fewer output tokens. In the API, GPT-6.2 Astra's input and output token prices are 20% lower than GPT-6 Astra's, with a 60% discount on cached input at $8 for input, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 for output, all per million tokens, while GPT-6.2 Sol keeps GPT-6.1 Sol's API token prices.

OpenAI said GPT-6.2 Astra sets a new quality bar for AI in complex professional work, with slides, spreadsheets, and documents that read less like AI and follow the templates and conventions of a user's field. OpenAI said the model writes cleaner code and builds frontends that look and work better, particularly for websites, gaming, and 3D design. OpenAI said it believes GPT-6.2 Astra is the best model in the world for scientists. OpenAI said GPT-6.2 Sol is smarter and more efficient than GPT-6.1 Sol and lets users complete more tasks on the same paid plan. OpenAI said many of its employees use GPT-6.2 Sol as their default model for technical and non-technical tasks.

On Agents' Last Exam, GPT-6.2 Astra scored 5.2 points higher than GPT-6 Astra at less than a third of the cost and 5.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost, with Fable 5.2's leaderboard results excluding nine tasks that used a fallback model. GPT-6.2 Astra scored 9 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 at less than one-third the cost and set a new high on the Vals Science Index. In Cognition's FrontierCode 2.0, GPT-6.2 Sol came within 0.5 points of GPT-6.2 Astra at about one-fifth the cost, both at max. On LifeVal, GPT-6.2 Sol outscores GPT-6 Astra at about one-seventh the cost. On Harvey LAB-AA v1.1, GPT-6.2 Astra more than doubled Claude Fable 5.2's pass rate at about one-sixth the cost, and Astra for Law scored even higher.

On the internal GDPval v2 benchmark, GPT-6.2 Astra was up 6.2 percentage points from GPT-6 Astra while using 22% fewer output tokens, and GPT-6.2 Sol improved 5.3 points from GPT-6.1 Sol. On Artificial Analysis's AA-AnalystAgent, GPT-6.2 Astra answered 62.5% of questions correctly on all five independent attempts. Marquis Wong, Principal AI Engineer at IMC, said Astra's documents were a significant step up from GPT-6 Astra. Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, said Astra used 62% fewer tokens than GPT-6.1 Sol on complex legal-agent tasks and scored higher than alternative models on 8 of 10 research tasks across tax, M&A and litigation work. Niko Grupen, Head of Applied Research at Harvey, said Astra completed more than 3x as many Legal Agent Benchmark tasks with 34.5% fewer output tokens.

Jay Hack, Head of AI at ClickUp, said GPT-6.2 Astra edged out ClickUp's production model in blind testing with about 40% fewer tokens and 30% fewer review rounds. OpenAI said Astra's more precise computer use lets it work down to individual parts and connections in CAD and simulation tools. OpenAI asked GPT-6.2 Astra to visualize chassis dynamics of a car on a mountain road, and Astra created the 3D model, wrote a Python solver to simulate dynamics between the tires and suspension, and animated the results in Blender. OpenAI's team used GPT-6.2 Astra to turn the scalloped balconies of Chicago's Marina City towers into a paper lamp, and the site generated by the model can be used to create your own paper lamp. OpenAI said GPT-6.2 Astra brings stronger visual reasoning to web design, choosing layouts and imagery that give each site a distinctive look.

stories.Headline: Razorpay plans updated DRHP filing next week for February 2027 IPO
stories.Summary:
Razorpay plans to file its updated Draft Red Herring Prospectus next week, targeting a potential initial public offering by February 2027, according to a Bloomberg report cited by TechGig. The Bengaluru-based fintech firm had confidentially filed its draft IPO papers in June 2026, and the Securities and Exchange Board of India cleared that confidential filing on November 3. Investor roadshows are expected to begin immediately after the public filing of the updated prospectus. The public issue is reportedly planned at around $600 million, comprising fresh shares and an Offer For Sale component.

The IPO could value Razorpay at approximately $5 billion, or about ₹47,000 crore, which marks a markdown from its $7.5 billion valuation in 2021. Razorpay reported a 65 per cent year-on-year increase in operating revenue to ₹3,783 crore in FY25, but it recorded a loss due to ₹1,209 crore in ESOP expenses and one-time costs linked to its domicile shift from the US to India. The company is also exploring a 0.4 per cent merchant discount rate on eligible UPI transactions above ₹2,000 to boost monetisation, though its rollout might be delayed until after the 2027 state elections due to concerns over merchant backlash. Beyond payments, Razorpay is expanding into AI-led products, including its Agent Studio platform for deploying task-specific AI agents.

Razorpay was founded in 2014 by Shashank Kumar and Harshil Mathur, and it offers payment processing, business banking, payroll, and lending solutions. The company has raised over $800 million from investors including Tiger Global Management, Y Combinator, Ribbit Capital, and Lightspeed. India's IPO market has seen firms raise around $18.6 billion through initial share sales so far in 2026. The articles do not include direct statements from the founders or other company officials about the filing or the listing plans.

stories.Headline: Anthropic researcher warns superhuman AI may arrive by late 2027
stories.Summary:
Anthropic AI researcher Tao Lin predicted on November 20, 2026, that broadly superhuman artificial intelligence could emerge within about 1.3 years, potentially by the end of 2027. Lin said this AI would rival or surpass human skills in fields such as programming, medicine, law, and filmmaking. He highlighted risks including major workforce displacement and permanent reliance on state welfare. Automation-driven job cuts are already affecting technology firms like Salesforce, Amazon, and Oracle, according to the report.

The forecast sets a timeline of roughly 1.3 years from the November 2026 report to a possible arrival by late 2027. Lin cautioned about losing control over autonomous systems as one of the risks of rapid progress. He urged AI developers to slow progress so that comprehensive safety testing can take place. The article names programming, medicine, law, and filmmaking as the fields where such a system could match or exceed human skills.

Lin, an AI researcher at Anthropic, is the person responsible for the prediction and the warnings that came with it. He said developers should slow down to allow for comprehensive safety testing before such systems arrive. He also pointed to workforce displacement and permanent reliance on state welfare as risks of the technology. The article does not say what Anthropic itself plans to do in response to his remarks.

The context is that automation-driven job cuts are already affecting technology firms including Salesforce, Amazon, and Oracle. Lin's warning comes as those cuts show the workforce effects that he says could grow much larger. The article does not say what happens next beyond his call for slower progress and safety testing. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Mike Diegel argues AI oversight must govern actions as he builds Pulpo in Arizona
stories.Summary:
A letter published on November 19, 2026 in The Gila Herald, written by Mike Diegel of Pima, Arizona, responded to a November 18 article about Senator Mark Kelly’s new framework to protect Americans from the most advanced AI models. Diegel wrote that Senator Kelly is right about the problem, saying companies should not grade their own homework and that self-regulation has failed. He added that oversight which only arrives after an incident is not oversight at all. The letter argued that Kelly’s proposed fix still misses the core issue because it governs the model rather than the action.

The framework described in the letter calls for a rulebook of hazard levels, independent examiners embedded at AI companies to review safeguards as models are built, and testing and liability before and after deployment. Diegel wrote that none of that stops a consequential action at the moment it happens, because a test can pass, an examiner can sign off, and a company can disclose a risk while the AI system still makes the transfer, deletes the file, or sends the data. He argued the danger is not only how smart a model is but what authority it has been given to act, since a safe model with write access is dangerous and a dangerous model with no authority does nothing. For that reason he said his team is building Pulpo in Arizona, with governance sitting before execution as a narrow, one-use permit for one specific action, with durable evidence afterward.

Diegel wrote that no permit should mean no governed effect, and that anything else is monitoring dressed up as prevention. He said he respects Senator Kelly’s intent and his service, but that protecting Americans requires governing what AI is allowed to do, not just how it is tested or watched. The letter was signed by Mike Diegel of Pima, Arizona. The articles give no further details on the framework, on Pulpo, or on what happens next.

stories.Headline: Sara Jacobs and Don Beyer introduce bipartisan AI safety framework
stories.Summary:
Representatives Sara Jacobs of California and Don Beyer of Virginia introduced a new artificial intelligence framework on November 19, 2026. This legislative outline aims to establish essential guardrails for the development and deployment of advanced technology. Representative Celeste Maloy of Utah joined the Democratic lawmakers to support this bipartisan effort. The proposal represents the second attempt by members of the House to address these issues.

The proposed SAFE AI Act would require the federal government to establish a set of minimum safety standards. These baseline requirements would then allow individual states to build their own additional regulations upon the federal foundation. This structured approach seeks to balance national consistency with the specific needs of different state jurisdictions. The framework focuses on creating a reliable safety net for the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence.

Representatives Jacobs and Beyer are responsible for the outline as they prepare to advance the issue during the next Congress. While the provided text does not include direct quotes, the lawmakers intend to create a bipartisan path for AI oversight. This initiative follows other House efforts, such as a separate framework by Sam Liccardo and Kevin Kiley regarding engagement with China. The broader goal is to mitigate risks while maintaining technological progress through legislative cooperation.

stories.Headline: Intuit opens Bengaluru campus as its second-largest engineering centre worldwide
stories.Summary:
Intuit inaugurated a new two-tower campus at Embassy Tech Village on Outer Ring Road in Bellandur, Bengaluru, on November 20, 2026, and the facility now serves as the company's second-largest engineering centre worldwide. The campus consolidates all Intuit India teams, which the company says is designed to foster seamless collaboration and innovation. The Bengaluru site brings together teams working on core product, platform, and AI capabilities for global customers. The expansion reflects Intuit's continued investment in India as a significant innovation hub, according to the company.

Nearly 25 per cent of Intuit's global technology talent is based in Bengaluru, where teams have operated since 2005. Those teams develop platforms, products, and AI-driven experiences for consumers, businesses, and accountants worldwide. The new campus reinforces Intuit's commitment to driving global AI innovation from India, the company said. The articles do not give the cost of the campus, its seating capacity, or a headcount for the new facility.

Saurabh Saxena, Senior Vice President, Product Development and India Site Leader at Intuit, said the campus aims to bring top tech talent together for growth and innovation in India. Alex Balazs, Chief Technology Officer at Intuit, emphasised that the Bengaluru teams are central to building AI-driven experiences that help customers prosper. The articles do not say what happens next, such as further hiring targets or additional phases of construction. No other next steps are given.

stories.Headline: Local authority teams learn to assess AI risks to human rights at Paris academy
stories.Summary:
Teams from 20 local and regional authorities took part in the first HUDERIA Academy for Local Authorities, held in Paris from 17 to 19 November 2026, where they learned to assess the risks that artificial intelligence poses to human rights, democracy and the rule of law. The event was organised by the Centre of Expertise for Multilevel Governance at the Congress of Local and Regional Authorities, working closely with the Council of Europe's Steering Committee for New and Emerging Digital Technologies. Over the three days, participants from 18 member states applied HUDERIA, the Council of Europe's methodology for assessing the impact of AI systems, to a fictional AI-supported public consultation. They identified risks, mapped stakeholders and designed measures to mitigate those risks. The authorities represented included Camden from the United Kingdom, Fingal County from Ireland, Amaroussion from Greece, Bergen from Norway, Valongo from Portugal, Lviv and Rivne from Ukraine, Arezzo from Italy and Harghita County from Romania.

The list also included Ventspils from Latvia, Vigo from Spain, Diyarbakır from Türkiye, Bitola and Resen from North Macedonia, Bălți from the Republic of Moldova, Shkodër from Albania, Kutaisi from Georgia, Szentendre from Hungary, Turnišče from Slovenia, Nõo from Estonia and the Association of Netherlands Municipalities. Participants described HUDERIA as practical and relevant, and several began applying it to their own projects while obtaining feedback from their peers. They committed to maintaining an alumni network and called for follow-up and continued opportunities to engage with HUDERIA. The Academy is an official event on the Road to Geneva AI Summit 2027 and a contribution to the Council of Europe's New Democratic Pact for Europe, and it supports implementation of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence.

Annika Vaikla, the Congress co-rapporteur on AI and Deputy Mayor of Viimsi in Estonia, urged authorities to use AI to give public servants more time for people while keeping people in control. She called for AI literacy among political leaders, staff and citizens, and for smaller municipalities to have access to shared expertise. The articles say several themes ran through the Academy, including that local AI should be human-centred, socially anchored and community-led, and that public trust has to be earned through openness and clear accountability by keeping humans in the loop. The articles do not say what specific follow-up measures were agreed beyond the alumni network and the calls for continued engagement.

stories.Headline: Snowflake's Vivek Raghunathan says skipping rollout stages causes uneven AI coding results
stories.Summary:
Many engineering organisations have deployed AI coding tools but frequently encounter uneven results, according to insights from industry leaders reported by TechGig on November 20, 2026. This outcome is often attributed to overlooking critical phases in the rollout, specifically the transition from initial experimentation to codified best practices. Vivek Raghunathan, senior vice president of engineering at Snowflake, outlined a five-stage progression for AI rollouts that draws inspiration from Intel's Andy Grove. The initial phase involves allowing chaos to reign, followed by discovering effective practices, codifying them into a shared language, scaling that language across the organisation, and finally reorganising around the new operational reality.

Organisations often bypass the second and third stages, which involve discovering and codifying what actually works, because of an eagerness to demonstrate a quick return on investment for new tool purchases. Skipped stages frequently lead to measuring inappropriate metrics too early, such as lines of code or merged pull requests, instead of focusing on tool adoption across diverse tasks. A lack of a shared vocabulary for effective practices also prevents individual successes from becoming organisational knowledge. Raghunathan's team at Snowflake identified approximately 14 named patterns, including plan in writing before you write code and fence agents into separate git worktrees, which provide a concrete framework for teaching and measuring AI-assisted work.

Scaling AI adoption through mechanisms like regular focus weeks, where dedicated time is allocated for learning or innovation, proved more effective than relying on mandates. Reorganising roles and responsibilities, the final stage, should only occur once a clear understanding of reliable AI-assisted work is established within the company. The article attributes the uneven results to skipped rollout stages rather than to problems with talent or the tools themselves. It does not say what happens next for organisations that follow the model or what further steps Snowflake plans.

stories.Headline: Security leaders shift focus to securing how employees use AI as enterprises balance adoption with data leak risks
stories.Summary:
Enterprises are facing a conflict between adopting generative and agentic AI for tasks such as debugging code, summarizing contracts and automating decision-making, and preventing proprietary data from leaking into unauthorized models. Security and compliance leaders are working at the same time to stop proprietary source code, financial projections and regulated customer records from leaking into unauthorized AI models. For most Chief Information Security Officers the question is no longer whether employees are using AI, because that use is now acknowledged. Their focus has shifted to understanding what employees are doing with AI and to securing that use rather than blocking it. Semantic DLP is presented as a way to secure enterprise generative AI data without hindering adoption.

The story requires enterprises to balance the adoption of generative and agentic AI against the risk of data leakage, and it changes the focus of security leaders from whether AI is used to how it is used. The tasks named in the articles are debugging code, summarizing contracts and automating decision-making, and the data at risk includes proprietary source code, financial projections and regulated customer records. The articles give no numbers, no dates beyond the publication date of November 20, 2026, and no named individuals. The only named technology is semantic DLP, which the articles say helps secure enterprise generative AI without hindering adoption. The articles do not describe how semantic DLP works or what it costs.

Chief Information Security Officers are the people responsible, and the articles say they acknowledge that employees use AI and have shifted their focus to securing it. Security and compliance leaders are also described as working to prevent proprietary data from leaking into unauthorized models. The articles paraphrase no individual by name and carry no direct statement from any officer or company. The context is a tug-of-war between adopting generative and agentic AI for everyday work and keeping sensitive data inside authorized systems. The articles do not say what happens next, beyond the stated aim of securing generative AI use without hindering adoption.

stories.Headline: Soket AI raises nearly $4 million from Bajaj Finance and Pennant Technologies for on-premise enterprise LLMs
stories.Summary:
Bengaluru-based Soket AI, a frontier AI research lab and an IndiaAI Mission startup, has raised nearly $4 million from Bajaj Finance and Pennant Technologies, according to a TechGig report published on November 20, 2026. Bajaj Finance invested about $2 million through Bajaj Finserv Intelligence, its applied research and innovation initiative, while Pennant Technologies, a lending software company in which Bajaj Finance holds a stake, contributed another $2 million in the same round. The funding will support Soket AI's work on large language models focused on coding, mathematics and reasoning, which are intended for enterprise applications, particularly within financial services. Soket AI's models are designed to run on an organisation's own infrastructure, including on-premises environments, an approach the company says allows training and deployment at lower costs with full control over data.

The startup was founded in 2019 by Abhishek Upperwal and focuses on what it describes as frontier AI for work where a wrong answer has a cost. Soket AI was selected by the IndiaAI Mission in May 2025 to build foundation models, and it unveiled its 26.3-billion-parameter EKA-1 model on November 3 this year, trained on nearly 7.5 trillion tokens. EKA-1 is an open, sparse hybrid language model that supports all 22 scheduled Indian languages and English, and it is designed for mathematics, code generation, reasoning and agentic applications. Soket AI and Pennant plan to jointly develop banking-specific language models and AI agents targeting applications such as know-your-customer checks, onboarding, collections, compliance and fraud detection.

Rajeev Jain, Vice-Chairman and MD of Bajaj Finance, said the next phase of AI will be defined by outcomes at sustainable cost, and he noted that Soket AI's models can make advanced AI economically viable for financial services while ensuring secure deployment within their infrastructure. Sanjiv Bajaj, Chairman and MD of Bajaj Finserv, highlighted the importance of indigenous research for AI as critical information infrastructure, adding that the investment reflects Bajaj Finserv's commitment to strengthening India's sovereign AI capabilities. The funding round places the on-premise model approach at the centre of the company's plans for financial services, where data control and cost are presented as the main considerations. The report does not say what happens next beyond the joint development work with Pennant.

stories.Headline: Nicholas Matsakis introduces Symposium and Agent Client Protocol to guide AI agents in using Rust
stories.Summary:
Nicholas Matsakis, a lead designer of the Rust programming language and a senior principal engineer at Amazon, introduced two new projects on November 20, 2026, according to TechGig. The first is Symposium, an agent-oriented toolchain designed to guide AI agents in using Rust, and the second is the Agent Client Protocol, which proposes a standardised way for AI agents and clients to communicate. Matsakis presented the projects as a way to integrate Rust with artificial intelligence more effectively. The report was published by TechGig on that date.

Symposium aims to give AI agents tailored Rust guidance, such as recommending Rust 2024 and the latest crate versions, while letting crate authors write skills that instruct agents on how to use their libraries. The Agent Client Protocol is intended to improve interoperability across various agents and front-end tools, moving beyond current vendor-specific implementations. The projects address current large language model limitations, including agents using outdated library versions or older Rust editions, because current LLMs often struggle to keep up with the fast pace of software development and library updates. By embedding skills directly within Rust crates, Symposium aims to prevent agents from hallucinating application programming interfaces or generating non-compiling code. Matsakis also introduced the concept of battery packs, which provide best-practice guidance for recommended sets of libraries such as an opinionated network service pack.

Matsakis emphasised Rust's memory safety as a significant advantage, noting its adoption in critical systems like the Linux kernel and at companies such as Microsoft and Amazon. He cited statistics indicating that switching to Rust reduces memory-safety-related vulnerabilities, which account for a large percentage of overall software flaws. The initiatives are part of a broader vision for a more extensible ecosystem that supports open-source maintainers through a Rust commercial network. The stated goal is to streamline language choice for developers by offering robust tooling and community support for Rust development, particularly when combined with AI.

stories.Headline: Justice department launches Super Intelligence Task Force to coordinate AI enforcement
stories.Summary:
The Department of Justice has launched a Super Intelligence Task Force, known as DOJ-SITF, to promote American artificial intelligence and to coordinate criminal and civil enforcement against actors who misuse AI, according to a November 19, 2026 article by McCarter & English attorneys Lindsey R. Harteis, Zachary Myers and Erin Prest. The Attorney General’s press release announcing the Task Force signals that enforcement will be forthcoming for those who use AI to engage in fraud or other criminal conduct. The new body merges the Artificial Intelligence Task Force that the former Attorney General announced in January 2026. Under Executive Order 14434, the executive branch uses the terms Super Intelligence and SI instead of Artificial Intelligence or AI.

The Task Force is charged with organizing the Department’s criminal and civil enforcement efforts involving AI and with deconflicting investigations, cases and other matters among Department components and United States Attorneys’ Offices. It will recommend enforcement priorities meant to promote public safety and prevent misuse of AI, serve as the Department’s point of contact with the President’s separate AI Task Force and other federal agencies, and coordinate the Department’s affirmative civil litigation involving AI. It will also develop guidance on prosecuting AI-related unlawful conduct and on evaluating compliance measures, and advise on legislative or regulatory proposals that promote AI innovation without burdensome regulation. The announcement does not establish a new regulatory or legislative framework for AI, so potential enforcement would proceed under existing laws.

The Task Force will be led by the Attorney General or his designees, with the Associate Attorney General and Associate Deputy Attorney General serving as co-chairs. Additional members will include representatives of the Antitrust Division, the Attorney General’s Advisory Committee, Civil Division, Criminal Division, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the National Fraud Enforcement Division, the National Security Division and the Office of the Solicitor General. The DOJ release says the Task Force will ensure a comprehensive approach across the Department and will ensure that America’s leadership in AI is not compromised by misuse by foreign state and state-sponsored actors, transnational criminal organizations, and individual or corporate actors engaged in fraud or other unlawful conduct. The Task Force will work in partnership with the separate AI Task Force established by President Trump.

The article says the DOJ does not explain what constitutes misuse of AI or establish the precise scope of conduct that could result in civil or criminal liability. It says companies’ use of AI in connection with government payment claims, cybersecurity controls, and representations made while negotiating and performing government contracts could present potential exposure under existing federal statutes. Using AI to present false claims for payment from the government, failing to maintain necessary cybersecurity controls while using AI resources, and making material misrepresentations about AI use in government contracts might conceivably result in liability, according to the article. The authors write that companies should understand the Task Force’s objectives and composition and should consider steps to mitigate potential civil or criminal exposure from their use of AI technologies and platforms.

stories.Headline: Researchers find no AI dependency tool reports responsiveness or cross-cultural validity
stories.Summary:
Wenhai Fan, Lijun Wang, Lihong Li, Xiaoxia Zheng, Zhaoqing Miao, and Mingming Yu conducted a systematic review of AI dependency tools. This research was published on November 20, 2026, in the journal Psychology Research and Behavior Management. The authors evaluated the methodological quality and measurement properties of instruments used for college students. They searched eight databases from their inception until January 21, 2026, to find relevant studies. The team used the COSMIN Risk of Bias Checklist and the mGRADE approach to grade the evidence.

The review examined nine studies evaluating nine different AI dependency assessment instruments for students in higher education. The AI dependence scale and the reliance on ChatGPT scale for nursing students were both classified as category A. The scale for dependence on artificial intelligence was placed in category C, while the other instruments were category B. No instruments reported responsiveness, measurement error, or cross-cultural validity across different countries and cultures. The protocol for this review was registered in PROSPERO under the registration number CRD420251269989. The researchers stated that reliable assessment instruments are needed to identify AI dependency and its behavioral consequences. They noted that existing tools exhibit limitations in measurement quality, conceptual clarity, and applicability due to varying frameworks.

The authors preliminarily recommended the AI dependence scale and the reliance on ChatGPT scale for evaluating students. They argued that improved tools will support future research on psychological mechanisms and interventions to reduce dependency. The team concluded that future research should develop more robust and theoretically grounded instruments for this purpose. The authors noted that AI tools are a double-edged sword that can support learning or reduce independent thinking. Students are affected by potential problems including academic dishonesty, ethical dilemmas, privacy concerns, and technology-induced anxiety.

A study by Kaabi found that 78.3 percent of university students in the United Arab Emirates depend on AI. That same study reported that 94.5 percent of those students experienced detrimental effects on linguistic skills and critical thinking. Dependency is associated with negative outcomes like sleep disturbances, academic procrastination, and negative emotions. The articles explain that AI dependency is a state of cognitive inertia and behavioral attachment toward AI-generated content. This condition is characterized by a difficulty in independently correcting or verifying the outputs generated by AI.

It is distinct from addiction, which involves withdrawal and impaired control, and problematic use, which denotes impaired use. AI dependency may lead to superficial learning where students complete assignments without understanding the core concepts. Such dependency can reduce cognitive engagement and substitute independent thought with automated responses from AI tools. Future research should more comprehensively evaluate psychometric properties and develop instruments that are more theoretically grounded.

New tools must be tested to see if scores stay stable when measured again over a period of time. Researchers need to determine if these instruments can detect real changes in student dependency levels over time. The articles leave open how to unify the concepts of AI dependency, addiction, and problematic use in literature. They also leave open how to resolve the lack of uniformity in current assessment methods and content dimensions.

stories.Headline: Brazil's Senate approves an AI regulation bill while Peru enacts a general AI law
stories.Summary:
Brazil’s Senate approved a bill on December 10, 2024 regulating the use, development, and deployment of AI, and that general framework remains before a special committee in the Chamber of Deputies with no vote date confirmed. On February 25, 2026, another law turned Brazil’s National Data Protection Authority into a full regulatory agency with greater technical, administrative, and financial authority. Peru passed legislation in 2023 establishing principles including data privacy, the development of national AI talent, and cooperation on AI development at home and abroad. In 2025, a supreme decree approved regulations implementing Peru’s law, setting out financing provisions, accountability mechanisms, and implementation periods. The Atlantic Council published the analysis on November 19, 2026, written by Olivia Torres, a project assistant at its GeoTech Center, and Angel Ortega, a Panamanian attorney and policy researcher.

An attached proposal in Brazil would expand the role of the National Data Protection Authority, making it the default AI regulator alongside sectoral regulators. Peru’s 2023 law designates regulatory authority to the existing Secretariat of Government and Digital Transformation. Peru’s 2025 decree clarifies how responsibilities are divided among government institutions and enforcement authorities, and provides that when the Secretariat encounters a regulatory breach it has authority to consult the competent authorities. In Peru, the National Data Protection Agency handles AI-related personal data breaches, the National Institute for the Defense of Competition and Protection of Intellectual Property handles industry competitiveness and consumer protection, and the National Police specializes in cybercrimes. The Organization of American States launched the Inter-American Framework on Data Governance and Artificial Intelligence, known as MIGDIA, a regional initiative developed by multisector stakeholders and governments.

Ahead of the 2026 Brazilian elections, Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court issued fourteen resolutions governing the electoral process, including restrictions on AI use. The resolutions barred AI systems from recommending candidates or signaling voting preferences and required disclosure of AI-generated or digitally manipulated campaign content. The court was able to enforce the resolutions through the suspension of profiles. Dilmar Villena, director of Hiperderecho, one of Peru’s leading digital safety organizations, warned the authors in an interview that without additional resources institutions will have limited bandwidth to oversee all emerging AI technology concerns. Villena noted that oversight of most emerging technologies, including cloud computing and platform regulation, falls under the Secretariat of Government and Digital Transformation, which faces concerns around its budgetary capacity due to its reliance on funding from the Presidency of the Council of Ministers.

Brazil’s first AI proposal was criticized for insufficient inclusion of Indigenous voices in the legislative debate and failure to consider structural racism in public security. São Paulo’s Smart Sampa city surveillance pilot project was heavily scrutinized by civil society since its presentation in 2022, as it was found to disproportionately profile black individuals. Brazil’s legislative debates incorporated concerns about racial discrimination and other contextual issues. Peru has launched digital government indicators that track the implementation of digital government initiatives and institutional capabilities and show where administrative capacity is thin. The indicators do not yet measure whether AI implementation itself is working, but are described as an important building block for future institutional readiness assessments.

Countries in Latin America are developing AI regulatory frameworks, many drawing on European regulatory traditions, from data protection to emerging risk-based AI rules. Brazil and Peru have become regional leaders in regulation while still at an early stage of AI governance, pioneering different approaches. Brazil has begun strengthening its institutions while its general AI framework remains in development, and Peru has become one of the first Latin American countries to pass a general AI law coupled with implementation mechanisms. One MIGDIA recommendation is to clearly define the processes, roles, and responsibilities of actors involved across the data lifecycle. Brazil has already taken steps in this direction by assigning a role of AI regulator to the National Data Protection Authority.

Brazil is developing authority before its regulatory framework is concretized into law, while Peru has a more clearly assigned authority now that AI legislation has been approved and is beginning to be applied. The articles leave open whether Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies will vote on the general AI framework and when. They leave open whether the attached proposal making the National Data Protection Authority the default AI regulator will be adopted. They leave open whether Peru will scale up institutional resources as regulatory responsibilities expand. They leave open whether Peru’s digital government indicators will later measure whether AI implementation itself is working.

stories.Headline: Researchers propose Vision-as-a-Tool to let text-only agents offload visual reasoning
stories.Summary:
Haolin Yang, Wenshan Wu, Jin Jiang, Yu Cheng, Yan Xia, Ting Song, Yangyu Huang, Zhiliang Peng, Wenhui Wang, Hangbo Bao, Yuzhe Zhang, Wen-Da Wei, Tengchao Lv, Li Dong, Lei Cui and Furu Wei posted a paper titled Vision-as-a-Tool: Visual Harness for Multimodal Agentic Coding to arXiv on 20 November 2026. The paper argues that multimodal agentic coding needs strong visual reasoning to analyze observations and to evaluate the artifacts that agents generate. Current frameworks mostly rely on a Thinking-with-Images paradigm, in which agents depend on their own intrinsic vision to carry out visually grounded tasks. That architectural coupling creates a fundamental bottleneck, because agent performance stays strictly bounded by internal perceptual limits, and text-only agents lack native perception entirely.

The authors introduce the Vision-as-a-Tool paradigm, which reframes general-purpose multimodal large language models as callable external utilities rather than as the agent's own eyes. Earlier visual tool use merely manipulated images for an agent's intrinsic vision to read, whereas this approach lets text-only agents completely offload visual reasoning during agentic execution. Vision-capable agents can meanwhile augment their native perception on demand, and the authors instantiate the paradigm in VHarness, a unified framework driven by five atomic actions. They evaluate VHarness across Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG and Image-to-3D generation tasks, and the results show that it consistently improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy for both text-only and multimodal coding agents.

The paper is listed under Artificial Intelligence and Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, and its authors conclude that modularizing visual reasoning into callable utilities gives a flexible and scalable foundation for future agentic coding systems. The abstract does not assign responsibility for any failure to a named person or organization, and it reports no statements beyond the authors' own framing of the bottleneck and their proposed fix. The article also carries standard arXivLabs boilerplate describing a framework through which collaborators develop and share features on the site, and noting that arXiv works only with partners who adhere to its values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy. The posting invites ideas for projects that would add value to the arXiv community through arXivLabs, but the articles give no further details on deployment, timelines or follow-up work.
