stories.Headline: Ejaaz Ahamadeen examines Anthropic's AI models ahead of its IPO and the race to self-improvement
stories.Summary:
In a Yahoo Finance video published on November 19, 2026, In the Loop host Ejaaz Ahamadeen examined Anthropic's evolving AI models ahead of the company's highly anticipated initial public offering and the accelerating race toward more advanced artificial intelligence. Ahamadeen broke down the latest predictions for recursive self-improvement, the point at which an AI system could autonomously improve its own capabilities. He described recursive self-improvement as an AI model so smart that it can design, build and research the next version of itself, an AI smarter than the smartest AI researcher. He said the researchers paid hundreds of millions of dollars to work at these AI labs are, in effect, building their own replacement. He added that the part exciting investors is not the self-improving part but what it means, because such a model could theoretically be pointed at any profession, any vertical or any hard task.

Ahamadeen referred to an AI 2027 report whose authors made predictions back in 2025 or perhaps 2024, and he said they had one of the most accurate predictions so far. One of their cases covered when self-improving technology would arrive and when white-collar work would be replaced by AI. He said they have now moved up their dates, having been about 10 months late, and they predict this to happen as early as the end of next year, 2027. He described a world where an AI model can automate 99% of white-collar work, which makes up trillions of dollars worth of value in the economy. He then posed the question of what one would value the company that created such a model, if the leading model that does that is an Anthropic Claude model.

Ahamadeen acknowledged that listeners might hear him and say he is just selling propaganda for Anthropic, but he said he has looked into the research and the data. He said it is not just Anthropic proving it, but also OpenAI and Google, and that all three companies have made public statements saying they are very close to achieving recursive self-improvement. He said OpenAI has solved a bunch of really complex hard math and physics problems, and Google is solving a lot of complex science problems and advancing its own scientific experiments internally. He said Anthropic is focused on biology and medicine and cancer specifically. He noted that all of this assumes Anthropic is able to overcome a number of challenges that still lay ahead of it.

The video ran alongside coverage of Anthropic's Nasdaq debut, with a live blog inviting readers to follow the big listing, and the stock was quoted at 94.62, up 11.62 or 14.00%, in one snapshot and at 95.40, up 12.40 or 14.94%, in another. stories.Headline: Shawn Tsao launches Snapp AI with $4.6M seed to bring agentic sports intelligence to bettors and teams
stories.Summary:
Shawn Tsao, who co-founded and sold the food delivery startup Caviar, has raised a $4.6M seed round for his new venture, the sports intelligence firm Snapp AI, as reported on November 19, 2026. The investors in the round include a16z Speedrun, Dorm Room Fund, Gold House Ventures, House Fund and Valia Ventures. Snapp's co-founders are Andrew Tamura as chief technology officer, Alex Marshall as chief AI officer, Tsao as chief executive and Min Park as chief operating officer and chief financial officer. The company's agentic AI has both consumer and enterprise applications, helping users answer questions, surface insights and make data-driven analysis more efficient. Fantasy players and bettors make up the majority of individual users, while Cal football is Snapp's first team client.

The original plan for Snapp was to use open-source large language models, but Tsao found the data quality and accuracy too poor for use at a sophisticated level. Instead, he said his team combined Gemini, OpenAI and Claude to build a tool he described as 44% more accurate and 3.2 times faster than a general LLM. Snapp seeks to take the fragmented sports data ecosystem, including player stats, tracking data, betting lines and prediction market odds, to help analyze the action, build predictive models and surface advantageous betting lines. Tsao noted that the AI will sometimes even steer bettors away from poorly conceived parlays.

The spark to investigate AI for sports data was a conversation Tsao had with Marshall about WNBA betting lines, and he likens Snapp to an AI agent like Muse, Dots or Duet but fully dedicated to sports. Tsao said the core goal is to become the best sports intelligence company, whether for consumers or for teams, since the same AI services both. On prioritizing one market over the other, he said it will probably dual track at the moment because Snapp is a young company and AI tooling for productivity lets it scale products for both sides very quickly. He described one use in which a Cal football coach dictates into his AirPods a request for Snapp to pull as much available data as possible on a recruit and then adds the player to his worksheet for later reference.

Tsao said feedback from bettors, fantasy players and teams is that work which used to take hours, or things they did not want to get to, now gets done for them instantly. Tsao was one of five Cal Berkeley students who started Caviar, which they later sold to Square and then to DoorDash for $410M. As a student he had worked as a manager for Cal football and was exposed to the inner workings of administering and operating a college program. He wanted to return to sports, which he called his passion, second only perhaps to eating, and in conversation with the football staff he learned how large a gap there was for AI to help coaches identify talent and recruit prospects.

stories.Headline: Advisor360 CEO Milind Mehere calls AI a reckoning for wealth management
stories.Summary:
Milind Mehere, CEO of Advisor360, said in an interview with InvestmentNews at Impact 2026 in Boston that AI is a reckoning for wealth management, bigger than robo-advice. He said a consumer with one click can now upload tax returns and financial statements and get very smart. He said the responsibility has shifted to the adviser to be smarter than what GPT can answer. He has been in the CEO role 5 months and was on the board for 2 and a half years before that. He has been building in wealth management and asset management for the last 13 years.

He said efficiency happened two years ago and is old news, and that the first use case was an AI layer on top of CRM for things such as meeting prep. He described Advisor360's concept of a unified data layer, which he said long predates AI's popularity and is foundational to its software. He said the company serves large insurance company broker-dealers, supporting millions of households and tens of thousands of advisers. He said its products include meeting prep, Pulse signals from macro and micro signals, agentic onboarding, and talk to your data. He said a mortgage resetting from 2% in the ZIRP era to 6% today could mean $1,000 of extra payments a month.

He said his mandate in the next 12 to 24 months is to separate noise from signal and launch products for the adviser ecosystem. He said data and trust are the foundational elements for proving which use cases stick, and that success will be measured by adoption. He said the company's meeting prep has provenance of where data came from, so it can say data came from one system versus another. He said advisers should not sit on the sidelines and should pick two, three or four problems and find partners to solve them. He said advisers should be careful with data privacy and security, and that data capture is free and software is almost becoming free.

He said hyper-personalization does not take away from the adviser-client relationship at all. He said a client whose mortgage is resetting and who gets that call would see trust in the adviser go up 10x. He said advisers have 400 other customers and are battling memory, which machines are very good at. He said advisers should outsource that to machines and spend time on growing their business, which he called a big problem for the industry, and on playing a little more golf. He said advisers should treat each customer as if they were the only customer.

He said in December 2023, when GPT came out, it reset many expectations, not just for software or finance but for how we operate generally. He said the rate of change is extremely fast but there is a lot of noise. He said the adviser ecosystem is so fragmented that getting clean data to run a context or intelligence layer on is not easy, and everybody in the industry is grappling with it. He said the machine sees a consumer's changing financial life daily, including markets, income, bonuses, job loss, a house purchase, mortgage payments and expenses. He said data the adviser had yesterday is already outdated.

He said the next 12 to 24 months will bring many use cases similar to meeting prep, and that agentic workflows will solve the problems they identify. He said the company is launching a bunch of use cases and workflows in its marketplace in the service of getting advisers to be super advisers and ultimately in the service of the consumer. He said AI and the companies supporting it are going to be very innovative. He said advisers should jump in and test a few workflows to see where the technology will truly help them. He said the question is how to blend context and stitch workflows together that actually solve the problem, which he said will be the differentiation.

stories.Headline: UBS upgrades Box to buy and lifts price target to $55 on AI demand
stories.Summary:
UBS upgraded Box Inc, which trades on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker BOX, to a buy rating from neutral on November 19, 2026, according to a report published by Proactive. The brokerage also raised its price target for the shares to $55 from $37 after customer checks strengthened its confidence in the company's artificial intelligence prospects. UBS said ten field checks indicated that recent AI-driven growth could extend beyond the initial Enterprise Advanced upgrade cycle. The analysts concluded that this growth could support revenue growth of about 10% annually through financial year 2030.

UBS raised its financial year 2028 revenue growth forecast to 10% on a constant-currency basis from 9%, a figure that sits above the market consensus of approximately 9% year-on-year. The analysts said Box was moving beyond its traditional role as a content repository into higher-value AI-powered workflows, including client onboarding, loan underwriting, insurance claims, contract analysis and human resources processes. Customers cited demand for document extraction, content analysis and automated workflows, with Box benefiting from access to companies' unstructured data while maintaining existing permissions and governance controls. The checks also indicated that artificial intelligence was supporting higher customer spending through Enterprise Advanced upgrades, additional user seats and consumption-based services.

UBS estimates that Enterprise Advanced upgrades and AI consumption could together contribute about five percentage points to annual revenue growth over the next three years. Several customers expected total spending to increase by 5% to 15%, while one anticipated doubling its spending from $5 million to $10 million within approximately 18 months. UBS raised its valuation multiple to 15 times calendar 2028 estimated free cash flow from 11 times, citing improving AI traction and the potential for mid-teens or higher free cash flow growth. The report did not say when Box itself would next report results or how the company responded to the upgrade.

Articles.Title: Box upgraded to 'buy' by UBS as AI demand supports growth outlook

stories.Headline: Liveops survey finds 60% of customers arrive better prepared using their own AI tools
stories.Summary:
Liveops surveyed 750 adults in the United States who use their own artificial intelligence tools for customer service, and the company published its findings on 19 November 2026. The survey found that 60 percent of those customers feel more prepared before they contact a company, while 72 percent have fixed a problem without contacting the company at all. Some 84 percent have had to repeat information that a chatbot already had, and 65 percent say there is little point reaching a representative who only repeats what their AI said. Liveops said agents need context and authority to act, not just information.

The findings change what customers expect when they arrive, because many have already done the work before they make contact. A majority feel ready before they reach a company, and nearly three quarters have solved a problem on their own without any contact. The repeat information figure of 84 percent shows that the handover from chatbot to human often fails to carry what the customer already provided. The 65 percent who see little point in a representative who repeats their AI shows that a scripted response adds nothing at that stage.

Liveops is responsible for the survey, which covered 750 adults who use their own AI tools for customer service. The company said agents need context and authority to act, not just information, which is a paraphrase of its stated conclusion. The article does not name any individual at Liveops or give a direct quotation from a named person. The survey is the source of every number in the report, and the article presents the findings without naming the executives involved.

The context is a customer service market where buyers already bring their own AI tools to the interaction, and the article places the survey alongside other vendor announcements from the same day. The article does not say what Liveops plans to do next, and it gives no date for any follow-up research or product change. It also does not say how the survey respondents were recruited or how the questions were worded. The article ends with the conclusion that agents need context and authority to act, not just information.

Articles.Title: Customers Now Arrive With AI Homework Done, Liveops Finds

stories.Headline: KraneShares argues AI demand outruns supply as chip rental prices rise
stories.Summary:
KraneShares published a market update on 19 November 2026 arguing that the AI trade is being misread. Semiconductors sold off, hyperscaler earnings sparked worries about spending, and headlines about data center permit freezes added anxiety. Many investors concluded the AI trade is running out of demand. KraneShares said the market is reading the signals backward. The firm said the situation is a supply shock, with more demand for AI computing power than the industry can build, power, and deliver.

KraneShares manages the KraneShares Public-Private AI & Technology ETF, ticker AGIX. Rental prices for Nvidia's H100 chips rose about 32% last month, and prices for its newer B200 chips rose 25%, per Ornn data as of 13 November 2026. IREN, an Australia-based cloud computing and AI infrastructure company, said this week that prices for its compute are still rising, per CNBC as of 5 November 2026. Microsoft described capacity, not demand, as the main constraint on its growth. Microsoft's commercial remaining performance obligations reached $677 billion, up 73%, per LongYield as of 31 October 2026.

KraneShares said rising prices, full capacity, and a growing backlog are the signature of scarcity, not a slowdown. The firm said the drop in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index partly reflects investors repricing the slope of growth. KraneShares said scarcity raises the earning power of installed capacity, pointing to stronger revenue at lower valuations across the AGIX portfolio. Over the past 30 days, analysts raised forward earnings estimates for AGIX's holdings while the portfolio's forward price-to-earnings ratio came down. KraneShares called earnings expectations going up while valuations come down an attractive setup for long-term investors.

KraneShares said a permit slowdown can act as a healthy brake, especially for a portfolio like AGIX. A year ago, roughly 23 gigawatts of data center capacity was already under construction worldwide, about three-quarters of it in the U.S., per BloombergNEF as of 24 March 2026. UBS estimates about 30% of expected 2028 additions are at risk, per Yahoo Finance as of 7 November 2026. Meta, Microsoft, Google, SpaceX, and Nebius are building multi-gigawatt data centers with power plants they pay for themselves, and all five were AGIX holdings as of 31 October 2026. ERCOT, the operator of the Texas power grid, has 474 GW of large-load connection requests in its queue, about five times the grid's peak demand, per Dave Manuel as of 4 November 2026.

In the September quarter, capital spending exceeded operating cash flow at three of the largest hyperscalers, and only Microsoft stayed positive. Earnings for the 493 S&P 500 companies outside the Magnificent 7 appear to be growing 32.6%, compared with 22.6% for the Magnificent 7 themselves, per FactSet as of 30 October 2026. Roche added 2,176 Nvidia Blackwell GPUs this spring, bringing its total above 3,500, per Roche as of 15 March 2026. Morgan Stanley Research estimates nearly $3 trillion of AI-related infrastructure investment will flow through the global economy by 2028, per Morgan Stanley as of 9 March 2026. Anthropic grew its annualized run-rate revenue from approximately $1 billion in early 2025 to $47 billion in May of 2026, per Anthropic's website as of 28 May 2026.

McKinsey's predictive models say advances in AI could produce a $17.1-25.6 trillion boost to the global economy annually. KraneShares said the AI trade has run hard for two years and leveraged liquidity has left the market structure vulnerable. The firm said a reset is not the end of the story, citing rising compute prices, record backlogs, disciplined supply, and broadening demand beyond the Magnificent 7. AGIX is designed for a ten-year horizon, aiming to capture long-term growth of an innovation still in its infancy. KraneShares said it expects growth to continue on a different slope, steadier, healthier, and more durable.

stories.Headline: Bret Taylor's Sierra seeks $1.5 billion at near $30 billion valuation
stories.Summary:
Sierra, the AI customer service startup led by Bret Taylor, is in early talks to raise about $1.5 billion at a valuation near $30 billion, according to a report from The Information cited by Techmeme. That figure would nearly double the $15.8 billion valuation the company reached in May. Sierra has not confirmed the round, and the terms could still change. The report says investors are paying software-platform prices for AI agents that resolve customer issues, which puts pressure on every incumbent's roadmap.

stories.Headline: Anthropic prices IPO at $83 and starts Nasdaq trading as AI bug hunters lift cyber stocks
stories.Summary:
Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share on November 19, 2026, above its $70 to $78 range, and began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. Jared Blikre wrote the Yahoo Finance article published that Thursday at 9:00 AM CST. The debut followed weeks of outages at Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase and Apple, each blamed on internal problems rather than hackers. Ben Emons of research firm FedWatch Advisors called the situation the "Patchpocalypse" in a note written Wednesday. Anthropic unveiled Claude Mythos Preview on April 7, a bug hunter so strong that Anthropic limited its release to a small group of partners.

Newly reported software security flaws in the federal National Vulnerability Database hit a record high of almost 17,500 in October, about four times the level a year earlier, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. This year's count, more than 100,000, already tops 2024 and 2025 combined. Since April 7, CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks shares have doubled or better. The First Trust Nasdaq Cybersecurity ETF is up nearly 50%, more than twice tech's gain, and has fallen less since the Oct. 6 tech peak, about 11% versus nearly 20% for tech. Palo Alto was surging early Thursday after raising its full-year outlook, lifting other cyber stocks.

Emons wrote that a flood of AI-found bugs means a flood of patches, and every patch is a chance for something to break. Mustafa Suleyman, who runs Microsoft's AI unit, told Deirdre Bosa on Deirdre Bosa Live that Microsoft's models are finding flaws which humans haven't found for years or even decades. Palo Alto CEO Nikesh Arora told analysts that unintended consequences of patching and configuration changes were partly behind the recent outages. Somesh Dash, a general partner at Anthropic investor IVP, told Deirdre Bosa that if last year was token maxing, this year is going to be SOC maxing. Dash said the outages were growing pains and that we're actually doing the really necessary plumbing to be able to prepare for this next generation.

Y2K, short for year 2000, was the late-1990s fear that computers storing years as two digits would read 2000 as 1900. Fixing it cost US companies and governments more than $100 billion, according to a 1999 Commerce Department estimate. That spending stopped when the clock ran out, but this bug hunt has no deadline, since the models keep getting better. Twelve of the 15 larger US IPOs DataTrek Research tracked this year trade below their offer price, and the firm says Anthropic at least needs a decent first-day gain. Last year companies raced to use as much AI as they could, so-called token maxing, and Dash sees this year's race in security operations centers, the teams that watch for attacks around the clock.

Anthropic's new shareholders are still waiting while the bug fixers have already been paid. The article's chart shows the S&P 500 at 7,216.16, down 107.47 or 1.47%, and the Nasdaq at 24,057.87, down 372.01 or 1.52%. The VIX stood at 27.50, up 2.94 or 11.98%, and gold at 3,677.80, down 64.10 or 1.71%. Bitcoin was at 62,862.99, down 235.22 or 0.37%, and December crude oil at 83.27, up 0.96 or 1.17%. Anthropic traded at 94.69, up 11.69 or 14.09%, in the session snapshot.

Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft the post, and humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked it before publication. Blikre is the global markets and data editor for Yahoo Finance, reachable on X at @SPYJared or by email at jaredblikre@yahooinc.com. The page lists related headlines, including one saying Anthropic locked down Claude Mythos over hack risk and another saying cybersecurity stocks slid after Anthropic's AI tool launch. The article leaves open whether Anthropic holds a decent first-day gain, with its new shareholders still waiting. It also leaves open how far the bug hunt runs, since the models keep getting better and the hunt has no deadline.

stories.Headline: Family offices raise stock allocations to 36.4% while holding lower AI exposure than the S&P 500
stories.Summary:
Family offices increased their allocation to public stocks to 36.4% of their portfolios in the third quarter, up from 35.6% in the second quarter, according to the CNBC Family Office Portfolio Tracker. Their stock holdings have jumped from 33.6% in 2024, a substantial increase for family offices, which rarely deviate from their long-term financial allocations. The Tracker is powered by data from Addepar, a data and artificial intelligence platform used by financial professionals globally that now has over $10 trillion on its platform. Unlike surveys, Addepar's data provides a real-time look into the portfolios of hundreds of single-family offices, aggregated and anonymized, representing a total of more than $1.4 trillion in family office assets. The increased allocation to stocks, whether from passive market gains or active buying, shows that family offices aren't pulling back from the market despite growing fears of an AI bubble and weakness in tech stocks.

Eric Poirier, CEO of Addepar, said family offices have demonstrated over more than 15 years of study that they take the long view, but they do like staying invested. He said that with the run-up in AI thematically, they are staying exposed and risk on. At the same time, family offices are hedging their tech bets, and according to Addepar they have lower exposure to AI stocks when compared to the broader S&P 500. While tech stocks account for 40% of the S&P market cap, family offices have an average allocation of 28% of their equity portfolios in tech stocks, according to the Tracker. They are offsetting the tech risk in part with financials, which account for 11% of the S&P but make up an average allocation of 18% for family offices.

Poirier said the lower tech weighting and higher financials exposure suggests that family offices see financials as a potential offset to AI risk, and that they are fading the AI trade to some extent but still staying quite exposed. Family offices are also continuing to dial back their exposure to alternative investments, which account for 47% of their portfolios, down from 48.5% a year ago. The biggest decliner was real estate, down to 7.2% from 9.4% in the third quarter of 2025, and higher interest rates have driven down valuations in many real-estate portfolios and funds, likely accounting for much of the drop. Hedge funds also saw a decline, from 8.9% a year ago to 7.5%, as many funds grapple with more volatile stock markets and declining tech stocks. Their investments in private credit declined slightly to 1% of their portfolios, and their private equity holdings fell for the second straight quarter to 6.4% of their portfolios.

Family office holdings of private companies, held directly rather than through a private equity fund, fell 0.3% to 15.7%, likely due to slight declines in valuations, though private companies remain by far their largest segment among alts. Cash piles grew slightly for family offices to 8.6%, suggesting they want to keep adequate dry powder on hand in case of a market correction or crisis. The big question for family offices this year and next is how they manage rising yields and inflation fears, and some were positioning for inflation at the start of the year with bets on infrastructure and real estate, yet the surge in yields driven by oil prices was faster than many expected. Family office holdings of fixed income have steadily increased for three straight quarters, to 8.1% in the third quarter. Poirier said family offices tend to be able to withstand market volatility more so than other investors, but that their response to the historic rise in fixed income and rates has been more muted relative to even five-year averages.

Articles.Title: Family offices move more money into stocks, hedge AI risk, according to CNBC Family Office Portfolio Tracker

stories.Headline: Pete Warden discusses the shift toward local AI and open-weight models
stories.Summary:
Pete Warden discussed the shift toward local AI and open-weight models during a podcast interview hosted by Ben Lorica for O'Reilly. The conversation focused on why AI is moving from the cloud to local hardware and the progress of open models. Warden, a deep learning engineer and co-creator of Moonshine Voice, explained the current state of edge computing and voice interfaces. He explored how low-latency speech models could make voice a more natural interface for users. The discussion also covered the economics of local AI and emerging hardware that challenges GPU-centric infrastructure.

Running local AI requires specific hardware, such as the Apple M5 Studio which offers a configuration with 256 gigabytes of system memory. Warden noted that a 9 billion parameter model from the Qwen family can fit into a four-gigabyte graphics card using Q4 weight quantization. He mentioned that Ollama is one of the most well-known tools for users to run these models on laptops. The interview highlighted that local models are only a few months behind the capabilities of commercial models from OpenAI and Anthropic. These tools allow AI to run in browsers or on-device, providing enterprises with more control over their data.

Pete Warden stated that local AI is more capable than most people realize and that hardware barriers are lower than perceived. He argued that the biggest remaining obstacles are usability and a lack of marketing from big tech companies. Warden explained that companies prefer subscription revenue models over local tools, which leads to a lag in consumer awareness. He suggested that local AI capabilities should eventually be integrated directly into the operating system for apps to use. He also noted that commercial models often have restrictions and guardrails that can hinder professional work, such as cybersecurity.

Ben Lorica suggested that open-weight models will ultimately prevail because they are essential parts of the technology stack. He noted that privacy and intellectual property security are primary arguments for adopting local AI over cloud services. The discussion affected knowledge workers who might need to code or write documents while offline, such as on an airplane. Lorica questioned if consumers would prefer local models for personal uses, like AI therapists, to ensure total ownership. He compared the current shift to the historical rise of open-source projects like Linux, Postgres, and MySQL.

The articles provide background on the dot-com boom when people paid high prices for SPARC servers and Microsoft IIS. Warden compared the current AI landscape to that era, noting how Apache and Nginx eventually replaced expensive commercial alternatives. He mentioned that the industry is currently dealing with DRAM price increases that slightly hobble hardware manufacturers. The background includes the development of specialized versus end-to-end models and the role of high-bandwidth flash in hardware. The conversation also touched upon the difference between multimodal models and specialized speech models.

Future developments include the potential for local AI to fully replace cloud models for various types of knowledge work. The articles leave open whether local models will completely wipe the floor with commercial alternatives as open-source web servers did. There is ongoing debate regarding the regulation of frontier AI and the effectiveness of different hardware accelerators. The transition toward integrating AI into operating systems, particularly by Apple, remains a key point of interest. It is unclear how quickly usability will improve for the average civilian user.

Articles.Title: Pete warden on local AI, open models, voice interfaces, the future of hardware

stories.Headline: Boltz raises a $110M Series A led by Bessemer to speed up drug discovery with AI
stories.Summary:
London-based Boltz, an AI research startup that develops models to speed up drug discovery, has raised a $110m Series A funding round, less than a year after emerging out of stealth. The company was spun out of MIT in the United States but is now located in London, where it employs 40 AI researchers in the King's Cross district. Bessemer Venture Partners led the round, with existing investors including Andreessen Horowitz, Amplify Partners, Zetta Venture Partners and Obvious Ventures participating. New investors include Greycroft, F-Prime Capital, Hummingbird and Benchling, joining Nvidia, which also announced an investment earlier this year during Jensen Huang's visit to the UK. The round follows Boltz raising a $28m seed round at the start of the year.

Boltz builds software which helps pharmaceutical and biotech researchers design potential drugs and decide which candidates to test in labs. Its AI models can predict what protein and drug candidates look like when bound together, estimate how strongly they bind, and propose new molecules designed to bind to a target. The startup develops open-source AI models and other models through its own platform and API. At MIT, the co-founders released open-source AI models that matched the performance of closed-source models like DeepMind's AlphaFold3, and these models are now part of the default setting for early-stage drug discovery. Boltz has announced collaborations with Pfizer, GSK, Takeda and Bristol Myers Squibb, and revenue is generated through partnerships and providing access to its platform and models.

Boltz said it believes it is still just at the beginning of an exponential trajectory in model capabilities, and that its upcoming models are already showing substantial improvements in the quality of the molecules they generate. The company said its long-term goal remains a world where a scientist can go from a therapeutic hypothesis to a human-ready molecule without leaving their computer. It said reaching that goal will require further advances in the models and substantial investment in compute and data. Boltz says it will use the funding to invest in compute and data, and expand its team.

stories.Headline: Marsh finds 71 percent of employees have used AI at work but only 37 percent use it regularly
stories.Summary:
Marsh, the professional services firm listed in New York under the ticker MRSH, released on November 18, 2026 the results of a survey it conducted on how HR technology affects employees, drawing on more than 6,700 workers across ten countries: Canada, France, Germany, Japan, Mexico, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom and the United States. The survey found that 71 percent of employees have used AI in their work, nearly double the 39 percent recorded in 2024, while only 37 percent, roughly one in three, use AI regularly in their day to day work. The gap between rapid adoption and organizational change remains wide, and Marsh's global workforce leader Ravin Jesuthasan said the 71 percent figure shows an unusually fast two year expansion for a workplace technology survey, though he added that behind the number lies stalled transformation. He said that without sufficient support, upskilling opportunities and job redesign, the use of AI tools does not necessarily lead to effective and sustained use. The survey found wide differences by role and industry, with 59 percent of high tech and IT employees using AI regularly, about three times the 22 percent in healthcare and 19 percent in government, and with 64 percent of executives using it regularly against 20 percent of entry level professionals.

These gaps reflect differing access to AI training and support: 78 percent of executives said their employer provided AI training in the past year, compared with 44 percent of experienced professionals, 32 percent of entry level professionals and 20 percent of hourly workers, and executives also had more access to mentoring, coaching and sandbox environments for experimenting with AI. Confidence in AI's effects reached 89 percent among executives and 60 percent among entry level professionals, above the 69 percent of experienced professionals, while high tech and IT employees, who have the most access to AI, were most likely to report negative effects on their work at 26 percent, nine points above the overall average, citing increased workload at 41 percent, more time needed to complete tasks at 40 percent, and concerns about accuracy and privacy at 35 percent. More than one in five employees said they use AI tools their employer does not provide, the share of employees who do not follow organizational AI guidelines nearly tripled over the past two years, and more than one in ten said their company has no AI guidelines at all. Jesuthasan said shadow AI is not only a governance and compliance issue but a sign of a gap between what organizations ask of employees and the tools available to them, which capable employees try to close themselves.

Among employees who strongly agreed their digital tools are well equipped, 84 percent use company provided AI and 85 percent follow AI guidelines, while among those who strongly disagreed those shares fell to 42 percent and 54 percent. One in three employees said no one had explained how AI affects their job or department, and among those who had been told, only 21 percent named their direct supervisor or manager as the source, leaving many to interpret AI policy themselves; nearly one in three said they are somewhat or very reluctant to try new technology at work. Many organizations focus AI training on technical skills, but judgment, critical thinking and contextual knowledge are what turn AI use into business results, and 90 percent of executives said they are confident doing their work with AI tools against 50 percent of hourly workers, while only 30 percent of employees strongly agreed it is easy to understand the skills needed to advance their careers. Jesuthasan said the practical question for leaders is whether the conditions for responsible AI use exist in their organization, and that how leaders act, demonstrate AI use, set and communicate norms, and invest in human skills determines the return on AI investment.

stories.Headline: Trustpoint Xposure completes over 200 AI visibility audits for professional services firms
stories.Summary:
Trustpoint Xposure, a New York-based public relations agency, announced on November 19, 2026 that it has completed more than 200 AI visibility audits for professionals and firms across professional services, including the legal, medical, financial and technology sectors. Each audit records how AI search platforms, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews, describe a professional or firm when users ask about them. The audits note whether the subject appears, how accurately the platform describes them, and which sources it cites. The company says its audits use a fixed set of questions a prospective client might ask, run across four platforms, recording the answers, the sources cited, and any competitors named instead. The same questions can be repeated later to show whether the description has changed.

In the company's internal analysis, 88% of the professionals audited were either absent from AI answers or described inaccurately. Of those, 54% were absent and 34% were described inaccurately, while 12% were described correctly. The company also found inconsistent entity information, such as differing names, titles or descriptions across profiles, in 64% of audits. The figures are based on internal analysis, have not been independently audited, and individual results may vary. The company says no AI platform publishes its exact selection rules and no result can be guaranteed.

Common reasons a professional is missing or misdescribed include inconsistent details across websites, limited independent editorial coverage, missing structured data such as schema markup, and no Google Knowledge Panel. Trustpoint Xposure says its Answer Engine Optimization work focuses on consistent entity information across the web, credible editorial coverage, structured data such as Person and FAQPage schema, and a Google Knowledge Panel or Wikipedia entry where a subject is eligible. The company says Google and Wikipedia's editors make those final decisions, so it does not guarantee either outcome. It advises businesses to ask ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google the questions their customers ask, record the answers, and repeat the check monthly, since AI answers can change from day to day and trends are more reliable than any single result. The company offers a complimentary AI and Media Visibility Audit that follows this approach.

It also says professionals in regulated fields, including law and healthcare, should follow their licensing body's advertising and confidentiality rules when acting on audit findings. Trustpoint Xposure describes its AEO Certification Framework as its own proprietary standard and not an independent third-party certification. The company provides Answer Engine Optimization, AI visibility audits, SEO and digital public relations, and more information is available at its website. The media contact is Jack Smith, Media Director, at contact@trustpointxposure.com. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the audit process and the monthly checks the company recommends.

stories.Headline: Laurel Bridge Software adds web management and AI integration to Compass
stories.Summary:
Laurel Bridge Software announced on November 19, 2026, new and enhanced capabilities for its Compass DICOM Routing Workflow Manager, which the company describes as a tool for orchestrating complex DICOM and HL7 workflows across healthcare networks, imaging centers and cloud infrastructure. The Newark, Delaware, company said the release adds web-based management, greater workflow visibility, advanced query capabilities and broader cloud and AI integration. Laurel Bridge said it will showcase the enhancements at RSNA 2026 at Booth #4561, where visitors can see the capabilities in action and schedule a personalized demonstration. The announcement was issued by the company as a press release dated November 19, 2026, at 14:00 UTC. The new release includes a web interface that brings centralized, browser-based configuration and management to Compass while the familiar Compass Client continues to be advanced and supported, giving users flexibility in the environment they prefer.

Enhanced status capabilities provide immediate insight into DICOM and HL7 job queues, including queue position and the specific conditions preventing jobs from running, which the company says helps IT teams resolve workflow bottlenecks more quickly. Expanded job reporting adds visibility and auditability across the DICOM lifecycle, including association activity, individual image arrival and transmission times, and job status transitions from pending through completion or failure. New fuzzy matching extends multi-destination query spanning across DIMSE and DICOMweb endpoints, improving study retrieval and demographic reconciliation when patient names or metadata vary, and new Span Group transport modes expand flexibility across cloud, hybrid and multi-destination workflows. Jeff Blair, President of Laurel Bridge Software, said healthcare IT teams need clear visibility and direct control over the data pipelines that support clinical imaging workflows. He said the enhancements expand workflow visibility and simplify administration while providing the flexibility needed for increasingly complex on-premises, cloud and hybrid imaging environments.

For organizations managing Compass across multiple locations, the company pointed to Lighthouse Centralized Monitoring & Management, which provides centralized visibility and administration across deployed Laurel Bridge applications. The company said Lighthouse helps PACS and IT teams monitor activity, manage configurations, deploy updates and oversee DICOM and HL7 services across distributed environments. Laurel Bridge said Compass extends beyond traditional image routing to support configurable enterprise imaging workflows, with capabilities including DICOM and HL7 workflow automation, metadata normalization and transformation, DICOM SR measurement integration with dictation templates, EHR and encounter-based imaging integration, SCO-to-BTO conversion, DICOM, DICOMweb, HL7 and FHIR interoperability, secure imaging and AI data exchange, and AI and cloud workflow integration with AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. The company said it has helped healthcare organizations address imaging interoperability and workflow challenges for over 30 years. Laurel Bridge said it has thousands of installations in more than 50 countries, and it directed readers to its website for more information.

stories.Headline: Dell and Microsoft expand private cloud partnership to run AI models inside corporate data centers
stories.Summary:
Dell Technologies and Microsoft expanded their private cloud partnership on November 19, 2026, during the Microsoft Ignite conference. This collaboration introduces new infrastructure offerings that allow enterprises to run artificial intelligence models closer to their own data. The initiative aims to reduce the reliance of organizations on public cloud services while maintaining strict control over sensitive information. These systems are designed for companies facing regulatory requirements, data residency restrictions, or the need to protect proprietary corporate information.

The expanded offering integrates Dell Private Cloud, Microsoft Azure Local, Microsoft Foundry Local, and Nvidia acceleration. It utilizes the Dell PowerEdge XE9780 server, which is built upon the Nvidia HGX accelerated computing platform. Microsoft is also extending Azure Local support to Nvidia HGX B300 systems to provide more hardware options outside conventional public clouds. Azure Local provides the management foundation, while Microsoft Foundry Local enables organizations to run AI models internally instead of sending data to external services.

Dell and Microsoft stated that this integrated infrastructure allows heavy AI workloads to operate safely inside corporate data centers and firewalls. Dell noted that their Private Cloud platform can reduce Day 2 infrastructure operations time by 66 percent compared to traditional three-tier systems. The company also claimed potential cost savings of up to 65 percent when compared with hyperconverged infrastructure. They highlighted that blueprint-driven automation through the Dell Automation Platform simplifies the deployment and ongoing management of these systems.

The companies emphasized that private cloud infrastructure offers advantages in data sovereignty, security, latency, and operational control. Dell cited a September 2026 analysis by Signal65 and Futurum Group titled The Economics of Agentic AI. This study found that using Dell AI Factory infrastructure could lower the total cost of ownership by 90 percent over two years compared to cloud API models. The analysis further indicated that some hardware configurations could reach a break-even point within two to three months.

stories.Headline: Non-profit estimates 60% of Anthropic's mapped US data center power demand ties to natural gas
stories.Summary:
The Better Data Center Project, a US-based non-profit that advocates for frontline communities facing rapid AI growth, published research on November 19, 2026 claiming that about 60 percent of the mapped US data center power demand for Anthropic is tied to natural gas. The group mapped 19 US sites where Anthropic has leased between 5.9 and 9.6 GW of capacity, out of roughly 15 GW the company has contracted. Of those sites, the non-profit claimed that approximately 2.5 GW, or 26 percent, is powered by on-site natural gas, with the remainder tied to the grid. Because the US grid itself is powered by 47 percent natural gas, the group asserted that 60 percent of the mapped sites' power demand is tied to natural gas. Earlier in November, Anthropic signed a $3.4 billion deal for 1.7 GW of natural gas generators supplied by Caterpillar, working with OnePWR on units expected to be available within two years for use at Anthropic data centers, including engineering and construction needs.

Paweł Czyżak, CEO and founder at Ornaq, said the figures are estimates, noting that Anthropic does not disclose its sites, that at least 5 GW is not mapped, and that some attributions are speculative. He added that Anthropic is not the only AI company running on gas but that he had expected a higher standard. An Anthropic spokesperson told DCD that the company is working to add new power generation for its data centers so it is not drawing on supply used by local homes and businesses. The spokesperson said much of that new power is natural gas, which can be brought online quickly, ramps up and down as demand changes, and is abundant in the places being considered for data centers. The spokesperson also said the company is working to broaden its energy mix with geothermal, wind, solar and emerging technologies, and is designing projects that will rely on renewable energy in regions with strong renewable resources.

Anthropic also pointed to sustainability measures including joining the carbon emission buying consortium Frontier and working with Watershed, a carbon accounting and emissions disclosure platform. The news comes as the company completes its initial public offering this week, expected to value it at approximately $1.5 trillion after shares were priced at $83 ahead of its debut on the Nasdaq. Major data center firms have increasingly turned to on-site natural gas to bypass multi-year interconnection queues for a firm grid connection, with Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Google all signing deals in recent years for large-scale gas generators in the US market. Smaller players have also moved in, with Crusoe set to use natural gas power at its 1.8 GW Wyoming campus, and Elon Musk-owned SpaceX recently announcing plans for a data center and natural gas power plant in Texas.

stories.Headline: KR1 sells DIEM-backed AI inference capacity for USDC on Surplus Intelligence
stories.Summary:
KR1 plc has opened sales of AI inference capacity backed by its DIEM credits, taking payment in USDC as the London Stock Exchange-listed company puts Venice model capacity to work for third-party customers. The company holds 557 DIEM, purchased separately from its VVV position, and when staked each DIEM provides $1 in daily credit for running models on Venice, giving KR1 access to $557 in daily model credits. On Surplus Intelligence, KR1 chooses which models to list and sets their prices, and when the marketplace matches an offer with a buyer, Venice runs the model using KR1’s credits, and KR1 receives USDC. In the 90 days through Nov. 16, 2026, KR1 fulfilled about 1.92 million third-party requests through Surplus Intelligence, serving 101.5 billion AI model tokens. KR1 also supplies DIEM to Diem Relay, which stakes pooled supplier tokens on Venice and sells the resulting inference capacity, and suppliers receive a share of USDC proceeds in line with their stake, after fees.

October earnings pointed to an estimated annualized yield of 5.45%, calculated using the month-end fair value of DIEM KR1 supplied to the marketplace. The estimate is not a guaranteed or realized return, and KR1 said the rate varies with supply and demand for inference and computing capacity. Venice AI launched its VVV token on the Base blockchain on Jan. 27, 2025, and staking VVV provides access to Venice API inference capacity, while holders can lock staked VVV to mint Diem compute credits, as TokenPost’s earlier coverage of the token explained. The articles do not name any individual spokesperson or executive at KR1, Venice AI or Diem Relay, and they carry no direct quotations, so the only attributed statement is KR1’s note that the estimated yield varies with supply and demand for inference and computing capacity. Responsibility for the offering sits with KR1 plc, the London Stock Exchange-listed company that holds the 557 DIEM, lists models and sets prices on Surplus Intelligence, and supplies DIEM to Diem Relay.

Venice AI provides the underlying model capacity and runs the models when a marketplace offer is matched with a buyer, while Diem Relay pools supplier tokens and distributes USDC proceeds after fees. The articles do not describe any further statements from these parties about the arrangement. The context is that Venice AI launched its VVV token on the Base blockchain on Jan. 27, 2025, and staking VVV provides access to Venice API inference capacity, while locking staked VVV mints Diem compute credits. KR1’s 557 DIEM were purchased separately from its VVV position, and the October earnings figure of an estimated 5.45% annualized yield was calculated using the month-end fair value of DIEM KR1 supplied to the marketplace. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the open sales, the ongoing fulfillment of requests through Surplus Intelligence and the continued supply of DIEM to Diem Relay.

stories.Headline: Maria Salas-Fernandez leads an Iowa State project using AI to make bioenergy sorghum more lodging resistant
stories.Summary:
A one-year project at Iowa State University to improve sorghum for bioenergy has been selected by the US Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission, a national initiative aimed at accelerating breakthroughs in energy, scientific discovery and national security using artificial intelligence. The project is valued at $750,000 and was announced by World Grain on November 19, 2026, in a report by John Reidy. Maria Salas-Fernandez, a professor in the Department of Agronomy, is the lead investigator on the project to improve bioenergy sorghum’s lodging resistance. Lodging is a condition in which stalks bend, buckle or completely fall over in wind or heavy rains. She is collaborating with other researchers at Iowa State’s College of Engineering and the National Laboratory of the Rockies to develop AI tools that can harness sorghum genetic resources and eventually be used for other crops.

The project builds on Salas-Fernandez’s prior research to produce hybrids that deliver high biomass yields by improving sorghum genetics adapted to northern latitudes. She said much progress has been made in developing sorghum as a bioenergy crop, and the main goal of the first phase of the Genesis Mission is to eliminate sorghum’s lodging problem while keeping farmers and end-users in mind. She said part of the challenge is to make the sorghum plant stronger and more lodge-resistant without negatively impacting its value for bioprocessing. She said this is important because many times when you try to solve the lodging problem, you can change some characteristics that result in problems for the biorefinery.

As part of the project, researchers will leverage the existing data while collecting additional, very detailed biomechanical, chemical and nanoscale data on a small set of plant materials to feed AI models and create a digital twin, Salas-Fernandez said. A key objective in the first phase of the project is to demonstrate the potential of AI tools to develop plant designs much faster than traditional breeding and experimental approaches alone. If successful, the researchers said the framework should eventually be transferable to other crops, different traits and biological systems. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that first phase or when results are expected.

stories.Headline: Colorado lawmakers plan to revisit labor law, AI rules and Medicaid in 2027
stories.Summary:
Colorado’s 2027 legislative session will open less than two months after the November 19, 2026 article, with a new governor for the first time in nearly a decade and a Democratic supermajority in both chambers of the General Assembly. Democrats are expected to make their third attempt to eliminate Colorado’s Labor Peace Act, the only law of its kind in the country, which is 83 years old. The law currently requires employees at unionized workplaces to undergo two elections to establish a union security agreement. Democrats first introduced legislation eliminating the second election requirement during the 2025 session, and it passed both chambers. Gov. Jared Polis vetoed the measure, expressing concerns about requiring all employees to pay union dues regardless of membership.

Sponsors resurrected the bill during the 2026 session despite Polis’s threats to veto it again unless labor and business reached a compromise, and the measure passed and was rejected again. Sen. Julie Gonzales, D-Denver, who sponsored the 2026 bill, promised the measure would return for 2027, though Gonzales will not return to the General Assembly. Democrats now have enough members in both chambers to override a veto. Gov.-elect Phil Weiser stated last May that he would sign “a worker protection act,” and during an October candidate forum he called the Labor Peace Act antiquated while acknowledging business community concerns about Colorado’s competitiveness. Lawmakers introduced a pair of bills last session on artificial intelligence data centers, one focused on environmental impact and the other on the economic aspect, but neither passed, with the sponsor of the former asking for it to be killed and a committee voting down the latter.

Sen. Cathy Kipp, D-Fort Collins, who sponsored the environmental bill, said she plans to bring the measure back with her House cosponsor, Rep. Kyle Brown, a Louisville Democrat. Rep. Alex Valdez, D-Denver, sponsored a data center measure in 2026 but is term-limited and will not return, and his cosponsor, Sen. Kyle Mullica of Thornton, did not respond to questions about whether he would bring the bill back. Colorado passed Senate Bill 205 in 2024, the nation’s first law establishing a regulatory framework for artificial intelligence, targeting “algorithmic discrimination” in “high-risk” AI systems that review college, loan, or rent applications. Polis signed the measure but warned sponsors that certain provisions would need to change in the next legislative session. During a special session in the summer of 2025, lawmakers passed a bill delaying SB 205’s implementation date, and that fall Polis convened a working group whose recommendations informed Senate Bill 189.

Senate Bill 189 passed during the 2026 legislative session, replaced SB 205, and goes into effect Jan. 1. Lawmakers also passed policies during the 2026 session establishing regulations on chatbots and AI use in therapy settings. Medicaid spending accounts for over one-third of the state’s budget and continues to grow, and Polis has told legislators they will need to cut the program or cuts will have to come from other critical sectors like education. The legislature’s Joint Budget Committee made several difficult cuts to healthcare programs last session to close an over $1 billion shortfall, including capping reimbursement hours for family caregivers and slashing Medicaid provider reimbursement rates by 2%. Polis told JBC members last week that Colorado’s new graduated income tax rate will need to cover the state’s Medicaid spending by 2030.

Polis’s budget proposal includes a 4.3% increase in Medicaid spending, or about $250 million, which accounts for inflation and growth but is not enough to keep the program funded at its current level. All told, the proposal would cut more than $600 million in Medicaid spending. The JBC has until April to balance the state’s budget for the next fiscal year. Many communities across Colorado have issued moratoriums on new data center construction, choosing to wait for state or federal regulations before moving forward. The data center debate has only gotten more heated since the 2026 session ended in May, and some lawmakers hint at even more attempts at regulation in 2027.

It remains to be seen whether federal regulations for artificial intelligence systems will come anytime soon. As AI technology continues to develop and experts worldwide warn the public about its potential for malicious use, lawmakers will likely introduce even more guardrails this coming session. Weiser’s position on the Labor Peace Act might not matter, with Democrats holding supermajorities in both the House and Senate, meaning they could override a governor’s veto. Gonzales will not return to the General Assembly. Mullica did not respond to questions about whether he would be bringing the data center bill back.

stories.Headline: Google turns off Gemini and Search by default for K-12 student accounts
stories.Summary:
Google announced on Nov. 3 that access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search will be turned off by default for K-12 student accounts, and school administrators will have to enable access, with more details promised in the coming months before the new controls roll out. The change groups Search with the AI tools, and reporting on it says schools may not be able to turn off Google's AI features while keeping Search available. Google is also making Guided Learning available in Google Classroom globally and plans to pilot Guided Learning in Search at select U.S. schools before expanding access. Guided Learning is an interactive study tool that uses questions and step-by-step explanations to help students solve problems, and in Classroom teachers can assign activities tied to course materials and receive real-time insights into where students may need help. Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post that schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and that administrators should have controls to help them manage their approach.

Father McGivney Catholic High School in Edwardsville uses Chromebooks and Google tools, and asked whether it would enable or restrict any of the tools for students, the school did not say whether it had made a decision. Principal Joseph Lombardi said Google's expanded controls provide another opportunity to evaluate how these tools can best serve students, and he said decisions about student access to Gemini and other AI features would be based on the school's existing academic policies, student safety and the educational value of the tools. The school's policy, included in each course syllabus, prohibits students from using AI without permission from a teacher or administrator, and Lombardi said students are prohibited from using AI to complete assignments, write papers, create projects or take assessments without that permission. Lombardi said the school considers AI-generated work presented as a student's own to be academic dishonesty, and teachers decide whether AI is allowed for an assignment based on its learning objectives. He said the school sees potential uses for AI in brainstorming, organizing information and providing study support, while aiming to help students use emerging technology responsibly, and he said that when its use replaces independent thinking, original writing, problem-solving or genuine understanding, it becomes counterproductive to education.

Lombardi said the school's Catholic identity is central to its approach to artificial intelligence, and he cited Pope Leo XIV's encyclical "Magnifica Humanitas," which says technology should serve human development rather than diminish it. The school emphasizes personal relationships, authentic learning, moral development and the formation of conscience, and it teaches that every student is created in God's image and has unique gifts that technology cannot replace. Lombardi said AI should never replace the meaningful relationships between teachers and students or the intellectual growth that comes through personal effort, reflection and discovery, and he said the goal is to prepare students to navigate an increasingly technological world while remaining grounded in their Catholic faith and respect for human dignity. The Diocese of Springfield recently issued its "Technology and Artificial Intelligence Guidance for Catholic Schools," which calls for balancing technology's educational benefits with the responsibility to protect students' intellectual, emotional, moral and spiritual development, and Lombardi said it reflects the school's existing policies and commitment to educating the whole student, mind, body and spirit. Edwardsville District 7 schools do not use Google products and do not expect to be impacted by the changes, and St. Boniface School, Trinity Lutheran Schools and Metro-East Lutheran High School did not respond to requests for comment.

stories.Headline: Tool or trouble?: Teachers at WHS share different opinions on how to regulate AI for students
stories.Summary:
For the past four years, educators have scrambled to change curriculums around the emergence of AI to reduce the ability to potentially cheat with AI tools, and debates surrounding the topic have increased as AI use in schools becomes more prominent. Annabelle Hage, Fiona Peltonen and Kergan Hill wrote the Wayland Student Press article published November 20, 2026, in which teachers in different departments at WHS shared different opinions on how to regulate AI for students. While some teachers outright ban AI entirely, others allow for a more nuanced approach and even encourage students to use it. In a survey by Pew Research Center, about 32% of K-12 educators say there is an equal mix of benefit and harm using AI tools in an education background. At WHS, departments share different needs for AI, and in certain subjects teachers argue AI creates a lack of critical thinking, especially in an academic setting.

History Department Head David Schmirer said AI is literally taking away your power to be able to think for yourself, and that the ability to make critical decisions and choices as you get older is going to become a lot more difficult. Math teacher Emily Grant said AI can be useful in math when students use it to understand how to do problems and not to just get the answers, and that asking AI to make a similar problem and show the steps can be a really helpful way to learn the material. English Department Head Peter Galalis said he doesn’t believe there will ever be a use for AI in English classes, that writing is a human practice and always is going to be, and that there are certain legal barriers to producing something written by AI because AI isn’t protected under copyright. Galalis said it’s going to continue to be really important that human writers produce and own their own words, because what you produce with a chatbot is not the same as something that you’ve written. Galalis said writing is something we don’t do just to produce more words for other people to read, that writing is something we can do to change ourselves, and that if you outsource that to a chatbot you rob yourself of those opportunities.

Math Department Head Kanchan Kant believes policies should adapt to focus on teaching what will be helpful for students seeking a math degree in the world of AI, and since AI will have an impact on careers in math, she believes a specific part of math jobs will no longer be focused on writing proofs but instead on critiquing what already exists. Kant said that if critiquing AI’s work is a part of what our students will end up doing, we should be preparing them for that. Schmirer said AI’s capability and availability has increased so rapidly that it’s really difficult for any teacher at the school to keep up with it. In the history department, Schmirer said teachers are allowed to choose their own pathway regarding AI usage, and while some teachers give students zeroes on assignments completed with AI, his method is to inform students on how harmful AI can be and encourage them to use their own thinking. Schmirer said that ultimately all we can do is appeal to students to make good choices, just like we do in other areas of life.

The in-class essay, rather than a take-home essay, is becoming increasingly popular as a way to remove AI from the equation, and some teachers assign print-out readings rather than online readings that teachers worry will be copy and pasted into an AI tool. Research shows that reading off a paper, annotating and taking notes by hand is more helpful in successfully absorbing information than reading a screen, and Schmirer said steps like printing out readings are what teachers are taking to work around the edges to decrease the use of AI. One anonymous student was given a zero on a homework assignment after it was flagged by an AI detector, later met with their teacher to defend their academic integrity and was able to receive full credit. The anonymous student said they were very confused and thinking maybe there was a glitch, and that it should be a bit more holistic with teachers meeting with students before assigning a grade for AI use. Schmirer noted that in certain cases in which students are accused of using AI, it is sometimes unclear whether the AI detector is correct in its allegations. Schmirer said he’d rather get less than good work from a student that’s their own work and that they put time and effort into than something that is simply not their own at that point.

Up until last year, take-home essays were common, if not expected, in WHS humanities classes, whether an essay about “1984” or a write-up on Mercantilism, with assignments that sometimes stretched over the course of days. Junior Archie Baker said he started at WHS in 2024, so his freshman year and sophomore year were almost entirely take-home essays, which he appreciates a lot more. English teacher Phillip George said that in his first year teaching at WHS in 2023 he thinks he had something like 16 instances of catching students cheating using online resources, which shocked him and forced him after that first year to start revising his approach. George used the analogy of marathon runners and sprinters, saying students were trained to run literary marathons and now English assessments are akin to sprints, and he said he is making them sprint for at least an hour and he does think it brings the bottom up a little bit. George said the in-class essay is great for authentically assessing student thought and writing but is very narrow in scope, eliminating the opportunity for revision, improvement and the drafting process, which is usually so essential to writing, and limiting the kind of time under tension that students experience.

Baker said during an in-class essay he feels much more rushed and can’t refine his thoughts, so he just writes it and then that’s it, and that he is trying to develop ideas but can’t get as in-depth or as nuanced as he’d like to. George said what is lost is a sense of intellectual endurance and the reward for the virtue of prolonged thought and hard work, and that he does think that’s a real intellectual virtue. Schmirer described the situation as a fluid situation where teachers react in the interest of educating students and preparing them for their futures as new advancements in AI continue to present themselves. Schmirer said the most important thing teachers can do is convince students that in the end, even though this is an easy and accessible resource, it’s ultimately not in your best interest to become overly reliant on it. Teachers can’t predict how AI will affect the future, and one single AI policy cannot possibly work for all subjects.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: Tool or trouble?: Teachers at WHS share different opinions on how to regulate AI for students - Wayland Student Press

stories.Headline: Ondas, Palantir and Regna AI co-host defense technology summit in Las Vegas
stories.Summary:
Ondas Inc., Palantir Technologies Inc. and Regna AI co-hosted the Ondas Defense Technology Summit, a small, invitation-only executive session, on November 18 in Las Vegas. Ondas shared highlights from the summit in a press release dated November 20, 2026, issued from West Palm Beach, Florida and Miami, Florida. Executives and leaders from Ondas, Palantir, Regna AI and Aston Martin Performance Technologies attended, along with other defense technology and AI innovators and industry experts. The day opened with remarks from Ryan Hartman, President and Chief Executive Officer of Ondas Sentinel and Interim Chief Executive Officer of Regna AI. Palantir followed with a demonstration and presentation on sovereign AI for mission-critical operations.

The summit is one of the first activations of Ondas' Global Partner relationship with Aston Martin Aramco Formula One Team, announced as the "Speed to Decision" partnership. The partnership is a multi-year global partnership in the autonomous systems sector that extends through 2029. The Las Vegas Grand Prix will showcase Ondas through brand visibility, engineering collaboration and stakeholder engagement. Four panels covered autonomy in the air and at sea and where unmanned systems go next, investing in defense tech, how industry and the Department of Defense partner to deliver, and defense tech capital markets and mergers and acquisitions. Bob Bell, Business Development Consultant at Aston Martin Performance Technologies, led the session on Manufacturing and Supply Chains for Defense.

Eric Brock, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Ondas Inc., said defense technology is attracting growing demand and investment, and capital is following companies that can pair AI and autonomy with the ability to manufacture at scale. Brock said convening leaders from technology, defense and capital markets with Palantir and Regna AI reflects how Ondas is positioning itself at the center of that shift, turning innovation into fielded capability and creating long-term value for stockholders. Elias Davis, Office of the CEO at Palantir Technologies, said the companies are helping defense partners deploy sovereign AI on their own terms, with control over their data and operations. Davis said co-hosting the summit with Ondas and Regna AI reflects a deep and expanding partnership. Ryan Hartman said bringing the leaders into one room let them focus on how AI is changing the mission and what it will take to get capability into the field sooner.

Hartman said that across the demo and the panels the message was consistent: AI and autonomy only matter if operators can trust them, control them and rely on them. Hartman said that is where industry and government have to keep working side by side. The day closed with Q&A and closing remarks from Hartman. The focused, executive-level format allowed for candid conversations about AI across defense missions, including sovereign AI. The summit reflects Ondas' strategy of bringing together the software, autonomous platforms and production capability that modern warfare requires.

Ondas Inc. (NASDAQ:ONDS) describes itself as a leading provider of advanced autonomous systems and next-generation defense and security technologies. Ondas develops and deploys integrated unmanned and autonomous platforms across air, ground and stratospheric environments, including autonomous drone systems, counter-UAS technologies, robotic ground systems, advanced unmanned aircraft and propulsion solutions, demining and engineering systems, and integrated sensing and communications technologies. Ondas' solutions are deployed globally by government, defense and commercial customers to protect infrastructure, borders, transportation networks, personnel and strategic assets. Regna AI says it is building the sovereign AI layer for defense, putting mission intelligence under the customer's command through specialized AI models that governments and defense organizations can own, control and deploy wherever the mission demands. Formula One is one of the most technology-driven sports in the world, and the engineering, data and rapid manufacturing developed for the track are increasingly being applied in other industries.

stories.Headline: Huawei introduces AI scaling methods for the financial sector at Singapore FinTech Festival
stories.Summary:
Huawei presented new methods for scaling artificial intelligence within the financial sector on November 20, 2026, during the Singapore FinTech Festival. The company shared insights regarding the acceleration of financial AI and the promotion of agentic finance with various international partners. Jason Cao, the CEO of Huawei Digital Finance, and Alvin Feng, the President of Huawei International Financial BU, delivered keynote presentations. They showcased a variety of solutions for central banks, insurance, securities, and the modernization of applications.

The proposed transition to large scale AI requires financial institutions to develop their own internal capabilities rather than relying solely on model performance. Huawei introduced the Fintelligent AI Solution, which utilizes an open hybrid infrastructure and three intelligent factories to deploy AI agents. These include the Agent Factory for governance, the Token Factory for lifecycle management, and the Data and Knowledge Factory for high quality information. This framework allows banks to use two super agents for customers and employees alongside multiple specialized agents for risk and wealth management.

Jason Cao explained that an open ecosystem makes AI affordable while technical optimization and commercialization ensure it functions reliably within business operations. He stated that institutions must maintain control over their own data and business logic to build a distinct competitive advantage. Alvin Feng emphasized that the new enterprise framework addresses critical requirements for security, sustainability, and scalability. He noted that standardized engineering is necessary for the mass production of AI agents across different scenarios.

Huawei has served over 7,100 financial customers over the last 16 years, including 54 of the world's 100 largest banks. The company is now focusing on creating a flywheel that connects data, execution, and feedback to make services accessible to customer AI agents. This strategy aims to transform essential processes like credit lending and mobile banking through deep integration. Future efforts will focus on capturing expert knowledge to develop self learning systems at the enterprise level.

stories.Headline: GIGABYTE showcases local AI deployment and agent development at partner summit
stories.Summary:
GIGABYTE held its AI Partner Summit on November 13 at the Pacific Palms Resort in Los Angeles, and the company highlighted the event's success in a release dated November 20, 2026. The summit carried the theme "Build Your First Business AI Agent" and brought together industry experts and enterprise leaders to show practical, secure and scalable AI solutions for business operations. A central highlight was a live demonstration of the GIGABYTE AI TOP ATOM, which the company says is designed to simplify local AI deployment. The event also featured technical insights from NVIDIA, executive presentations from GIGABYTE and real-world deployment stories from enterprise clients.

The technical sessions focused on three core operational areas, the first being local AI and RAG, which runs local large language models with proprietary business data to generate context-aware insights while maintaining total data security. The second area was AI model fine-tuning, which customizes AI models using LoRA techniques to meet specific organizational needs. The third was AI agent development, which builds functional AI agents to automate complex workflows and boost workplace productivity. GIGABYTE says the summit was centered on helping businesses build, customize and deploy AI agents as artificial intelligence moves from theoretical concepts into daily operations.

GIGABYTE presents itself as the responsible party behind the event and says it remains dedicated to advancing accessible AI hardware and software frameworks by bridging the gap between AI innovation and enterprise implementation. The company states that it will continue collaborating with industry partners to empower businesses of all sizes to convert AI possibilities into measurable, long-term growth. GIGABYTE describes itself as a developer, manufacturer and distributor of high-performance hardware solutions, from monitors and graphics cards to advanced data center infrastructure. The release lists the GIGABYTE USA PR Team in City of Industry, California, as the media contact.
