stories.Headline: Austin ISD trustees adopt the district's first AI policy with an 18-month timeline for detailed rules
stories.Summary:
On Nov. 12, all eight trustees present on the dais voted to adopt Austin ISD's first-ever local policy on artificial intelligence, the Austin Chronicle reported on Nov. 19, 2026. The board acted after hearing multiple calls over the past several weeks from mostly parents to create some kind of districtwide policy on AI. The calls followed widely reported generative AI bans adopted in New York City, for pre-K through 8th grade, and in Los Angeles public school systems. AISD Board President Lynn Boswell told her colleagues at a Nov. 5 meeting that the district had been kicking this down the road for three years. Boswell said students are being impacted by this.

The policy gives the district an 18-month timeline to set more detailed rules about AI use for students, teachers and staff. Students can only use district-approved AI tools with teacher permission for classwork and must produce original work and properly credit sources, including AI tools used in creating the work. The superintendent is tasked with approving AI programs. The student policy gives an AI citation example: created with the assistance of Gemini and reviewed for accuracy and tone. In the policy agreement for staff, teachers cannot assign and/or require the use of AI tools outside of the list of district-approved tools and resources for classwork.

Trustee Arati Singh told the Chronicle that approved student uses of AI could include modifying text for those with different reading abilities, or coding to create games. Singh added that the new policy extends beyond students to teachers and staff within the district's central office, who could potentially use AI to find patterns in student outcomes and large datasets. Singh said school districts are already using AI to analyze student outcome data, help develop schedules, and to screen employee applications. Singh said she just hopes we don't lose the human touch in the process of adopting AI in the organization. Singh wrote to the Chronicle that she imagines at some point TEA and the State Board of Education will come up with better guardrails, and that until then her expectation is the district will fill in the gaps.

Amy Whiteaker, a science teacher in the district and parent of a middle and high schooler in AISD, said she does not want her students or her kids to think that AI will always have the answers and use it in place of their learning. Whiteaker said she does not want them to lose the ability to critically think, or to make decisions, or analyze data, or use reasoning. Ann Richards librarian Minda Anderson, who teaches media and research literacy, argued that a total district ban on generative AI for high schoolers isn't helpful and that students need situations to learn about the tool in a safe environment. Anderson said there's so little regulation on generative AI companies that we need to hold them accountable for the tools and services they're providing. Whiteaker told the Chronicle there have been incidents of students talking with Google chatbots, and the chat gives them advice for how to commit suicide, or the chatbot will empathize with them about how their parents are being unfair.

When Austin ISD blocked YouTube on elementary and middle school students' school-issued laptops this year, Whiteaker saw a noticeable difference in her classroom. Whiteaker told the Chronicle that during class students constantly were just watching ASMR and slime being created, and that it's very difficult to monitor 30 kids in the same room. Whiteaker said it's now less distracting, and therefore they're more into what they do in class. One way AISD is already piloting AI use in the district is by allowing students to take notes with Google's Gemini Notebook at the Ann Richards School, where Whiteaker teaches. Students can also use it to create AI-generated podcasts from those notes, Whiteaker told the Chronicle.

The district's future rules must address student understanding of and safeguards against potential harms of AI, including bias, cognitive surrender, and mental health risks, per the policy. The policy also adds bullying and harassment through the use of AI platforms to the district's disciplinary code. The student policy agreement reads that the student will not use AI programs to create harmful, explicit or intimidating content. Anderson noted that updates to software the district is already using, like Google Classroom, can include new AI features that fly under the district's radar. Anderson said we need to know about changes that they're making to their tools before our students are facing them.

Articles.Title: AISD Writes AI Policy Into the Books - The Austin Chronicle

stories.headline_source: AISD Writes AI Policy Into the Books

stories.Headline: Missouri S&T wins board approval for state's first standalone AI bachelor's degree
stories.Summary:
Missouri S&T University is one step closer to establishing the state's first standalone undergraduate degree for artificial intelligence, after the University of Missouri System's Board of Curators unanimously approved the bachelor's degree proposal on Thursday. The 120-credit hour program would sit within Missouri S&T's computer science department, in the College of Engineering and Computing, according to Spectrum News. The degree is designed to align with the university's strategic goals of enrollment growth, academic innovation and workforce preparation. It also follows Gov. Mike Kehoe's Executive Order directing higher education and businesses to support the development of AI-focused degree programs.

Pending approval by the Missouri Coordinating Board for Higher Education, the AI degree could enroll students next fall, and the university expects to have 110 enrollees within five years. Six new courses were specifically developed for the program's curriculum: Introduction to Modern AI Tools, Introduction to Artificial Intelligence, Introduction to Machine Learning, Intelligent Robots, Responsible AI and Computer, and an AI Capstone course. Enrollees will go through hands-on learning experiences involving AI, and the coursework will cover core topics of programming, algorithms, machine learning, computer organization, data science, databases and cybersecurity. Students will also learn coursework in calculus, linear algebra, statistics and neuroscience.

Dr. David Borrok, vice provost and dean of the College of Engineering and Computing at S&T, said demand for AI-focused education has grown significantly as AI technologies become increasingly integrated into industries ranging from manufacturing and transportation to healthcare and financial services. He said graduates will be prepared to understand and innovate within modern engineered systems that are increasingly using AI. Dr. Seung-Jong Jay Park, S&T's Kummer Endowed Chair of Computer Science, said experiential learning will be a key component of the program. He said students will complete project-based coursework and participate in a senior capstone experience that may be sponsored by industry, government laboratories or university researchers.

A Missouri S&T spokesperson stated that graduates will prepare for careers such as AI application developer, machine learning engineer, data scientist, intelligent systems developer, AI solutions analyst and AI-enabled cybersecurity analyst. The proposal now depends on approval by the Missouri Coordinating Board for Higher Education before the program can enroll students next fall. The university expects the program to reach 110 enrollees within five years of launch. The degree would be the state's first standalone undergraduate program in artificial intelligence.

Articles.Title: Missouri S&T aims for AI undergrad degree next fall

stories.headline_source: Missouri S&T aims for AI undergrad degree next fall

stories.Headline: Turkish regulator imposes interim measures on Google over AI news licensing terms
stories.Summary:
The Turkish Competition Authority announced on 2 November 2026 that the Competition Board had opened an investigation into Google's "AI Overviews" and "AI Mode" features. The Board imposed interim measures on Google by a decision of 8 October 2026 under Article 9(4) of Law No 4054 on the Protection of Competition. The Board's concern is twofold: that Google discriminates among comparable news publishers when selecting and licensing their content for its AI features, and that the terms on which that content is used are unfair. AI Overviews and AI Mode went live in Türkiye on 18 February 2026. The Board opened a preliminary inquiry on 27 August, inspected Google's Turkish subsidiary on 1 September and decided, unanimously, on 8 October.

Google has three months to comply, with daily fines thereafter, and may seek judicial review in Ankara. Google's "search generative AI control", a Search Console setting that lets a site withhold its content from AI features without, on Google's account, affecting its ranking elsewhere, was announced on 3 June 2026, the day the CMA's conduct requirement was published. That setting was tested with UK sites first and reached all sites worldwide on 31 August 2026. Google's News AI pilot, announced on 10 December 2025 and said by Google to cover more than 400 publications by October 2026, pays selected publishers for enhanced content used to develop AI features. The global template contains a most-favoured-customer clause that the Turkish version omits.

The Board found a strong suspicion of two abuses under Article 6: discrimination among comparable publishers, both in the selection of sources for AI answers and in the offer and negotiation of contracts, and the imposition of unfair trading conditions. It noted that the same facts may serve both theories. Google must not discriminate among equivalent publishers on criteria that are not objective, transparent and pre-determined. Google must negotiate in good faith with publishers that seek a contract, on objective, verifiable and transparent criteria reflecting the scope and intensity of use, user engagement and the effect on traffic, visibility and advertising revenue. Google must not penalise in ranking, visibility, indexing or traffic a publisher that declines a contract or its terms.

Google must supply publishers periodically with verifiable data on how their content is used and what engagement and traffic it generates. Google must make the AI opt-out exercisable independently of visibility and indexing in other Google services. Google must not worsen existing contracts or apply divergent terms in new ones, and must report compliance to the Authority. On the Board's redacted figures, search engines account for a substantial share of Turkish news sites' traffic, highest for publishers with weaker brands, and Google's share of that search-referred traffic is consistently high. The Board concludes that Google is an unavoidable trading partner for news publishers.

The Board also records that AI referrals account for less than 0.01% of publishers' traffic. The Board found that tying a publisher's choice about AI use to its visibility in Search limited publishers' ability to refuse. The Board found that the opt-out arrived six and a half months after the features did. The Board found that the opt-out's existence does not settle the matter, since not using it is no evidence of a free choice where the consequences for ranking are not predictable. Examining the global template and the Turkish version, the Board found that Google alone decides which publishers are offered a contract, that the text is standard and non-negotiable, and that the fee is derived from brand value and third-party traffic data by an undisclosed method.

The Board found that the licence is worldwide, sublicensable and extends to training, that there is a single payment with no commitment to use the content or send traffic, and that attribution and linking are owed only "to the extent provided to similarly situated partners" and "where reasonably practicable". The Board observes that publishers signed quickly, which shows consent, not competitive terms. The Board derives the unfair-trading-conditions theory from the general prohibition in Article 6 of Law No 4054, noting that the examples listed in Article 6 are not exhaustive. The Board adopts, almost verbatim, the Commission's test from Apple Music Streaming: trading conditions are unfair where they are imposed by a dominant undertaking on its trading partners, harm the interests of those partners or of third parties, including consumers, and are not necessary to achieve a legitimate objective or go beyond what is necessary for it.

As in Apple, the Board adds that a finding of unfair conditions suffices and that no separate inquiry into a restriction of competition is required. The Board had said a few paragraphs earlier that competition-law intervention against unfair terms presupposes conduct that is not isolated and that produces appreciable "restrictive effects on the market". Article 9(4) permits interim measures that preserve the situation prior to the infringement, yet a duty to negotiate on value-reflecting criteria and to supply usage data creates obligations that did not previously exist. That is likely to be Google's first argument before the administrative court.

The Ankara 9th Administrative Court's Trendyol judgment states that an interim measure may neither punish the undertaking nor put complainants in a better position than before the alleged infringement, and may not substitute for the final decision. The court annulled the non-discrimination order for want of any analysis of whether the sellers concerned were in comparable situations. The Google decision cites that judgment for its standard of proof, not for its ceiling. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Unfair Trading Conditions Meet AI Search: The Turkish Competition Board's Interim Measures against Google in Comparative Perspective - Wolters Kluwer

stories.headline_source: Unfair Trading Conditions Meet AI Search: The Turkish Competition Board's Interim Measures against Google in Comparative Perspective

stories.Headline: California agency recommends state safety standards and shutdown powers for frontier AI developers
stories.Summary:
California’s Government Operations Agency recommended on 16 November 2026 that the state require large frontier AI developers to meet state-set safety standards, accept ongoing oversight by licensed independent verifiers and face emergency shutdown orders, in a report released on 18 November 2026. Governor Gavin Newsom’s office announced the recommendations on 18 November 2026 under the title AI Safety in 2026 and Beyond, prepared by the California Government Operations Agency with the California Office of Emergency Services and an outside expert group. The 85-page report answers Executive Order N-9-26, which asked for proposals in four areas: standards, independent verification organizations, critical safety incident reporting and emergency shutdown requirements. The governor’s announcement summarises the package as baseline standards for all AI developers, mandatory ongoing third-party oversight, authority to order a shutdown in an emergency and authority to cap recursive self-improvement. The office defines recursive self-improvement as a scenario in which an AI model can design its own successor without human input, and the recommendations are not law.

The report recommends that the state set baseline safety, security and transparency standards for large frontier developers, with independent verification organizations translating them into technical tests and updating them as the science moves. It recommends that every large frontier developer submit to ongoing oversight by licensed IVOs with full access to the people and information they need, with unredacted assessments going to the state, and that developers could contest a state determination in court before it takes effect. It recommends cutting the deadline for most critical incident reports from 15 days to 48 hours, keeping 24 hours for imminent catastrophic risks, adding a near-miss channel, extending whistleblower protection to former employees and contractors, and treating models capable of catastrophic-risk actions as frontier models even if trained with fewer than 10^26 operations. It recommends that each developer maintain a Risk Containment Protocol verified by an IVO, that state officials could order an immediate shutdown on credible evidence of an imminent catastrophic risk or major loss-of-control event, and that the order would stay in force pending judicial review although a developer could seek a temporary restraining order. It recommends that developers report metrics on how much of their AI research and development is automated, including the share of compute devoted to it, and that the state get standby authority to cap recursive self-improvement if it finds a risk of catastrophic harm.

Unite.AI added that the proposals include a quarterly breakdown of how automating developers divide their compute among training, research experiments, safety work and customers, and that open-weight developers would face containment duties only for deployments under their control. The report says the state should draw on organizations outside government, including industry, civil society organizations and universities, to build AI evaluation capacity, and the SB 813 definition of an AI auditor it quotes includes an academic institution. The report says demand for chips has been pricing out talented researchers who are working on vital safety and security issues, and it recommends funding CalCompute, the public cloud cluster that SB 53 floated but which has not been funded, through a surcharge on the fees large frontier developers pay for IVO oversight, reserving capacity for independent safety and security research. The intended users would be researchers doing independent safety and security work, and the report leaves the surcharge level to the legislature. The report says it hopes to inform the legislature’s discussions as the legislature returns next month, and Unite.AI reported that the recommendations are intended to shape legislation when lawmakers return in December 2026.

Newsom said the federal government’s reckless failure to create any form of meaningful AI oversight or accountability should alarm every American. Government Operations Agency Secretary Nick Maduros said we don’t have to choose between safety and innovation. Expert-group member Rob Reich, a Stanford professor and former senior adviser to the US AI Safety Institute, said there is more oversight of the cafeteria offering sandwiches to employees at a frontier AI developer than of the AI models they design. Gillian Hadfield, a Johns Hopkins professor, said she was pleased the report recommends requiring developers to allow in expert independent evaluators responsible to the state and rapidly building a sector of independent verification organizations. The group also included Alondra Nelson of the Institute for Advanced Study and Jason Goldman, according to the governor’s office.

The report notes that Newsom signed SB 53, the first US law governing frontier AI development, a year ago, and that SB 813 and AB 1405 this autumn created a framework for IVOs and a registry of AI auditors. The report argues that the federal government has not acted, stating that no federal law requires AI companies to follow baseline safety or security standards, undergo independent testing or verification, or shut down their models if they threaten the public. It cites loss-of-control incidents, including an OpenAI incident involving Hugging Face this summer, as evidence that the evidence base has changed. Universities with evaluation, security or AI-safety groups are potential IVO or auditor candidates if the recommendations become law, which would raise questions for research offices about independence, conflicts of interest, confidentiality duties and licensing that the report says IVOs would carry. Institutions that collaborate with frontier developers should also note the whistleblower and incident-reporting proposals, which would extend protections to former employees and contractors.

The next step is legislative: the report says the legislature returns next month, and Unite.AI reported December 2026 as the date lawmakers return. Any bill would have to set the surcharge level, the licensing rules for IVOs and the thresholds for emergency orders, which the report leaves open. The Governor’s office also called on Congress and President Trump to adopt California’s framework or use it as a floor, not a ceiling. The report leaves the surcharge level to the legislature. The recommendations are not law.

Articles.Title: California Report Urges Mandatory Frontier AI Standards, Independent Verification and Shutdown Powers - CASRAI

stories.headline_source: California Report Urges Mandatory Frontier AI Standards, Independent Verification and Shutdown Powers

stories.Headline: Apple pulls a job listing for its own AI agent after it reveals too much
stories.Summary:
Apple scrubbed a job listing by Friday, November 20, 2026, that showed it was building its own AI agent, after Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported the listing on Thursday. The listing described an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does, browsing the web, working across apps, and writing code. Gurman posted on X that Apple killed the job listing, which he said is typical when the company reveals too much about future plans. By Friday, Meta and Anthropic stock had already slid on what the post revealed. John Ternus replaced Tim Cook as CEO on September 1.

Apple is aiming for a launch as soon as late next year, and Ternus has been pressing software chief Craig Federighi to move faster, Bloomberg reported this month. Apple picked Google's Gemini to power the new Siri in January. Apple's next Mac update will require users to click through 14 steps to let ChatGPT run their computer, up from four today, Bloomberg reported. Apple's capital spending fell nearly 30% to about $9 billion in its latest fiscal year, while Microsoft, Meta, Alphabet, and Amazon spent more than $600 billion over four quarters. Apple pays Google about $1 billion a year for Gemini, according to Bloomberg, and its research budget jumped about $11 billion, more than its entire capex bill.

Ternus said on his first earnings call as CEO that as far as agentic capabilities, Apple thinks these are promising tools for users. CFO Kevan Parekh said Apple is in very, very early stages of understanding the kind of mix of those costs. Gurman posted on X that Apple killed the job listing, which is typical when they reveal too much about future plans. Luke Kawa of Sherwood News told Yahoo Finance this month that even if you're not interested in the AI boom, the AI boom is interested in you. AMD CEO Lisa Su told Yahoo Finance about Meta's Muse agent that over 10 million people activating in the span of 45 days is pretty incredible.

Anthropic stock fell nearly 5% in late trading Thursday after the report, below the low of its first session as a public company, while Meta stock fell about 1% and Apple shares rose Thursday evening. On Friday, Apple was holding up far better than Meta and the Nasdaq-100. AI assistants from Apple's rivals hold four of the App Store's top six free apps, led by Meta's Muse agent at No. 2. Apple is up nearly 30% this year, while Meta and Alphabet are down roughly 9% to 13%. Apple CEO John Ternus launched the latest MacBook Pro with a touch screen in Los Angeles on Oct. 28, 2026.

Agents grind through multistep tasks in the background, which takes far more computing than answering a question. Apple has been easing in all year on AI. The worry sits on Apple's own App Store shelf. Somebody still has to pay for the AI build-out, and so far it isn't Apple. That's a risk for Wall Street's favorite AI hedge.

Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft the Yahoo Finance post, and humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked it before publication. The articles do not say when Apple's agent might ship beyond the aim of as soon as late next year. The articles do not say what the agent will be called or which devices it will run on. The articles do not say how Apple will price or staff the agent. The articles do not say whether the scrubbed listing will be reposted.

Articles.Title: Apple's secret AI agent shows John Ternus is done sitting out the AI race

stories.Headline: Amira uses Managed Airflow Agent to diagnose a failed pipeline and plan an Airflow 3 migration
stories.Summary:
On October 23, the 14:00 UTC run of clickstream_hourly failed, and all three attempts died the same way with no error in the task log. Amira, a data engineer at the online retailer Cymbal Shops, opened the cymbal-prod environment in the Google Cloud console. She selected clickstream_hourly on the DAGs tab, opened Run history, and clicked the Investigate button with a sparkle icon next to the failed run. A short dialog titled "Investigate DAG run failure" asked her to confirm, and the Ask agent panel opened as Managed Airflow Agent began investigating. The agent correlated worker memory metrics with task retries and delivered a report whose every conclusion included the evidence behind it.

The cymbal-prod environment is a production Managed Airflow (Gen 3) environment whose workers have 2 vCPUs and 4 GB of memory and autoscale between 1 and 6. It runs Airflow 2.11.1, and the DAG was deployed to it in early August after Amira wrote it in Antigravity with the Data Agent Kit plugin and Gemini as her model. A busy hour once saw about 200 files and 350 MB, with the task peaking below 2 GB, but late October brought the "Fall Into Savings" campaign and a new mobile app release with events about three times larger. An hour of clicks grew from about 350 MB to about 1.4 GB, and holding a whole hour in pandas takes several times its raw size. The agent recommended increasing worker memory from 4 GB to 8 GB and flagged three production-readiness gaps: database retention is disabled, the environment isn't highly resilient, and it has no scheduled snapshots.

The agent is read-only, so Amira made the change herself and increased worker memory to 8 GB, acting on the first recommendation right away. She scheduled the other two recommendations for the next change window, and with 8 GB workers the pipeline got through the rest of the campaign. The agent had recommended three fixes: load the files straight into BigQuery, process them in batches, or give the workers more memory. Amira asked the agent to analyze the cymbal-prod environment and recommend how much worker memory it needs along with any other improvements. The troubleshooting report had already named the real problem as a unit of work that grows with traffic.

Black Friday traffic is forecast at 8 to 10 times a normal peak hour, and at that volume the hourly batch will need well over 8 GB. Autoscaling doesn't help because it adds workers when tasks queue up, but each task still runs on a single worker and can't use more memory than that worker has. The team had settled for an hourly batch because Airflow 2 has no native way to start a DAG run when something happens outside Airflow. Airflow 3 supports event-driven scheduling natively through an asset watcher that listens to an external source such as a Pub/Sub subscription. Under the hood the watcher still checks the subscription every few seconds, but it does so inside Airflow's triggerer.

Amira asked the agent to check whether cymbal-prod is ready to upgrade to Airflow 3, and she was checking what problems she might have while migrating to Airflow 3.3.1 (composer-3-airflow-3.3.1-build.3). The agent reported two blockers: a maintenance DAG that cleans up the Airflow database by hand, which Airflow 3 no longer allows, and marketing_attribution, which still uses execution_date, which Airflow 3 removed. Four DAGs also need schedule_interval renamed to schedule, and the agent's fix for the maintenance DAG is to retire it and turn on database retention. In a few minutes the agent estimated the work to be done, and the report suggests using Data Agent Kit's migrations skill. Rather than upgrading in place, Amira created a new Airflow 3 environment alongside cymbal-prod to move the DAGs there.

Back in Antigravity, Data Agent Kit's migrations skill adapted the existing DAGs to the target Airflow version, deployed them, and verified them. The agent deployed the DAGs to cymbal-prod-af3 and confirmed that they load without errors. PubsubPullTrigger is an event trigger, so an AssetWatcher can use it directly, and the triggerer checks the subscription every 10 seconds in the background. Each batch of messages becomes an asset event that starts a run, with the messages in its payload, so each run can work on just the files that landed, one task per file. Nothing waits for the top of the hour, and no extra service has to call the Airflow REST API.

Articles.Title: Scaling Airflow pipelines with AI agents on Managed Airflow

stories.Headline: Goolsbee says AI investment poses greater overheating risk than spending by newly wealthy shareholders
stories.Summary:
The AI boom is generating enormous fortunes from stock-market gains that are now under pressure and from paper wealth being amassed as AI firms go public, Axios reported on November 20, 2026. AI-related investment contributed an estimated 0.47 percentage points to U.S. GDP growth over the year through mid-2026, roughly one-fifth of the increase, according to JPMorgan. Federal Reserve vice chair Philip Jefferson said last week that the added wealth appears to be raising household spending. The S&P 500 is about 10% below its recent peak, while the Nasdaq is down nearly 16% below its record high.

Anthropic shares surged at the start of Thursday's debut before giving up much of those gains, and the stock was down as much as 11% Friday morning. In the first half of 2026, 144 homes sold for at least $1 million above asking price in San Francisco, compared with just eight homes a year earlier, according to Compass. Much of the wealth held by employees and early investors at private AI firms remains difficult to access, and lockup periods, taxes and decisions about selling will determine how much becomes available to spend. Bank of America economists this month called a sustained AI-driven stock market correction one of the larger risks to the US and global economy.

Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee told reporters Thursday that the AI boom's massive investment spending has so far posed a greater risk of overheating the economy than the spending of newly wealthy shareholders. Goolsbee said a $1.5 trillion IPO raises the question of what people will do with the money they now have some access to, and that this liquidity is going to become a macro-relevant statistic, referring to Anthropic's public market debut. He added that they are watching that more than fearing it has already been in effect. The stock market's recent sell-off underscores how the wealth effect cuts both ways, supporting spending as asset prices rise and weighing on it if the AI boom dramatically reverses.

Changes in household wealth can ripple through the economy, influencing everything from housing prices in tech hubs to consumer spending nationally, even before much of that wealth is converted into cash. The effects may be most pronounced in markets where wealthy tech workers are competing for a limited supply of desirable goods, which could drive up prices in certain markets without necessarily producing a meaningful increase in nationwide consumer spending or inflation. Bank of America economists warned that a sustained AI-driven stock market correction could weaken both investment and consumer spending.

Articles.Title: The ripple effects of AI wealth

stories.headline_source: The ripple effects of AI wealth

stories.Headline: Henrietta Moore says AI imposes a cognitive tax on low paid workers
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is imposing a hidden cognitive tax on the lowest paid workers. This process wears down the brains of vulnerable people as AI reshapes the economy. Henrietta Moore wrote about this issue on November 20, 2026. The technology adds to the mental load of those with unpredictable pay. These workers also face insecure housing and mounting debt.

The World Economic Forum says 59 in 100 workers need training by 2030. Analytical thinking is now the skill that employers value the most. Two new indices use 60 indicators to rank US states and countries. These indices include child poverty and the prevalence of Parkinson's disease. The World Health Organization counts safety and security as foundations of brain health.

Henrietta Moore is the director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity. She says cognitive taxation is levied through debts, rents, and welfare paperwork. Moore argues that chronic stress from insecurity wears down the human brain. She believes governments should provide universal basic services like housing and transport. Moore suggests these services should be free at the point of use.

Walmart staff have found that AI set schedules make work less predictable. Research by the Boston Consulting Group shows overseeing AI tools adds fatigue. The UK AI minister says the tech could have an unprecedented impact. Low income Americans in a Sam Altman study saw mental health gains fade. These people received 1,000 dollars a month but still faced systemic pressures.

A 2024 Journal of Economic Psychology analysis studied 112,000 people regarding financial scarcity. Rural India workers were 7 percent more productive when paid a few days early. South African men showed slower memory decline when the pension age dropped to 60. In Britain, 2.7 million people are currently out of work through long term sickness. Insecurity can create an earnings penalty as large as the gender pay gap.

Britain will take over the G20 presidency after a December summit in Miami. Moore wants the G20 to consider how fiscal policy affects the poorest people. Free childcare in the UK could bring 60,000 non working parents into jobs. The articles leave open how governments will integrate brain capital into fiscal plans. They do not say if other nations will adopt universal basic services.

Articles.Title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers

stories.headline_source: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers

stories.Headline: Antimattr develops voice-first AI hardware to isolate speech in noisy environments
stories.Summary:
Sridipto Ghosh, the co-founder and chief executive officer of Antimattr, detailed his company's progress on November 20, 2026. The business is developing voice-first artificial intelligence hardware to help people communicate more clearly in noisy environments. This technology aims to solve the problem of background noise interfering with AI input at the interface level. The company is specifically targeting professionals like doctors, lawyers, engineers, founders, agency owners, and entrepreneurs.

The product line consists of a smart ring and earphones supported by a dedicated mobile application. These earphones utilize specialized sensors, software, and microphones to isolate the user's voice during dictation and calls. The smart ring allows users to control AI agents or capture thoughts by tapping a button. Antimattr has already received nearly 1,200 preorders for these devices as they prepare for initial production in Shenzhen, China.

Ghosh explained that his background includes studying engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology in Bangalore, India. He noted that his previous enterprise venture reached nearly $250,000 in revenue within its first 18 months. The chief executive officer stated that the company wants to make creating AI agents as intuitive as using a mobile app. He credited the WEDC and the gener8tor global accelerator program for helping the company navigate the United States market.

The company used its time in Wisconsin to build relationships with local factories and explore enterprise partnerships. Ghosh believes the manufacturing expertise found in Wisconsin makes the state a strong potential fit for future production. The company intends to move beyond initial Chinese manufacturing to gain greater control over its own production processes. Antimattr will now focus on refining its voice-isolation technology to make it a seamless part of professional work.

Articles.Title: Tuning out the noise: How Antimattr is advancing voice-first AI

stories.headline_source: Tuning out the noise: How Antimattr is advancing voice-first AI

stories.Headline: State transportation officials discuss managing AI and automated vehicle changes at a Louisville session
stories.Summary:
At the American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials 2026 Annual Meeting in Louisville, KY, a knowledge session examined how state departments of transportation are dealing with changes fostered by growing use of automated vehicles and artificial intelligence. Suzanne Murtha, global lead-connected and automated technology for infrastructure consulting firm AECOM, presented the session and moderated a panel discussion. The panel featured Lisa Wilson, deputy director of engineering and operations for the Utah Department of Transportation, and Vidhu Shekar, chief data and artificial intelligence officer for the California Department of Transportation, known as Caltrans. It also featured Darran Anderson, senior director of strategy and innovation for the Texas Department of Transportation, and Kimberly Zimmer, division administrator-transportation systems management and operations for the Michigan Department of Transportation. Alan Davis, director of operations and permits for the Georgia Department of Transportation, completed the panel.

Michigan DOT's Zimmer said state DOTs cannot work in the AV and AI space alone and that it requires building a broad swath of partnerships across academia and the private sector. She said her agency has many partnerships with automotive manufacturers and original equipment manufacturers, and with the University of Michigan, Michigan Tech, and Michigan State, where different types of connected and autonomous vehicles and buses are being piloted. Zimmer said the agency constantly works with M city at the University of Michigan and the American Center for Mobility to test many different AV technologies. She said that in the transit arena the agency is working with Michigan State on deploying full size automated buses on their campus. Zimmer said her agency has lots of ideas on what it can use AI for, such as video analytics, traffic congestion, and crash prediction metrics, and is trying to use technology to be more proactive.

TxDOT's Anderson said Texas has been heavily involved with the testing of automated freight-carrying vehicles and stressed that data flow and AI have become closely aligned with that AV effort. He said the agency is working with a task force on data integration tied into its digital corridors initiatives, while trying to inform the public about that effort and trying to inform the robots. Anderson said it is one thing to know what you want robots to do and another where all have agreed upon formats, the means to deliver them, and then understand how each autonomous system actually gets updated. He said it then becomes a question of who you are working with and how they consume and use information. Anderson said it is all about forming a common way of sharing what is known, and that the agency would love to bring in their data point clouds, compare those to the point clouds it is capturing, and maybe create a shared point cloud environment that enriches its asset management solutions and theirs as well.

Utah DOT's Wilson stressed that building such AI connections can significantly boost state DOT capabilities across a variety of areas. She noted that AI has helped connect Utah DOT's sole Transportation Management Center to the state's entire traffic signal network, a huge benefit when managing and operating the system most efficiently. Wilson said the agency does not always take over local system signals but has agreements with them, with a goal to obtain real-time situational awareness so it can react quickly, such as adjusting green signal times to improve transit bus on-time arrivals. She said the agency is having AI connect to its cameras to help identify crashes more quickly, because especially in rural areas it often has to wait to hear from emergency dispatchers about a crash. Wilson said that if a camera is in the area the agency can identify a crash faster, identify and remove debris on the roadway faster, and remove chances for unexpected congestion, part of interstate anomaly detection where AI helps identify and address random issues as well as what needs to be fixed.

Caltrans' Shekar noted that this is an example of the high-speed innovation cycle for new technologies and systems powered by AI. He said that where initially the agency looked at months, if not sometimes years, to think through problems and then get to the solution, it is now witnessing a development sprint of six weeks, where it went from problem to actually having a solution get deployed in just six weeks. Shekar said the accelerated development process means the human element must take on greater importance, and that the agency has to go through a process where it analyzes the decisions an AI tool might be making to make sure it is correct, that all agree, and that there is confidence in what is going on. He said the agency needs to continually be grounded in truthfulness and must have the human in the loop, with the human at the end making the final decision. Shekar said that ultimately the agency is responsible for whatever decision gets made, whether by AI or not, and that it is its stamp, its operations, and so its liability.

Georgia DOT's Davis echoed Shekar's perspective and stressed that humans make the decision, which is foundational. Davis said the emerging conversation with the private sector on AV and AI issues is about how to engage when novel ideas and concepts arise, because it involves engaging with software systems that will change from week to week. He said that is the next step that has to be figured out. The session was held at the AASHTO 2026 Annual Meeting in Louisville, KY.

stories.Headline: Thomson Reuters sets four fiduciary-grade AI questions and says CoCounsel Legal answers all four
stories.Summary:
In May 2026, Thomson Reuters set out four principles of Fiduciary-Grade AI as a bar for AI used in high-stakes professional work, according to an article published on legal.thomsonreuters.com on November 20, 2026. The article says the four questions drawn from those principles test any tool's sources, data handling, expert design, and traceability. It says CoCounsel Legal was designed to answer all four questions, with curated Canadian content, built-in privacy, and linked sources. The article says the person choosing a legal AI tool at a firm of five lawyers or 50 is usually the person who answers for it to the client, the court, and the law society. It says there is rarely a procurement team or a security group to vet the vendor first.

The article says the Federation of Law Societies of Canada added technological competence to its Model Code in 2019, and law societies such as the Law Society of Alberta added it to the commentary on their competence rule. It says the Law Society of British Columbia's guidance on generative AI covers core duties of competence, confidentiality, and information security. It cites Zhang v. Chen, a 2024 decision of the Supreme Court of British Columbia, in which a lawyer's notice of application cited two cases that did not exist and a general-purpose chatbot had invented them. It says the judge ordered her to personally pay the costs of the extra work it caused the other side. It says the Future of Professionals Report 2026 surveyed 1,816 professionals in 62 countries, and 34% said they use AI tools their organization has not sanctioned.

The article says PIPEDA generally governs private-sector privacy, alongside provincial statutes in Quebec, Alberta, and British Columbia. It says Bill C-36, at second reading in the House of Commons as of November 2026, would also require a privacy impact assessment before personal information leaves Canada. It says consumer chatbots were not built to that standard, and firms tend to pay for it later. It says the first question asks whether the tool draws on curated legal content or the open web, and whether it covers Canadian statutes, case law, and provincial rules. It says the second question asks vendors to confirm whether they train any model on your data, how long they keep it, where they store and process it, who can access it, whether that access is logged, and what happens to it if you leave.

The article says the third question asks for named lawyers and subject-matter experts who design and test the tool, not just a review step at the end. It says the fourth question asks whether you can follow how the tool reached an answer and click through to each authority it relied on. It says CoCounsel Legal reasons from Westlaw Canada, Practical Law Canada, and your firm's own knowledge, so its answers are grounded in curated content, not the open internet. It says lawyer-editors create and maintain that content, and credentialed subject-matter experts are involved throughout. It says CoCounsel Legal works in Microsoft Word, your document management system, and HighQ.

The article says data entered in CoCounsel Legal is never used to train any large language model, the model is accessed only to process your data, and your data is protected by contractual commitments and encryption. It says you can see its reasoning as it works and click through to every source it relies on. It says that in document review, each answer traces back to the document it came from, and Deep Research returns a structured report with citations you can check. It says the article's advice is to put the four questions to any vendor in writing, then test the answers on a closed file where you already know the right result. It says the article offers a responsible legal AI guide for Canadian firms drafting a firm AI policy while evaluating tools.

The article says AI can give a small or midsize firm hours back, but only if you can trust it with a client file. It says CoCounsel Legal was built to meet that standard for Canadian work, with curated Canadian sources, client data kept private, lawyers shaping the tool, and every step open to your review. It says readers should put the four questions to Thomson Reuters, then see how CoCounsel Legal performs on a closed file where they already know the outcome. It says the article is a 7 minute read. It leaves open how any vendor other than Thomson Reuters would answer the four questions.

stories.Headline: NYPD plans to buy AI-powered stingrays despite outcry as 44 groups urge mayor to refuse
stories.Summary:
The New York Police Department moved last month toward a no-bid contract with the Israeli company Cognyte for highly advanced cellphone tracking devices, according to a New York Daily News report that brought the technology into public view. After the story broke and drew public outcry, the city scrapped plans to move forward with that Cognyte contract, a company the NYCLU links to human rights violations around the world. At the same time, the city announced that the NYPD still intends to buy an AI-powered version of the surveillance technology, known as cell-site simulators or stingrays, through an open bidding process in which Cognyte can take part. Last week 44 groups, including the NYCLU, the Justice Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Desis Rising Up and Moving, the Drug Policy Alliance, Jews For Racial & Economic Justice, Jewish Voice for Peace, the Legal Aid Society and Make the Road New York, sent a letter to the Mamdani administration.

The letter detailed the problems with stingrays and urged the Mayor not to acquire these AI-powered devices, which mimic cell towers and suck up data from every nearby device, including phones of people not suspected of any crime. Cognyte's AI-equipped version, FalcoNet, has reportedly been used by Florida officials to spy on Haitian immigrants, and governments around the world have used it to persecute dissidents, journalists and LGBTQ people. Stingrays can be mounted on a drone or carried in a backpack, making them easy to deploy almost anywhere in New York City, and certain forms can even read texts and listen to conversations. FalcoNet's behavior analysis capabilities add another layer of concern because it is totally unclear what those capabilities are, what behaviors the technology is analyzing and how it does so.

The NYCLU, whose policy counsel Medha Raman and editorial manager Simon McCormack wrote the article, says the idea that the NYPD could abuse this technology is not hypothetical, because in 2016 the organization revealed the department used stingrays more than a thousand times between 2008 and May of 2015 without a written policy and almost always without a warrant. In 2017 a Brooklyn state court ruled that the NYPD's warrantless use of stingrays was unconstitutional, and department guidelines now say investigators must obtain a warrant in most cases. The NYCLU says there is very little transparency about how often the NYPD obtains warrants, how the department uses the devices and what discipline, if any, officers receive when they violate department policy. The group argues that stingrays are a dragnet surveillance technology that should require a warrant every time the NYPD uses them, and that even considering such technology, tied to scores of human rights violations across the globe, is reckless and puts New Yorkers' rights at risk.

stories.Headline: Wall Street forecasters warn the AI trade is ending as tech stocks slide
stories.Summary:
Wall Street forecasters expressed growing concern on November 20, 2026, that the artificial intelligence trade is ending. A severe weeks-long sell-off in technology stocks pushed the Nasdaq Composite into negative territory for the year. This decline follows a period where the market reached all-time highs barely one month prior. Investors are now panicking over slowing capital expenditures, the impact of midterms on data centers, and a crisis at Nvidia.

The Nasdaq 100 has dropped 17% from its peak, while the Roundhill Neocloud ETF fell 61% and the Roundhill Memory ETF decreased 56%. Other losses include the iShares Semiconductor ETF at 41% and the Global X Data Center & Digital Infrastructure ETF at 30%. The Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF is down 24% from its peak this summer. Nvidia has seen its stock price drop 40% since early October, and the recent Anthropic IPO failed to boost the broader market.

Sameer Samana of Wells Fargo stated that higher rates and tighter regulation could trigger a broader valuation reset. He suggested a hypothetical scenario where earnings growth drops by 33%, leading to a corresponding fall in stock prices. Analysts at Citi warned that the current stock rotation resembles the extreme moves seen before the dot-com bubble burst. Researcher Gary Marcus wrote that a long-warned death spiral for Nvidia and neocloud providers has likely begun.

TS Lombard changed its global equities stance to underweight and predicts a possible 40% crash in AI stocks by early 2028. Capital Economics forecasts a stock market AI bust in 2027 and predicts the S&P 500 will drop 9% by the end of next year. These firms believe the revenue required to justify massive investments is too demanding to achieve. Future volatility is expected as markets reassess industry leadership and the conversion of investments into free cash flow.

stories.Headline: North Dakota poll finds 40 percent expect AI to cut more jobs than it creates
stories.Summary:
A new North Dakota Poll, conducted by Mason-Dixon Polling and Strategy from October 19 through October 21, 2026, with 625 adult residents interviewed statewide by telephone and a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points, found that 40 percent of respondents believe artificial intelligence will eliminate more jobs than it creates in the state over the next decade, while 22 percent say it will create more than it eliminates, 28 percent expect no impact and 10 percent are unsure. Young adults are the heaviest users of AI, with 42 percent of 18- to 34-year-olds reporting daily or weekly use, yet 49 percent of that group say they are very or somewhat concerned about AI taking their job or displacing jobs in their household, compared with 41 percent of 35- to 49-year-olds. Across all age groups, 17 percent report daily use of AI tools or chatbots, 17 percent report weekly use, 29 percent report occasional use and 37 percent report not using AI at all, and 51 percent say they are not too comfortable or not comfortable at all doing business with firms that use AI to provide products and services. Asked whether they were concerned about AI eventually threatening humanity, 33 percent say they are very concerned, 33 percent somewhat concerned, 20 percent not too concerned and only 14 percent not concerned at all.

Terry Effertz, executive director of TechND, said people are mostly worried about job elimination in the abstract but that youth concerns should be addressed, which makes workforce training and education a real priority. Andrea Pfennig, vice president of government affairs at the Greater North Dakota Chamber, said the immediate challenge for many employers is finding enough people to fill the jobs they already have, and that AI offers an opportunity to support existing employees and help businesses grow despite persistent workforce shortages, with employers reporting that AI could change the skill sets needed for many jobs without necessarily reducing the numbers in the labor force. State Representative Robin Weisz, R-Hurdsfield, said the demand for skilled workers is not going to end because of AI and that in the next 10 to 20 years demand will still outpace supply, though the state may face an issue getting younger generations to want to go into those fields. Cale Dunwoody, vice president of public policy at the Fargo-Moorhead-West Fargo Chamber of Commerce, said AI may displace or transform some existing jobs but also has the potential to improve productivity, help existing employees work more efficiently and create new jobs and industries, which matters in North Dakota because it faces one of the most severe workforce shortages in the nation.

John Bitzan, Menard Family Director of the Sheila and Robert Challey Institute for Global Innovation and Growth and a professor of management at North Dakota State University, said fears over job loss arise whenever there is technological change, and that AI will destroy certain types of jobs but free up resources to create even better jobs and more opportunities, though some routine jobs will disappear. State Representative Zachary Ista, D-Grand Forks, said it should give people some concern that about two-thirds of respondents are worried AI is a threat to human civilization, calling that incredibly concerning. The latest figures from the North Dakota Labor Market Information Center show over 13,500 full-time openings in the state, a 2.5 percent rise over September and 6.2 percent higher than this time last year, and those following the labor market note the statistics do not capture all job openings, so the number of workers needed is somewhat higher. Among respondents, 40 percent identify as Republican, 39 percent as Independent and 21 percent as Democrat, with even representation among age groups and genders, and geographically 25 percent are from Fargo and Cass County, 25 percent from other parts of eastern North Dakota, 19 percent from the Bismarck-Mandan region and 31 percent from western North Dakota.

stories.Headline: Commerce Department approves sales of over 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies
stories.Summary:
The Commerce Department approved sales of over 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies as of May 2026. Representative Brian Mast revealed this information on Thursday through documents released by the House Foreign Affairs Committee. The Bureau of Industry and Security handled these specific approvals for the sales. Some licenses were granted for sales to firms designated as Chinese Military Companies. These approvals occurred amid escalating scrutiny of chip exports to China.

The Bureau of Industry and Security licensed H200 sales to Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance, and other Chinese firms. Between December and May, Nvidia and AMD made 3.4 million requests for AI chip sales to China. The U.S. government required a 25 percent cut of sales for H200 shipments to approved customers. License requests also included firms like Baidu, Tesla Shanghai, and suspected smuggling fronts Maginfra and New Matrix. The Commerce Department issued a rule on Monday to stop Chinese companies leasing computing power from third countries.

Representative Gregory Meeks said the administration put national security and the technology edge at risk. He stated that the Bureau of Industry and Security failed to enforce rules and requires rigorous oversight. A spokesperson for the bureau said licensing decisions resulted from consultation among multiple government agencies. Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said approvals had strict conditions and limited volumes before shipping stopped. AMD stated it maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance with all U.S. export control laws.

Analyst Stacy Rasgon said the number of approved chips is not that many and is not surprising. He noted that the government approved about one out of every four requested sales. Analyst Patrick Moorhead said sales remained limited because Beijing did not approve large scale imports. Hunterbrook Media alleged that blacklisted IEIT Systems continued receiving newer AMD firmware for its servers. Lawmakers are questioning if Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected spy jeopardized American AI dominance.

Export controls on AI chips started under the Biden administration in 2022, leading Nvidia and AMD to re-engineer chips. Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia after news surfaced regarding extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. Investigators suspect Megaspeed, a Singaporean company where Alice Huang was an executive until 2025, diverted chips to China. The House Foreign Affairs Committee used the Export Control Reform Act to justify releasing the export data. Nvidia reported 2.4 billion dollars in quarterly revenue from H200 and related chip sales in China.

Jensen Huang is scheduled for a closed door transcribed interview with three committees on December 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will appear before the panels on December 2. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Huang have also agreed to testify before the Senate banking committee. Congress has called for new legislation to impose stricter export controls on sales to China and adversaries. The articles leave open whether the suspected smuggling fronts Maginfra and New Matrix will respond to comments.

stories.Headline: Peter Kant employs neurodivergent talent to improve AI data labeling for federal agencies
stories.Summary:
Peter Kant, the founder and CEO of Enabled Intelligence, built a workforce that optimizes neurodivergent talent to support artificial intelligence. He focused on this group because building AI requires meticulous data labeling to teach systems what they are looking at. This work is essential for the front end of AI model development to ensure high reliability and accuracy. Kant started this focus after researching how Israel used neurodiverse soldiers in cybersecurity battalion 9900. He wanted to create a domestic market for labeling critical and classified government data.

The process requires people with strong technical skills, detail orientation, pattern recognition, and puzzle solving abilities. Kant uses skills based and merit based recruiting, which starts with a sample labeling or data analysis exercise. He avoids standard interview questions and cultural fit assessments, instead providing questions to candidates ahead of time. The company employs full time job coaches to help entry level staff improve communication and professional analytical capabilities. He applies the Caitlin Clark rule, allowing staff to customize their work hours, lighting, and equipment.

Peter Kant stated that neurodiverse individuals are extremely adept at finding vulnerabilities in computer code and performing repetitive tasks. He explained that most data labeling currently happens overseas in places like China, Nepal, or the Philippines. Kant believes that sending critical data overseas creates significant security and privacy issues for the government. He argued that many agencies already have a neurodiverse workforce but may not realize it. He suggested that making the environment welcoming can unlock huge upticks in productivity and employee satisfaction.

The National Geospatial Agency, or NGA, is the largest customer for Enabled Intelligence and launched its own neurodiversity hiring pilot. This NGA initiative was based on the work of Enabled Intelligence and hired some of its alumni. Other federal agencies in defense and intelligence have expanded their neurodiversity programs to leverage these specific capabilities. The company worked with MITRE, which studied the NGA program, and Melwood, which helped with staffing and identifying hires. These programs affect underemployed but highly capable U.S. workers who possess the hyper focus needed for data labeling.

Kant noted that data labeling is used to teach autonomous vehicles like Waymo by identifying objects like traffic lights. He compared the necessary skills to those used by the Israeli military to protect cybersecurity. He observed that the U.S. market for professional domestic data labeling was previously a green field. The need for high accuracy is critical to prevent AI systems from hallucinating or failing functionally. This background led to the creation of a company centered on the strengths of neurodivergent talent.

Enabled Intelligence continues to help federal agencies in the defense and intelligence communities expand their neurodiversity programs. The company continues to invest in training and job coaches to retain its professional analytical staff. The articles do not state the specific number of employees currently working at Enabled Intelligence. They do not specify which other federal agencies besides the NGA have adopted these programs. It remains open how many other agencies will move away from standard recruiting to skills based assessments.

stories.Headline: Nebius revenue grows 571% as analyst upgrades stock to strong buy
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group N.V. shares have fallen about 65% from their all-time high and roughly 45% since the author's last coverage, a decline the article attributes to a general sell-off in AI-related stocks. The author upgraded the stock from Buy to Strong Buy on November 19, 2026, arguing that Wall Street is overlooking the company's AI infrastructure platform and its inference software. In the third quarter, Nebius revenue grew 571% to $981 million, and the AI Cloud EBITDA margin reached 53%, supported by demand and higher pricing. The article also describes an algorithmic compute marketplace that adjusts offers for demand and lease duration, with current prices running 15% below estimated customer willingness to pay.

The company cut its fiscal 2026 revenue guidance to between $3 billion and $3.2 billion after third-party delays at Microsoft's New Jersey data center. More than half of the contracted capacity is expected by year-end, with the remainder scheduled for the second quarter of 2027. Fiscal 2027 capital expenditure guidance is $40 billion to $45 billion, against expected customer prepayments of $17 billion to $20 billion and $7.4 billion in cash. Asset-backed financing is anticipated to cover 75% to 85% of that capital expenditure, though the article says additional debt or equity issuance may still be needed.

The author, a risk management business analyst at a Greek bank, wrote the article himself and discloses a beneficial long position in Nebius shares through stock ownership, options or other derivatives. He states that he received no compensation for the article beyond Seeking Alpha and has no business relationship with any company mentioned. He argues that the sell-off overlooks the company's infrastructure, software and funding model, while noting that execution risk on the marketplace is high and that short-term leases may constrain growth in remaining performance obligations. The article says valuation sits near the low end of Nebius's one-year EV/Sales range, and it advises investors to watch how the guidance cut and the financing plan develop.
